text:
Musk to Texas Democrats: Our Success Came From Freedom, Not Your Favors

Elon Musk just slapped down a Wall Street Journal story claiming Texas Democrats plan to yank the "white-glove treatment" for SpaceX and Tesla now that they've flipped the state. He made it plain: the companies thrived here because the government stayed out of the way.

"SpaceX and Tesla have prospered in Texas, because we were not constantly operating under an oppressive and extractive state government," Musk wrote.

He explained the practical reasons too. Factories need hands-on leadership. "And I need to be close to the factories, so that I can walk the floor in person. That’s why the first major SpaceX factory was in LA and first major Tesla factory was in SF Bay Area."

Then California turned hostile. "As California became increasingly difficult, due to extreme taxes and overregulation, we moved our major domestic expansions and HQ to Texas."

This is the same pattern that hollowed out California's tech and manufacturing base. High taxes, endless rules, and politicians treating productive companies like piñatas drove the growth elsewhere. Texas offered the opposite: lower burdens, faster permitting, and room to build. Jobs followed. Investment followed. Rockets and cars got built instead of lawsuits.

Now the new Democratic leadership is signaling they want to change the deal. They talk about ending special treatment, scrutinizing land deals, slowing data centers, and reviewing incentives. Translation: they see a successful employer and reach for the regulatory toolbox. The same approach that chased SpaceX and Tesla out of California is being imported to Texas.

Musk is not asking for favors. He is stating the obvious. Companies locate where they can operate without constant extraction and interference. Texas gained by being less California. If Democrats reverse that, the next expansion, the next factory, the next launch complex will simply go somewhere else. Florida has already been mentioned. Other red states are open for business.

The left celebrates the blue wave as a rebuke to Musk's spending. What they are actually celebrating is the chance to punish the companies that create the jobs and tax base they want to spend. History shows how that ends. California wrote the playbook. Texas is now being invited to copy it.

text:
Tesla announcing the end of Cybertruck production in mid-2027 has honestly left a bad taste in my mouth.

I’ve dreamed of owning a Tesla since I first drove one in 2018. I finally made that happen in 2025, although my delivery experience was far from pleasant. Today, I own a 2026 Model Y Premium AWD, but the Cybertruck has always been what I REALLY wanted.

The problem? Every time I got closer to comfortably affording one, the price seemed to move further out of reach. Now we’re looking at over $92K, and production is coming to an end.

Could I buy one? Absolutely. I have enough in savings to pay cash. But just because you CAN afford something doesn’t mean it’s financially responsible to buy it.

So now I’m questioning what’s next.

I drive roughly 30 miles a day, and I rarely use FSD (Supervised) outside of road trips. While I enjoy my Model Y, its ground clearance leaves something to be desired, especially as an essential employee who needs to get to work during Connecticut snowstorms.

That leaves me considering three options:

Keep my current Model Y.
Upgrade to another Model Y Premium AWD with the tow package, larger 16-inch screen, and black headliner.
Leave Tesla and consider the Rivian R2, which offers the additional ground clearance I’m looking for.

And here’s the thing: I don’t necessarily need FSD (Supervised) or Autonomy+. They’re nice features, but I barely use them. Rivian’s technology will continue improving, and the R2 might actually better fit my needs.

I’m not a Tesla hater. Quite the opposite. I’ve been a fan for years. But watching Tesla walk away from the vehicle I’ve been saving for has genuinely made me question whether my next vehicle should even be a Tesla.

So I’m curious: If you were in my position, would you stick with Tesla, make the jump to Rivian, or just keep what you already have?

text:
John Stuart Mill

“But the price paid for this sort of intellectual pacification, is the sacrifice of the entire moral courage of the human mind.”

When institutions seem distant or fragile, the next moral decision is often painfully local. Being steady inside oneself does not require withdrawing care from the world. Our character is tested most sharply when nobody can promise us a predictable outcome.

Silence and reflection can help prevent other people from becoming the targets of our distress. The quotation is not a promise that trouble will disappear. It asks what sort of person we become while trouble continues. Read this passage as a challenge to examine our next response, not as a claim that any philosopher foresaw our election or that injustice is harmless.

The magical turning point begins with a single deliberate gesture rather than a victory over strangers. A rosequartz glass dragon moves through a valley of shattered bells while the wizard faces a meaningful choice. The decision is not a spectacular attack. Instead, the steady light guides a boat to shore. In the background, two differing speech circles etched onto a stone forum floor with shared middle space quietly points to freedom of thought without forced agreement.

For us, the practical beginning is smaller than the cinematic one: pause long enough to name your real concern, then offer one calm response to another person. A little restraint does not settle every argument, but it may make the next conversation possible. What does your inner life need before your next public act?

Source: On Liberty, public domain English edition

text:
judiciary possesses institutional independence. This staggered architecture prevents the entire government from moving in one direction at the same instant. The nation is given both momentum and resistance.

Equilibrium among the three branches

Constitutional equilibrium should not be confused with equal power in every matter. The branches are not symmetrical. They are functionally distinct.

The legislative branch** makes general rules, controls appropriations, represents political constituencies, and conducts oversight.
The executive branch** administers law, directs foreign and domestic policy within its authority, and provides the decisiveness necessary for government.
The judicial branch** resolves legal controversies and determines whether governmental conduct conforms to higher law.

The equilibrium emerges from interaction. Congress may enact legislation, but the president may veto it. The president may execute policy, but Congress may limit funding or conduct oversight. Congress and the president may produce a law, but courts may invalidate it if it violates the Constitution. Judicial review permits federal courts to examine governmental action and declare legislative or executive acts unconstitutional.[5] The doctrine was famously articulated in Marbury v. Madison in 1803, even though the Constitution does not expressly use the phrase “judicial review.”9

This structure is not designed to make government effortless. It is designed to make power answerable. Delay may be the price of liberty. Friction may be evidence that constitutional boundaries are operating. A government that can act quickly in every circumstance may also be a government that cannot be effectively resisted.

Judicial review and the preservation of constitutional boundaries

The Supreme Court’s role is not to settle every political disagreement. Its judicial authority is most legitimate when it translates a concrete legal controversy into a question of constitutional limits. Judicial review is therefore not a substitute for elections, nor a general license for judges to govern. It is a mechanism by which the constitutional order can adjudicate whether one branch has exceeded the authority assigned to it.

The Court’s intervention becomes especially important when ordinary political safeguards fail. If Congress is captured by the same partisan incentives as the executive, legislative oversight may weaken. If the electorate is deeply polarized, electoral correction may produce only a different form of paralysis. If fundamental rights are placed at the mercy of temporary majorities, the judiciary may be required to enforce constitutional guarantees against popular excess.

The Supreme Court itself describes judicial review as a means of ensuring that each branch recognizes the limits of its own power and of protecting rights against governmental violation.[7] This is the paradox at the heart of constitutional democracy: the majority governs, but the majority does not possess unlimited authority. The Constitution places some principles beyond the reach of ordinary political convenience.

H. L. A. Hart and the legal grammar of equilibrium

H. L. A. Hart offers a valuable philosophical vocabulary for understanding this system. Hart distinguished between primary rules, which impose duties, and secondary rules, which determine how rules are identified, changed, and adjudicated. At the center of the legal system is what he called the rule of recognition: the shared institutional criteria by which officials identify what counts as valid law.3

Applied to the American constitutional order, the rule of recognition is not merely a written sentence. It is a complex practice through which judges, legislators, administrators, and citizens recognize the authority of the Constitution, statutes, judicial decisions, elections, procedures, and institutional offices. The Constitution is the supreme legal framework; legislation must be enacted

text:
A viral chicken sandwich can bring customers through the door. It cannot guarantee lasting success. 🍗

Popeyes started in Louisiana in 1972. Its spicy chicken helped build a global franchise brand, and its 2019 chicken sandwich became a nationwide sensation.

But the latest chapter tells a tougher story.

According to Mashed, Popeyes faced declining same-store sales, growing competition and a slow response to customers demanding better value.

One major franchisee, Sailormen, filed for bankruptcy in 2026 after reporting $223 million in annual sales—and an $18 million net operating loss.

That was a franchisee bankruptcy, not the bankruptcy of the entire Popeyes brand.

The company is pursuing value offers, stronger marketing and operational upgrades to regain momentum.

My takeaway: Brand recognition gets attention. Store economics determine what owners keep.

Before buying a franchise, look beyond the logo. Understand the costs, debt, local competition and actual owner earnings.

Would you rather own a famous brand—or a less familiar business with stronger margins?

𝐋𝐎𝐔𝐈𝐒𝐈𝐀𝐍𝐀'𝐒 𝐀𝐓𝐓𝐎𝐑𝐍𝐄𝐘 𝐆𝐄𝐍𝐄𝐑𝐀𝐋 𝐁𝐋𝐎𝐂𝐊𝐄𝐃 𝟐𝟐 𝐎𝐅 𝟐𝟑 𝐈𝐍𝐍𝐎𝐂𝐄𝐍𝐂𝐄 𝐏𝐀𝐘𝐎𝐔𝐓𝐒 — 𝐄𝐋𝐕𝐈𝐒 𝐁𝐑𝐎𝐎𝐊𝐒 𝐈𝐒 𝐇𝐄𝐑 𝐓𝐀𝐑𝐆𝐄𝐓

Elvis Brooks was 19 years old when prosecutors sent him to Angola for a 1977 bar s∗ooting he says he never committed. He spent the next 42 years inside the walls of one of the most violent prisons in America before a judge finally threw out his conviction. “𝘚𝘩𝘦 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘴 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘤𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘴𝘩𝘦 𝘥𝘰𝘦𝘴𝘯’𝘵 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘦,” Brooks said of the woman now fighting to keep him from collecting a dime.

The reason he’s free at all is a cover-up. Prosecutors sat on fingerprint evidence lifted off beer cans handled by the actual gunmen — prints that did not match Brooks — for decades, until one of their own finally admitted it had been buried. 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐚 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐫 𝐰𝐡𝐨 𝐡𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐡𝐚𝐬 𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞. Brooks’s attorney, Harry Daniels, said the state only started treating his innocence as a problem the moment he tried to collect what it owed him: “𝘐𝘵’𝘴 𝘰𝘯𝘭𝘺 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘥𝘦𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘩𝘦’𝘴 𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘵𝘭𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘣𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨𝘧𝘶𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘷𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘮𝘦 𝘢𝘯 𝘪𝘴𝘴𝘶𝘦.”

Louisiana law says a man exonerated after decades in prison is entitled to up to $480,000. Brooks filed his claim two years ago. He still hasn’t gotten a hearing. Attorney General Liz Murrill, the state’s top lawyer, has 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝟐𝟐 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟑 𝐰𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐟𝐮𝐥-𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐦𝐬 𝐟𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐞, insisting in her own filings against Brooks that he’s still guilty. A law professor who studies these cases didn’t mince words: “𝘐 𝘤𝘢𝘯’𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬 𝘰𝘧 𝘢𝘯 𝘢𝘵𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘯𝘦𝘺 𝘨𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘲𝘶𝘪𝘵𝘦 𝘢𝘴 𝘢𝘨𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘷𝘦.”

This isn’t the first time Murrill has gone after an exoneree who pushed back. When one man tried to withdraw and refile his claim, she threatened to report him to the bar and block his law license unless he dropped it. Brooks says he’s not backing down either: “𝘉𝘶𝘵 𝘪𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬 𝘐’𝘮 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘨𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘶𝘱, 𝘸𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘵𝘦 𝘧𝘭𝘢𝘨, 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘨𝘰𝘵 𝘮𝘦 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨.” He gets around New Orleans by bicycle now, living alone in a one-bedroom apartment at a senior center on a $𝟗𝟗𝟒-𝐚-𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡 𝐒𝐨𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐜𝐤 — the only income he has after the state took 42 years of his life and offered nothing back.

Louisiana’s own prosecutors created this mess by hiding the truth for decades. Now its attorney general is spending your tax dollars fighting the men her own state already admitted it wrongly locked up — instead of paying what they’re owed. She may win in court. But she will never undo the four decades she’s forcing an innocent 69-year-old man to relive every time he asks for what the law already says is his.

𝐋𝐨𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐚’𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐬 𝐛𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐡𝐢𝐦 𝐢𝐧 𝟏𝟗𝟕𝟕. 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐲-𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞’𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐭𝐨𝐩 𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐲𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐛𝐮𝐫𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥.

text:
Happy Birthday Hedy Lamarr 

A great star of Classic Hollywood, the raven-haired Lamarr was one of the most beautiful women of her era, described as “enough to make strong men faint.” Her high octane glamour belied the brilliancy of her mind; during World War II, she co-invented a frequency-hopping radio guidance system which served as an underlying mathematical and technical foundation for modern spread-spectrum communications. Lamarr was born in 1914 in Vienna. In 1933, aged 18, she starred in the Czech film, “Ecstasy.” It made her internationally notorious, for simulating an orgasm and briefly appearing nude. Later that year, Hedy impulsively married the older munitions manufacturer Friedrich Mandl, the third-richest man in Austria. It was an unfortunate alliance, as Lamarr was of Jewish descent and her husband was pro-fascist, controlling and kept her a virtual prisoner. In 1937, no longer able to bear her confinement, Hedy persuaded Mandl to let her wear all of her jewelry to a party and then absconded. After travelling to London she met Louis B. Mayer and secured a contract. Lamarr arrived in Hollywood in 1938 and MGM began promoting her as the "world's most beautiful woman". Her first film was “Algiers” (1938), with Charles Boyer. According to one viewer, when her face first appeared on the screen, "everyone gasped ... Lamarr's beauty literally took one's breath away." She starred in “Boom Town” (1940), one of her most popular films, opposite Clark Gable, Claudette Colbert and Spencer Tracy. MGM reteamed her and Gable in  “Comrade X” (1940), another hit. Lamarr then appeared with James Stewart in “Come Live with Me” (1941), playing a refugee. She described Stewart as "one of the sweetest men in the world" and liked the film because “it was my first chance to do a charming, humorous story.” This was followed by the hugely successful “Ziegfeld Girl” (1941), with Judy Garland and Lana Turner, “H. M. Pulham, Esq.” and “Tortilla Flat” (1942). Lamarr played the exotic Arab seductress Tondelayo in “White Cargo” (1942), with Walter Pidgeon. The film contains what is arguably her most memorable line: "I am Tondelayo. I make tiffin for you?" She looked stupendous, but none of her roles were challenging and Lamarr took up inventing to relieve her boredom. Inexplicably, she turned down the leads in “Laura” and “Gaslight” to star with William Powell in the mediocre comedy “The Heavenly Body” (1944), and the histrionic melodrama “Experiment Perilous”. A highly proficient actress, she was never given the chance to prove herself. Around this time Lamarr asked to join the National Inventors Council, but was told that she could better help the Allies by using her appearance to sell war bonds. After peace was declared, she had her biggest success in Cecil B. DeMille's “Samson and Delilah”, with Victor Mature, in which she shone as the conniving but tender Biblical seductress. Lamarr also made the psychological thriller “The Strange Woman” (1946). Her performance won high praise from critics. The New York Times wrote, "Undoubtedly every actress yearns for a tour de force and Hedy Lamarr can consider that yearning fulfilled.” In the 1950s, her acting career declined, and her last film was the “The Female Animal” (1958). Perhaps Lamarr’s greatest contribution to the world was her frequency-hopping system, invented during the War with pianist George Antheil, to prevent torpedo jamming. It was granted a U.S. patent in 1942, and offered to the Navy, who rejected it on the basis that it was too large to fit in a missile. In the late 1950s, Lamarr designed and developed the Villa LaMarr ski resort in Aspen, Colorado. In 1966, she was arrested for shoplifting but the charges were dropped. The actress became increasingly reclusive and retired to Florida, dying in 2000, aged 85. First, the Midwest was the North. Lincoln was from Illinois. Grant, Sherman, and Sheridan were from Ohio. The Midwest supplied the manpower, breadbasket, and industrial backbone of the Union war effort. The idea that the Midwest and South could have teamed up to beat the North is like saying Texas and the South could have beaten the South.

But surely, indeed, the Midwest wasn't naturally hostile to the South. They broke because of the Republican Party's "Free Soil" bargain. "Free soil" was a racist exclusion zone. The territories were for "free white people" alone (see: Lincoln's own commentary), while Illinois Republican Lyman Trumbull proudly declared the GOP the "white man's party." The Midwest didn't ally with the South because the Republican Party offered them a better deal, to keep the black man out of the territories, and in turn receive federal land grants, railroad subsidies, and a protective tariff for their industry.

Kansas voted overwhelmingly pro-slavery in 1855. The free-state settlers refused to accept the ballot box, set up their own illegal legislature, and funded armed terrorists (Jayhawkers) with "Beecher's Bibles" to murder pro-southern settlers. Yet again, the North rejected popular democracy and chose violence.

And the South did have Northern allies. They were called Copperheads, and they were concentrated in the Midwest. But even with their help, a military takeover of Washington and the Northeast was impossible. The North had 22,000,000 people, 90% of the nation's manufacturing, and 70% of the railroads. text:
After years of delays, Evander Holyfield and Mike Tyson finally meet on November 9, 1996, with "The Real Deal" scoring an 11th round TKO, in Las Vegas, of the heavily favored WBA Heavyweight Champion.

This was Tyson's first title defense and the third time the pair had been scheduled to meet.

Tyson and Holyfield were originally scheduled to fight on June 18th of 1990, in Atlantic City, New Jersey. 

Tyson, at the time the undisputed World Heavyweight Champion, was guaranteed more than $22 million, and Holyfield, the undisputed #1 ranked heavyweight contender, was guaranteed more than $11 million. 

However, those plans went down the drain when Tyson lost the title to James (Buster) Douglas, a 42-1 underdog, by a 10th-round knockout on February 11, 1990, in Tokyo, Japan. Eight months later, on October 25, Douglas would lose the title to Holyfield by a third-round knockout in Las Vegas, Nevada.

The second time Tyson and Holyfield were scheduled to fight was for November 8th of 1991, at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas. It was to be then champion Holyfield's second title defense. Holyfield was guaranteed $30 million, and Tyson was guaranteed $15 million. But, on September 9th, Tyson was indicted on charges of raping a beauty-pageant contestant in Indianapolis, Indiana. Although some felt that the fight should have been canceled, it was still set to happen. Then, on October 19th, it was announced that Tyson had injured his ribs, and the fight would have to be postponed. With Tyson's trial set to begin on January 27th of 1992, no new date was scheduled for the fight. On February 10th, Tyson was convicted of rape and sent to prison.

Tyson would be released from prison on March 25th of 1995 and he regained the WBC heavyweight title with a third-round TKO of Frank Bruno on March 16, 1996, and then regained the WBA heavyweight title with a first-round TKO of Bruce Seldon on September 7, 1996. Tyson then relinquished the WBC title to fight Holyfield instead of the mandatory challenger, Lennox Lewis.

Richard Hoffer reported the following in the November 18, 1996, issue of Sports Illustrated:

Tyson and Holyfield met in the center of the ring at the opening bell and engaged in the kind of furious combat that no heavyweight fight fan had seen in years. They swung wildly and then collapsed into clinches, shoved each other away and finally resumed battle as the cycle began again. It was breathtaking, especially when it became clear that Holyfield would not be flattened by Tyson's straight-ahead fusillades. Suddenly Holyfield, the built-up cruiserweight, seemed formidable at 215 pounds, his 77 1/2-inch reach putting him out of range of Tyson's 71 inches.
In the second round Holyfield, who is not known as a big puncher, hit Tyson with a left hand that seemed to stagger him. At the end of the round Tyson paused on his way to his corner and looked at Holyfield as if puzzled. In fact he was, as he admitted later, "blacked out." The fight went eight more rounds, until referee Mitch Halpern stopped it less than a minute into the 11th, but afterward Tyson could recall none of them. For everyone else the bout was unforgettable. Holyfield's constant pressure was a welcome sight after the weak-kneed efforts of Tyson's previous opponents, but the challenger was providing something more than action. By crowding in, he was taking away Tyson's hook, which is more effective from outside, and generally he was keeping Tyson too occupied to put together more than two punches.
Tyson was always a threat, of course, and in the fifth round he unleashed a right to Holyfield's body and an uppercut to his chin, reminding everyone of his power. But Tyson was plainly befuddled, strangely ineffective. The two fighters would clash, tie up and get broken apart by the referee, and there Holyfield would be, still standing in front of Tyson.
Later Tyson would say he remembered nothing from the third round on. Not the sixth round, when Holyfield opened a small cut above Tyson's left eye with an unintentional head butt and then decked him with a left hand to the shoulder as 16,325 people chanted Holyfield's name. Tyson was definitely in trouble. In the seventh he kept looking to Halpern, complaining about head-butting. And later in that round he rushed Holyfield face-first and inadvertently smashed his left eye into Holyfield's shaved head. Tyson gasped in pain, stood straight up and appealed to the ref again.
A sense that Holyfield really could win swept the crowd, and chants of "Let's go, Mike!" were squashed by choruses of "Holy-field!" Tyson tried trading punches with Holyfield in the 10th, but that turned ugly for him when Holyfield hit him with a powerful combination, followed shortly by a right to the head and, with eight unanswered punches, backed him into the ropes. In all, Holyfield hit Tyson 23 times in the 10th. It had been a long time since anyone had seen Tyson saved by the bell.
The fight was effectively over, but it went 37 seconds into the 11th round, when a big right to Tyson's head slammed him into the ropes again and Halpern embraced him in protection. "I don't remember that round," Tyson would say. "I got caught in something strange."
Holyfield's dominating win would send thousands of happy betters to sports book windows in Vegas clutching winning tickets.
Rob Terry, the race and sports book director at Boulder Station, said that no Las Vegas book he knew of had managed to escape a beating on this fight. To understand how much money it takes to bet a fight down from 25-1 to 5-1 odds  is to understand the beating the books received.
"It was devastating," Terry said. "When you consider the fight opened at 25-1 and closed at 5-1, then you know there was a lot of movement. There was a huge amount of Holyfield money."
"Everybody I've talked to was basically pasted," added Jay Kornegay of the Imperial Palace. "That's a typical Tyson fight because people have to lay such big odds on him. In such one-sided action we always need the big favorite."
Terry said sports books had little choice but to offer the large odds on Tyson, especially considering how easily he had dispatched his four previous opponents while Holyfield had struggled in his recent fights. Tyson came in off a first-round knockout of Bruce Seldon, while Holyfield was unimpressive against a faded Bobby Czyz.
"It was based on what was seen over the previous four fights," Terry said. "But it was still pretty steep considering the types of fights he (Tyson) had. The line was put up based on fights against nobodies.
"The public got the better of it in this one for sure. Pure and simple, the sports books took a bath."

text:
Chapter Eight

There was absolute silence in Wienis’ chambers when the image of Prince Lefkin appeared at the televisor. There had been one startled gasp from the regent at the haggard face and shredded uniform of his son, and then he collapsed into a chair, face contorted with surprise and apprehension.

Hardin listened stolidly, hands clasped lightly in his lap, while the just-crowned King Lepold sat shriveled in the most shadowy corner, biting spasmodically at his gold-braided sleeve. Even the soldiers had lost the emotionless stare that is the prerogative of the military, and, from where they lined up against the door, atom blasts ready, peered furtively at the figure upon the televisor.

Lefkin spoke, reluctantly, with a tired voice that paused at intervals as though he were being prompted – and not gently:
‘The Anacreonian navy … aware of the nature of its mission … and refusing to be a party … to abominable sacrilege … is returning to Anacreon … with the following ultimatum issued … to those blaspheming sinners … who would dare to use profane force … against the Foundation … source of all blessings … and against the Galactic Spirit. Cease at once all war against … the true faith … and guarantee in a manner suiting us of the navy … as represented by our … priest-attendant, Theo Aporat … that such war will never in the future … be resumed, and that’ – here a long pause, and then continuing – ‘and that the one-time prince regent, Wienis … be imprisoned … and tried before an ecclesiastical court … for his crimes. Otherwise the royal navy … upon returning to Anacreon … will blast the palace to the ground … and take whatever other measures … are necessary … to destroy the nest of sinners … and the den of destroyers … of men’s souls that now prevail.’
The voice ended with half a sob and the screen went blank.

Hardin’s fingers passed rapidly over the Atomo bulb and its light faded until in the dimness, the hitherto regent, the king, and the soldiers were hazy-edged shadows; and for the first time it could be seen that an aura encompassed Hardin.
It was not the blazing light that was the prerogative of kings, but one less spectacular, less impressive, and yet one more effective in its own way, and more useful.
Hardin’s voice was softly ironic as he addressed the same Wienis who had one hour earlier declared him a prisoner of war and Terminus on the point of destruction, and who now was a huddled shadow, broken and silent.

‘There is an old fable,’ said Hardin, ‘as old perhaps as humanity, for the oldest records containing it are merely copies of the other records still older, that might interest you. It runs as follows:

‘A horse having a wolf as a powerful and dangerous enemy lived in constant fear of his life. Being driven to desperation, it occurred to him to seek a strong ally. Whereupon he approached a man, and offered an alliance, pointing out that the wolf was likewise an enemy of the man. The man accepted the partnership at once and offered to kill the wolf immediately, if his new partner would only co-operate by placing his greater speed at the man’s disposal. The horse was willing, and allowed the man to place bridle and saddle upon him. The man mounted, hunted down the wolf, and killed him.

‘The horse, joyful and relieved, thanked the man, and said: “Now that our enemy is dead, remove your bridle and saddle and restore my freedom.”
‘Whereupon the man laughed loudly and replied, “The hell you say. Giddy-ap, Dobbin,” and applied the spurs with a will.’

Silence still. The shadow that was Wienis did not stir.

text:
Every American family has one man who is racing the GPS.

He has been racing her for fifteen years.

She does not know.

My coworker Sakai found out in New Mexico.

Last month, he spent two weeks at a supplier in Albuquerque. On Friday, a guy from the plant named Kurt invited him along for the weekend. His mother's 80th birthday. In Denver.

"It's a little drive," Kurt said.

Saturday. 4:58 a.m. A minivan in a driveway. Kurt, his wife Lisa, two kids, a cooler, and Sakai.

Kurt held up his phone.

A calm woman's voice said, "Your destination is six hours and twelve minutes away."

Kurt looked at the phone the way a boxer looks at a man at the weigh-in.

"We'll see," he said.

Lisa leaned back to Sakai. "He's been fighting that woman since 2009."

"What is her name?"

"We don't say her name in this car."

Then Kurt explained the rules.

"Rule one. We stop when the tank is empty. Not when your bladder is full. The tank."

Sakai raised his hand. "And if the bladder is full first?"

"Then you made choices back in Albuquerque."

"Rule two. Every stop is gas, bathroom, snacks. All at once. In and out. Like a bank robbery. But polite."

"Rule three. The only legal reason to stop early is green chile."

The eleven-year-old asked, "What if somebody throws up?"

Kurt did not look back. "Window."

Sakai understood immediately.

In Japan, our bullet trains are famous for running on time, to the minute. It takes thousands of engineers and billions of dollars.

In America, the same job is done by one man in a minivan, powered entirely by spite and sunflower seeds.

Sakai is an engineer. He took out his phone and started a stopwatch.

Kurt saw this in the rearview mirror.

He did not say anything. But something passed between them. The way it does between two men who have both checked the time while someone else was talking.

The children had gained a second father. They had not asked for one.

First stop. Gas, bathroom, snacks.

Sakai came back to the van in two minutes and fifty seconds.

Kurt looked at his watch. Then at Sakai.

"...You're hired."

Outside Santa Fe, the calm woman spoke again. "A faster route is available."

"No, it isn't," Kurt said.

She offered four times. He declined four times.

Sakai asked, "But if her route is faster—"

"It's not about faster," Kurt said. "It's about who's driving."

Lisa said, "Kurt. He's a guest."

"Then he can hold it like a guest."

Sakai kept records. It's what he does.

"We're making good time": 9.

"Are we there yet": 14.

"Kurt, slow down": 6.

"I'm not even speeding": 6.

Sunflower seeds: one bag. The whole bag. Kurt.

At 10:58 a.m., in a driveway in Denver, the calm woman said, "You have arrived."

Her estimate had been 11:10.

Kurt did not get out.

He turned off the engine. He looked at the phone for a long moment. Then he said, very quietly:

"Twelve minutes, sweetheart."

Then he got out of the van like he had just landed on the moon.

His mother opened the front door. Eighty years old. Apron. Flour on her hands.

"You're early. The ham isn't done."

"Worth it," Kurt said.

He hugged his mother. He hugged his kids. Then he hugged Sakai, and slapped his back twice, which Sakai says is how American men sign a contract.

"Best wingman I ever had."

The eight-year-old ran inside and told her grandmother, "Dad has a Japanese son now."

Her grandmother thought about this.

"Does he want ham?"

Sakai came home to Tokyo last week.

Yesterday morning, Google Maps told him the walk to the station would take nine minutes.

He did it in seven.

He texted Kurt. Kurt replied in four seconds.

"Proud of you, son."

His wife asked him who he was racing.

Sakai said, "Her."

text:
My conclusion is that Iran either already possesses at least one nuclear weapon or will possess one by January 2029 at the latest, around the next U.S. presidential transition. If it does not already have a bomb, I suspect at least some of its uranium may have been enriched beyond the last verified 60%, potentially to 70% or higher by now. Neither possibility has been independently verified.

Iran has been enriching uranium to 60% since April 2021, five and a half years ago. Its stockpile reached approximately 400 kg in May 2025 and 440.9 kg by June 13, 2025. If further enriched to 90%, approximately 400 kg could theoretically provide enough fissile material for 9–10 nuclear weapons, although producing functioning bombs requires additional steps.

Iran restricted IAEA monitoring in 2021, removed surveillance equipment in 2022, and inspectors have been unable to verify its enriched uranium inventory since June 2025. We have had incomplete oversight for years and no verified accounting of the stockpile for nearly seventeen months. We do not know what survived, where it is, whether any has been further enriched, or whether Iran has already manufactured nuclear weapons.

The latest reported Qatari proposal suggests another apparent acknowledgment that Tehran still possesses approximately 400 kg enriched to 60%, offering to dilute it to 3.67% in exchange for lifting the American naval blockade, releasing $6–10 billion in frozen assets, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, renewed IAEA inspections and regional concessions. The terms remain unconfirmed. Iran’s president had already publicly offered dilution in September.

After two rounds of major strikes and more than eight months of war, the United States still cannot account for the uranium or demonstrate that Iran’s nuclear-weapons capability has been eliminated. Facilities were damaged, but the material remains unaccounted for. I consider this one of the largest American strategic and military blunders in modern history, potentially comparable to Afghanistan and Iraq.

In my assessment, Iran has maintained strategic leverage throughout the confrontation, extending back to the killing of Soleimani in January 2020, while the United States became increasingly inward-looking, politically divided and preoccupied.

Now add accelerating AI development, potentially shortening research and engineering timelines without eliminating the physical requirements of nuclear-weapons production. By January 2029, Iran will have had nearly eight years since reaching 60% enrichment and nine years since Soleimani.

After years of sanctions, intelligence operations, diplomacy and military strikes, Washington is still negotiating over approximately the same 400 kg of uranium it set out to neutralize, without independently establishing what survived, what was moved, what has been further enriched, or what may already have been built.

text:
Morning.

Last week in Indian markets was one trade, and it was oil. Brent closed 30 October at $117.64. This morning it is about $97.30. That is a fall of more than 16% in a week, the steepest since the early Covid period, and it happened because Washington and Tehran started talking. Trump said renewed strikes on Iran are "highly unlikely" if a strong deal comes through, with the nuclear programme and the Strait of Hormuz reportedly both on the table.

Everything else here was downstream of that. The Nifty rose about 8.4% on the week to 24,986, the Sensex had its best week since February 2021, the rupee jumped 1.2% to 93.91, its strongest since April, and foreigners bought Rs 48,263 crore of equities. The shape of it matters: this is an FII-led, crude-led rally priced on a deal nobody has signed.

Gold and silver had a good week and a weak Friday. MCX December gold closed at Rs 1,42,224 per 10g and silver at Rs 1,84,095 a kg, both up on the week, both knocked back once strong US payrolls lifted the dollar. Base metals are the soft spot, with copper weak and Chinese credit growth projected to drop sharply this month. For India, cheaper crude reads the familiar way: better for paints, tyres, aviation and the oil marketers, worse for upstream realisations, and quietly helpful for the current account.

Asia is repairing this morning after an ugly Friday, Nikkei up about 3.1% and Kospi 1.3%, having fallen 6% and tripped a circuit breaker respectively in a global AI selloff. GIFT Nifty is around 25,080. The US 10-year sits near 4.87% and the market still prices roughly a 70% chance the Fed hikes in December.

On the names, Tata Steel is the print to look at: consolidated profit up 16% to Rs 3,700 crore, EBITDA of Rs 10,665 crore, margin up 90 basis points to 16.1%, volumes doing the work against softer prices. Divi's Labs put up a big quarter with profit up 64% to Rs 1,127 crore. Tata Chemicals went the other way, a Rs 50 crore loss against a Rs 154 crore profit last year. Nuvama moved Tata Steel, Hindalco and Power Grid to Buy. On the primary side, Hindustan Coca-Cola Holdings filed its DRHP for a pure offer for sale of 99.75 crore shares.

Three things to watch today. One, any headline out of the Iran talks, because that is the hinge under crude, the rupee and the index. Two, the US CPI print tomorrow, which lands while we are shut for Balipratipada, so Wednesday opens on a gap. Three, India's October CPI on Thursday, where consensus sits near 5.93% and some forecasts go to 6.2%, against the RBI's 6% upper tolerance. India VIX closed up 20% at 18.43.

More after the close.

text:
When Jensen Huang was 17, he asked a 19 year old girl named Lori Mills at Oregon State University if she wanted to see his homework. At that time, the two were lab partners in an electrical engineering class. Jensen offered her a deal: if they studied together every Sunday, she would get straight A’s. Somewhere along the way, he made her another promise that he would be a CEO by 30. They exchanged marital vows  five years after they met.

Today, Huang wrote an emotional letter to NVIDIA’s employees about betraying that girl he had met in college: 

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children.”

The New York Times has reported that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang, an executive at a company that bought NVIDIA chips, was gathering information for Beijing. She and Jensen Huang are unrelated, but it seems she supplied “high voltage electricity” to the CEO of one of the world’s best employers. 

Long before anybody cared what Jensen Huang knew about computer chips, he was a boy from Taiwan whose parents sent him and his older brother to the United States ahead of them. When the family reunited, his mother worked as a maid at a Catholic school and his father was an engineer.

As a teenager, Huang cleaned tables at Denny’s. After college, he worked in the chip industry and earned a master’s degree at Stanford. And when he turned 30 in 1993, he and two fellow engineers, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, founded NVIDIA. The idea was borne at a Denny’s in California: to make chips that could put convincing 3D graphics on a home computer so people could play better games.

The three partners nearly went out of business. NVIDIA had a contract to build technology for Sega, the Japanese video game company, and Huang realized they had  taken the wrong technical approach. He flew to Japan to tell Sega the work would not deliver what NVIDIA had promised. Then he had to ask Sega to let them out of the contract and pay them anyway. Sega agreed. That money bought NVIDIA time to build another chip.

Isitoshe, 

Years later, NVIDIA made it possible for researchers to program those graphics chips for work that had nothing to do with games. In 2012, researchers used NVIDIA chips to train AlexNet, a system that made a big leap in teaching computers to recognize what was in a picture. The same ability to do many calculations at once is a big reason those chips are now used to train AI. It also explains why governments care so much about who can buy the most advanced ones.

Lori earned her own electrical engineering degree from Oregon State. She went on to lead the foundation she and Jensen established, and in 2022 they gave $50 million to help build a research center at the university where they had met. 

Earlier this year, at Carnegie Mellon’s commencement, Jensen told the students about the girl from his lab class and announced they had been married 40 years. In today apology letter, Jensen writes that he hopes over time, he could earn back the trust of his wife and two children.

text:
Nature Biotechnology: Low-n epitope-targeted antibodies via AF-Multimer × IgLM co-optimization.

Mille-Fragoso, Hie, Gao and colleagues at Stanford and the Arc Institute design de novo CDRs onto a user-specified antibody framework, instead of relying on immunization or large library screens that offer little control over which epitope is hit.

Hard readout
→ Functional antibodies across four diverse targets — PD-L1, IL-3, IL-20 and the viral protein BHRF1 — and across binder formats, after testing only 43–101 designs per antigen
→ Experimental success rates of 4–22%; the paper reports nanomolar binding affinities, and BLI examples include 170 nM (PD-L1), 280 nM (IL-3) and 190 nM (IL-20)
→ Validated designs showed robust expression in mammalian cells and high sequence and structural novelty; code and full protocols are open-sourced

Worth reading when epitope-targeted antibody design still sounds like a high-n screen.

Injectable Chiral Single-Walled Carbon Nanotubes (SWCNTs), Silicon Nanowire Arrays, & Graphene-Intrgrated Meshes are the physical infrastructure for the Human Embedded System.

Injectable Chiral SWCNTs represent a frontier in nanobiotech, serving as high-performance interfaces between biological neural networks & digital hardware. When integrated into a biological matrix, they can effectively function as the raw physical layer of a "human embedded system"—an integration of biological computing (the brain) & synthetic cybernetics.

Brain Machine Interface (BMI) Tech

A brain–computer interface (BCI), sometimes called a brain–machine interface (BMI), is a direct communication link between the brain's electrical activity & an external device, most commonly a computer.

https://t.co/Xk2ieUuAgQ

The use of single walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) as a coating material for electrodes is a promising strategy for the implementation of deep brain stimulation (DBS) & brain computer interface (BCI) strategies.

https://t.co/7l8IIYo1QL

SWCNT-coated electrodes have outperformed traditional brain implants – such as tungsten & stainless-steel electrodes – by improving electrical stimulation of & recordings from neurons, both in in vitro & in vivo studies.

https://t.co/GUwkCVxS3K

SINGLE-WALLED CARBON NANOTUBE-POLYMER-BASED FLEXIBLE ELECTRODE

Objective — The development of electrode arrays able to reliably record brain electrical activity. 

We undertook a comprehensive physico-chemical, physiological, histological & immunohistochemical characterization of new single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNT)-based electrode arrays grafted onto medium-density polyethylene (MD-PE) films. 

Approach — The long-term electrical stability, flexibility, & biocompatibility of the SWCNT arrays were investigated in vivo in laboratory rats by two-months recording & analysis of subdural electrocorticogram (ECoG). Ex-vivo characterization of a thin flexible & single probe SWCNT/polymer electrode is also provided. 

Main Results — The single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) arrays were able to capture high quality & very stable electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals across 8 weeks. The histological & immunohistochemical analyses demonstrated that SWCNT arrays show promising biocompatibility properties & may be used in chronic conditions.

The SWCNT-based arrays are flexible & stretchable, providing low electrode-tissue impedance, &, therefore, high compliance w/ the irregular topography of the cortical surface. Finally, reliable evoked synaptic local field potentials in rat brain slices were recorded using a special SWCNT-polymer-based flexible electrode.

Significance — The results demonstrate that the SINGLE-WALLED CARBON NANOTUBE (SWCNT) ARRAYS GRAFTED IN MEDIUM-DENSITY POLYETHYLENE (MD-PE) THIN FILMS ARE SUITABLE FOR MANUFACTURING FLEXIBLE DEVICES FOR SUBDURAL ELECTROCORTICOGRAM (ECoG) RECORDING & might represent promising candidates for LONG-TERM NEURAL IMPLANTS FOR BRAIN MACHINE INTERFACES.

https://t.co/5YUZPUyxDK

No matter what the application is, the signal processing chain is the same. The  BCI system consists of 4 sequential units: 

(1) signal acquisition, (2) feature extraction, (3) feature translation, & (4) device output.

https://t.co/iZSLUMZ9ft

SENSORS (BASEL, SWITZERLAND) 

These 4 units are controlled by an operating protocol that defines the onset & timing of operation, the details of signal processing, the nature of the device commands, & the oversight of performance. 

Today, due to the wide spread of the embedded system & the computational resources that can offer, it becomes a priority to implement BCI technologies in embedded platforms. 

An embedded BCI (EBCI) is a microprocessor or microcontroller based system of hardware & software. It is designed to analyze the EEG signals & translates them into commands, that are relayed to an output device to carry out a desired action or useful info for practitioner.

​
What is Traumatic Brain Injury? ​

​Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a physical injury to the brain resulting from a variety of causes including vehicle crashes, falls, sports related injuries, military combat, and assaults. 

As a result, the severity of the injury can fluctuate in degree from mild to severe, sometimes resulting in death. 

While TBI mostly prompts physical damage to the brain, it is also associated with an array of psychological and hrmonal problems. 

These include cognitive disabilities, sleep pattern problems, lack of attention, dizziness, confusion, etc. 

Current Diagnosis of TBI

TBI is currently diagnosed with a subjective physical examination, psychological screen & the typical Glascow test. The patient's injury is usually confirmed with a CT scan. 

CT scans are effective in depicting bleeding around the brain as well as swelling, but limited in their ability to diagnose mild TBI, especially concussions. 

MRIs are more powerful in their imaging ability in comparison to CT scans. But like CT scans, they are unable to detect injury to nerve fibers inside the brain. 

Hence, axonal damage remains undetectable in most occasions. Other radiological exams like positron emission tomography scans are developed for mild TBI but with extremely high cost. 

The most successful first response test is the imPACT test, which is computerized version of the physical and psychological tests. It allows health care personnel to diagnose TBI at the scene of injury by using an integrated electronic applications, but not reliable.

Atom NanoElectronics has developed air-stable thin film field effect transistors based on these nanotubes with high ION/IOFF ratio (>10^8). 

These field effect transistor devices outperform chemiresistors and amperometric/potentiometric sensors in terms of detection limits and sensitivity resulting from the signal amplification by gate modulation. 

Additionally, these field effect transistors can be easily incorporated into sensor circuits such as ring oscillators and power gain differential amplifiers to enhance detection performance parameters such as low detection limits and background elimination. 

Moreover, these integrated sensor circuits can be remotely powered and read-out through wireless communications & can be further combined with microfluidic channels for real-time monitoring of implanted patients.

Key Factors:

> Sportsbook consensus: Seattle -8.5, total 39.5, Seattle moneyline -440 (about 81.5% implied).

> Internal model: Seattle 73.4% to win, projected score Seattle 24.7 to Arizona 17.7 (margin 7.05, total 42.45). Fair moneyline is about -277, so -440 is too short to offer value.

> Best value gap: the model margin of 7.05 vs the market 8.5 is a 1.45-point gap toward Arizona. We still have no lean on the spread. The 42.45 projection is 2.95 above the 39.5 total, but we have no lean on the total either, since the run-leaning pace (-4.6% pass rate over expected) pulls it back toward the market.

> Quarterbacks: Drew Lock (SEA) is at +0.116 EPA/dropback (12th) with +1.24 CPOE, filling in for Darnold. Gardner Minshew (ARI) is at +0.035 (21st) with +0.92 CPOE in his first start of 2026. Both are sacked on 5.9% of dropbacks.

> Trenches: pass rush is a wash. Seattle's rush gets home on 6.1% of dropbacks (15th) and Arizona's on 6.1% (14th). Seattle's line is patched with Charles Cross and Quenton Nelson out, which caps Lock's deep game.

> Arizona's backfield is gutted: James Conner and Jeremiyah Love are on IR and Bam Knight is out, leaving Tyler Allgeier as the lead back. Arizona's red-zone touchdown rate is 48.1%.

> Rest, travel and weather: Seattle has 6.0 days of rest vs 7.0 for Arizona, and the Cardinals travel 1,104 miles. Conditions at Lumen Field are 56.7F with 10.1 mph wind, so there is no real weather impact on passing or kicking.

It is 8:00 PM on a Sunday.

Before Monday morning hits, you need to see two quiet reports that just dropped from the Federal Reserve and Visa—because they expose the exact trap banks are setting for the next 6 weeks:

1. Visa just projected U.S. holiday retail spending will surge 4.5% this November and December, pushing toward a record $1 TRILLION.
2. At the exact same time, the Fed's latest bank lending survey revealed that while consumer demand for credit cards is climbing, banks are actively "getting choosier" and tightening credit standards.

Here is the plain-English translation of what is happening behind the scenes:

Banks want you to swipe their cards at 24% APR to fund that $1 trillion holiday boom—while quietly raising the FICO score requirements on the 0% APR and high-cashback cards that actually help you win.

Take 15 minutes tonight (Sunday at 8:00 PM) to lock in this 4-step @CreditDeskHQ defense before the Monday rush begins:

[1] Protect Your Credit Utilization Before Banks Tighten Further
When banks get "choosier," a 680 FICO score no longer gets you Tier-1 approval or 0% balance transfer lifelines—you need a 740 to 760+ score.
- Open your banking app right now and check your Statement Closing Dates for this week.
- Credit bureaus snapshot your balance on the Statement Closing Date, NOT the Payment Due Date.
- Pay your current balance down under 10% of your credit limit tonight so the bureaus record single-digit utilization this week.

[2] Never Let a Store Cashier Talk You Into a "20% Off" Retail Card
Over the next 6 weeks, every retailer will offer you 15% to 20% off at the register if you open their store credit card.
- Do not take the bait. Store cards carry predatory 28% to 32%+ APRs, tiny credit limits (which wreck your utilization ratio), and burn a hard inquiry on your credit report.
- Instead, route your November and December shopping through a real, no-annual-fee 2% to 5% cashback card you already own—with Autopay locked to "Full Statement Balance."

[3] Build a Separate "Holiday Spoke" Inside Your HYSA
Never mix holiday gift and travel spending with your monthly rent and utility money.
- Keep strictly 1 month of essential bills in your $0-fee checking "Hub."
- Keep your 3 to 6 month emergency fund untouched inside an FDIC-insured 4.00%+ High-Yield Savings Account (HYSA)—never at a 0.01% brick-and-mortar bank.
- Only spend what you can clear in full to $0.00 before the statement closes.

[4] Quarantine Any Card Carrying a Balance Tonight
If you are already carrying credit card debt heading into mid-November, remember the golden rule of banking:
- The moment you carry a balance from one month to the next, your 25-day interest-free grace period is dead.
- Every new coffee, bag of groceries, or holiday gift you put on that card gets hit with 24% interest the exact second you swipe it.
- Freeze that card in your app tonight and move Monday's normal spending to a clean, $0-balance card.

Spend 15 minutes setting up your accounts tonight so you wake up Monday morning on the winning side of the bank's math.

Bookmark this Sunday night checklist, and hit Follow + Subscribe on @CreditDeskHQ for weekly plain-English banking and credit blueprints!

text:
Vietnam Day4. MEKONG DELTA – THE FRENCH LEGACY AND THE AMERICAN WAR

The Mekong Delta has witnessed dramatic chapters of Vietnamese history.
During the French colonial period (1858–1954), the region became an important agricultural and commercial center. French colonial administration expanded waterways, transportation infrastructure, and agricultural production, particularly rice cultivation. Saigon and other southern towns developed as important trading centers.
Today, traces of this period can still be found in old colonial buildings, churches, bridges, traditional townhouses, and historic urban streets.

The region later experienced another turbulent chapter during the Vietnam War (with American) (1955–1975).
Because of its strategic importance, the Mekong Delta became a major area of military operations. Rivers, canals, villages, and agricultural lands were deeply affected by the conflict.

Yet, despite decades of hardship, local communities demonstrated remarkable resilience.
Today, visitors can discover historical sites, old houses, religious architecture, and local museums while listening to stories passed down through generations.

Cycling through the countryside offers a different perspective on history. Instead of seeing the Mekong Delta only through historical photographs and museums, you can witness how people rebuilt their lives and transformed the region.
History is not only found in books. Sometimes, it lives in the villages, buildings, and stories along the road.

Explore the Mekong delta, Vietnam, one ride at a time -

text:
On the ninth of January 1966, a farmer went on the radio in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, and made his neighbours an offer.
You can come and register to vote at my shop, he told them. And if you cannot afford the two dollar tax, do not worry about it. I will pay it for you.
Within 24 hours he was dead.
His name was Vernon Dahmer, & this is what that offer cost him.
Vernon was born in 1908, near Hattiesburg, in a Mississippi where a Black man was beaten down by the law from the day he was born.
And he still built something.
He worked a farm of 200 acres. He ran a sawmill. He opened a grocery store. By the 1960s his family was one of the few well off Black families for miles, & he put his neighbours to work and helped the ones who were struggling.
There was one more thing about Vernon.
His skin was light. Light enough that he could have moved somewhere new, called himself a white man, & lived an easy life.
He never gave it a moment's thought.
What he wanted was the vote. Not just for himself. For all of them.
He had a saying he repeated to anyone who would listen. If you do not vote, you do not count.
So he took over the local NAACP branch, & he went to work.
But Mississippi had built a wall around that ballot box.
There was a reading test you could fail no matter how well you read, because the man marking it decided who passed.
And there was the poll tax. 2$, paid at the county courthouse, before you were allowed to vote at all.
2$ was groceries for a family. But money was not even the worst of it.
Klansmen used to loiter outside that courthouse. Standing about. Watching the door. Staring at any Black person who came near.
Most people took one look and kept walking. Who could blame them.
So Vernon began walking them in himself. He and his sons went along, so that nobody had to face those men on their own.
Then he thought of something better.
He talked the local sheriff into letting the voter registration book be kept in his own grocery store.
No courthouse. No men at the door. You could sign up for the vote in the same shop where you bought your flour.
That was what he announced on the radio. And then he added the part about paying the two dollars himself.
The Klan heard it too.
That night, two carloads of them drove out to his farm in the dark.
They opened fire on the house and threw firebombs through the windows. The house caught. The store caught.
Vernon woke to gunshots and flames and his children screaming.
He picked up his shotgun and went to the front of the burning house, and he stood there shooting back at those men in the dark.
He held them there. And while he held them, his wife Ellie got the children out through a window at the back.
Every one of them lived. His little girl was burned, but she lived.
Vernon did not. He had been breathing fire the whole time he stood there, and his lungs were finished. He died in hospital that same day.
While it happened, some of his own sons were serving in the United States military, in uniform, far from home.
Their father had just been killed for helping people vote in the country they were defending.
The Klan leader who ordered it was a man named Sam Bowers. He was tried four times in the 1960s, and four times an all white jury could not bring itself to convict him.
He walked free for thirty two years.
But the Dahmer family never stopped. Not for three decades. They pushed, and they wrote, and they pestered, until a journalist helped them prise the case back open.
In 1998, Sam Bowers stood trial for the fifth time. This jury needed about two hours. Guilty. Life in prison, where he died.
In 2020, a statue of Vernon Dahmer was unveiled outside the Forrest County Courthouse. The same building his neighbours had once been too frightened to walk into.
Vernon Dahmer owned more than almost any man in his county. Land, a mill, a shop, a house he had built with his own hands.
He gave every bit of it, and his life on top, over two dollars that were not even his to pay.
~Professor Calcue

text:
The richest person in the room is not always the one with the most money. Sometimes, it’s the one who can afford to say no. ✍🏾

Mahabharata ❤️

Duryodhana had an empire. Yudhishthira lost his kingdom, his wealth and almost everything he owned.

Yet, when Krishna offered a choice before the Kurukshetra war, Duryodhana chose Krishna’s vast army. Arjuna chose Krishna himself, knowing he wouldn’t even carry a weapon.

One chose resources. The other chose wisdom. History remembers who made the better choice.

Think about that for a moment.

We spend years accumulating things. Bigger houses, better cars, premium memberships, expensive holidays and impressive designations.

But how much of it actually belongs to us if we cannot walk away from a bad job, say no to a toxic relationship or take a day off without feeling guilty?

A person with ₹10 crore and a lifestyle that demands ₹12 crore is not necessarily wealthy.

A person with ₹50 lakh, no debt, enough savings and control over their time might be far richer.

We confuse the ability to buy things with the freedom to choose. There is another lesson here.

Krishna didn’t fight Arjuna’s war for him. He offered guidance. Arjuna still had to pick up his bow.

That’s an uncomfortable truth about life.

Your parents can give you a head start. Your friends can open doors. Your mentors can show you the way. But nobody can live your life on your behalf.

Eventually, you have to make your own choices and live with their consequences. Perhaps success isn’t about having everything the world can offer.

It’s about reaching a point where you don’t need everything the world offers.

Build wealth. But don’t become its servant.

Earn well. But protect your time.

Have ambitions. But know when enough is enough.

The ultimate luxury isn’t owning everything. It’s needing very little to feel complete.

⚽ 35 YEARS OF KENTUCKY GIRLS SOCCER: The dynasties, Final Four regulars and numbers behind the championships  ⚽ 

Sacred Heart and South Oldham have won nearly half of Kentucky's girls soccer state championships since 1992, but a 35-year review of Kentucky High School Athletic Association tournament results reveals a different advantage when public and private schools meet for the title.
Public schools have won 14 of the 20 championship games against private-school opponents, despite private schools making more championship-game appearances overall.
The historical review, covering every state championship from 1992 through 2026, identifies 14 different champions, 19 programs that have reached the final and 37 schools with at least one documented Final Four appearance.
The results illustrate the dominance of a handful of programs, the difficulty of converting postseason appearances into championships and the streaks that have helped shape Kentucky girls soccer.

⚽ Sacred Heart and South Oldham lead championship history ⚽ 
Sacred Heart holds the state championship lead with nine titles, followed by South Oldham with eight. Together, the programs have captured 17 of the 35 championships, accounting for 48.6% of the titles awarded since the KHSAA sanctioned its inaugural girls soccer tournament in 1992.
Notre Dame ranks third with four championships. Highlands, Male and West Jessamine have won two apiece, while Ballard, Bethlehem, Central Hardin, Greenwood, Lafayette, Lexington Catholic, St. Henry and Tates Creek each have one.
Those six multiple-title programs account for 27 championships, or 77.1% of the tournament's history.
Sacred Heart also leads with 14 championship-game appearances, compiling a 9-5 record in the final. South Oldham, Notre Dame and Lexington Catholic have each reached the championship game 10 times, but their results reveal sharply different levels of success.
South Oldham has won eight of its 10 championship appearances, an 80% winning percentage that leads all programs with at least four finals. Notre Dame is 4-6, while Lexington Catholic has endured nine championship losses since winning its lone title in 2002.
The nine runner-up finishes are the most of any school. Notre Dame follows with six, while Sacred Heart has five.
Highlands, meanwhile, has reached six championship games and won twice, capturing consecutive titles in 2005 and 2006.

⚽ Reaching the Final Four does not guarantee a championship opportunity ⚽ 
Sacred Heart's postseason consistency extends beyond its championship appearances. The Valkyries lead the compiled records with 17 identified Final Four berths, followed by Notre Dame with 15, Lexington Catholic with 14 and South Oldham with 11.
Those four programs account for 44 of the 70 championship-game appearances in the tournament's history, or 62.9%.
South Oldham has been particularly successful in the semifinal round, winning 10 of its 11 documented appearances. Sacred Heart has a 14-3 record in identified semifinals, while Highlands has reached the championship game in six of seven appearances.
Other programs have experienced very different postseason outcomes.
Greenwood has made eight Final Four appearances but reached the championship game only once. That breakthrough came in 2019, when the Gators defeated Highlands 1-0 to capture their state title.
Bowling Green has reached five Final Fours without advancing to the championship match, the most among the identified programs that have never played for the title. Woodford County has made five semifinal appearances and reached the final twice, finishing as runner-up in 2004 and 2007.
West Jessamine offers another contrast. The Colts have reached six Final Fours, advanced to two championship games and won both, defeating Lexington Catholic in 2016 and Notre Dame in 2017.

⚽ Public schools hold the championship advantage ⚽ 
The public-private comparison is among the most notable findings of the historical review.
Private schools have accounted for 40 of the 70 championship-game appearances, compared with 30 for public schools. However, public schools lead the overall championship count 19-16.
Of the 35 championship matches, 20 paired a public school against a private school. Ten featured two private schools, while five matched public schools.
Public schools won 14 of the 20 head-to-head meetings, a 70% winning rate.
The composition of the Final Four has also produced two unusual tournaments.
In 2015, Sacred Heart, Lexington Catholic, Bethlehem and Owensboro Catholic formed an entirely private-school Final Four. Sacred Heart defeated Lexington Catholic 1-0 for the championship.
The 2026 tournament featured an entirely public-school field: Central Hardin, South Oldham, Highlands and Paul Laurence Dunbar.
Central Hardin defeated South Oldham 1-0 on Nov. 7, completing an undefeated 25-0-3 season and claiming its first girls soccer championship.
The 2015 and 2026 tournaments represent the only completely private and completely public Final Four fields, respectively, among the 32 seasons with fully identified semifinalists.

⚽ Championship dynasties and postseason streaks ⚽ 
South Oldham owns the longest championship streak in the tournament's history, winning four consecutive titles from 1998 through 2001 under coach Cy Tucker.
The Dragons also captured consecutive championships in 1995 and 1996, giving the program six titles in seven seasons from 1995 through 2001.
Sacred Heart won three consecutive championships from 2007 through 2009 and added back-to-back titles in 2024 and 2025.
Male captured consecutive championships in 1993 and 1994, Highlands repeated in 2005 and 2006, and West Jessamine followed with its two-title run in 2016 and 2017.
But championship streaks tell only part of the story.
Greenwood holds the longest fully documented streak of consecutive Final Four appearances, advancing five straight seasons from 2001 through 2005 without reaching the championship match during that span.
South Oldham reached four consecutive Final Fours from 1998 through 2001, winning the championship each season. Notre Dame reached four straight from 2011 through 2014, winning twice, while Sacred Heart recorded four-year runs from 2006 through 2009 and 2017 through 2020.
Those streaks illustrate the difference between sustained postseason success and the ability to finish a season with a championship.

⚽ The significance of the historical records ⚽ 
The 2026 championship completed 35 seasons of KHSAA-sanctioned girls soccer, beginning with Lafayette's 1-0 victory over Notre Dame in the inaugural 1992 final.
All 35 champions and runners-up have been identified, accounting for 70 championship-game appearances and an equal number of semifinal victories.
The compiled records also identify 134 of the 140 possible Final Four berths. Complete semifinal fields are available for 1992-94 and 1998-2026, while the six losing semifinalists from 1995-97 remain unidentified.
Championship-game statistics are complete. Final Four appearance totals and semifinal loss records should be considered provisional because those six missing positions could affect individual school totals and historical rankings.
The championship finalists from 1995-97 are credited with semifinal victories, since each necessarily advanced through that round.

They fled violence in search of safety. Now reports allege that death found them where they sought refuge.

In Ethiopia's East Wollega region, disturbing accounts describe drone strikes against displaced Amhara civilians, including women, children, and the elderly.

Local reports allege more than 30 deaths. One mother is reportedly fighting for survival after losing both legs.

These specific claims require independent verification. But the wider catastrophe is undeniable.

On October 29, drone strikes struck another displacement camp in Ethiopia, killing at least 15 people, including children, according to Reuters.

Consider what these families have endured.

First, they lose their homes. Then their communities. Then their ability to find shelter, food, and medical care. And now, even the places where they seek refuge may offer no safety.

What kind of world allows those fleeing violence to become victims of violence yet again?

What kind of civilization possesses the technology to observe an entire village from the sky, yet cannot guarantee that a wounded child will receive medical treatment?

A mother should not have to lose her legs while searching for a place where her children might live in peace.

A child should not have to learn that even running away may not save his life.

And no government should ever regard the suffering of civilians as an acceptable consequence of its military or political objectives.

I am a Catholic and Knight Commandeur of the Sovereign Military Order of the Temple of Jerusalem.

Our faith teaches that every human life possesses sacred dignity. Our Templar heritage calls us to remember the vulnerable, defend the innocent, and place service above recognition.

The Cross is not an ornament of convenience. It is a call to sacrifice.

To the Ethiopian government and Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed: These allegations demand an independent investigation. Establish who ordered the strikes, who carried them out, what was targeted, and whether civilians were unlawfully attacked.

Ensure that the wounded can reach medical care. Open humanitarian routes. Protect displaced families. Preserve evidence and hold perpetrators accountable wherever the facts lead.

To @UNHumanRights @WHO @UNOCHA @amnesty: The wounded cannot survive on expressions of concern. They need access to hospitals, medical supplies, emergency assistance, and protection.

To His Holiness Pope Leo XIV, @Pontifex:

Holy Father, our Ethiopian Orthodox brothers and sisters have endured terrible suffering. Their cries belong to the conscience of the entire Christian world.

The Sovereign Military Order of the Temple of Jerusalem continues raising its voice from the sidelines while innocent communities suffer.

We are willing to present our Order's history, principles, and humanitarian vision before the Holy See.

We ask for meaningful dialogue about what properly authorized humanitarian cooperation might contribute to the preservation of innocent human life.

Not conquest. Not vengeance. Not glory.

Service, mercy, justice, and peace for all.

Our concern does not end with Christians. Every innocent Amhara, Oromo, Muslim, Christian, or person of any faith deserves protection from violence.

I stand by the words of my oath:

“If my strength can become another man's shelter, my courage his hope, my voice his defense, or my life the price of his tomorrow, then none of it was ever mine to keep.”

We have prayed over enough graves. It is time to protect the living.

God is love. Let our humanity reflect it.

Chevalier Richard J. Kraemer, KCTJ
Sovereign Military Order of the Temple of Jerusalem

Non nobis, Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam.

Ad Majorem Dei Gloriam. ✝️⚔️🇻🇦

text:
Real history. Not the " Arab Palestinian reinvention"

In 1947, partition was accepted as a legitimate way to end British rule and create new states. India and Pakistan were born. Around 15 million people were uprooted and hundreds of thousands were killed. Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs were massacred, raped, abducted and driven from their homes.

And Partition didn't simply end when the borders were drawn. Refugee movements continued for years, particularly in Bengal, with millions displaced over subsequent decades. Its effects on families, communities and the psychology of the subcontinent are still part of its history.

Yet nobody turned that continuing trauma into an argument that Pakistan had no right to exist.

Now look at the British Mandate for Palestine.

The UN proposed dividing the Mandate into two states  an Arab state and a Jewish state. The Jews accepted. The Arab Palestinian leadership and Arab states rejected partition and went to war.

The 1937 Peel Commission recognised that Jews could not safely depend on an Arab-majority government. The Arab Revolt had exposed the depth of that conflict. The Commission concluded that partition offered the most practical way forward: separate states for Jews and Arabs.

Their partition plan was for two states. One Jewish with almost equal Jewish and Arab citizens and an Arab state.

The proposed Jewish state was not an Arab free territory. It contained almost equal numbers of Jews and Arabs and was to guarantee equal civil and political rights and freedom of religion.

The Jews accepted sharing the land.

The Arab leadership rejected the partition.

War followed.

And there is another fact routinely left out of this story: many Arabs remained inside Israel. They became citizens. They stayed, built families, businesses and communities, and their descendants are now a large part of Israel's population. Israel's first population registration was explicitly intended to register the residents of the new state.

At the same time, around a million Jews were driven from or fled Arab and Muslim countries in the following decades. They lost homes, property and livelihoods and rebuilt their lives.

That is the comparison that matters.

Displacement after the collapse of empires was not unique to Jews or Arabs.

India and Pakistan demonstrate the enormous human cost of partition.

Jewish refugees demonstrate that entire communities can suffer dispossession and still rebuild.

What became different was the politics built around  "Palestinians". The fact that after 1950 arabs in Judea and Samara , renamed West Bank by Jordan, were made Jordanian citizens forgotten in the story telling.

It was not allowed simply to become part of the painful history of the collapse of the British Mandate. It became an inherited political grievance, with refugee status passed down generations and the creation of Israel itself continually presented as the unresolved injustice.

And that tells you something important.

If this were simply about land, the argument would be about borders.

But Israel has surrendered territory for peace, returned Sinai to Egypt, made peace with Jordan and withdrew completely from Gaza.

The question keeps returning to something deeper: the legitimacy of Jewish sovereignty itself.
 
Partition created Pakistan amid vastly greater population upheaval and continuing trauma, yet Pakistan's existence was not made into a permanent accusation against Muslims.

The difference is not Partition. It is what was subsequently made of Jewish statehood.

Other peoples born from partition were allowed to heal,rebuild and move forward.

Jewish national self-determination was turned into the permanent crime that supposedly explains everything that followed.

It is the old idea that Jewish sovereignty is uniquely illegitimate. Jews have maintained a continuous presence in the holy land of Israel, families tracing their history back to the second temple

text:
Good, thoughtful post. I wasn't planning on meditating on this tonight, but here are my thoughts (which are informed by the Reformed tradition and Westminster: but I'm not trying to square this with any creed beyond those required of all Christians by the ecumenical councils), if I may offer them. I am not dogmatic about anything which follows.

1) I believe Psalm 103:12 is literal. It's the only way I can square Job 32:1-2 with Job 42:7. God literally forgot Job's sin after he repented. He was permitted to serve as mediator for his friends without any  apparent need of offering for himself, even though he was unclean with visible, oozing, bloody sores. This is amazing.

2) In the covenant community, old and new, I think God deals with the  "venial sin" (for lack of a better term) of the weaker among us (virgins, infirm, slow, babies, deaf, blind) differently than he does with the sin of men like you and I and Job. If I may be so bold, I would suggest that the economy of salvation for virgin women like Mary is different from the economy of salvation for able-bodied men of Adam (and non-virgin, non-married women of Eve) who are "positionally" in high-handed sin at all times without grace. The weaker among us have special favor (which is why feminism is so stupid and destructive.) This is suggested by 1 Tim 2:15 read literally but contemplatively with Genesis 3-4 read literally and cotemplatively, and the patristic understanding that Mary was a perfected Eve, just as Christ was a perfect Adam.

3) If the tradition is true that Mary was placed in the service of the temple from youth, as a virgin, and then placed in submission to Joseph, it is probable that any "venial sin" of Mary's from her youth was forgotten by God the moment she submitted herself to her various superiors: first those in the temple, then Joseph, and YHWH by extension, before she had an opportunity to commit any high-handed sin. If so, her womb was purified and God saw no sin in her, as he saw no sin in Job (who did not need to make sacrifice for himself). In other words, Job and Mary were deemed righteous by God in the O.T. sense and economy, in different ways than us in the New Covenant economy, but also differently from each other: Mary was a virgin, Job was a patriarch and a priest in the order of Melchizedek of some kind.  

4) Accepting these premises, Mary was chosen among the virgins of Israel because she and her womb were elected before time to be filled with the Holy Ghost, but not because of any accident of her birth, other than that she was a holy virgin from the prophecied clan and tribe "in the fullness of time," Gal. 4. For Christ to have been born under the law, Mary could not have been ontologically special. In other words, God could have elected any other holy virgin of Israel and none of them needed any birth of supernatural significance in order for their womb to be deemed cleansed and fit for Christ's presence. 

Tl;dr, Mary was "saved" from sin before the Lord entered her womb in the normal way any other virgin woman of Israel would be saved, by submission to headship and holy living. As I understand the Orthodox to believe, she and all other justified OT covenant saints only needed to be cleansed from ancestral sin to be perfected in Christ and fit for the resurrection, their individual sins having been forgotten, like Job's, and Mary's, the latter having never sinned high-handedly or mortally anyway.

Conclusion: Mary was favored among women because she was elect, not because of any supernatural accident of birth.

P.S. You mentioned the quadriga, so I am obligated to draw @UPuritano's attention to this.
