text:
NQ / NASDAQ — PRE-OPEN REGIME RADAR
A Fragile Monday Rebound Meets Nvidia Leadership Risk as US Inflation and AI Infrastructure Earnings Set the Week's Direction — 9 November 2026

9 NOVEMBER 2026 | 12:07 SWITZERLAND | 05:07 CME/CHICAGO | 06:07 NEW YORK
FIRST REPORT OF THE DAY — PRE-OPEN AND WEEKLY OUTLOOK
MARKET DATA REFERENCE: REUTERS, 05:10 NEW YORK / 11:10 SWITZERLAND

MAIN CONCLUSION
US equity futures are attempting to recover after four consecutive weekly declines in the Nasdaq Composite, but the initial improvement is distinctly weaker in technology than in the wider market. At 05:10 New York on Monday, Reuters recorded Dow futures up 0.73%, S&P 500 futures up 0.40% and Nasdaq-100 futures up just 0.21%. Nvidia was down approximately 4.5% in pre-market trading after its board announced an independent investigation concerning reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The board said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security had been compromised and expressed confidence in his leadership. The Nasdaq therefore begins the week with two competing forces: renewed willingness to buy equities after last week's severe losses, and fresh uncertainty affecting one of its most influential AI companies.

KEY CONFIRMATION / RISK
Tuesday's October US Consumer Price Index, Friday's Producer Price Index and earnings from CoreWeave, Cisco and Applied Materials will test three separate assumptions underpinning technology valuations: the path of inflation, the future cost of capital and the financial returns from AI infrastructure. Friday's stronger-than-expected employment report increased market pricing for a December Federal Reserve rate rise to around 80%. Lower oil prices are providing some relief, but rates, corporate financing and semiconductor breadth remain decisive information variables. A positive pre-market futures quotation is not evidence that the correction has ended.

FRIDAY'S CLOSE — THE REBOUND DID NOT REPAIR THE WEEK
Friday's US cash session delivered a rebound after Thursday's historic technology decline. The Nasdaq Composite rose about 1.1% to 24,579.43, the S&P 500 gained 0.32% to 7,376.86 and the Dow fell 0.46% to 51,285.73. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index recovered 4.2%, with AMD up approximately 11% and Nvidia up 2.8%.

The weekly record tells a different story. The Nasdaq Composite still lost 3.4%, its fourth consecutive negative week. The S&P 500 declined 2.7%, its weakest week in more than a year, and the Dow lost 0.9%. The Nasdaq has fallen more than 10% from its recent peak, meeting the conventional correction threshold. Friday's advance therefore represented a partial recovery from extensive selling, not a restoration of the previous market condition. The figures refer to cash indices, not the NQ futures contract.

MONDAY'S FUTURES — DOW LEADERSHIP, NASDAQ RESTRAINT

REUTERS OBSERVATION, 05:10 NEW YORK / 11:10 SWITZERLAND:

DOW E-MINI FUTURES: +0.73%.
S&P 500 E-MINI FUTURES: +0.40%.
NASDAQ-100 E-MINI FUTURES: +0.21%.

NQ is participating in the recovery but substantially lagging the Dow. Reuters also reported modest weakness in Intel, Marvell and Qualcomm before the US opening, while Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta were up by less than 1% each. The divergence points to selective risk-taking rather than broad confidence in technology. These percentages are a published snapshot, not live prices at the report's publication minute; no current NQ futures price, VWAP, POC or support level is assumed.

NVIDIA — AN UNEXPECTED COMPANY-SPECIFIC RISK

Nvidia's board announced on 8 November that an independent committee, assisted by external counsel, would investigate reports that Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The company expressly stated that it had no reason to believe national-security interests or company secrets had been compromised, and that it retained confidence in its leadership. An investigation is not evidence that the reported allegations have been substantiated.

Nevertheless, the shares were indicated 4.5% lower before the opening on Monday. Nvidia's weight in major technology benchmarks, its position in the AI supply chain and investors' sensitivity to leadership uncertainty explain why the announcement matters to Nasdaq sentiment. The near-term market question is whether this reaction remains company-specific or weakens semiconductor participation more broadly.

AI INVESTMENT — DEMAND, FINANCING AND RETURNS ARE DIFFERENT THINGS

The market is not simply deciding whether artificial intelligence will expand. Chip demand, cloud adoption and the installation of data centres remain material sources of spending. Investors are increasingly reassessing how much of that spending is financed through corporate cash flow, debt, leasing arrangements or new equity, and when the resulting infrastructure may generate attractive financial returns.
An equipment supplier may recognise revenue as chips and networking systems are delivered. A data-centre operator must then recover construction, power, cooling, financing and operational costs over time. A hyperscaler may have ample liquidity but still face declining free cash flow during an exceptionally capital-intensive expansion phase. These businesses cannot be evaluated as if they possessed identical financial characteristics.
The October correction has made the distinction more visible. This week's earnings will test whether revenues and contractual demand can support the costs of the build-out, rather than simply confirming that companies are spending more on AI.

COREWEAVE — TUESDAY'S DIRECT TEST OF AI FINANCING

CoreWeave is scheduled to report on Tuesday, 10 November, after the US cash close, with its earnings call at 23:00 Switzerland. It provides access to AI computing capacity and is therefore exposed to both strong demand and the financial consequences of extensive infrastructure investment. Its previous quarter generated around $2.58 billion in revenue, more than double a year earlier, but investors remain focused on debt, cash generation and the cost of increasing capacity.

The key disclosures will be revenue growth, remaining performance obligations, capital expenditure, customer concentration, project timing, borrowing costs and management guidance. A large revenue increase alone may not settle the question of financing sustainability. The report could influence other data-centre operators and the wider technology sector outside regular cash-market hours.

CISCO AND APPLIED MATERIALS — THURSDAY'S SUPPLY-CHAIN TESTS

Cisco and Applied Materials are scheduled to report on Thursday, 12 November, after the US market closes. Both have management calls planned for 22:30 Switzerland. Cisco's networking products can offer evidence about the scale and timing of infrastructure orders. Applied Materials, a supplier of semiconductor manufacturing equipment, can provide information on chipmakers' investment plans and the capacity expansion pipeline.

For Cisco, relevant variables include orders, revenue guidance, margins and the contribution of AI networking demand. For Applied Materials, semiconductor equipment demand, foundry and memory investment, customer spending priorities and forward guidance are especially important. Strong results from either company would be informative, but neither alone could guarantee an NQ rebound.

ASIA — A RELIEF RALLY WITH MIXED REGIONAL CONFIRMATION

Taiwan's Taiex rose approximately 4.9% and Japan's Nikkei gained about 2.3% on Monday, following heavy losses the previous week. The Korean Kospi was weaker in an Associated Press observation, declining approximately 0.8%. Europe began the day with modest equity gains. The rebound suggests that some investors are returning to previously sold technology exposure, but it is not uniform across regional markets.

For NQ, the most useful question is whether that improvement carries into US semiconductor trading. Different market structures, currencies and company weights prevent Asian percentage changes from acting as automatic indicators for the Nasdaq's next move.

OIL — IMMEDIATE RELIEF, CONTINUING GEOPOLITICAL UNCERTAINTY

Brent crude declined around 2% to $96.29 a barrel in a Reuters global-market observation. President Trump said further US attacks on Iran were unlikely while diplomatic negotiations continued to make progress. Lower crude prices may moderate near-term inflation pressure and operating costs, but the underlying geopolitical situation and energy-supply risks remain unresolved.

Power availability and electricity costs are especially relevant to data-centre economics. Even sustained oil relief would not, by itself, resolve grid-connection constraints, construction schedules or corporate financing requirements. Energy should be monitored as one component of the week's financial backdrop, not as a single-factor prediction of NQ direction.

TREASURIES AND THE FEDERAL RESERVE — THE RATES RISK IS BACK

The US Treasury's official par-yield curve for Friday, 6 November, recorded the 2-year yield at 4.51%, the 5-year at 4.64%, the 10-year at 4.86% and the 30-year at 5.26%. These are previous-session reference values, not synchronised Monday quotations. A separate Monday market observation put the 10-year close to 4.87%.

October nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000, well above the roughly 65,000 expected, while unemployment fell to 4.1%. After the report, market pricing for a 25-basis-point December Fed rate increase moved towards 80%. That is an implied market probability at the time of observation, not a policy decision or a reliable forecast. The Fed's next decision is scheduled for 9 December.

For NQ, the key relationship is not merely whether Treasury yields rise or fall. It is whether the reason for the move improves the outlook for corporate earnings and financing. Lower yields driven by declining inflation expectations differ from lower yields driven by defensive demand. Company borrowing spreads can also move independently from government yields.

DOLLAR AND CROSS-ASSET CONDITIONS

Reuters reported the dollar index around 101.88, down approximately 0.3%, in a Monday global-market observation after Friday's sharp advance. Currency moves reflect differences in monetary expectations, capital flows and demand for defensive assets. They do not give a reliable stand-alone signal for the next NQ movement.

Bitcoin and other risk-sensitive assets have also been volatile following the technology correction and the US elections. Their performance may provide context for overall risk appetite, but it should not replace direct observation of Nasdaq liquidity, semiconductor participation and equity breadth.

THE WEEK'S CENTRAL EVENT — OCTOBER CPI ON TUESDAY

TUESDAY, 10 NOVEMBER | 14:30 SWITZERLAND | 07:30 CME/CHICAGO | 08:30 NEW YORK.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release the October Consumer Price Index and Real Earnings. A Federal Home Loan Bank of New York survey snapshot lists consensus for headline CPI near +0.3% month on month, against September's +0.6%, and core CPI near +0.2%, against the previous +0.3%. Consensus values may change and should not be confused with results. September headline inflation was 3.7% year on year.

The composition will matter: shelter, energy, services and core inflation can produce different implications even when the headline matches expectations. A softer release could reduce some concern about December tightening; a stronger release could reinforce it. The actual response of Treasury yields and technology shares will be more informative than assuming either release must generate a specific index direction.

WEDNESDAY — VETERANS DAY CHANGES THE BOND-MARKET ENVIRONMENT

WEDNESDAY, 11 NOVEMBER.

US equity markets are scheduled to remain open, but SIFMA recommends a full closure for dollar-denominated US fixed-income trading in observance of Veterans Day. Some Treasury-related reference markets will therefore have different liquidity and publication schedules. NQ and equity traders should not treat Wednesday as an ordinary day for reading cross-market confirmation from cash Treasury trading. Consult the relevant futures exchange's contract-specific holiday schedule for execution hours.

THURSDAY — CLAIMS, HOUSING AND TECHNOLOGY EARNINGS

THURSDAY, 12 NOVEMBER | 14:30 SWITZERLAND: INITIAL AND CONTINUING JOBLESS CLAIMS.

THURSDAY, 12 NOVEMBER | 16:00 SWITZERLAND: EXISTING HOME SALES.
THURSDAY, 12 NOVEMBER | AFTER 22:00 SWITZERLAND: CISCO AND APPLIED MATERIALS RESULTS; CALLS EXPECTED AT 22:30.
Claims provide fresh evidence on layoffs and continued unemployment; housing is sensitive to financing costs. Neither is a direct measurement of NQ earnings, but surprises can affect rate expectations and broader risk appetite. The corporate reports may have more direct consequences for networking, semiconductors and the AI supply chain.
FRIDAY — OCTOBER PPI AND COST PRESSURE

FRIDAY, 13 NOVEMBER | 14:30 SWITZERLAND | 07:30 CME/CHICAGO | 08:30 NEW YORK.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics will publish October Producer Price Index data. A Federal Home Loan Bank of New York survey snapshot shows consensus near +0.4% month on month for headline PPI, following +1.3% in September, and about +0.3% for the index excluding food and energy, following +0.7%. These are forecasts, not released results.

The report will offer additional evidence on producer costs after the CPI release. Together, Tuesday's CPI and Friday's PPI can materially alter the market's assessment of inflation persistence and monetary policy. Cost pressure in goods, energy and services should be analysed separately instead of treating one headline number as a complete description of inflation.

TODAY'S CALENDAR — MONDAY, 9 NOVEMBER, SWISS TIME

15:30 — US cash equities open.

16:00 — September US Wholesale Trade data.

17:00 — New York Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations, October; the one-year inflation-expectations reading was 3.9% previously.
19:00 — US Treasury three-year note auction.

22:00 — Regular US cash-market close.
After the close — Take-Two and selected other companies report; Constellation Energy is among the day's relevant earnings releases for energy supply and data-centre demand.

Monday's economic calendar is relatively light compared with Tuesday and Friday. Nevertheless, the market has a significant pre-opening company-specific catalyst in Nvidia and remains sensitive to positioning after last week's sharp correction.
WEEKLY EXPECTATION — BASE CASE

The base case is a fragile and uneven attempt at stabilisation, punctuated by substantial event risk. Investors have demonstrated a willingness to buy some beaten-down AI shares, but they have not yet restored uniform technology leadership. Nvidia's pre-market decline, a roughly 80% market-implied probability of a December rate increase and this week's inflation releases make an uncomplicated risk-on recovery difficult to assume.

A possible pattern is alternating directional impulses around major data and earnings, separated by periods of indecision. This is a description of conditions that could develop, not a forecast that the market must trade in a range or follow a particular intraday path.

BULLISH SCENARIO — CONDITIONS FOR BROADER RECOVERY
Inflation comes in sufficiently moderate to ease expectations of additional tightening; semiconductor losses stabilise beyond an isolated rebound; Nvidia-specific uncertainty remains contained; and CoreWeave, Cisco or Applied Materials provide reassuring evidence on demand, margins and financing. The strongest confirmation would be a broadening in Nasdaq participation and more durable NQ performance relative to ES. A decline in yields would be more supportive if it accompanied improving equity breadth rather than flight-to-safety demand.

BEARISH SCENARIO — CONDITIONS FOR RENEWED SELLING
Inflation proves persistent or broad, increasing the expected cost of capital; Nvidia's problems spread into sector sentiment; AI infrastructure results raise further concerns about debt, capital expenditure or delayed returns; and Nasdaq breadth deteriorates. Under these conditions, rallies may remain vulnerable to selling and the correction could extend. A bearish macroeconomic assessment still does not determine the next minute of NQ trading.

ANALYTICAL EDGE

SELECTIVE EQUITY RECOVERY / CAUTIOUS TECHNOLOGY REGIME / HIGH CPI AND AI-EARNINGS SENSITIVITY. The evidence does not justify a statistically calibrated probability of the week's direction. Today's Dow-led futures strength and Nvidia weakness argue against treating the improvement as a confirmed Nasdaq-led recovery.

CURRENT REGIME

POST-CORRECTION BARGAIN HUNTING / NVIDIA LEADERSHIP UNCERTAINTY / AI INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCING REASSESSMENT / FED RATE-HIKE RISK / LOWER OIL / UPCOMING CPI AND PPI / SELECTIVE GLOBAL SEMICONDUCTOR PARTICIPATION.

OPERATIONAL CONCLUSION

The market's macroeconomic narrative is useful for assessing uncertainty and exposure, not for claiming advance knowledge of the next candle. For NQ and MNQ, the coming CPI release and company earnings create conditions in which price movement, trading costs and stop execution may differ from quieter sessions. Positions should remain governed by defined initial risk, size and maximum acceptable loss, regardless of conviction about an economic outcome. No unverified levels or trade signals are presented here.

text:
Noctis had read his fair share of peculiar stories throughout his years of existence. Transmigration, reincarnation, soul swapping, the sort of fantastical concepts he would usually dismiss with mild amusement, finding them far too absurd to be anything more than fictional entertainment. Yet, as he slowly regained consciousness, he began to wonder whether the universe had decided to play a rather cruel joke on him.

For starters, his body felt unusually heavy. His limbs were terribly short, his vision blurry, and the unfamiliar sensation of being unable to properly control his own movements was enough to make him frown. Except, the frown never quite formed. Instead, a rather pitiful whimper escaped his lips. He blinked for a few times before he came into a horrifying realisation.

He was a baby. An ordinary, few months old baby, judging by the inability to even sit upright without assistance. Surely, this was some elaborate dream. Perhaps he had fallen asleep while reading one of those transmigration novels and somehow found himself trapped in its ridiculous plot. Except, if that were the case, why on earth had he transmigrated into an infant instead of an adult? Had the universe run out of better options?

Before he could gather his thoughts, his surroundings offered another mystery. The room was enormous, furnished with elegant antique furniture, intricately embroidered curtains and an absurdly large cradle. Beyond it stood several maids dressed in elaborate European-style uniforms, moving about with the sort of grace and discipline one would expect from an aristocratic household. Everything, from the furnishings to the clothes, practically screamed wealth.

And then came the next problem.

The bedroom doors swung open, followed by the hurried footsteps of a rather cheerful looking man dressed in what appeared to be an outrageously expensive ensemble. His face lit up the moment he spotted the little figure in the cradle, and before Noctis could so much as process his arrival, the man was already scooping him into his arms, showering his cheeks with an alarming number of kisses. Apparently, this overly affectionate stranger was his father. More specifically, a duke.

As though waking up in an unfamiliar body was not troublesome enough, he had apparently been reborn into an aristocratic family, as their fifth child. The revelation only became more overwhelming when several other children and young adults began gathering around him, each wearing expressions ranging from curiosity to barely concealed amusement. Apparently, they were his older siblings, and they seemed rather entertained by the sight of their youngest brother.

Noctis stared at them, silently attempting to make sense of his new circumstances. Five children? A duke? A mansion full of maids? He had gone from being a 228 years old vampire to an infant who could not even hold his own head properly. He could already feel a headache forming.

If this was indeed transmigration, he sincerely hoped the author had at least been kind enough to provide him with a decent plot. Because, judging by the way his father was currently kissing his forehead for the third time, surviving this childhood was going to be considerably more difficult than surviving two centuries of vampiric existence.

text:
Somewhere right now, a dog is standing in a kitchen, staring at a freezer door like it owes him money.

Not hungry. Not thirsty. Not even hot. Just certain, with the full weight of his entire canine soul, that behind that door lives the greatest object in the known universe.

A frozen cube of water.

I want to talk about this, because I think we have been laughing at something that deserves more respect.

Dogs have lived beside us for somewhere between fifteen thousand and forty thousand years, depending on which researcher you ask and which skeleton they trust. In that time they have helped us hunt, herd, guard, haul, track and search. They have sat through our worst singing. They have forgiven every bath. They have waited at windows for people who were gone for eight hours and greeted them like they were back from war.

And after all of that history, after all of that evolution, after all of that devotion, a significant number of them will drop everything, including loyalty, dignity and dinner, for something that is going to be a puddle in four minutes.

That is either the funniest thing about dogs or the most honest thing about them. I have decided it is both.

There is a video I have been thinking about for days. I will not tell you what is in it beyond this: it is about dogs and ice, it is a lot of different dogs, and every one of them is operating at a level of commitment that most humans reserve for their wedding day or their last slice of pizza.

I am not going to describe it. Descriptions ruin it. What I want to do instead is explain why it hits the way it does, because I went down a rabbit hole and the rabbit hole turned out to be about something much bigger than frozen water.

Let me start with the part nobody asks about.

Why ice?

Not why dogs like cold. That one is easy. Why do dogs treat ice as if it were a different category of thing from water? Water sits in a bowl all day. It is free, it is always there, it is the same temperature as the room, and most dogs drink it with all the enthusiasm of a man reading terms and conditions.

Freeze that exact same water and you get a creature who will pace, whine, scheme, perform and negotiate.

Same molecules. Different universe.

The answer is that ice is not water to a dog. Ice is an event.

Think about what a cube actually offers a mouth that has spent its whole day on kibble and lukewarm bowl water. It is cold in a way that almost nothing else in a house is cold. It makes a sound when it moves. It cracks. It slides. It changes shape while you are holding it, which means it is, in some sense, alive. It tastes like almost nothing, and then suddenly like everything, because the cold wakes up every nerve on the tongue at once.

And it disappears. That last part matters more than you think. A toy is the same toy tomorrow. A cube is a story with a beginning, a middle and an end, all of it happening in the dog's own mouth.

There is a reason you cannot get bored of something that keeps ending.

Now, the sound.

If you have ever lived with one of these dogs, you already know what I am about to say. You can be in another room, asleep, with a fan running, and the second the ice maker drops a load into the tray, a dog materializes beside you. No footsteps. No warning. Just a sudden, expectant presence, like a very small bouncer who has heard the guest list change.

This is not magic. This is learning, and it is the oldest, cleanest kind.

More than a century ago, a Russian physiologist named Ivan Pavlov noticed that dogs began to salivate not only at food but at the things that reliably came before food. You know the bell. What people forget is why it matters: it showed that a dog's mind is constantly building a map of what predicts what. Footsteps predict a walk. Keys predict a car ride. A certain rustle predicts dinner.

Now look at a modern kitchen from the dog's point of view. The freezer door opens with a seal-breaking hiss. Then comes the clatter of cubes into a cup. Then the human walks over holding something that glitters.

That is not a kitchen. That is a perfectly designed training program, and the dog graduated years ago, with honors.

Here is the part that I think is genuinely clever, and I say that with respect for the dogs and zero respect for ourselves.

It does not work every time.

Sometimes the cup is for the human. Sometimes the cube lands on the floor. Sometimes the person just walks past with a sparkling water and the dog is left standing there, heart hammering, having prepared for a celebration that was not for him.

Psychologists have a name for what that does to behavior. When a reward arrives unpredictably, the habit becomes harder to extinguish, not easier. It is the same principle that keeps people at slot machines. A guaranteed reward gets boring. A maybe gets under the skin.

So every time you have ever given a dog a cube on a whim and ignored the next ten requests, you have not taught patience. You have built a gambler.

I know that sounds harsh. I am saying it with love. I am one of the people who built one.

Which brings us to something I think is the most overlooked fact in this entire conversation.

Every ice-obsessed dog has a patient zero.

There was a first cube. There was a hot day, or a dropped piece, or a clumsy moment at the fridge door, and a dog who had never given it a second thought suddenly had something cold slide across a kitchen floor. And the dog did what dogs do with everything that moves. He chased it. He pinned it. He tasted it. And then the cube did something no toy has ever done: it vanished into a little wet nothing, and he had to find another one.

From that second on, the human was the supplier.

Nobody planned it. Nobody ever does. That is how every great obsession starts, in a kitchen, by accident, with someone saying "oh, here you go" in a tired voice.

And you know what is strange? Almost nobody regrets it.

Ask someone with one of these dogs and they will tell you, a little sheepishly, that they now keep ice on purpose. That the ice bin is a shared household resource. That there is a whole negotiation, a whole language, a whole tiny economy of who gets what, when, and how many. You do not get that with a bag of treats. A treat is food. A cube is a ceremony.

I have thought a lot about the word "ceremony" here, and I do not think it is an exaggeration.

A dog's life is repetitive by design. Same walks, same bowls, same couch, same hours. Predictability is their comfort, but it is also their ceiling. So when something small and strange enters that routine, something that crackles, shines, escapes, and tastes like winter, they do not treat it as a snack.

They treat it as the best part of the day.

And honestly? They might be right.

There is a theory I keep coming back to. Dogs are not simple. They are focused. A dog does not carry a mortgage, an inbox or a group chat. When a dog wants something, the want is total, undivided, frictionless, and entirely visible on the outside. There is no filter between desire and body.

When you watch a person want something that badly, you see strain. When you watch a dog want something that badly, you see joy.

That difference is the whole reason this kind of video travels.

Neuroscientists have actually studied it, in a way. A researcher named Gregory Berns trained dogs to lie still in an fMRI scanner, awake and willing, so he could watch what their brains did when they anticipated something good. The finding that stuck with a lot of people was that the reward centers lit up in response to cues for things the dogs loved. In other words, the anticipation was not an afterthought. It was a feeling in its own right.

I think about that when a dog hears the ice maker. The cube is not even in the room yet, and already the best part has begun.

Let me slow down and say something sensible, because a post this long should earn some trust.

Ice is not a medical tool, and it is not a substitute for water. Most vets are comfortable with plain ice cubes as an occasional treat for most healthy dogs, but there are real caveats. Small dogs can choke on large cubes. Powerful chewers can crack a tooth on something rock-hard, and a fractured tooth is a miserable, expensive way to learn that lesson. A dog that gulps a huge amount of very cold water at once can end up with an upset stomach.

And if a dog is genuinely overheating, with heavy panting that will not settle, drooling, weakness, wobbling, a bright red tongue, that is not an ice cube situation. That is an emergency, and the answer is cool water, shade, and a call to a vet, immediately.

I mention it because the joy on display in these clips is real, and the joy is only worth celebrating when the dog is safe. Love is allowed to be funny and careful at the same time.

Okay. Back to the good part.

Because there is a thing that happens when a dog meets ice that I have never been able to shake, and I think it is the real reason you will keep watching.

Dogs cool themselves differently from us. We sweat across most of our skin. A dog mostly pants, moving air over a wet tongue and the lining of the mouth, with a little help from the pads of the paws and the nose. A summer day is not an inconvenience to a dog. It is a negotiation with physics.

So a cold object, for a dog, is not a luxury. It is relief with a taste.

You can see it, if you know where to look. The body language of a dog that has just discovered something cold on a hot day is not the body language of a dog that got a treat. It is looser. Slower. Almost grateful. It is the posture of someone who has just been handed a glass of water in the desert.

And yet, if that were the whole story, you would only see it in July.

You do not. You see it in cold months, in kitchens with the heat on, in dogs who are not hot at all. Which means temperature cannot be the whole explanation. Something else is going on, and I think it is this:

Dogs love anything that reacts.

A ball does not react. A bone does not react. A cube reacts to everything. It skids when you paw it. It chatters when you drop it. It leaves a trail. It melts where you hold it. It changes under your tongue. A dog can spend ten minutes with a single piece of ice and feel, honestly, like it is in conversation with it.

That is what a good toy is, whether it is designed or found.

Something that answers back.

Here is where the comedy comes in, and I want to be precise about it, because comedy has rules.

Things are funny when the size of the feeling does not match the size of the object. A grown man furious at a parking meter is funny. A toddler weeping at a banana that broke in half is funny. A dog that has decided, with the force of a thousand generations, that a piece of frozen water is the thing it was born for is funny.

But look at what is actually happening. The mismatch is not the dog being silly. The mismatch is us. We have forgotten how to be that excited about something that small.

I think about the last time I wanted something as simply as that. No strategy. No guilt. No "I should not." Just a pure, uncomplicated yes.

I could not tell you the date.

And I suspect, if I am being honest, that is why these videos are not really about dogs at all. They are about a version of happiness that adults quietly stopped believing was allowed.

It costs nothing. It is available in nearly every home on earth. It requires no talent, no luck, no preparation. It just requires a living thing that has not yet learned to be embarrassed by delight.

We buy these dogs sleek toys that cost more than my first car. We stock shelves with enrichment puzzles, snuffle mats, elk antlers, treats shaped like tiny steaks. And all along the real prize was in the freezer door, next to a tray of peas.

There is a kind of poetry in that. A dog does not know what anything costs.

He only knows what it does.

Let me tell you what I noticed about the ones who love it most.

They are not the same. That is the thing that surprised me. Different sizes, different breeds, different ages, different houses with different counters and different floors. If this were a quirk of a single animal, I would shrug.

It is not. It is a pattern. The obsession shows up in very different dogs, in very different kitchens, and it looks nearly identical every time.

The same stillness before the sound. The same slight tilt of the head. The same ridiculous, shaking, full-body anticipation. And then, after, the same expression, which I can only describe as the face of someone who has gotten away with something.

There is a word in behavioral science for a shared, repeating pattern across individuals: a species-typical behavior. But I do not think the scientific term does it justice here. I would call it a language. A small, unspoken, global dog dialect whose single word is "cold."

And the people at the other end of the language, the ones holding the cup, they have learned to speak it back.

Have you noticed how the humans in these situations never seem annoyed?

Think about it. Here is a creature that has interrupted a meal, a phone call, a nap, a film, with a stare so intense you can feel it on the back of your neck. And the person does not scold. The person sighs, smiles, stands up, and says something like "okay, okay, fine."

That "fine" is the sound of a human being delighted to be manipulated.

I think that is the second half of the story, the part the clips only hint at. This is not a story about a dog getting what he wants. It is a story about a household that has quietly reorganized itself around the happiness of one small animal, and finds the arrangement worth it.

Every home with one of these dogs has the same invisible rule. If the dog is thrilled, the day is a little better. Nobody wrote it down. Everybody follows it.

So here is the question I cannot put down.

What, exactly, is a dog feeling in that moment?

I want to be careful, because the honest answer is that nobody knows. We can measure heart rate, posture, brain activity, saliva, cortisol. We can run a scanner and watch a reward system light up. What we cannot do is step inside the experience and tell you what it is like to be a dog who has just heard the sound.

Anyone who tells you with total confidence that they know is selling something.

But we are not completely in the dark either. We know dogs are capable of anticipation. We know they can be frustrated, and we know they can be thrilled. We know that when a dog has a strong positive association, its whole body tells the truth about it, from the ears to the tail to the way the back legs cannot quite stay on the floor.

We know, in short, that something is happening in there. Something big. Something that looks a great deal like joy.

And maybe that is enough. You do not need to prove what a dog thinks to know that watching one come alive is good for you.

Let me add a layer that most people skip.

The ice obsession is, quietly, one of the best demonstrations of how dogs learn from us rather than just about us.

A dog does not wake up one day and decide that a refrigerator is interesting. A dog learns, over many repetitions, that when a certain human stands in a certain place and makes a certain sound, something good tends to follow. Over time, the dog starts paying attention to us as the source of the thing. The cube is the reward. The person is the doorway.

That is a profound kind of trust, if you think about it. A dog that waits at the fridge is not waiting for ice. It is waiting for you to be the person who opens the door.

Every time you do, the relationship gets a little stronger. Every time you do not, the dog stays hopeful anyway.

I have no idea how to feel about that, except humbled.

Now let me do something a little unfashionable and defend the dogs against the idea that they are just being greedy.

Greed is wanting more than you need, and taking it from someone else. What you see in these dogs is almost the opposite. They are not hoarding. They are not guarding. They are asking, in a very visible way, and then enjoying, in a very visible way, with a transparency that humans find nearly impossible.

When was the last time you asked for something you wanted that openly? With your entire body? Without rehearsing a speech in your head first?

Dogs are not greedy. Dogs are honest about wanting.

And honestly, the world might be a little kinder if more of us were.

There is a funny thing about internet culture that I have been watching for a long time. The clips that spread furthest are rarely the dramatic ones. They are the ones that make a stranger on the other side of the world feel, for a few seconds, like they know exactly what is going on.

When someone sends one of these videos to a friend, the message is almost never "look at this dog." It is "this is yours." Or "this is mine." Or "this is us."

Because everybody who has ever loved a dog has one thing their dog is irrationally devoted to. A specific ball. A particular sock. A rumpled blanket. A neighbor's cat. A single tree in a single park. A word, a sound, a snack, a person.

For a lot of dogs, apparently, it is ice.

So what is yours?

I mean that seriously. What is the small, ridiculous, unreasonable thing that your dog treats as sacred? And did you ever teach it to them, or did they find it, and you simply made the mistake of noticing?

I ask because the answer says something about the household. The thing a dog loves is often a reflection of what the home has quietly made possible: the heat of a long summer, a particular routine, a person who is too soft to say no.

Dogs hold up a mirror. The reflection is usually kinder than the one we expect.

Let me return, for a minute, to the dogs in this particular video, because I promised I would not describe it and I intend to keep that promise.

What I will tell you is how it made me feel, because that is the only honest report I can give.

I started watching with the half-attention that you give to anything in a feed. I expected to smile and keep scrolling. That is not what happened. I watched it again. Then I watched it a third time with the sound on, because I realized the sound was doing half the work. Then I sent it to two people, and both of them wrote back within a minute, one with a single word and one with a long string of laughing faces and an unprompted story about her own dog.

That is a reaction I cannot manufacture. I can only report it.

And I will say this much about the structure, because it is the part I find so quietly impressive. The clips are different, the dogs are different, the homes are different. But by the time you are a few seconds in, you stop thinking of them as different dogs at all. You start thinking of them as one dog. One enormous, scattered, multi-breed, multi-household dog, carrying a single enormous, very serious conviction.

It is the closest thing I have seen to a universal truth about the species, delivered with absolutely no ceremony.

If you only have time to watch one thing today, I will not pretend this is the most important thing you could do. But I will say that I have rarely watched anything that so reliably changed the temperature of my mood.

It is a very short trip to take, and you will come back lighter than you left.

There is one more angle, and it is the one that has stayed with me longest.

We live in an age that treats attention as a resource to be harvested. Everything we scroll was designed by someone, tested by someone, tuned to keep a thumb moving. Most of it succeeds, and most of it leaves us a little emptier than it found us.

Then a clip appears in which nobody is selling anything. No one is performing for a camera in the way a person performs. The star of the show has no idea there is an audience, no idea what a feed is, no idea that its private obsession is about to be seen by strangers on three continents. It is just a creature in a kitchen, in a yard, in a hallway, completely absorbed in a thing it loves.

That absorption is rare now. We can feel its absence in our own lives, and we recognize it instantly in someone else's.

I think that is what we are really hungry for when we watch videos like this. Not cuteness. Cuteness is easy. We are hungry for a person, or an animal, who is fully where they are.

A dog with a cube is fully where it is.

It is worth asking what that does to us when we watch. I do not believe it is only entertainment. I believe, a little, that it is a reminder. Not a lecture. Dogs are terrible lecturers. A reminder in the way that smelling cut grass reminds you of being nine years old.

There is a version of you that used to want things this simply. It did not leave. It is just quiet.

Now let me be fair to the skeptics, because every good argument deserves its opponents.

Some people will say this is only a funny clip, and that I am inflating it. They will say a dog likes ice for the same reason a dog likes everything: it is novel, it is cold, it is edible-ish, and it tastes like a treat. They will say that a long post about it is a waste of everyone's time.

They might be right. I will give them that.

But I would gently point out that the funniest and most revealing things about any species are almost never the grand gestures. They are the small, repeated, unnecessary ones. We learn more about a person from the way they treat a waiter than from their résumé. We learn more about dogs from what they do at the freezer door than from what they do in a trial.

The ordinary is where character lives.

And if what character looks like, in a dog, is an unembarrassed, wholehearted, shaking-tail commitment to a frozen cube, then I think that tells us something rather good about the species.

Here is another thing worth sitting with.

Humans have domesticated an enormous number of animals. Very few of them have developed the habit of looking up at us with an expectation of delight. Cows do not. Chickens do not. Horses might, in their way, but their way is considerably more aristocratic.

Dogs are different, and they are different in a way that has to be partly learned. They look at us as if we were the weather, the sun, the possibility of something wonderful. And what do we do with all that hope? Very often, we hand them something small and cold and watch them lose their minds.

It is an exchange so lopsided, and so happy, that it should probably be studied by economists.

You put in a few seconds of your time and a few drops of water. You get back, in return, a living creature's undisguised celebration.

If you could invest in anything at that rate of return, you would.

One last detail, because it is the one I find most moving: the wait.

Watch any dog in the seconds before a cube arrives and you are watching hope in its purest form. There is no guarantee and no contract, only a history of good things and a belief, built from that history, that another one is coming. People spend years learning to hope like that. A dog does it on kitchen tile, on four legs, with no vocabulary, in under three seconds.

Maybe that is the real trick of the whole thing. Not that dogs love ice, but that they know how to wait for what they love without ever deciding it will not come.

Let me give you a few questions to carry with you, because I think good posts leave something behind.

What is the smallest thing that has ever made you feel completely, unreasonably happy, and when did you last give yourself permission to want it that much?

Who in your life is the dog at the freezer door, the one who is delighted by things you have stopped noticing, and are you taking enough time to be delighted with them?

And what would change in your own days if you treated one ordinary object, one cup of coffee, one cold drink, one quiet hour, with the full seriousness a dog gives a cube of ice?

I do not have answers. I only know the questions get louder when you watch. Mine have been loud for days on end.

So.

If you have a dog, you already know why you will watch this, and you probably already know which dog in your life it will remind you of. If you do not have a dog, I will not pretend it will convert you, but I will say it will leave you a little more tempted.

If you grew up with a dog and lost them, I will warn you gently that this one may arrive with a lump in the throat, the good kind, the kind that comes from remembering exactly how much joy one small animal could carry into a room.

And if you are having one of those weeks where everything is heavy, where the news is loud and the inbox is endless and nothing seems to fit, I would ask you for just a little while to borrow the dogs' sense of priorities.

Forget the inbox. Forget the news. Forget, for a minute, the whole grown-up machinery of being tired.

Someone, somewhere, is standing at a freezer door.

They are not asking for much. They have never asked for much.

They are just waiting for you to open it.

Watch the video.

text:
Today in History 
November 9th
1922
Born on this Day
Dorothy Jean Dandridge was born on November 9, 1922, in Cleveland, Ohio. She was a groundbreaking American actress, singer, and dancer who became one of Hollywood’s most celebrated African American stars. Renowned for her beauty, elegance, and extraordinary talent, Dandridge challenged racial barriers in an entertainment industry that offered limited opportunities to Black performers.

Raised by her mother, Ruby Dandridge, an actress and entertainer, Dorothy began performing at an early age alongside her older sister, Vivian. The sisters formed a singing and dancing act known as the Wonder Children, later performing as part of the Dandridge Sisters. Their performances took them to prestigious venues, including the Cotton Club in Harlem, where Dorothy developed the stage presence that would define her career.

Dandridge made early film appearances during the 1930s and 1940s, often receiving minor roles because of Hollywood’s racial discrimination. Despite these obstacles, she gained recognition as a nightclub singer, captivating audiences with her sophisticated performances and powerful voice.

Her breakthrough came in 1954 when she starred in Otto Preminger’s Carmen Jones, portraying a passionate and independent woman opposite Harry Belafonte. Her remarkable performance earned her an Academy Award nomination for Best Actress, making her the first African American woman nominated in that category. This historic achievement established Dandridge as an international star and a trailblazer for future generations of Black actresses.

In 1959, she starred alongside Sidney Poitier in Porgy and Bess, portraying Bess in the film adaptation of George Gershwin’s celebrated opera. Her performance earned her a Golden Globe nomination and further demonstrated her dramatic range.

Despite her success, Dandridge struggled against racism, restrictive Hollywood casting practices, financial difficulties, and personal heartbreak. She married dancer Harold Nicholas in 1942, and they had a daughter, Harolyn, who was born with significant developmental disabilities. The marriage ended in divorce in 1951. Her second marriage, to businessman Jack Denison in 1959, also ended in divorce.

Throughout her career, Dandridge fought to be recognized as a serious actress rather than confined to stereotypical roles. Her determination helped open doors for African American women in film, even as discrimination continued to limit her own opportunities.

On September 8, 1965, Dorothy Dandridge died in Los Angeles, California, at just 42 years old. Her death was attributed to an accidental overdose of the antidepressant imipramine.

Although her life ended tragically, her legacy remains extraordinary. In 1999, Halle Berry portrayed her in the acclaimed television film Introducing Dorothy Dandridge, introducing her remarkable story to a new generation.

Dorothy Dandridge is remembered not only as a glamorous Hollywood icon but also as a courageous pioneer who broke racial barriers, challenged discrimination, and helped transform the possibilities for Black women in American cinema. #OTD

text:
My 23-year-old daughter told me she had a man in her life, but they weren't boyfriend and girlfriend.

I looked at her.

ME: "So what exactly are you people?"

DAUGHTER: "Mummy, we're exclusive, but we haven't put a name to it."

ME: "Exclusive? Meaning he doesn't date other women?"

DAUGHTER: "Yes."

ME: "And you don't date other men?"

DAUGHTER: "Of course."

ME: "Does he take care of you?"

DAUGHTER: "Sometimes."

ME: "Does he introduce you as his girlfriend?"

She laughed.

DAUGHTER: "Mummy, you people like titles too much."

I dropped my spoon.

ME: "My dear, if he doesn't want another man to have you, why is he afraid to call you his woman?"

She went quiet.

Then she said something that surprised me.

DAUGHTER: "Mummy, what if I ask him and he says he's not ready?"

I looked at her and smiled.

ME: "Then at least you'll know where you stand instead of spending your life guessing."

She shook her head and went to her room.

I thought that was the end of the conversation.

Until three days later, when she came home crying.

The problem: Punjab's dairy farmers produce milk that is vulnerable to adulteration and feed contamination. The existing testing infrastructure is centralized. A farmer in Faridkot must travel to Ludhiana to get a sample tested. The cost of travel and the time lost often exceeds the value of the test. The result is a quality-verification gap that punishes honest farmers and rewards adulterators.

The solution: Guru Angad Dev Veterinary and Animal Sciences University (GADVASU) has secured a ₹1.55 crore CSR grant from Kemin Industries South Asia to deploy a state-of-the-art Mobile Feed and Milk Testing Laboratory (MFML). (The Tribune, 12 Jun 2026)

The scope: Free testing of milk, cattle feed, fodder, and silage. Detection of milk adulteration. Screening for aflatoxins, toxic substances in animal feed that can enter the milk supply chain. (Times of India, 25 Oct 2026)

The operational plan, the implementation timeline, and the stated goals are now on the record.

🛠️ 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗢𝗣𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗔𝗟 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞𝗜𝗡𝗚

The mobile laboratory is not a van with a testing kit. It is a fully equipped laboratory-on-wheels. The university has procured the vehicle and is currently undertaking fabrication to install the laboratory facilities. (Times of India, 25 Oct 2026)

The testing protocol is designed for speed and accessibility. Farmers bring milk or feed samples to the mobile unit at a designated location. The sample is tested on-site. The results are generated. The farmer receives a scientific assessment of their product without paying a fee.

The testing menu is specific:
• Milk quality and adulteration: Detection of common adulterants to ensure the milk entering the supply chain is safe. (Dairy Dimension, 26 Oct 2026)
• Aflatoxin screening: Identification of toxic substances in animal feed that can affect livestock and contaminate milk. (Times of India, 25 Oct 2026)
• Feed, fodder, and silage analysis: Assessment of nutritional deficiencies to help farmers improve feeding practices. (GADVASU, 2026)

The outreach strategy is decentralized. The mobile lab will be stationed at university campuses, Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs), and other government locations. The target coverage includes the central, south-western, and Kandi regions of Punjab. (Dairy Dimension, 26 Oct 2026)

The advisory layer is integrated. The lab will offer ration formulation services and farmer awareness programmes on feed safety, mastitis prevention, and silage management. (The Tribune, 12 Jun 2026)

📅 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗧𝗜𝗠𝗘𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗘 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗚𝗢𝗔𝗟𝗦

The grant was secured in June 2026. The vehicle has been procured and fabrication is underway. The launch is scheduled for January 2027. (Times of India, 25 Oct 2026)

The first-phase goal is operational proof. A single mobile lab covering three regions, serving farmers at KVK and government locations, with free testing and advisory services.

The expansion goal is explicit. If the project succeeds, GADVASU and Kemin Industries plan to introduce additional mobile laboratories, with the long-term objective of covering all districts of Punjab. (The Tribune, 12 Jun 2026)

RT @velitesgear | Full Text Article: https://t.co/4mVujombEt | Author: @Helionbooks "From the Hindenburg to the Hermann 

By Dr Bill Mitchinson

As many readers will know, in the weeks following the stunning victory at Amiens in August 1918, the Allied armies struck further massive blows against the increasingly demoralised German forces. The Allies were able to keep the withdrawing enemy off balance by the use of deception, surprise and swift concentration of force. They applied overwhelming fire power and a developing doctrine for open warfare, and possessed confidence in a system of sustainment capable of delivering men, munitions and provisions to a fluid front. When the momentum of one offensive waned, tempo was maintained by launching another in a different sector. Progress in terms of mileage gained was not always substantial but by continuously tying down German forces and limiting Ludendorff’s ability to move his ever-diminishing reserves, the Allied advance was becoming inexorable. The successes came, however, at considerable cost.

An earlier volume, The Battles for the Wastelands, explained how in August and September 1918 British Third and Fourth Armies fought their way eastwards to retake the devastated areas lost during the German Spring Offensive. The old Somme battlefields were recaptured as were the sectors taken during the Advance to the Hindenburg Line in the dreadful spring of 1917. On 2 September the Canadian Corps of First Army, assisted by the operations of Third and Fourth Armies to its south, carried the formidable Drocourt-Quéant Line and continued its advance towards Cambrai. By mid-September Third and Fourth Armies were again in front of the daunting Hindenburg system and in positions close to those they had occupied on 21 March 1918. These defences comprised a successive series of trench lines stretching back in places to a depth of 12 miles. During the course of four days later in the month the foremost defensive lines were to be broken. Once clear of the Masnières -Beaurevoir Line the advance continued across unbroken ground towards the river Selle.

The series of attacks on the Hindenburg Main and Support Lines, or what the Germans termed the Siegfriedstellung, were to be staggered over a period that stretched from 27 September to 12 October. These 16 days embraced what later became known officially as the Battle of the Canal du Nord, the Battle of the St Quentin Canal, the Battle of Beaurevoir, and the Battle of Cambrai, 1918. The final phase of the combined operations is known as the Pursuit to the Selle. Once the river was reached, the Germans were expected to make a stand. While First and Second Armies, together with the French and Americans, continued their coordinated offensives elsewhere, Third and Fourth Armies were compelled to instigate an operational pause. Preparations were begun for a set-piece offensive which was scheduled to commence on or around 17 October.

The assaults on the Hindenburg Main Line in late September have been well described in other volumes. These illustrate the thorough preparation, the evolving tactical doctrine, and the means of sustaining crushing fire power which by that stage of the war characterised the British armies’ operations. What is less widely known is what happened during the next phase of the advance. The area under discussion in this volume lies roughly between the rivers Escaut and Selle. During the war the Escaut and its associated nearby canal were, and still are today, known by different names. The canal can be referred to as both the Canal de L’Escaut and also as the Canal de St Quentin. Some trench maps and contemporary accounts and reports refer to it as the Schelde Canal.

In late September and October 1918 the boundaries of Third and Fourth British Armies, which in total comprised seven corps, ran from a little west of Cambrai and then, from the eastern side of the city, along the modern D114 to Saulzoir. In the south from a few miles north of St Quentin it essentially followed today’s D8 to the vicinity of Vaux Andigny. This arable, undulating land was crossed by the defensive lines which lay behind the Hindenburg Main System. They are sometimes referred to by different names but for the purposes of this guide they will be known as the Hindenburg Support Line, the Marquion-Cantaing Line, the Marcoing Line, the Le Catelet-Nauroy Line, the Masnières-Beaurevoir Line, and the Fonsomme Line. Although not as formidable as the Hindenburg Main Line all of these defensive systems had, to varying degrees, sections of well-developed trench networks protected by wide swathes of barbed wire and concrete pill boxes housing multiple machine guns. Observation and command posts were connected by buried telephone cable to supporting artillery. Once clear of the Beaurevoir trenches and strong points, and until they approached the Selle, British, American, and Australian forces had the opportunity to advance through still undamaged villages and across partly cultivated terrain.

In the same way as its companion volume (a third is in preparation) the examination and description of the engagements together in one book accompanied by maps and photographs offers a pragmatic and practical touring alternative. The countryside is little changed from what it was in mid-1918. The villages and small towns have expanded but the fields are again verdant, the woods and copses re-grown, the farms re-established, and the roads largely follow their original course. There are also the mouldering remains of pill boxes. Traffic is infrequent and the farm lanes, field headlands, wind farm access points, pavé roads, and the former metre gauge railway tracks offer good off-road opportunities for gravel bikes. Allied cemeteries lie scattered across the landscape but many of them away from the 1914 battlefield are only infrequently visited by British and Australian travellers. The few visitors that do cross the area are often travelling from the Somme to Ors en route to visit the grave of Wilfred Owen.  It is a beautiful landscape to explore and, with the use of the maps and imagination, the work of Third and Fourth Armies on their way to final victory can be put into their wider operational context.

From the Hindenburg to the Hermann: British Third and Fourth Armies Operations; 27 September to 16 October 1918 is available to buy here.

text:
The other day I had a conversation with a hiring manager who told me, with deep concern, “It’s just so hard to find qualified candidates these days.”

I said, “Really? Let me see the job description.” Five minutes later, I understood the problem. They weren’t hiring a person. They were trying to recruit a supernatural creature with a LinkedIn profile, a master’s degree, and a willingness to work for cake.

The position was listed as “Entry Level,” which apparently means you entered the workforce during the Clinton administration. Requirements included 15 years of experience with software released four years ago. I asked whether they were accepting applicants with time machines. She said, “We prefer candidates who can demonstrate initiative.” Fine. I’ll invent the software in 2008 and circle back. The ideal candidate needed to be a visionary leader, a humble team player, a strategic thinker, a hands on problem solver, and someone who “thrives in ambiguity.” Translation: nobody knows what this job is, but you’ll be blamed when it goes wrong. Ma’am, you’re advertising for an operations director, not a hat rack at Burlington.

Then came the responsibilities. Manage 12 departments. Lead global initiatives. Build the budget. Fix the printer. Bring innovative ideas to the table, but don’t question management. Be available nights and weekends while maintaining “excellent work life balance.” I guess the balance is that work gets your life and you get a branded water bottle.

The salary? “Competitive.” Competitive with what? A middle school lemonade stand? She explained they offered a dynamic compensation package. I asked whether the package contained actual money or just complimentary access to the office microwave. And the culture! “We’re a family here.” Of course you are. A family where Thanksgiving dinner is a performance review and Grandpa fires you because the mashed potatoes didn’t meet quarterly targets. Benefits included flexible hours, meaning you answer whenever they call. Even the desk plant resigned, citing unrealistic growth expectations and no PTO.

I asked how many interview rounds. “Just six, plus a case study, personality assessment, panel presentation, and a casual coffee chat with the CEO.” Casual? That’s not hiring. That’s an international adoption process with a background check conducted by the Avengers.

Finally, she sighed and said, “People just don’t want to work anymore.” I looked at the description again. You want a Harvard trained astronaut, a Navy SEAL, a therapist, an accountant, a software engineer, and a motivational speaker, all rolled into one person who will cheerfully accept $52,000 and bring their own laptop. I told her, “Your candidate exists. He’s called Batman. But he has better benefits, his own transportation, and even he doesn’t answer emails after Gotham closes.”

Maybe qualified candidates aren’t impossible to find. Maybe the unicorns read the job posting, saw the salary, and decided to remain mythical.

text:
Joe, I totally accept that comparing the raw ordination figures of an international priestly fraternity with those of an individual diocese would be statistically misleading. But surely that is an argument for using the correct statistical measures, rather than dismissing the phenomenon altogether?

What we ought to examine is the number of vocations relative to the population from which they emerge, ideally adjusted for age and religious practice. Consider the Diocese of Lincoln, Nebraska. According to the 2025 Official Catholic Directory, it has one diocesan seminarian for every 2,007 Catholics, compared with a US diocesan median of one for every 14,671. That is a vocational rate more than seven times the median, and importantly, those figures exclude the FSSP seminarians studying in Lincoln. The FSSP itself ordained 25 priests in 2026, substantially above its recent annual average. That represents real vocational fruit, whatever the geographical distribution of its congregations.

You may be right that self-selection plays a part, but that raises another fascinating question: why are young men selecting these communities in the first place?

My argument isn't that every diocese should become the FSSP, or even that the traditional liturgy is the sole explanation. It is that communities characterised by liturgical seriousness, doctrinal clarity, a strong priestly identity and confidence in the supernatural seem to offer something that attracts vocations (I mean it seems blindingly obvious to me). Surely, when so much of the Church is preoccupied with managing priestly decline, we should be curious enough to investigate what these flourishing communities are getting right?

text:
THREE AND A HALF STEPS TO DEATH

The following text was dictated by Billy Vickers to Hank Skinner, another death-row inmate, after he survived an execution date on December 9, 2003 at "The Walls" Unit, in Huntsville, Texas. 

Billy waited until midnight (when the death warrant expires) in a death-watch cell next to the execution chamber. Billy Vickers wanted to share his experience with as many as possible. Billy and Hank Skinner were in cells next to each other, and Billy no longer had the strength to write. He asked Hank to transcribe their conversations about the last weeks of his life between two execution dates. Billy was executed on January 28, 2004." - DPN Editor

"It all started when I got "the date" in September. Up until then it was just something in the distance. Now it was all too real. It seemed like a giant weight descended onto my shoulders.

"Suddenly the calendar seemed bigger and every number on it had ominous portent. Every day, hour and minute that passed I kept having these recurring thoughts like "Well, I’ll probably never get to do (or: see, hear, say, read, etc.) this again.

"Everything seemed to take on this flavor of oppressive finality. My mind would run on and on and on for hours and hours. Every new day I woke up to the realization that it’s one less I’d be here.

"I remember sometimes thinking of people I’d known in the world who’d died horrible deaths and I found myself envious of them. For them, bad as it was, it was still over and done with in a few minutes/ moments. For me, it’s stretched out over eleven (11) years. It’s always been there (death). But now it’s right on top of me. Yet still days away. I couldn’t imagine how in the world I was going to survive it until the end, then laughed at myself for the insanity of that thought.

"On the day of execution I haven’t slept at all. I don’t seem to think cohesively for any length of time at all. It seems like an eternity, yet I keep wondering where the time went. Then the regrets start in, as I’m mostly thinking of my family and how this is hurting them. I keep thinking about things I should’ve said to my family but forgot. Things I should’ve written. But now it’s too late. It seemed time kept growing less and less, as I visit with them and tell them over and over that I love them and goodbye.

"The next think I know I’m being shackled and loaded in the van and it’s too late to say anything. All those thoughts and regrets are repeated over and over in my mind during all those hours I sat in the death house waiting to die at any time.

"In the death house, I keep thinking of my family. I pray for some way to release them from the pain and torment, for me to just go on and handle this alone, as my problem, to face it. Then I caught myself thinking of the thoughts I had during the ride to Huntsville, with my senses heightened to the point of being painful. I hear the van tires on the pavement as a rushing noise in my ears with every car, tree, building or house we passed I thought, "Well, I’ll never see that again".

"Then, I start to hear every beat of my heart as if I’m holding it up to my ear. But at the same time, it really hurts and I can’t figure out how it can keep beating and beating that hard.

"Then my thoughts are broken when the warden comes into the death house to tell me what will be taking place when the time comes. He points to a door I can see from my cell and tells me behind that door is the execution chamber. When the time comes they will come and get me. If I can’t walk, they will carry me, but either way I’m going. He tells me the chaplain will be here soon.

"The chaplain comes and tells me, while I’m on the gurney he will be there holding my ankle to offer comfort.

"As these people talk to me, I know they’re people, but at the same time I think of them as something else or, in a bad way. As these thoughts just seem to hang there and it seems to be getting dark but it’s the middle of the day and there’s lights everywhere. Then I see the door that the ambulance will back up to, to pick up my body and that’s when it strikes me all over again, "this is it". There’s no way to describe the pressure I feel as I pray they’ll hurry up and get it over with.

"Every time the walkie-talkie bursts to life, a door slams, the phone rings, I nearly jump out of my skin. This is almost constant for six (6) hours. The chaplain tells me that if I hear rustling and movement in the back, he says It’s just the execution team getting ready and for me not to be "alarmed", (they’re just coming to kill you. Don’t be “alarmed"! H.W.S.). They kept me "alarmed" for those long hours of torture.

"I talk to the chaplain some while pacing the cell. I’m thinking I’m going to have a heart attack before they get me onto that horizontal cross with needles in my arms instead of nails. I’ve been broke out in a cold sweat for 2 hours. Can’t think. Just pace, pace, pace. Back and forth, back and forth. 3 ½ steps. I can’t remember the subjects or details of anything the chaplain said, just a bunch of words.

"I eat some of my last meal but I can’t taste a thing. I just look down and see that some of it is gone.

"Six o’clock comes. Nothing. Pace, pace, pace those 3 ½ steps. Seven o’clock. 8 o’clock. Same thing. My mouth is so dry no amount of water can wet it. I know they’re going to open that door any minute and confront me with that gurney and those needles. This is it. This is it. Every time I blink the sweat out of my eye I see it open, I think, that door.

"Nine o’clock. I’m still pacing. I can’t take any more of this! Can’t escape it. "Lord," I pray, "just let it be over. Just let it be done one way or another". It feels like my mind has been stretched in a million directions until it has stress holes like Swiss cheese.

"Ten o’clock. Pace, pace, pace. I know the attorneys are filing stuff and I want to have hope, but that door… I believe, if a stay was coming they’d already have announced it.

"Eleven o’clock. Pace. Pace. My whole body feels like it’s going to explode into a mist. This can’t be real.

"Ten minutes to midnight. I’ve gotten so confused and fuzz-minded that all these jumbled thoughts, in pieces, are plying through my mind every direction, so fast it just seems like a constant hum or moan. They say it’s too late, they can’t do it. Tell me to get ready to go back to Polunsky. I can’t comprehend this. I’m supposed to be dead. I barely remember coming back. I can’t walk straight.

"The next days I feel so strange, like I’m out of place, out of reality somehow. I’m not able to think, I can’t believe I’m still here. They let the warrant expire. I think now that they must be required to give me life. I got only one set of appeals so it follows they get only one chance to execute me, right? There was no legal reason not to they just failed to. Maybe I should feel lucky but I just feel cheated and cursed. I can’t even get executed right! Yet, I am so grateful and happy to be alive, just for my family. My greatest worry was thinking of them having to go through all this with me, on account of me.

"Then, last week I found out from my lawyer that they have set me another execution date. On January 28th, 2004 I’ll have to go through all this again. I can’t believe it. I don’t know what in the world I’m going to say to my wife and kids. I sit down in my cell, trying to comprehend this and start crying. I think I have never shed so many tears over others over so many days in a row or had my heart twisted out of socket this bad. There just are no words for how this feels. Now the whole nightmare starts all over again. I cannot believe it. I know I won’t last through another round of this."

By Billy Frank "Sonny" Vickers
January 2004

Aaliyah Jack, 28, was sentenced on November 5, 2026, to life without parole for the second-degree m*rder of her son Legend, plus an additional 15 years for cruelty to juveniles. Judge Michael Canaday ordered the sentences to run consecutively.

The horrific case began on July 8, 2024, when authorities discovered Legend's body in shallow water behind the Vinton Welcome Center in southwest Louisiana, near the Texas border.

His little brother, Kingtrail, was still missing.

The following morning, a truck driver spotted the 1-year-old crawling in a ditch alongside Interstate 10, approximately eight miles from where his brother's body had been recovered.

The toddler had somehow survived roughly TWO DAYS outdoors during Hurricane Beryl, enduring wind, rain, and exposure without anyone caring for him.

He was dehydrated and covered in insect bites but had escaped serious injury. Authorities called him a "miracle baby."

Prosecutors said Jack deliberately led Legend into the water despite knowing the little boy was terrified of it and couldn't swim.

Investigators also recovered surveillance footage from a Beaumont, Texas, gas station showing Jack dragging her 1-year-old son across the floor by his arm the day before Legend's body was discovered.

Even more disturbing was what Jack admitted afterward.

During a recorded jail conversation with her mother, Conswella, Jack declared, "I hurt my kids before anybody hurt my kids."

When her mother directly asked whether she had done it, Jack answered, "Yes, ma'am."

Jack later admitted to a KPLC reporter that she had k*lled Legend and abandoned Kingtrail, claiming she was under the influence of drugs at the time. She said she had taken two pills from an associate in Houston that she believed turned out to be ecstasy.

Authorities arrested Jack in Mississippi on July 9, following a car crash, the same day her surviving son was rescued.

In September 2026, a Calcasieu Parish jury convicted her of second-degree m*rder and cruelty to juveniles after hearing testimony and reviewing evidence that included autopsy photographs.

At sentencing, Jack made a rambling statement about spending money on someone's birthday, but reportedly offered no apology for what she had done to her children.

Legend's paternal grandmother, Dion Polk, revealed that the little boy had been living with her since May before Jack took both children on July 6, just days before the tragedy.

Calcasieu Parish District Attorney Stephen Dwight said the sentence holds Jack accountable for taking an innocent child's life and inflicting unimaginable suffering on another. First Assistant District Attorney Jacob Johnson said she belongs behind bars for the remainder of her life.

Jack's life sentence without parole, followed by another 15 years, ensures she will never be released from prison. Is that enough?
