text:
President Trump shares claims about 'unusual patterns' in midterm elections and questions James Talarico's victory in Texas... despite saying he would accept the results | James Gordon, Daily Mail

President Donald Trump has sparked fresh controversy by sharing a series of posts questioning the results of the midterm elections, including Democrat James Talarico's stunning victory in Texas – just days after promising to accept the outcome.

The president spent part of Saturday amplifying claims about 'unusual' voting patterns, dramatic increases in Democratic support and election-night figures that some conservative commentators suggested were difficult to believe.

Trump shared several charts and messages on Truth Social that appeared to cast doubt on the scale of the Democrats' sweeping victories, which saw Republicans lose control of both chambers of Congress.

But none of the material he circulated provided evidence of election fraud or wrongdoing.

The posts mark a striking change in tone from Tuesday night, when Trump told The New York Times he was 'absolutely willing' to accept the election results and work with the incoming Democratic majorities.

One of the most provocative messages concerned Talarico's crushing victory over Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race.

The president reposted a message from an account called The Lone Raccoon, which featured a graph showing the candidates' vote totals rising throughout election night, including several sharp jumps.

The graph highlighted sudden increases in the Democratic candidate's tally, although such jumps can occur when election officials release large batches of counted ballots.

Trump shared a post questioning Democrat James Talarico's victory in Texas, featuring a graph of election-night vote totals and asking: 'Does anyone believe this at all?'

Talarico's victory was one of the biggest shocks of Tuesday's elections, making him the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Texas since 1988.

The 37-year-old former teacher defeated Paxton by approximately 12 percentage points in a state that Trump carried comfortably just two years earlier.

Paxton has already conceded the race and congratulated his Democratic opponent.

Trump also circulated another message highlighting what its author claimed was an extraordinary surge in Democratic votes nationwide.

The post, originally published by Kevin Bass, declared: 'Republican votes stayed the same. Democrats materialized 20 million new votes.'

An accompanying bar chart compared the popular vote in House elections in 2022 and 2026.

It showed Republicans receiving 54.2 million votes in 2022 compared with a projected 55.6 million this year.

But the Democratic figures appeared dramatically different, rising from 51.3 million in 2022 to a projected 70.4 million in 2026.

Crucially, the 2026 numbers were projections based on an assumption that just 85 percent of votes had been counted, rather than final election totals.

An independent examination of the figures found that the suggestion of 20 million additional Democratic votes was misleading, with the eventual increase likely to be considerably smaller.

Trump shared a third post raising questions about the extraordinary Democratic turnout in Texas, where Republican Governor Greg Abbott was defeated by Gina Hinojosa.

The message, written by Donald Ward, noted that Abbott had actually increased his vote total compared with his successful 2022 reelection campaign.

But Hinojosa received approximately 1.7 million more votes than Democratic candidate Beto O'Rourke managed four years earlier.

'Those are Looney Tunes numbers,' Ward declared.

He also claimed Hinojosa received 400,000 more votes in Texas than Kamala Harris did during the 2024 presidential election.

'These are not normal midterms numbers,' he wrote. 'Not a single opinion poll before the elections came close to predicting this.'

Ward suggested that polling places should have experienced enormous lines to account for such high turnout.

However, comparisons between different election years do not themselves establish irregularities, and the post offered no evidence that ballots were improperly counted.

Another message circulated by Trump highlighted unusually consistent Democratic gains across multiple states and demanded closer scrutiny of ballot totals, voter records and turnout.

'A pattern this even demands answers at the ballot level,' the post declared, calling for hand counts and checks of voter registration records.

The flurry of online activity came less than four days after Trump appeared ready to acknowledge the Republicans' devastating election defeat.

'I am absolutely willing to accept those results,' he told The New York Times during a telephone interview on Tuesday night.

'We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out.'

At the time, Trump blamed Republican losses partly on his own absence from the ballot, suggesting his personal popularity could have helped struggling candidates.

He also insisted he had no regrets about supporting defeated Republicans, including Paxton and South Carolina Senator Darline Graham.

The president's latest online activity now raises questions about whether he will maintain that conciliatory position as Democrats prepare to assume control of Congress.

Their victories will give them new powers to launch investigations into his administration and potentially block key parts of his legislative agenda.

Aaron Tucker had been out of prison for just seven days.

The 32-year-old was living in a halfway house in Bridgeport, Connecticut, trying to rebuild his life from scratch. He had almost nothing to his name. "I came out here with nothing, literally nothing," he said.

But he had something important that morning: a job interview at a barbecue restaurant. He put on a dress shirt someone at the halfway house had given him, and got on a bus.

On the way, in Westport, Aaron watched as a car slammed into a tree and flipped over. It was upside down and smoking.

Aaron asked the bus driver to stop. The driver told him that if he got off, the bus would leave without him.

Aaron got off anyway.

He ran to the wrecked car, unbuckled the driver's seatbelt and dragged him out, just as the car started to catch fire. The man's head was bleeding badly, so Aaron took off the dress shirt he'd been given for his interview and pressed it against the wound. A few workers from a nearby auto body shop rushed over with a fire extinguisher to help.

Aaron stayed by the man's side until the ambulance arrived.

By then, his interview was long gone.

"I feel like a job can come and go," he said, "but a life is a one-time thing."

When his story spread, people were so moved that a fundraiser for him raised more than $50,000. And the job he missed? He ended up getting several new job offers instead.

He gave up his chance at a fresh start to save a stranger. The world made sure he got another one 💛

Why Women Sleuths Make Cozy Mysteries Spark

A missing heirloom can upset an entire town. A suspicious alibi can spoil a church fundraiser. And when women detectives start asking gentle, persistent questions, people often reveal far more than they intended. That combination of curiosity, courage, and people skills is one reason women detectives feel so at home in cozy mysteries.

They do not need to kick down doors to hold a reader's attention. Often, their greatest strength is noticing what has changed: a neighbor who suddenly skips her usual coffee stop, a friend protecting someone with a poorly told lie, or a worried dog who keeps returning to the same patch of garden. A good sleuth sees patterns. A memorable one also understands the people caught inside them.

## Why Women Detectives Feel So Right in Cozy Mysteries

Cozy mysteries are built around community. The setting may be a small Florida town, a village square, a seaside neighborhood, or a close-knit retirement community, but it is never just wallpaper. The place has memories, routines, local opinions, and history tucked into every storefront and front porch.

Women detectives often move naturally through these spaces because relationships are part of their investigative toolkit. They may volunteer at an event, work in a local shop, care for animals, teach school, practice medicine, or know exactly which neighbor has heard the latest bit of gossip. Their connections give them access, but more importantly, they give the mystery emotional stakes.

When someone is in danger, the case is rarely abstract. It may involve a friend, a beloved local business, a family with old wounds, or a town tradition worth preserving. The detective wants answers not only because a crime has occurred, but because she wants to make her community safer and kinder.

That does not mean she is perfect. The best amateur sleuths can be stubborn, curious to a fault, and occasionally too willing to follow a hunch before breakfast. Those flaws make the clever moments feel earned. A detective who doubts herself, makes a mistake, then looks again with fresh eyes is far more satisfying than one who always has the answer tucked in her pocket.

### Curiosity Is More Than a Cute Trait

A cozy detective's curiosity has to carry real weight. It gets her through awkward conversations, puzzling clues, and the occasional warning to mind her own business. She asks a second question when everyone else has accepted the first answer. She remembers a detail that seemed small at the time. She listens when a witness is talking around the truth instead of saying it plainly.

This kind of curiosity is especially appealing because it is recognizable. Readers may not have access to a crime lab or a police badge, but they understand the power of paying attention. The mystery becomes an invitation to observe alongside the sleuth. Was that muddy shoeprint really from the gardener? Why did the antique clock stop at precisely the wrong moment? And why is the cat sitting so calmly beside the one person who claims to hate animals?

In a well-crafted whodunit, those answers cannot come from luck alone. The detective has to gather information, sort through competing motives, and test what she believes. A warm setting can still hold a smart puzzle.

## Women Detectives Bring Heart Without Losing Edge

There is a mistaken idea that a cozy mystery must choose between warmth and suspense. It does not. In fact, the warmth makes the suspense sharper. When readers care about the baker whose reputation is at risk or the shy newcomer accused too quickly, the stakes feel personal.

Women detectives are often written with a strong sense of empathy, but empathy is not the same as softness. It can be a form of intelligence. A sleuth who understands grief, embarrassment, jealousy, and fear can recognize why a person is lying. She may even know when a lie is meant to protect someone rather than hide guilt.

That nuance matters because mysteries are about more than identifying a culprit. They are about understanding how a secret affected a group of people. A satisfying ending explains the method and motive, but it also restores a measure of order. The innocent are cleared. The overlooked person is heard. The community has a chance to mend.

Of course, a detective should not excuse bad behavior simply because she understands it. Compassion works best when paired with clear judgment. The sleuth may feel sorry for someone, yet still insist that the truth comes out. That balance gives her moral center without making her preachy.

### Skills Make the Sleuth Believable

The most enjoyable women detectives have useful skills that belong to their lives rather than appearing only when the plot needs them. A veterinarian may notice an animal's behavior that points toward a hidden timeline. A librarian may recognize a rare book or track down a historical record. A gardener can tell when soil has been disturbed. A former reporter knows how to make a source feel comfortable enough to talk.

These talents should help, not solve everything. A specialized clue is fun when it opens a door, but the detective still needs to do the patient work of connecting it to motive, opportunity, and means. Readers want to be surprised, not cheated.

Animal knowledge offers particularly delightful possibilities in cozy mysteries. Dogs and cats do not testify, but they observe plenty. A dog may react to an unfamiliar scent, lead someone toward an overlooked object, or make a beeline for the person who has been sneaking around after dark. Canine forensics can add a fresh twist while keeping the investigation grounded in plausible observation.

In Doc and Daisy Mysteries, that blend of skilled sleuthing and a warm snout is part of the fun. A dog narrator can notice the odd smells, nervous gestures, and snack-related clues that human investigators might miss, while also reminding us that loyalty is its own kind of wisdom.

## The Joy of a Detective With a Full Life

A strong detective needs more than a case file. She needs friendships, responsibilities, habits, and perhaps a little unfinished business in her own life. She might be caring for a parent, rebuilding a career, learning to trust after a loss, or figuring out how to accept help from the people who love her.

These threads should enrich the mystery rather than wander away from it. A personal conflict can make an interview difficult. A family history can shed light on an old town secret. A new friendship can provide a valuable perspective. The case still comes first, but the detective's life gives the story its heartbeat.

There is also room for humor. Even a serious clue can arrive at an inconvenient time, such as during a charity auction, a book club meeting, or while a determined dog is trying to inspect someone's picnic basket. Humor does not erase danger. It gives readers a breath between tense moments and makes the town feel lived in.

## What Makes a Woman Detective Memorable

The memorable ones are not copies of one another. Some are bold and chatty. Others are observant, private, and quietly fierce. Some work closely with law enforcement, while others must earn the trust of a skeptical sheriff. Some solve crimes with a circle of friends, and some begin the story believing they have to do everything alone.

What they share is a willingness to look closer when it would be easier to look away. They care about truth, but they also care about the people truth will affect. That makes every clue feel like more than a puzzle piece.

The next time you settle in with a cozy mystery, watch what the detective notices before anyone else does. It may be a crooked picture frame, a missing recipe card, a nervous laugh, or paw prints where paw prints should not be. In the hands of the right sleuth, even the smallest detail can lead the whole town toward the truth.

An Essay on Freedom

November 9, 2026

Two hundred and fifty years ago, a group of men got together and started an experiment based upon the prospect of individual freedom. They envisioned a nation that would prioritize life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.

But living in a free country is hard.

I remember growing up as a poor child in Panama City Beach, Florida. Even at ten years old, perhaps younger, I was already reflecting on my stature in life.

How am I going to make a living in this world? How am I going to take care of myself?

Because everything I was hearing told me that eventually, it was going to be on me.

I could see that my own mother struggled to get by. Even my grandfather, whom I loved dearly, struggled to make ends meet.

And I was reminded of our circumstances every time someone punched my free meal ticket at school or I watched my mother check out at the grocery store with actual paper food stamps.

So I worried.

Turns out, that's what you're supposed to do when you're free.

You're supposed to worry about yourself. You're supposed to figure out how you're going to contribute to your own success. You're supposed to take responsibility for your own future.

And sometimes you're going to fail.

That's the price of freedom. But it's also the beauty of freedom. You have the opportunity to get up, dust yourself off, and try again.

Now, here we are, nearly 250 years into this great American experiment, and people are seriously entertaining the idea that socialism might offer us something better.

Well, I have a suggestion.

Let's look at the results.

History has already given us examples of what happens when governments attempt to manage economic life from the top down. The Soviet Union, for example, struggled with shortages of basic consumer goods. People waited in lines for bread and spent years waiting for automobiles.

Meanwhile, here in America, ordinary citizens have access to an abundance of goods and services that previous generations could scarcely have imagined.

I walk into a Walmart or a Kroger today, and I look around.

The shelves are stocked. The choices are almost endless. Food from all over the world is available to ordinary Americans, including people who grew up as poor as I did.

And all I can say is:

Good God, thank you, America.

I know our country isn't perfect. I know people struggle. I certainly did. And I know that freedom doesn't guarantee happiness or success.

But it gives us something extraordinarily precious.

The opportunity to pursue them.

I don't want a government that promises to take care of every aspect of my life. I want a government that protects my freedom to make something of it.

That's the America those men envisioned 250 years ago.

And that's the America I hope we never lose.

Good day.

𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐈𝐑𝐒 𝐄𝐌𝐏𝐓𝐈𝐄𝐃 𝐋𝐘𝐍𝐃𝐎𝐍 𝐌𝐂𝐋𝐄𝐋𝐋𝐀𝐍’𝐒 𝐁𝐀𝐍𝐊 𝐀𝐂𝐂𝐎𝐔𝐍𝐓 𝐈𝐍 𝟏𝟑 𝐒𝐄𝐂𝐎𝐍𝐃𝐒 — 𝐖𝐈𝐓𝐇𝐎𝐔𝐓 𝐂𝐇𝐀𝐑𝐆𝐈𝐍𝐆 𝐇𝐈𝐌

Lyndon McLellan ran the register at his own convenience store in rural Fairmont, North Carolina, for more than ten years — following his bank teller’s own advice to deposit under $10,000 at a time. “𝘐𝘵 𝘵𝘰𝘰𝘬 𝘮𝘦 13 𝘺𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘮𝘶𝘤𝘩 𝘮𝘰𝘯𝘦𝘺, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 13 𝘴𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘥𝘴 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘨𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘢𝘬𝘦 𝘪𝘵 𝘢𝘸𝘢𝘺,” he said after the IRS wiped out his account.

The IRS never accused him of a single underlying crime. He had 𝐩𝐚𝐢𝐝 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐫 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐝. Agents simply decided his legal cash deposits matched a pattern called “structuring,” got a federal judge to sign a seizure warrant, and never called McLellan or his accountant to ask why — before officers walked into his store and told him his account was already empty.

The government’s own case wasn’t even filed against McLellan — it was captioned “𝘜𝘯𝘪𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘚𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘈𝘮𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘤𝘢 𝘷. $107,702.66 𝘪𝘯 𝘜𝘯𝘪𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘚𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘴 𝘊𝘶𝘳𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘺,” as if the cash itself had committed a crime. When the case drew attention, the U.S. Attorney’s opening move wasn’t an apology — it was an offer to keep half: “𝘔𝘺 𝘰𝘧𝘧𝘦𝘳 𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘳𝘦𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘯 50 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘤𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘯𝘦𝘺,” prosecutors told him. McLellan said no.

This is civil asset forfeiture, and it lets federal agents treat an ordinary bank account as presumed guilty the moment a deposit pattern looks convenient to flag — no crime, no charge, no trial required, just a judge’s signature. 𝐈𝐭’𝐬 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐩𝐭𝐬, 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝, 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐜𝐤 that can get treated the same way the next time an agent decides a pattern looks suspicious.

Facing the backlash, the U.S. Attorney folded, moved to dismiss the case for “no probable cause,” and handed back every cent of the $107,702.66. But 𝐌𝐜𝐋𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐥𝐲 $𝟐𝟐,𝟎𝟎𝟎 in legal and accounting fees the government never reimbursed — the price of proving his own money was his.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐈𝐑𝐒 𝐚𝐝𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐭 𝐧𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐡𝐚𝐝 𝐚 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐭 𝐡𝐢𝐦 — 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐥𝐞𝐟𝐭 𝐚𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐫 $𝟐𝟐,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐩𝐨𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐫 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐬𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐰𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐡𝐢𝐬.

text:
TALK TO HEALTH™ | THE MANIFESTO

Health is the restoration of meaningful participation in life.

We’ve built systems to diagnose illness, manage crises, administer benefits, measure outcomes, and deliver services.

Yet one question remains:

Does a person believe their participation in life still matters?

Someone can be medically stable yet socially disconnected. Receive services yet remain isolated. Survive a crisis without believing tomorrow offers anything different.

Survival matters. But survival alone is not the entirety of health.

Talk to Health™ exists to address what happens between surviving and participating.

We are building public-benefit infrastructure connecting human experience, artificial intelligence, health, and social systems around one objective:

Create conditions where people believe tomorrow holds genuine possibilities because their participation in life matters.

OUR FRAMEWORK

Meaningful participation develops through six interconnected stages:

1. ORIENTATION
Understanding where we are, what’s happening, and what is real.

2. BELONGING
Recognizing opportunities for connection, community, and participation.

3. BECOMING
Exploring identity, meaning, and possibilities beyond present circumstances.

4. ACTIVATION
Moving from understanding toward intentional participation.

5. INTEGRATION
Connecting new understanding and experiences with everyday living.

6. POSSIBILITY
Recognizing and participating in futures previously difficult to imagine.

These stages are not a rigid prescription. They provide a framework for understanding and supporting human participation.

REALITY SUPPORT, NOT REALITY REPLACEMENT

Artificial intelligence can expand access to information, strengthen human capabilities, and help people navigate complex systems.

But technology must not replace human judgment, manufacture certainty, or exploit vulnerability.

It should help people orient themselves within reality.

That requires distinguishing confirmed facts, observations, reasonable inferences, and unknowns.

Our operating principle:

Notice First. Name Later.™

Observe before concluding. Investigate before declaring. Separate evidence from interpretation. Update understanding when new information emerges.

Do No Harm. Update the Model.

HUMAN PARTICIPATION IS THE POINT

People are not merely patients, consumers, cases, data points, or problems awaiting solutions.

They are participants in interconnected human systems.

Their experiences contain information. Their relationships create possibilities. Their contributions matter.

Meaningful participation should not be reserved for those with sufficient money, health, influence, or institutional access.

Systems should expand participation, not merely manage exclusion.

WHAT WE ARE BUILDING

Talk to Health™ is developing a public-benefit ecosystem supporting reality literacy, human connection, responsible AI, education, and meaningful participation.

Our work includes tools, frameworks, experiments, and community-centered approaches that strengthen people’s ability to understand their circumstances and shape what comes next.

We do not claim to possess every answer.

We are building infrastructure where better questions can be asked, evidence examined, understanding updated, and possibilities created.

OUR COMMITMENT

We will distinguish spiritual meaning from empirical evidence.

We will separate observation from interpretation.

We will protect privacy, consent, and human dignity.

We will challenge assumptions, welcome correction, and update our understanding as evidence evolves.

And we will continue building toward a world where meaningful participation is recognized as fundamental to health and collective possibility.

Design follows reality.

Meaning can be participated in.

Health is the restoration of meaningful participation in life.

This is Talk to Health™.

And we’re just getting started.

Talk to Health, Inc. | 501(c)(3)
North Carolina, USA

text:
Police shot him in his own driveway during a warrant, and the county would not release the video.

Andrew Brown's family were eventually allowed to watch twenty seconds of it.

Twenty seconds. That was the offer.

Elizabeth City, North Carolina. 21 April 2021.

Deputies came to serve drug warrants on Andrew Brown Jr, forty-two, a father of seven. He was in his car in the driveway.

Deputies fired. He was struck in the back of the head.

Then came the fight over the tape, and that fight is why this case belongs in this week rather than among a hundred others.

In North Carolina, police recordings are not public records. A court order is required to release them.

The sheriff's office did not release the footage. The family asked to see it.

They were shown a twenty-second clip, redacted, with officers' faces blurred.

Twenty seconds, of an incident in which multiple deputies fired multiple rounds at a man in his own driveway.

The family's lawyers held a press conference about it. A judge later allowed the family limited private viewing and permitted some release, while declining to make the footage public, citing the investigation.

The district attorney announced that the shooting was justified and no charges would follow. A federal investigation was later closed without charges. The county settled with the family.

Most of the footage has never been released to the public.

And that is the point to take, because it applies far beyond this one driveway.

Whether you ever see what happened to a man in his own home depends entirely on which state he happened to be standing in.

In some, footage goes out in days. In North Carolina, his children had to go to court to watch twenty seconds of their father dying.

text:
"The Latin American player doesn’t get the recognition he deserves.
Neither does the Negro player, unless he does something spectacular, like Willie Mays.
We have self-satisfaction, yes.
But after the season is over, nobody cares about us.
Zoilo Versalles was the Most Valuable
Player in the American League, but how many times has he been asked to make appearances at dinners or meetings during the winter?
Juan Marichal is one of the greatest pitchers in the game, but does he get invited to banquets?
I am an American citizen, but some people act like they think I live in the jungle someplace.
This is a matter of sports, of a  man’s ability and his accomplishments.
What matters what language he speaks best."
Roberto Clemente.
When John Candelaria was getting ready to sign with the Pittsburgh Pirates he visited with the team and met Roberto Clemente. After speaking for a few minutes, Roberto left, then came back  into the room and in Spanish said to John and his parents, that he knew how much they were going to offer John to sign, but that the actual number they were willing to spend was much higher, so they should ask for that.
Since none of the Pirates officials spoke Spanish, they had no idea what Roberto Clemente had told him.
"Roberto Clemente"

✝️The Blood of Christ✝️

A Bible verse for you

Hebrews 9:13-15 NIV 

The blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean sanctify them so that they are outwardly clean.  How much more, then, will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse our consciences from acts that lead to death, so that we may serve the living God!  For this reason Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance—now that he has died as a ransom to set them free from the sins committed under the first covenant.

Commentary:
Jesus cleans house from the inside out. The Old covenant represented a purification of the flesh, but that covenant would not deal with iniquity in our hearts. Only through Jesus Christ can our conscious be cleared, our hearts renovated, our minds renewed, and our lives transformed. 2 Corinthians 5:17 says, “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, the new creation has come: The old has gone, the new is here!” (NIV) Romans 12:1-2 says, “Therefore, I urge you, brothers and sisters, in view of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God—this is your true and proper worship. Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God’s will is—his good, pleasing and perfect will.” (NIV)

text:
Kheel Batasha..

Why Kheel? for those who do not know this name, this is Laja.. puffed paddy actually.

Take a raw paddy seed & put it in the soil.. it will grow again.

In Vedanta, a raw seed represents Vasanas & pending karma.. the seeds which still have the capacity to fructify and create another cycle

But when that same paddy touches agni, it bursts open & becomes white kheel.

If you sow Kheel in the ground, it never sprouts again.. yet it becomes light and nourishing.

There is an old principle called Dagdha Bija.. a burnt seed. Once the seed is burnt, its capacity to germinate is gone.

Laja itself is not an ordinary grain. We even have the Laja Homa, where puffed paddy is offered into Agni.

So when we offer Kheel to Maa on Diwali, I see the same tattva here.. may the heavy seeds of our past Daridrya and old negative Karma be transformed by Agni so they do not sprout again in the coming cycle.

There is an agricultural layer also

Diwali comes around the paddy harvest and traditionally Kheel was made from the new crop & offered before we consumed it ourselves.

Astrologically also, Rice carries a strong moon connection, while the whiteness, rasa, abundance and Lakshmi association of Kheel Batasha bring in venus tattva.
a
Batasha is sweetness and rasa.. very venus.. but it too reaches the puja thali only after transformation through agni.

So Kheel-Batasha carries three things together.. Dhanya, Agni Samskara and Samriddhi.

text:
I accidentally found out I make $11,000 more than the woman who trained me.

I've been at my company 14 months. Priya has been there three years and taught me everything. She handles our biggest account and quietly fixes my mistakes before anyone notices.

Finance sent me a spreadsheet for an expense thing and left another tab open. I wasn't looking, but I saw it. Me: $68,000. Priya: $57,000.

I asked my boss Greg about it, carefully, saying I'd seen a number I wasn't meant to. He sighed and said, "Look, you negotiated. Priya took what we offered. That's not unfair, it's how hiring works."

Then he said, "I'd appreciate it if this stayed between us."

I googled it afterwards. In most places it's legal to discuss your own pay. But legal didn't make it feel easier.

Two weeks later we were eating lunch at our desks and Priya said, "Random question. I was looking at job listings for my title. Do you think I'm underpaid?"

My mouth was full of rice. I chewed for about nine seconds.

"I don't know," I said.

She smiled. "Okay. I just figured you'd tell me if you did."

That was Tuesday. It's Friday now and I still haven't said anything.

If I tell her, she'll probably leave and the team falls apart. If I don't, I'm the reason she stays underpaid.

And I haven't even asked myself the worst question yet. Why am I the one who got paid more?

text:
Trump says he was 'only kidding' about naming UFC CEO Dana White as White House press secretary amid hunt for Karoline Leavitt's replacement | James Gordon, Daily Mail

President Donald Trump on Sunday said he was 'only kidding' when he suggested UFC CEO Dana White could become his next White House press secretary.

On Saturday, Trump stirred speculation about recruiting his feisty ally and signaled a combative approach to dealing with Democrats as they prepare to take control of Congress.

Trump said White, a prominent supporter, 'loves the idea' of taking the job but insisted he had not been serious about the prospect, describing the suggestion as 'just a little fun.'

'I will tell you, I was only kidding,' Trump told reporters, explaining that he had posted photographs of prominent UFC fighters as potential assistants to White as part of the joke.

In Saturday's post, Trump described White as a 'violent Fighter and Warrior' and suggested he bring several current or former UFC champions to serve as assistants, saying they were needed to 'defend us against the Lunatic Left.'

Trump said White would visit him at the White House on Monday, but added that the meeting was planned for other reasons.

White, who has led the Ultimate Fighting Championship for more than two decades, has been a close Trump ally and helped mobilize support for his 2024 presidential campaign.

He has also appeared alongside Trump at several political events and helped bring UFC fights to the White House lawn this year.

On Saturday, White broke his silence revealing he would be flying to Washington, DC, immediately and meet the president face-to-face on Monday.

The UFC boss chuckled when questioned about the extraordinary offer by a reporter in London, before declaring: 'I'm flying to Washington, DC, right now.'

White, 57, refused to reveal whether he had already discussed the position with Trump but confirmed he would be meeting his longtime friend at the White House.

'I'm sure we'll have more to talk about after that,' he teased, keeping speculation swirling over whether he could actually become the administration's next chief spokesperson.

'I've got a lot of jobs already,' he added when pressed by a reporter at a press conference.

His comments come after conflicting reports emerged over whether White was seriously considering the job or had already rejected the president's offer.

TMZ reported that the fight promoter would meet Trump in the Oval Office on Monday to discuss the position, citing sources with direct knowledge of the planned meeting.

But CNN claimed White had already turned down the unorthodox proposal with one White House aide suggested Trump had been joking.

The drama comes as Trump scrambles to fill one of the most high-profile jobs in his administration following the disastrous five-day tenure of Katie Zacharia, who was fired after just one rocky press briefing.

The position has taken on even greater importance following the Republicans' crushing midterm election defeat, which handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress and the power to investigate the administration.

Trump made the offer on Truth Social on Saturday, writing: 'I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States.'

But the president went further, proposing that White bring an extraordinary collection of mixed martial arts stars to Washington as his assistants.

'I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris,' Trump wrote, apparently referring to UFC star Kayla Harrison in the final name.

'We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!'

The message immediately raised questions about whether Trump was making a genuine employment offer or simply having fun with his close friend.

White appeared willing to play along, reposting Trump's announcement on Instagram and sharing an image of himself standing behind the White House briefing room podium.

'On to the next chapter,' he wrote alongside the picture, without explaining whether he was accepting the offer or joining in the joke.

White House communications director Steven Cheung also enthusiastically backed the idea, reposting Trump's announcement with the message: 'Hell yeah! Do it, @DanaWhite!'

The president's interest in White comes amid a chaotic search for a replacement for Zacharia, whose spectacularly brief stint in the job ended last month.

She was dismissed after just five days, leaving the White House scrambling to find someone capable of handling the relentless scrutiny of the Washington press corps.

Her predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, had served for approximately 18 months before departing in August to spend more time with her young family. She subsequently joined Fox News as a contributor.

The search has produced some surprising names, with White House staffers even reportedly floating rapper Nicki Minaj as a possible candidate shortly before the midterm elections.

White, meanwhile, has spent years building one of Trump's closest relationships outside politics.

The UFC chief has spoken at the last three Republican National Conventions and played a significant role in connecting Trump with younger male audiences during his successful 2024 presidential campaign.

Trump has previously credited White with introducing him to an entirely different generation of voters.

'He introduced me to people I never heard of, young kids,' the president said earlier this year.

'I mean, I was being interviewed by 20-year-old kids. I'm saying, 'Where the hell did you meet these people?' They're called influencers.'

That relationship reached new heights in June, when Trump hosted a UFC event on the White House lawn as part of celebrations marking America's 250th anniversary.

However, the president's efforts to maintain his appeal among young men suffered a setback during Tuesday's midterms, with the demographic shifting toward Democrats.

The White House personnel shake-up has also reached the very top of Trump's administration.

On Friday, he ousted longtime chief of staff Susie Wiles and announced that hardline adviser Stephen Miller would replace her beginning Monday.

'I'll be doing maybe a few changes,' Trump told CBS News on Friday.

text:
Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

1. How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb and why?

He takes 21 steps — symbolizing the 21-gun salute, the highest military and foreign tribute.

2. How long does he pause before turning to walk back and why?

He waits 21 seconds, again in honor of the same tradition.

3. Why are his gloves damp?

They are lightly moistened to ensure he never loses his grip on his rifle.

4. Does he keep his rifle on the same shoulder, and if not, why?

He always carries it on the shoulder farthest from the Tomb. After each crossing, he performs an about-face and moves it to the outside shoulder.

5. How often are the guards changed?

Every 30 minutes, 24/7, 365 days a year.

6. What are the physical requirements for a Tomb Guard?

Applicants must be between 5'10" and 6'2" and have a waist no larger than 30".

Other expectations of the Guard:

They devote two years to the Tomb, live in the barracks beneath it, and must refrain from drinking alcohol on or off duty for the rest of their lives.

They can never swear in public or dishonor the uniform or the Tomb.

After two years, they earn a wreath pin signifying their service — fewer than 400 are currently worn.

If they violate the code, they must relinquish the pin.

Their shoes have thick soles to protect against extreme temperatures and metal heel plates that create the crisp click when they halt.

Uniforms must have zero wrinkles or lint and are inspected in a full-length mirror.

For the first six months, guards do not speak to anyone and do not watch television.

Their off-duty time is spent studying the 175 notable individuals buried at Arlington National Cemetery, memorizing who they are and where they rest.

Among them: President Taft, Joe E. Lewis, and Audie Murphy, the most decorated WWII soldier.

Every guard spends five hours daily preparing their uniform.

ETERNAL REST GRANT THEM, O LORD, AND LET PERPETUAL LIGHT SHINE UPON THEM.

When Hurricane Isabel approached Washington, D.C. in 2003, Congress shut down for two days. The guards were offered permission to suspend duty due to danger.

They replied: “No way, Sir!”

Drenched and marching through the storm, they insisted that guarding the Tomb is the highest honor, not just a task.

The Tomb has been continuously guarded — day and night — since 1930.

God Bless and Keep Them

I don’t often encourage sharing posts, but I would be honored if this one reached as many people as possible. We should always feel proud of the men and women who serve, wherever they are stationed.

Duty – Honor – Country

IN GOD WE TRUST — with Herbert F Wieland.

text:
TRUMP HASN’T ABANDONED ISRAEL. HE’S PREPARING FOR ISRAEL WITHOUT NETANYAHU.

The world is interpreting Trump’s changing rhetoric as evidence that Netanyahu has damaged Israel’s standing in Washington. But what if the real story is exactly the opposite?

For years, Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu have been more than political allies. They have stood together against Iran, defended each other’s positions, and pursued a shared strategic vision for the Middle East. Now both face political turbulence at home. Netanyahu is fighting to retain power, while Trump must navigate an increasingly hostile political environment in Washington. Trump’s shifting rhetoric toward Israel, including suggestions that Israel should shoulder greater responsibility for future confrontations, may not signal a falling-out with Netanyahu at all. It may be a calculated adjustment to the possibility of losing his closest Israeli ally.

And that brings us to Gadi Eisenkot. While much of the political establishment portrays Netanyahu as the problem and his potential successors as the solution, it overlooks a far more uncomfortable possibility: Trump’s tougher position may be emerging precisely because Netanyahu’s opponents are threatening the partnership Washington once relied upon. Why should Trump offer Eisenkot the same political protection, strategic cooperation, and diplomatic latitude he extended to Netanyahu? From Trump’s perspective, an Israeli leadership change could mean inheriting a government less willing to confront Iran decisively, less committed to holding strategic territory, and more inclined toward concessions. If Eisenkot wants Netanyahu’s position, Trump may be perfectly willing to let him inherit the pressure that comes with it.

The greatest miscalculation is believing that removing Netanyahu will automatically improve Israel’s relationship with America. Trump is not obligated to rescue an Israeli successor from the consequences of a different political agenda. On the contrary, he may find it politically advantageous to transfer responsibility for Israel’s security dilemmas directly onto the next prime minister. That would allow him to satisfy skeptical American voters while demonstrating just how much the Netanyahu partnership mattered. Eisenkot could discover that replacing Netanyahu is considerably easier than replacing Netanyahu’s relationship with the White House.

And Iran? The assumption that Trump’s changing language means the confrontation is over could prove dangerously premature. Trump may still act independently. But if Netanyahu survives politically, the old strategic alignment could return with extraordinary speed, potentially reopening the door to another devastating confrontation with Tehran. The world sees Netanyahu’s possible departure as the beginning of Israel’s diplomatic rehabilitation. It may instead mark the beginning of a much harsher reality for his successor. Trump has not necessarily changed his objectives. He may simply be preparing to pursue them without the man he trusted most in Jerusalem.

The message to Eisenkot could hardly be clearer: You wanted Netanyahu’s chair? Then inherit his enemies, his responsibilities, and his wars. Just don’t expect to inherit his friendship with Donald Trump.

text:
At last. The cause of the war has been identified.

Not the invasion. Not the tanks. Not the dead.

Bad manners.

On 60 Minutes, the President of the United States acknowledged that Russia invaded Ukraine. Then, with the solemn concern of a man discovering a stain on the tablecloth while the house burns down, he explained that Russia had been shown “great disrespect.”

How dreadful.

Imagine invading your neighbour’s home, destroying the furniture, burying his family beneath the staircase, and then filing a formal complaint because he neglected to welcome you properly.

Naturally, the neighbour is the difficult one.

Then came the magnificent proposal: Ukraine would emerge from the war “a little differently shaped.”

A little.

Such a charming word.

One can amputate a leg and describe the result as a modest alteration to the trousers.

One can remove a city from a map and call it a territorial adjustment.

One can take a country apart, provided the language remains sufficiently tidy.

I was born in the Soviet Union. I recognize this little linguistic miracle.

First, power takes what belongs to you. Then it takes the words with which you might describe the theft.

An invasion becomes a disagreement. Conquest becomes negotiation. Resistance becomes hatred. And the victim, still standing among the ruins, is summoned to explain his regrettable attitude.

The aggressor, meanwhile, is terribly sensitive.

There is something almost exquisite about this arrangement. The man holding the knife is offended by the blood.

Mr. President, Putin and Zelensky are not two gentlemen whose dinner party deteriorated over a disagreement about the wine.

One sent an army across an internationally recognized border. The other leads the country that army invaded.

To reduce that distinction to mutual hatred is to put the fire and the person trapped inside it on trial for failing to get along.

And to discuss the future shape of Ukraine as though it were a Manhattan property awaiting renovation is to forget that those lines contain homes, schools, graves, and living human beings.

But perhaps America should revisit its own revolutionary history.

Those troublesome colonists showed King George III a rather shocking lack of respect.

Imagine how much unpleasantness might have been avoided had someone simply explained the importance of good manners toward an empire.

Of course, Americans once had another word for people who refused to surrender their country.

Patriots.

What a curious evolution of the vocabulary.

The President was asked about trust. He offered personal relationships. He was reminded of an invasion. He offered wounded Russian dignity. He was asked about Ukraine’s future. He offered a new shape.

The facts entered the room.

The language escorted them out.

And here we arrive at the extraordinary moral accomplishment of modern diplomacy:

The aggressor may keep the territory. The victim may keep his grievances. The mediator may keep the applause.

Everyone receives something.

Except the dead, who remain remarkably uncooperative.

They refuse to become a negotiating position.

They refuse to applaud the revised map.

They remain where history left them, beneath the soil that someone has decided should now belong to somebody else.

And somewhere in Washington, the principal diplomatic injury remains Russia’s wounded pride.

What an extraordinary civilization we have built.

We have learned to negotiate the dimensions of a victim’s country while discussing whether he was sufficiently polite to the man who invaded it.

Apparently, the great offence was never crossing another nation’s border.

It was expecting the invader to endure the indignity of being told he had crossed it.

text:
This Russian innovation can change the game for India, Moscow’s all-weather friend!

Russia is racing to urgently expand its nascent low-Earth orbit satellite network, known as Rassvet (Dawn), to counter Elon Musk’s Starlink. On Friday, 6 November, Russia’s Security Council issued an official directive demanding a rapid scale-up in the mass production of these communications satellites and terminal equipment. The Kremlin warns that Western space-based systems like Starlink and OneWeb pose a direct threat to national security and could be weaponised to destabilise sovereign states.

Developed by the Russian aerospace firm Bureau 1440, Rassvet is already being deployed for military operations over Ukraine, specifically to secure drone operations and improve missile tracking.

Sooner or later, Russia will offer this technology to its long-term friend India. However, we must wait for the Russians to perfect it before we can thumb Musk’s nose.

Russia has successfully launched only 32 satellites so far this year (deployed in batches in March and July). In sharp contrast, SpaceX's Starlink operates more than 10,000 active satellites. The Russian expanse is thus limited.

Head of Roscosmos, Dmitry Bakanov, stated that Russia intends to have a constellation of ~300 satellites in orbit to achieve full baseline deployment by 2027. The ultimate roadmap aims for over 900 satellites by 2035, but observers are sceptical about the country’s ability to pull it off.

Ukrainian military intelligence (GUR) reports that Rassvet is currently insufficient for continuous operations. It provides only about 3 hours of connectivity per day, with roughly 50 minutes of continuous coverage as satellites pass overhead.

Once fully operational, Russia aims to use the high-speed, low-latency network to allow surveillance and attack drones to exchange data in real time, adjust flight paths mid-air, and evade electronic jamming.

However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has already imposed sanctions on 10 companies directly linked to the development of Rassvet. Furthermore, Ukraine has lobbied Washington for tighter controls, alleging that the project relies heavily on imported Chinese electronic components to bypass existing trade restrictions. A possible tech transfer to India after the Russian know-how is fully developed will, therefore, meet its fair share of geopolitical obstructions, especially given that none of the US, NATO or Ukraine is an enemy of India; we do business with all.

text:
Larry Page and Sergey Brin were Stanford grad students in their twenties when they emailed an offer to sell Google for $1.6 million. The investor in the middle talked them down, and the buyer still said no.

The buyer thought Google worked too well.

In the video below, Brin tells the story to the investor who tried to close that deal, Vinod Khosla. Then Khosla corrects the price.

"We don't really want to sell, but okay, for $1.6 million, you got a deal."

It was the late 1990s. Google was a research project that ranked web pages better than anything else.

The buyer was Excite, one of the biggest search sites on the internet. Khosla was one of its investors.

Page and Brin felt the project was eating their time at Stanford.

Khosla got the price down. By most accounts it ended at $750,000. In the video he remembers $350,000.

Excite's CEO George Bell still said no.

According to reports, he wanted Page to make the search worse, because it sent people off Excite's site too fast. Bell has disputed parts of this story.

Sites like Excite made money when you stayed on their pages and saw ads. Google found your answer and sent you away.

"Why would we work at a place that doesn't believe in search?" Page says.

In 1999 Excite merged with Home in a $6.7 billion deal. Two years later it was bankrupt.

Alphabet is now worth more than $4 trillion.

Google offered itself for $1.6 million.
Excite asked it to be worse.

Would you have taken $1.6 million as a grad student, or kept the search box nobody wanted to buy?

Save this video for the next time someone tells you your idea isn't worth it, and follow for more.

text:
Citi downgraded U.S. equities and global tech to Neutral from Overweight, citing AI fatigue and crowded positioning. The bank upgraded European stocks outside the U.K. to Overweight, favoring regions with less tech exposure.

Citi warns Nasdaq positioning could slip into net-short territory, though it estimates a roughly 5% additional drop is needed. AI sentiment has plunged as midterm results raise questions about long-term spending.

The bank remains constructive on AI long-term but seeks cleaner positioning first. Falling oil prices and lower bond yields offer support, though credit spreads have widened and earnings revisions slowed.

Citi expects global earnings growth to slow significantly in 2027. Historically, stocks have risen about 4% in similar years, with defensive and high-quality names outperforming. The bank now favors materials, health care, and food and beverage stocks in Europe.

U.S. Bancorp ($USB) trades at $59.90, up 0.76% in pre-market action. According to Yahoo Finance, the bank notes risks appear balanced rather than skewed to the downside, maintaining a cautious near-term outlook.

text:
$VRTS Q3 2026 earnings: Virtus cuts bonus costs, but client withdrawals speed up again

Virtus Investment Partners, which manages stock, bond and private-credit funds, kept its profit margin steady through lower bonus costs while client withdrawals worsened. Revenue excluding one-offs fell 8% from a year ago to $181 million because ending client assets dropped 16% to $141 billion, or 18% by our math without the Keystone private-credit purchase. Lower employee bonus accruals lifted the operating margin excluding one-offs back to the top of what the company's own cost targets pointed to.

• Ending client assets (AUM): $𝟏𝟒𝟏.𝟒𝐁 (-16.5% from a year ago (-17.8% excluding acquired Keystone assets at close))
• Net client outflows: -$𝟔.𝟏𝐁 (worse than -$5.6B last quarter and -$3.9B a year ago)
• Revenue, excluding one-offs: $𝟏𝟖𝟎.𝟖𝐌 (-8.1% from a year ago)
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟓.𝟖𝟔 (-20.3% from a year ago (+5.8% from last quarter))

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because last quarter's slowdown in client withdrawals and surge in institutional sales both reversed. Total net outflows widened again to $6.1 billion as institutional sales dropped in half to $1.1 billion, leaving the firm with a smaller asset base entering the fourth quarter. The good news: the average fee rate held at 43 basis points even as performance fees fell by half, proving the private-credit fee lift is sticking.

The question now is whether lower bonus accruals and higher-fee alternative funds can protect profit while stock funds keep losing 16% of their assets a year. Either institutional wins and stock performance finally stabilize the asset base, or shrinking assets push employee pay back above target as a share of revenue. Fourth-quarter net flows and the pay ratio will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫-𝐅𝐞𝐞 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐞𝐞 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝟒𝟑 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐬 𝐏𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬
Virtus Investment Partners, which runs mutual funds and separate investment accounts for individuals and institutions, earns most of its revenue as a percentage of the client money it manages. The firm bought private-credit manager Keystone National Group in March to add higher-fee products and lift its average fee rate. Critics argued last quarter's 43.1 basis point rate (0.431% of assets per year) rested on one-time performance fees.

The third quarter disproved that worry. Total average fees held at 43.0 basis points, up from 41.2 basis points a year ago, even as performance fees fell in half from 1.2 basis points to 0.6. By our math, the underlying fee rate without performance bonuses rose to 42.4 basis points from 41.9 in the second quarter because open-end fund fees climbed to 43.9 basis points.

Alternative funds and multi-asset portfolios now make up 30.0% of ending client assets by our math, up from 22.2% a year ago, as investors added money to "exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and tender offer funds". Still, by our math, quarterly fees from closed-end and tender offer funds slipped to about $27.7 million from $29.0 million in the second quarter, so the higher fee rate is only softening the blow of a smaller asset base.

What to watch: closed-end and tender offer fund inflows in next quarter's asset flow table. Rising inflows above this quarter's $68 million would show the private-credit purchase can grow on its own rather than just delivering a one-time step up.

🟢 𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐨𝐧𝐮𝐬 𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐫𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐁𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐏𝐚𝐲 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐁𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭
Employee pay and bonuses are the largest cost at Virtus. In the first two quarters of the year, pay excluding one-offs consumed a bigger share of revenue than finance chief Michael Angerthal had targeted on the prior earnings calls, raising concern that costs could not come down fast enough to match shrinking fee revenue.

In the third quarter, the asset manager brought pay excluding one-offs down 6.5% from the second quarter to $95.5 million. Virtus said the drop came from the absence of "a discrete non-cash expense item as well as lower variable incentive compensation". By our math, pay took 52.8% of revenue excluding one-offs, down 2.8 percentage points from the second quarter and below the 54.0% target set on last quarter's call.

That cost drop lifted the operating margin excluding one-offs by 2.6 percentage points from the prior quarter to 28.7%, hitting the top of the 27.7% to 28.7% band implied by last quarter's cost targets. However, compared with a year ago, pay still rose by 2.6 percentage points of revenue and overhead rose by 1.8 percentage points, pulling the operating margin down 4.3 percentage points from 33.0%.

What to watch: fourth-quarter employment expenses as a share of revenue excluding one-offs. Holding the ratio near 53% despite lower fourth-quarter starting assets would show management can protect margins through variable bonus cuts.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐝𝐫𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐤
The biggest risk for Virtus is steady client withdrawals from its stock portfolios. Management has argued for two years that clients are only pulling money because the market favors fast-growing tech stocks over its "quality-oriented equity strategies", which focus on steady, profitable companies. Last quarter, total net outflows narrowed to $5.6 billion from $8.4 billion in the first quarter, giving hope that the worst had passed.

Instead, net outflows widened again to $6.1 billion in the third quarter, while falling financial markets removed another $4.3 billion. Total assets under management (AUM), the pool of client money Virtus charges fees on, fell to $141.4 billion.

• Total ending AUM: down 16.5% from a year ago, or 17.8% by our math excluding the $2.3 billion acquired with Keystone at close
• Equity AUM: $59.5 billion, down 35.4% from $92.1 billion a year ago
• Total gross sales: $4.3 billion, down 31.7% from a year ago and 29.3% from last quarter
• Annualized net outflow rate: 16.1% of starting assets by our math, worse than 15.2% in the second quarter

Because Virtus enters the fourth quarter with $141.4 billion of ending assets — 5.4% below the third quarter's $149.5 billion average — management fees will step down again next quarter unless markets rally.

What to watch: fourth-quarter retail separate account and open-end fund gross sales. A drop below this quarter's $3.1 billion combined level would confirm that new client demand is drying up alongside persistent withdrawals.

driver faded — 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐟 𝐀𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐆𝐨𝐨𝐝 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫
Institutional accounts — money managed for pension funds, endowments and sovereign funds — make up a third of the firm's assets. Last quarter, chief executive George Aylward highlighted $2.2 billion of institutional sales as the highest in three years and described the sales pipeline as the strongest in a year, while cautioning that known upcoming withdrawals still exceeded known wins.

That sales rebound reversed in the third quarter. Institutional inflows dropped by half to $1.1 billion, even though the quarter included $0.4 billion from issuing a new collateralized loan obligation (CLO), a bundled pool of corporate loans. Without the large global real estate win that boosted the second quarter, institutional net outflows more than tripled from $0.7 billion to $2.2 billion.

At the same time, the average fee rate on institutional accounts fell to 30.7 basis points from 32.2 basis points in the second quarter and 31.6 a year ago. That shows the mandates Virtus is keeping or winning pay lower fees than the accounts clients are closing, cutting against last quarter's claim of a broad institutional recovery.

What to watch: institutional gross inflows and the institutional fee rate in the fourth quarter. Another quarter of inflows near $1.1 billion with a fee rate near 31 basis points would show the second-quarter surge was a one-off real estate mandate rather than a lasting turn.

🔴 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐮𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭
A standing concern is the wide gap between Virtus's standard accounting (GAAP) profit and the profit excluding one-offs that management emphasizes, alongside questions about how the acquired Keystone private-credit business is performing against its buyout targets. When Virtus bought Keystone, it recorded a contingent consideration liability — money it only has to pay the sellers if Keystone hits future revenue targets.

In the third quarter, Virtus cut the fair value of that contingent payout liability by $6.7 million, after cutting it by $4.4 million in the second quarter. Under accounting rules, lowering an expected buyout payment flows through the income statement as a gain, which boosted GAAP diluted profit by $0.74 per share this quarter. Meanwhile, unannounced restructuring charges rose to $2.2 million ($0.24 per share), bringing the nine-month restructuring bill to $5.9 million.

Even with the $0.74 earnout gain, GAAP diluted profit dropped 51% from the second quarter to $3.26 per share because investment marks flipped to a $1.08 per share loss and drove the GAAP tax rate up to 34% from 16% on the "meaningful sequential change to unrealized losses from unrealized gains in the prior quarter". Cutting the expected earnout payout two quarters in a row suggests acquired revenue is tracking below the upper payout targets.

What to watch: the contingent consideration footnote in the third-quarter 10-Q filing. It will show whether the $11.1 million of combined two-quarter liability reductions came from lower revenue projections at Keystone or discount-rate math.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐𝟐𝟑.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭  ⇘ decelerating
Net debt — total debt minus cash — fell 10.8% from the second quarter after Virtus made "a $15 million repayment of the amount drawn on the company's revolving credit facility". That leaves $15 million still drawn on the credit line, short of last quarter's plan to pay off the full $30 million balance near term. Working capital — short-term cash and receivables minus bills due within a year — dropped 37.8% from last quarter to $44.5 million.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟔.𝟕𝟕𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬  ⇘ decelerating
Diluted shares fell 1.4% from a year ago and were almost unchanged from 6.778 million in the second quarter. The investment manager spent $10.0 million to buy back 64,666 shares — matching the $10 million quarterly pace it has kept for four straight quarters while prioritizing debt paydown — and raised its quarterly cash dividend by 2% to $2.45 per share.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐕𝐢𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐬 𝐜𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐛𝐲 $𝟏𝟏𝐌?
The firm reduced its contingent consideration liability by $6.7 million in the third quarter after a $4.4 million cut in the second quarter. Management did not say in the release whether Keystone is tracking below the revenue growth targets required for the $75 million earnout.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐟𝐞𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐩𝐚𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬?
The earnings release contains no forward outlook table because Angerthal gives quarterly modeling targets for the fee rate, the pay ratio and overhead on the conference call. With ending assets down 7% from the second quarter, the fourth-quarter pay ratio target is the key margin test.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐄𝐓𝐅 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐊𝐞𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧?
The release reported $0.4 billion of gross ETF sales, but did not print ending ETF assets or the standalone management fee table from Note 3 of the 10-Q. Those figures show whether ETFs and private credit are still compounding organically.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟓.𝟗𝐌 𝐨𝐟 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐭𝐨-𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬?

text:
Your best partner is rented revenue. Rule 5.6 says they can leave tomorrow. Investors just offered 18x EBITDA for what stays.

And the rent is going up. 

David Morley's "Peak PE Partner" piece cites Josh Feltman's move from Wachtell to Kirkland in April at a reported $80M guaranteed over three years.

Morley asks whether the PE-driven lateral market is near its top. Weil's collapse is the backdrop. The reporting says Weil fell behind rivals on investment. How far behind, and in what, nobody outside the firm really knows, so I won't guess.

I'm more interested in what the money buys.

A lateral guarantee buys revenue the firm rents. If the partner leaves, the revenue leaves too.

Money spent tech enabling the practice buys something else: workflows, infrastructure, playbooks, the codified judgment of your best lawyers. 

Those stay when people go.

In a partnership partners pay in capital and typically take the same amount out when they leave. 

Shares don't usually rise in value when the firm builds something durable. 

For an initiative that has a 5 year break even, the partner retiring in three years has every reason to vote against funding it.

Outside capital has already put a price on that layer. 

Charlesbank signed an LOI to pay about $700M, roughly 18x EBITDA, for the MSO behind Wood Smith Henning & Berman, per PitchBook and the FT. 

They were valuing the platform, not one partner's book.

Outside Arizona and Utah's shrinking sandbox, Rule 5.4 keeps outside owners out of the law firm itself. 

For now the MSO is how a US firm gives that platform an owner.

Two things change when the platform sits in an MSO.

Partners can hold equity that appreciates. 

Holland & Knight, whose team told me they've closed more than $2B of law firm MSO deals this year, expects significant rollover equity in most of these transactions.

The people building the platform can own a piece of it too. Your engineers, data scientists and product leads can't hold law firm equity. 

However, they CAN hold MSO equity.

Trisha Rich made a point on my podcast that Rule 5.6 protects a lawyer's right to practice and their equity in the law firm. 

It says nothing about equity in a management company. That gives firms more room to reward people for staying. How much room will vary by state, and someone will test it.

PE professionals rarely switch firms because their carry is still vesting. Law firm partners have nothing vesting. The lateral market lives in that gap.

The firms on the upward leg of the K won't be the ones that paid the most for laterals. They'll be the ones that turned PE-funded fees into a platform someone can own.

If your top three rainmakers left on Friday, what would still be worth something on Monday?

text:
Things To Do Along The Beach: Songwriters, Walks and Superheroes

November is hitting the coast at full speed this week—and we’re here for it! The Frank Brown Songwriters Festival is filling our island with music, alongside local art, family fun, waterfront adventures, a comic hero’s luncheon, and a special day honoring our veterans. With something for just about everyone, it’s the perfect week to discover something new, cheer on local talent, catch live music, or simply get out and enjoy the coast. We’ve rounded up seven days of local happenings worth adding to your calendar. Grab your favorite people, bring your curiosity, and get ready to see what’s happening this week!

SEE FULL LIST AND LINKS:  https://t.co/lnphBXlH8q

Monday, November 9th- It’s an exciting week on the coast as the Frank Brown Songwriters Festival brings music to venues all across our 32-mile island. And Flora-Bama is turning up the excitement with special OPEN MIC sessions all week long! Hosted by “T-Bone” Montgomery, these crowd-pleasing events are full of surprises—you never know who might sign up and step on stage. Past award-winning songwriters could share the spotlight with anyone ready to perform. Bring your instrument, add your name to the list, and T-Bone will do his thing and get you on the schedule. Whether you're taking the stage or cheering on the performers, this week’s OPEN MICs promise to bring the house down. Open MIC times: Monday through Wednesday, noon to 5:30 PM; Thursday and Friday, noon to 3 PM. Happy tunes, y’all!

2026 Frank Brown Songwriters Festival Schedule

Tuesday, November 10th- Creating art is even more fun when there are no limits—and spray painting lets your creativity run wild! This Tuesday evening,  grades 6–12 are invited to the Orange Beach Library to create colorful planet and galaxy artwork inspired by the expressive style of street artists. It’s free to attend, but registration is required to make sure everyone has room to spread out and spray. Come ready to make a splash of color and take home a uniquely realistic spray-painted planet and galaxy painting! Before you head out, stop by the front desk to pick up the November calendar and discover more fun, free events happening at the Library this month. You might as well find a great book while you're there and keep your reading adventure going, too. Have fun!

Spray Paint @ the Library-OB

Wednesday, November 11th- What began as a holiday called Armistice Day, marking the end of World War I, expanded to honor all veterans in the 1950s. It is now firmly rooted in its deep historical context, with the date always falling on 11 November throughout the United States. It’s a day to remember and honor those we’ve lost in service, as well as those who are still here. Men and women who decide to serve dedicate their time and sacrifice their safety, and often their lives, for the common good and national security. There are many ways to honor veterans throughout the year. One simple way is to stop and take the time to say, “Thank you for your service,” if you see someone wearing a service hat or another indicator of service. It means more to them than we may ever know. On this day, many towns host events to honor veterans, and most businesses and schools are closed. The City of Foley will be hosting its annual Veterans Day commemorations and parade. The parade will begin at 11 AM at Max Griffin Park and conclude at the park near the city Veterans Memorial on South Alston. Please visit the link below for a detailed parade route. Come out and join others in the community to celebrate and honor our veterans, their families, and, of course, our country.

Veterans Day Parade & Route- Foley

Thursday, November 12th- Doc’s Seafood and Steaks offers an exceptional menu, game-day big screens, and open-air seating, along with live music on the Lawn from 5 to 8 PM. It’s a lovely spot for families and friends to enjoy dinner, sip a drink, and linger over the music and relaxed backyard atmosphere. And when the cooler nights arrive, heating stations will help keep everyone cozy. It’s difficult to beat a starry evening at a venue close enough to the Gulf to catch a hint of salty sea breeze, especially with a thick, juicy steak or a plate piled high with your favorite seafood and great live music. Make Live on the Lawn part of your weekly fall and winter plans—it's just that good.

Live on the Lawn @ Docs-OB

Friday, November 13th- On select Fridays in November, you’re invited to join a guided walk along the pier in Gulf Shores. You might wonder how this is different from paying to walk the pier on your own. The answer is that our diverse, complex ecosystem has so much to discover—and even more to protect. When we understand what makes our coastal waters and surrounding areas unique, we’re better equipped to care for them and avoid actions that could put them at risk. Parking is $15 for non-residents, and everyone is welcome to join, learn, and explore. During the walk, you’ll hear about the pier’s rich history, learn about local conservation efforts and how you can help, discover the marine life and bird species that call this area home, and learn how to protect them. Plus, sharing a wealth of fun wildlife and marine-life facts with friends is a pretty cool flex. The walk begins at 9 AM and lasts about an hour, but you’re welcome to stay longer if your parking pass is valid all day. Please arrive a few minutes early so you have time to find and meet up with your group.

Guided Pier Walk-GS

Saturday, November 14th- Bushwackers Landing is a sweet, somewhat hidden gem worth the short drive to Perdido Key for great food and beautiful scenery. This Saturday, it gets even sweeter with the Art Market: Local Art, Cold Bushwackers and More, from 10 AM to 5 PM! Come enjoy a different waterfront view, browse local artists and vendors, and get a head start on your holiday shopping. Then stick around for, you guessed it,  live music, delicious food, great drinks, and those unbeatable waterfront views. Interested in becoming a vendor? It’s not too late—visit the Bushwackers Landing Facebook page and fill out the form. Happy shopping, dining, and enjoying every little corner of the beach towns lifestyle!

Bushwacker Landing Art Market-Perdido Key

Sunday, November 15th- The Hangout in Gulf Shores is bringing the fantastic world of superheroes to life with a special visit from a friendly neighborhood hero at Character Lunch this Sunday from noon to 3 PM. The special guest will stop by to entertain and meet guests, and there’ll also be an exciting trivia game with prizes, one-on-one character meet-and-greets, photo ops for everyone, a character dance party, and plenty of delicious food options. No reservations are needed—just come hungry and ready to be dazzled by the hero, the theatrics, and more. Be sure to tell your friends and invite your neighbors. It’s going to be one epic day where 59 ends and the fun begins!

Character Lunch @ the Hangout-GS

Get out there, make memories, always support local, and enjoy what’s good this week on the coast!

text:
David Bowie and Iman had one of the most iconic and enduring love stories in music and fashion, lasting 24 years until Bowie's death in 2016...

They were introduced in Los Angeles in October 1990 by mutual friend and Bowie's hairdresser, Teddy Antolin. Bowie later described it as love at first sight, while Iman was initially hesitant to date a rock star. Bowie wooed her steadily, including flying out to see her in Paris and inviting her for tea. Iman fell in love with David Jones—the private man behind the Bowie persona—rather than the rock icon.

. . .

A hairdresser in Los Angeles was worried about his friend. The world's most famous rock star came home every night to an empty room.

His name was Teddy Antolin, and his friend was David Bowie.

Teddy was far more than the man who styled Bowie's iconic hair. He was one of his closest confidants. He saw the vulnerable human behind the legend. He knew that despite all the applause, Bowie was deeply lonely.

It was 1990. Bowie had spent three decades becoming Ziggy Stardust, Aladdin Sane, the Thin White Duke. He had played to hundreds of thousands of people.

And yet, after the shows ended, he returned to his hotel room alone.

"David was very lonely," Teddy later said. "All this hard work David did each day, and then he was alone."

Teddy had recently met Iman at a party in Los Angeles. The Somali supermodel, muse to Versace and Yves Saint Laurent, was guarded and intelligent, with no interest in dating a rock star.

But Teddy had a feeling. Underneath their glamour, they were two grounded souls who needed each other.

He invited them both to his birthday party in October 1990 — without telling either about the other. Only four people were in the room: Teddy, his boyfriend, Iman, and David Bowie.

Bowie arrived in a white Mustang wearing head-to-toe white denim. Iman arrived in a black Mercedes dressed in black leather.

"The minute she walked in, she had a big smile, and when she and David looked at each other, it was like love at first sight. You could feel the electricity."

Bowie offered to drive her home. She said, "No, I'm going to drive my car." Then she left.

"I was naming the children the night we met," Bowie later said. "It was absolutely immediate."

The next day, he invited her to tea. She discovered he didn't actually drink tea. He had offered it simply to be polite.

That's when she met David Jones. Not Ziggy Stardust. Just David — a shy, polite Englishman who listened.

"I fell in love with David Jones," she said. "I did not fall in love with David Bowie. Bowie is a persona. David Jones is the man I met."

He pursued her with quiet devotion. When her plane landed in Los Angeles two weeks later, he waited alone at the gate with flowers—no security, no entourage.

Once, when her shoelaces came undone on the street, he knelt down in the middle of the pavement and tied them for her.

"That's when I thought, this one's a keeper," she said.

He sent her flowers on the 14th of every month — the anniversary of the day they met.

Meeting her changed him. Bowie quietly decided to become worthy of her. He stopped drinking and cleaned up his life.

"You’re not just marrying me," Iman told him. "You’re marrying my tribe, my family." So Bowie went to meet them. When he returned, he proposed again — on a yacht in the Adriatic Sea. She said yes.
