text:
Subtle mood changes in late life may follow early Alzheimer’s brain changes, study suggests | Eric W Dolan, PsyPost

In older adults without memory problems, the buildup of Alzheimer’s-related tau protein in the brain tends to precede and predict a rise in mild depressive symptoms, with little evidence that mood changes drive protein accumulation. The findings, published in the Journal of Neuroscience, provide evidence that subtle emotional shifts in late life may be an early consequence of Alzheimer’s-related brain changes rather than an independent trigger for disease progression. This pattern was statistically significant only in cognitively healthy individuals, suggesting that early temporal windows offer the best opportunity to observe how brain pathology affects mood.

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive brain disorder that slowly destroys memory and thinking skills. It is biologically defined by the accumulation of two abnormal proteins: amyloid-beta, which forms sticky plaques outside brain cells, and tau, a protein that normally helps stabilize the internal skeleton of neurons but can misfold and form toxic tangles inside them. Long before a person shows noticeable memory loss, they often experience subtle changes in mood, such as apathy, anxiety, or mild depression.

Even mild depressive symptoms that fall short of a clinical diagnosis have been linked to a higher risk of developing dementia later on. Because tau accumulation and worsening mood often show up around the same time, it has remained an open question which process leads the other. One possibility is that early tau tangles damage deep brain regions that produce mood-regulating chemicals like serotonin, causing depressive symptoms to emerge as an early sign of disease.

Another possibility is that depression itself alters brain wiring or stress pathways in ways that make neurons more vulnerable to tau spread. Earlier imaging work linked the two in healthy aging. For example, a 2017 pilot study of cognitively normal older adults found that people with more tau tangles in memory-related brain areas also tended to report more depressive symptoms at a single point in time.

Don’t miss the next big psychology finding

Every morning, PsyPost sends a short briefing on the most interesting new peer-reviewed research in psychology and neuroscience.

Later longitudinal research tracked how these measures move together over several years. In a 2025 study by two of the same authors, Teodora Z. Markova and Anne S. Berry, analyzing shared data from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), rising depressive symptoms in cognitively unimpaired older adults were linked to tau buildup in the amygdala, a brain hub that processes emotion. Still, standard correlation studies could not establish whether tau buildup was driving the mood changes or if worsening mood was accelerating tau accumulation.

“Most of the work thus far in the field was correlational, just showing associations between more tau pathology and worsening depressive symptoms,” study lead author Teodora Z. Markova, who conducted the research as a doctoral student in the Neurochemistry and Cognition Lab at Brandeis University and is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of California, San Francisco Memory and Aging Center, told PsyPost.

“I wanted to leverage existing large-scale datasets like ADNI to really try and understand the dynamics between the two variables. While it’s hard to establish any ‘causal’ relationships with this kind of data, I wanted to use some creative statistical approaches to better understand which variable changes first, and get a better sense of whether tau accumulates before mood worsens (tau ‘causing’ disruptions in mood) or vice versa.”

To test the direction of this relationship, Markova, Berry at Brandeis University, and co-author Margo B. Heston at the University of California, San Francisco applied three statistical modeling approaches to multi-year brain scan and mood data. The authors originally hypothesized a two-way feedback loop in which tau and depressive symptoms would reinforce each other over time, with tau having the larger effect.

They examined records from 390 older adults (197 women and 193 men) enrolled in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, a large multi-site research project tracking brain aging. At the start of the tracking period, 226 participants had normal cognition, while 164 had either mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a stage of noticeable memory decline that does not yet interfere with daily independence, or Alzheimer’s dementia.

None of the participants had clinical depression when they entered the study, scoring 6 or lower on the 15-point Geriatric Depression Scale, a standard yes-or-no questionnaire that asks older adults about their mood and life satisfaction. Over an average follow-up period of roughly three years, each participant underwent at least two positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans to measure tau protein, paired with repeated depression questionnaires and memory tests. During a tau PET scan, a person receives a small injection of a radioactive tracer that binds to tau tangles in the brain, allowing a scanner to measure how much protein has accumulated in different areas.

Because tau spreads through the brain in a predictable sequence of stages, the researchers customized their measurements for each participant by tracking the most advanced brain region that had already crossed the threshold for tau positivity at their first scan. Most cognitively normal participants (194 of 226) had not crossed the positivity threshold anywhere at their first scan, so the researchers tracked tau in the earliest-affected region for them. They also took into account whether participants had amyloid-beta plaques on separate PET scans and whether they carried the APOE ε4 gene variant, the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s disease. The full statistical outputs were posted publicly on the Open Science Framework.

As expected, participants in the cognitively impaired group started out with more tau in their brains and more depressive symptoms than the cognitively healthy group, and both measures increased more rapidly over time in the impaired group. On the 15-point depression scale, the cognitively normal group started with an average score of 0.8, compared to 2.1 in the cognitively impaired group. Having amyloid plaques or carrying the APOE ε4 gene variant was linked to higher starting tau levels, particularly among those who already had cognitive impairment, though neither factor was significantly linked to differences in starting depression scores or how they changed over time.

When the researchers tested how rates of change in tau and mood interacted over time, a pattern pointing in one direction emerged in the cognitively normal group, running partly counter to their expectation of a two-way loop. Cognitively healthy participants whose tau levels rose the fastest also experienced the steepest increases in depressive symptoms over the follow-up period. In contrast, the rate at which a person’s depressive symptoms worsened was not significantly linked to how quickly they accumulated tau.

A simpler test of whether starting tau levels predicted later changes in mood, or the reverse, did not produce statistically significant results in either group. Next, the team used a mathematical technique called continuous time structural equation modeling, which estimates how one changing variable predicts future values of another variable across uneven time gaps between clinic visits.

Because this method requires a person’s scores to change at least slightly over time, 95 cognitively normal and 26 cognitively impaired participants whose depression scores remained completely flat across all visits were excluded from this specific analysis. Among the remaining 131 cognitively healthy adults, higher tau at a given scan predicted higher depressive symptoms at later visits, though the authors focused on whether this link existed rather than on how its strength changed over different time spans because each person had only a few scans.

Once again, the reverse pathway was not statistically significant: fluctuations in depressive symptoms did not predict later changes in tau. In the cognitively impaired group, neither pathway was statistically significant. To check that their statistical model was working properly with the available sample sizes, the researchers ran the exact same test using objective memory scores instead of mood scores, confirming that higher tau predicted subsequent memory decline in both the healthy and impaired groups.

For their third test, the scientists used an algorithm to estimate the age at which each participant first crossed the threshold into tau positivity in the entorhinal cortex, one of the very first brain areas near the hippocampus to develop tau tangles. Looking at the 62 cognitively normal and 96 cognitively impaired participants who had at least one tau-positive scan, they found that the cognitively impaired group had become tau-positive at an average estimated age of 67.6, about four and a half years earlier than the cognitively normal group’s average onset age of 72.2. Within the cognitively normal group, people who had been tau-positive longer showed steeper increases in depressive symptoms over time, whereas this relationship was not statistically significant in the cognitively impaired group.

“I was particularly surprised that we only observed significant tau-depressive symptom effects in the cognitively unimpaired sample and not in the MCI/AD dementia sample,” Markova said. “I think this really highlights the complexity of what is going on in MCI and AD dementia. To understand the dynamics of these relationships once there is a diagnosis, we may need different, more targeted approaches.”

“This particular study is contributing to a larger body of work demonstrating how late-life changes in mood from your baseline can really be indicative of developing neurodegenerative disease,” Markova explained. “So one major takeaway for a general audience could be about this field of research in general. A significant change in mood or a new neuropsychiatric symptom in later life could offer meaningful information about what’s going on in your brain. Along with complementary information about other biomarkers, tracking changing mood can help us identify who is at an elevated Alzheimer’s disease risk.”

“Also, while the effects in our particular study are small and subtle, we are still able to track significant relationships with tau PET imaging,” Markova added. “This really highlights the power of tau PET imaging.”

The rate-of-change and tau-onset results in the cognitively normal group held after the researchers adjusted for whether participants had amyloid-beta plaques or carried the APOE ε4 gene variant, while the continuous-time models did not include these or other background factors, which the authors left out to keep the models workable. Because about 59 percent of the cognitively normal participants were amyloid-negative at the start of the study, the authors suggest that early tau buildup can contribute to emerging depressive symptoms independently of amyloid plaque pathology.

The researchers propose that tau accumulation in emotion-related brain hubs like the amygdala, or in tiny brainstem clusters that supply mood-regulating chemicals to the rest of the brain, may underlie these subtle shifts in affect. The study itself did not test specific regions, and tau PET scans cannot measure tau in the brainstem.

To see whether concerns about memory loss were influencing the mood scores, the researchers ran an exploratory check by removing one question from the 15-item depression scale: “Do you feel you have more problems with memory than most people?” When they recalculated the models using the remaining 14 questions, the links between tau buildup and worsening depressive symptoms in the cognitively normal group were no longer statistically significant, and the continuous time model could not produce stable estimates. In the cognitively impaired group, slower increases on the 14-item mood score were unexpectedly associated with faster tau buildup.

The authors suggest that removing the memory question may have narrowed the range of scores too much to detect small statistical effects, but they also note that a person’s awareness of their own subtle cognitive decline likely plays a real part in the link between tau and mood. In the authors’ reading, declining mood and subjective memory complaints may represent overlapping expressions of early brain pathology.

There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because the study is observational, it can show which change tended to come first, not that tau directly causes mood changes. With only about two to three scans per person on average, the timing estimates remain rough, and the effects were small.

Because all participants were screened to exclude clinical depression at the start of the study and mostly reported very mild symptoms, the results cannot rule out the possibility that severe, clinical depression might actively speed up tau spread in a two-way feedback loop, as some animal studies of chronic stress have suggested. In addition, the statistical model used to test directionality over time had to drop more than 40 percent of the cognitively healthy sample because their mood scores never budged, meaning those specific findings apply only to older adults whose mood fluctuates over time.

“One common misinterpretation I want to highlight is that the participants included in these samples are not clinically depressed,” Markova noted. “Our results show that even subclinical changes in mood can significantly track with tau accumulation, and other papers have shown that these subclinical, below-threshold changes can also signify increased risk of going on to develop AD dementia later on. Additionally, the dynamics of these relationships could be very different in samples that have diagnosed depression.”

“As such, one of my long term goals is to follow participants across longer periods of time as some of them transition to a diagnosis of depression and/or a diagnosis of AD dementia,” she said. “This kind of work could give more valuable information about the factors that confer additional risk for or resilience against negative clinical outcomes.”

The lack of statistically significant findings in the mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s dementia group also highlights the difficulty of tracking mood in later stages of disease. The authors note that as memory and thinking decline, self-reported questionnaires become less reliable, and other complex behavioral symptoms or widespread brain changes may overshadow the specific influence of tau. Future studies could combine caregiver ratings with smartphone-based daily mood check-ins or wearable sleep trackers in more racially and ethnically diverse populations, including people with clinical depression, to map out how emotional health and brain biology interact across the full course of aging.

AI could transform mathematics, but humans will still need to be in the loop | Carolin Antos & Balthasar Grabmayr, The Conversation

OpenAI recently announced that one of its AI models solved one of the hardest problems in modern mathematics: the Navier–Stokes problem. The equations at the heart of this problem describe the movement of fluids like water and, according to the scientific definition, air.

The Navier-Stokes equations are essential to understanding phenomena such as ocean currents, blood circulation, and airflow over airplane wings. Yet, mathematicians have struggled for decades to determine whether coherent solutions to these equations exist.

It was for this reason that the US-based Clay Mathematics Institute, which is dedicated to disseminating mathematical knowledge, chose the Navier-Stokes problem as one of its seven Millennium Prize Problems.

These are the most important and challenging unsolved problems in modern mathematics, with a prize of US$1 million (£746,000; €895,000) offered for the first correct solution to each. A problem that resisted generations of mathematicians thus has apparently been solved by artificial intelligence.

While these advancements sent shock waves through the mathematical world, they seem to be only the tip of the iceberg: On October 6 2026, OpenAI presented its solutions to more than 300 longstanding unsolved problems across most areas of mathematics with their new internal model.

Does this mark the end of mathematics as a human endeavour?

Answering this question requires a closer look at mathematical proofs. Broadly speaking, a proof is an argument for a mathematical claim that starts from generally accepted assumptions and proceeds through the different steps of reasoning for the claim.

Before mathematicians accept such an argument as a proof, they need to check that each step is correct. Computers can increasingly help with this task, but for major AI-generated results, human mathematical supervision and expertise remains indispensable.

However, a fully verified proof is not the end of the story. Mathematicians do not only want to know that a theorem is true; they also want to understand why it is true and what can be learned from its proof.

Professor Terence Tao, from Unversity of California, Los Angeles, is one of the world’s leading mathematicians and a prominent supporter of AI’s use in mathematics. He recently coined the term “proof digestion” for the many ways that mathematicians continue to work with a proof after its correctness has been established.

They may reorganise the proof around more natural concepts, streamline a complicated argument, connect it to existing mathematics, or extract methods that can be applied elsewhere. Proof digestion itself can be highly fruitful and produce new mathematics.

Continuing work

Even after a proof has been digested, the mathematical work is rarely done. Major mathematical results often become stepping stones towards new open problems. Important variants of the Navier-Stokes problem, for example, cannot be solved by the methods of the recent proof proposed by OpenAI. This is typical of major breakthroughs: their importance often lies not only in answering a long-standing question, but also in introducing novel mathematical concepts and opening up new lines of research.

Often, one proof simply is not enough. Mathematicians regularly search for new proofs of results that have already been proven. Take, for example, the Pythagorean Theorem: a² +b² = c². This relates to the three lengths of a right-angled triangle.

This result was proved in antiquity, yet a book published in the 1920s collects more than 300 proofs for the Pythagorean Theorem that have been established over the last two millennia. If the only purpose of a proof is to establish that a result is true, all but the earliest of these proofs would be redundant.

Instead, the opposite is the case: different proofs may reveal new insights into why the result is true, uncover new connections to concepts from other mathematical areas, or suggest new methods of generalisation. Thus, proofs are not only valued for verifying mathematical results, but also for the explanation and understanding they provide.

What exactly makes a proof explanatory or illuminating is difficult to pin down – and remains an ongoing topic in the philosophy of mathematics. This makes explanation and understanding much less clear goals for AI than simply producing a correct proof.

The recent advancements in AI will likely transform mathematical practice profoundly. But mathematics is not simply the production of correct answers to unsolved problems. Proofs still need to be understood, reorganised, connected to other results and used to generate new questions.

As AI models become ever more effective at producing proofs, these other parts of mathematical research may become increasingly important. In the near future, it may therefore matter less who – or what – can produce a proof, than whether this can be used for mathematical progress.

$EVGO Q3 2026 earnings: EVgo charging sales rise 29%, but it cuts its outlook

EVgo, an operator of public fast-charging stations for electric cars, grew its main charging business while partner construction shrank and management lowered its full-year targets again. Charging network sales climbed 29% from a year ago to $72 million, lifting charging gross margin by nearly 4 percentage points. However, construction revenue from its eXtend partner program fell by half, leaving total revenue down 1%, and daily electricity dispensed per public charger dropped 4% from a year earlier. Chief executive Badar Khan expressed confidence in reaching sustained profit, yet the company reduced its 2026 plans for revenue, profit, and new stalls, while majority voting shareholder LS Power offered to buy the rest of the business for $2.00 per share.

• Charging network revenue: $𝟕𝟏.𝟖𝐌 (+29% from a year ago)
• Total revenue: $𝟗𝟏.𝟒𝐌 (-1% from a year ago (eXtend -49%))
• Daily usage per public stall: 𝟐𝟖𝟑 𝐤𝐖𝐡 (-4% from a year ago)
• Full-year 2026 outlook: 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐚𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬 (revenue middle down $27.5M; stalls down 313)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because management cut its 2026 targets for a second straight quarter and pushed fourth-quarter break-even out of reach. By our math, the middle of the new full-year profit plan leaves an operating cash loss before one-offs of about $1 million in the fourth quarter, and the stall cut delays the station openings needed to cover rising debt interest and corporate overhead. The good news: charging revenue growth sped up from the first half's 18% pace, and EVgo opened its first Tesla-built Supercharger station in Chicago.

The question now is whether the board accepts LS Power's cash buyout offer or stays independent to fund a delayed station rollout with more debt. Supporters of the standalone plan point to the 29% jump in charging sales and 900 future grocery-store plugs, while skeptics note that falling usage per charger, shrinking capital grants, and $17 million in equipment write-offs leave the 2030 targets out of reach. The special committee's decision on the buyout proposal and fourth-quarter stall openings will settle the path forward.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
EVgo's main business sells electricity to drivers at public fast-charging stations that the company owns and runs. Chief executive Badar Khan said this quarter's performance kept the business advancing toward sustainable profit. Sales from the charging network grew 28.7% from a year ago to $71.8 million, speeding up after two quarters near 18.5%.

Profitability on those electricity sales improved because fixed station costs spread across more revenue. Direct charging costs — electricity, station rent, and maintenance — fell by 3.7 percentage points of charging sales, lifting the charging network gross margin to 39.0% from 35.2% a year ago. Because total electricity dispensed rose 8% to 103 gigawatt-hours while revenue climbed 28.7%, higher revenue per kilowatt-hour and automaker fees did most of the work.

What to watch: the quarterly filing's breakdown of retail charging sales versus automaker contract fees. If one-time fee adjustments from expiring automaker credit programs drove the jump, charging growth will slow back toward stall growth in 2027.

🟢 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐥𝐚 𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐢𝐥 𝐏𝐢𝐩𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝
To attract more drivers — including rideshare and used-EV owners — EVgo is installing North American Charging Standard (NACS) plugs, the connector style developed by Tesla, and deploying EVgo-owned Tesla hardware. During the quarter, the company opened its "First EVgo v4 Supercharger site live in the Chicago area. EVgo Superchargers and EVgo sites with NACS available in Tesla navigation".

Total NACS plugs in operation passed 290 as of November 6, up from 240 in July. The network operator also "Grew relationships with Brixmor and Regency Centers to bring more than 900 new fast chargers to grocery-anchored shopping centers". Appearing on dashboard maps inside Tesla vehicles gives these plugs direct visibility to the largest fleet of electric cars on US roads.

What to watch: whether EVgo hits its earlier goal of 500 NACS plugs by year-end. Reaching that mark requires adding roughly 210 plugs in under two months, a steep jump from the 50 added since July.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐁𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐤-𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐎𝐮𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡
"We are as confident as ever in our path to sustained, positive Adjusted EBITDA and positioning EVgo to drive long-term value for our shareholders," Khan said. Adjusted EBITDA is operating profit before interest, taxes, depreciation, stock pay, and equipment write-offs. Management's multi-year plan calls for reaching $400 million to $600 million on that measure by 2030, starting with a profitable fourth quarter in 2026.

The company cut its 2026 targets across every line for a second quarter in a row, and the new numbers contradict that fourth-quarter goal. Also, EVgo pushed its next-generation 750-kilowatt chargers — previously expected to see initial field installations by year-end — to 2027.

• Full-year revenue plan: cut by $27.5 million at the middle of the range, to $375–400 million
• Full-year Adjusted EBITDA plan: lowered by $7.5 million at the middle, to a loss of $15–30 million
• Fourth-quarter Adjusted EBITDA: a loss of about $0.9 million at the middle of the range by our math
• New stalls added in 2026: reduced by 312.5 stalls at the middle, to 1,075–1,275

Even the reduced construction goal leaves roughly 535 new stalls for the fourth quarter by our math, after EVgo added just 160 in the third. Pushing station openings into next year delays the revenue needed to cover corporate overhead.

What to watch: fourth-quarter Adjusted EBITDA and gross stall additions in the full-year report. A negative EBITDA reading or fewer than 435 fourth-quarter stall additions would put the multi-year ramp further behind schedule.

🔴🔴 𝐃𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐲 𝐔𝐬𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐏𝐞𝐫 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐅𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐞𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫
EVgo makes higher margins when each plug dispenses more electricity per day, because station rent and fixed power fees stay the same as volume rises. Management's long-term targets assume daily volume per public charger climbs past 425 kilowatt-hours over the decade, even as the end of federal EV incentives slows car sales.

Instead, average daily electricity dispensed per public stall fell 4.1% from a year ago to 283 kilowatt-hours per day, down from 295 a year earlier. The company noted that excluding automaker free-charging programs, daily usage per stall rose 7% from a year ago. However, total volume per stall has now fallen against the prior year for three straight quarters, widening from a 1.8% drop in the second quarter.

That matters because the stations pay the bills with total electricity sold, regardless of whether an automaker or a driver picks up the tab. When automaker credit programs expire and those drivers do not keep charging at the same rate, the average station runs below last year's load.

What to watch: fourth-quarter daily usage per stall against last year's 292 kilowatt-hours. Because EVgo plans to open roughly 535 new stalls in the fourth quarter, newly opened plugs will likely keep average usage per stall below last year into early 2027.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭, 𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐆𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐬, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐬 𝐒𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐞𝐳𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡
EVgo funds its network expansion through government project loans, construction grants, and a partner program called eXtend, where it builds stations for partners like Pilot Company. While the $750 million Department of Energy loan and $300 million bank facility let EVgo build without issuing stock, borrowing enlarges its debt load while partner construction winds down.

• Partner construction (eXtend) revenue: $16.2 million, down 49% from $31.9 million a year ago
• Capital offsets (grants, automaker payments, and 30C tax credits): fell 52% to $10.6 million, pushing net capital spending up 482% to $24.2 million
• Total debt: rose 53% since December to $316.6 million, lifting quarterly interest expense 127% from a year ago to $4.3 million

With the federal 30C alternative-fuel tax credit expiring for stations opened after June 2026 and partner builds shrinking, EVgo must shoulder more of each new station's cost using interest-bearing debt.

What to watch: capital offsets and net capital spending in the fourth quarter. If grants cover less than a third of the heavy fourth-quarter construction wave, net debt will climb faster than the operational stall base.

🔴 𝐄𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐖𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐞-𝐎𝐟𝐟𝐬 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫
Khan said EVgo is "prioritizing higher-return sites, improving network utilization and implementing cost efficiencies", while replacing older chargers with faster hardware. Tearing out legacy equipment carries an upfront accounting cost that shows up inside general and administrative overhead.

Losses on disposed equipment and asset write-downs nearly quadrupled to $17.0 million from $4.4 million a year ago. Because of those write-offs, reported general and administrative expenses climbed by 18.8 percentage points of revenue to 65.8% ($60.2 million), pushing the operating loss to $49.4 million. Even excluding write-offs and stock pay, overhead rose by 5.0 percentage points of revenue to 39.3% ($35.9 million, up 13% from a year ago).

What to watch: fourth-quarter overhead excluding one-offs. Through nine months, that expense reached $109.9 million, leaving roughly $40 million for the fourth quarter if EVgo stays within its earlier $148–152 million full-year target.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐎𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐁𝐮𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐄𝐕𝐠𝐨
On November 2, EVgo's board received an unsolicited, non-binding proposal from LS Power Equity Advisors "to acquire all of the outstanding shares of EVgo’s Class A common stock not currently owned by LS Power for $2.00 per share cash consideration". LS Power already holds all 172.8 million Class B shares, giving it majority voting control. The board formed a special committee of independent directors to evaluate the offer.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟕𝟒.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Shrank for a third straight quarter, down 14.8% from $87.0 million in the second quarter and down 27.9% from $102.8 million at the end of 2025 by our math. Deferred revenue is upfront cash from automaker charging-credit and construction contracts not yet recognized as sales, and its decline shows those legacy programs are running off.

𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): -$𝟏𝟓.𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
Cash used in operating activities narrowed by 33% from a $22.8 million outflow a year ago, after a $6.5 million outflow in the second quarter and $35.4 million in the first. Across the first nine months of 2026, operating cash outflow tripled to $57.1 million from $19.0 million a year earlier as EVgo drew down $28.7 million of deferred revenue.

𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Customer accounts topped 1.9 million at the end of September, up about 19% from 1.6 million at the end of 2025. The fast-charging operator added over 95,000 accounts during the third quarter, keeping a steady pace with the 99,000 added in the second quarter and 86,000 in the first.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟑𝟕𝟓–𝟒𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $400–430 million
Cut. The middle of the range fell by $27.5 million to $387.5 million, leaving full-year sales up less than 1% (or 8.2% excluding last year's $25.9 million contract closeout payment by our math). By our math, that leaves $103.9 million for the fourth quarter, down 12.3% from a year ago (up 12.2% excluding the closeout). It is the second cut in two quarters: $0, -$25M, -$27.5M.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $(𝟑𝟎)–$(𝟏𝟓) 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
🠇 cut from $(25)–$(5) million
Cut. Management lowered the middle of the range by $7.5 million to a $22.5 million loss, the second consecutive reduction ($0, -$15M, -$7.5M). By our math, after a $21.6 million loss in the first nine months, the middle of the range leaves a $0.9 million loss for the fourth quarter (-0.9% of implied sales), backing away from earlier plans for a positive fourth quarter.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬: 𝟏,𝟎𝟕𝟓–𝟏,𝟐𝟕𝟓  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from 1,350–1,625
Cut. The company reduced its stall addition plan by 312.5 stalls at the middle of the range to 1,175, the second cut this year (0, -37.5, -312.5). Having added roughly 640 gross stalls across the first three quarters (including 160 in the third), the middle of the plan still requires adding about 535 stalls in the fourth quarter by our math, above last year's fourth-quarter record of 500.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐃𝐢𝐝 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐟𝐞𝐞𝐬 𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐣𝐮𝐦𝐩?
Charging revenue grew 28.7% while electricity dispensed rose only 8%. Because the press release does not separate retail charging from automaker contract fees, investors need the quarterly filing's revenue table to see if expiring automaker credit breakage inflated the quarter.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐍𝐀𝐂𝐒 𝐩𝐥𝐮𝐠𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐜𝐨𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐭 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠?
Daily usage per stall dropped 4.1% from a year ago to 283 kilowatt-hours. Management previously noted that 2025-vintage stations and NACS connectors trailed older plugs; without updated cohort figures in the release, it is unclear if Tesla navigation listings improved NACS usage.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐢𝐫𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 $𝟏𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧?
Write-offs of property and equipment jumped to $17.0 million from $2.9 million in the second quarter, even though net public stalls grew by 90. Management did not disclose how many legacy stalls it removed or impaired during the third quarter.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐠𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔?
Last quarter, EVgo gave full-year ranges for eXtend revenue ($90–95 million), autonomous-vehicle revenue ($40–45 million), and overhead excluding one-offs ($148–152 million). The third-quarter release omitted those lines when cutting total revenue by $27.5 million, leaving where the shortfall landed unexplained.

𝐃𝐢𝐝 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫, 𝐠𝐞𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐩𝐡𝐢𝐜, 𝐨𝐫 𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐨𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟑?
In the second quarter, California generated 46% of charging revenue, one customer accounted for 22% of total sales, and one vendor supplied 76% of charging hardware. Those concentration figures live in the quarterly filing's footnotes and are not yet readable from the release.

text:
$LDI Q3 2026 earnings: LoanDepot's home equity margins rise, but its loan outlook drops

LoanDepot, the non-bank mortgage and home equity lender, widened its lending margins while its loan volume and cash balance shrank. Revenue excluding servicing valuation swings fell 7% from a year ago, and net loss excluding one-offs widened to $31 million. Chief executive Anthony Hsieh pointed to rapid growth in higher-margin home equity lines, but the fourth-quarter plan calls for total loan originations to drop 32% from a year ago at the middle of the range.

• Revenue, excluding one-offs: $𝟑𝟎𝟐.𝟐𝐌 (-7.1% from a year ago)
• Net loss, excluding one-offs: $𝟑𝟎.𝟖𝐌 ($2.7M loss a year ago)
• Pull-through weighted margin: 𝟑.𝟗𝟗% (above 3.60–3.90% plan)
• Q4 funded loan volume outlook: $𝟒.𝟓–𝟔.𝟓𝐁 (-32% from a year ago at middle)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because selling $19 billion of mortgage servicing rights across the third and fourth quarters and buying back $87 million of bonds at a discount did not stop cash from falling or losses from widening. The good news: home equity lending pushed margins above the company's plan, and management doubled its annualized cost-savings target to $25 million.

The question now is whether home equity fees and cost cuts can stop the cash burn before the 2027 and 2028 bond maturities come due. Either the expanded savings programme and wider margins cover corporate overhead on a smaller loan base, or shrinking servicing fees and lower fourth-quarter volume drain more liquidity. The fourth-quarter cash balance and any debt refinancing terms will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐇𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐄𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐋𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐬
Chief executive Anthony Hsieh wants to grow home equity lending, which lets homeowners borrow against their home value without giving up low-rate first mortgages. He said loanDepot "ranked among the top three non-bank home equity lenders during the third quarter based on volume".

That product shift drove fee income and lending margins above the company's plan. Because home equity credit lines do not use a traditional interest rate lock, their revenue sits over a smaller rate-lock base and pushes the pull-through weighted margin higher.

• Other loan originations, which include home equity: $1.63 billion, up 118% from a year ago and 46% from last quarter
• Origination fee income: $64.6 million, up 86% from a year ago
• Pull-through weighted gain on sale margin: 3.99%, up 0.54 percentage points from last quarter

What to watch: the quarterly filing's breakdown of exact home equity volume and terms with technology partner Figure. If home equity growth merely replaces traditional cash-out refinancing, total lending revenue will keep shrinking.

🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥
The California-based lender is automating underwriting and closing tasks to cut what it spends per loan. This quarter it raised its target for annualized cost savings from $12 million to $25 million, expected through the rest of 2026.

Marketing and advertising spending fell 26.5% from a year ago to $27.7 million, dropping 2.6 percentage points as a share of revenue. Hsieh said the cost to produce a loan fell 16% from a year ago while funded loan units rose 33%.

What to watch: non-volume operating expenses in the fourth quarter. If the expanded $25 million savings programme takes hold, personnel and administrative costs should fall alongside the planned drop in loan volume.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐁𝐨𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐔𝐧𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐬
LoanDepot faces bond maturities in 2027 and 2028 while seeking to preserve cash and reduce its debt load. Finance chief David Hayes said the third-quarter asset sales and bond buybacks "strengthened our liquidity position and enhanced financial flexibility".

During the quarter the lender sold about $10 billion of Agency mortgage servicing rights for $165.7 million in net proceeds and repurchased $87 million of senior notes at an average price of 88% of face value. That trimmed net debt obligations by $114.1 million from June to $2.02 billion.

Even after collecting $165.7 million from servicing sales, unrestricted cash fell by $14.7 million from June to $214.4 million, less than half of the $459.2 million held a year ago. Total stockholders' equity dropped 28.2% from a year ago to $310.9 million, and Hayes offered no timeline for refinancing the remaining bonds.

What to watch: a formal agreement to extend or exchange the 2027 senior notes, and agency net-worth covenant headroom in the quarterly filing. Continued cash burn narrows the company's bargaining power with creditors.

🔴🔴 𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐏𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐚 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐩 𝐕𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩
Third-quarter funded loan volume fell 11.8% from the second quarter to $7.05 billion as higher mortgage rates slowed traditional home buying and refinancing. Traditional rate-and-term refinance volume dropped 63.3% from the second quarter to $287.1 million.

For the fourth quarter, management's plan calls for funded originations of $4.5 billion to $6.5 billion and pull-through weighted rate locks of $3.25 billion to $5.25 billion. At the middle of those ranges, funded volume drops 31.6% from a year ago and rate locks fall 41.6%.

Although the outlook projects pull-through weighted margins rising to a midpoint of 4.45%, higher margins do not offset the volume drop. By our math, the middle of the fourth-quarter lock and margin ranges points to about $189 million of origination revenue, down 19.9% from a year ago and 15.6% from the third quarter.

What to watch: fourth-quarter origination revenue against that $189 million mark. A drop of that size makes it harder to cover fixed corporate overhead and reach breakeven.

🔴 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐖𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞
LoanDepot has posted a loss excluding one-offs in every quarter of the past two years. In the third quarter, net loss excluding one-offs widened to $30.8 million from $29.4 million in the second quarter and $2.7 million a year ago.

While marketing and corporate interest expenses fell, employee compensation and direct lending fees took a much larger share of revenue than a year ago because total revenue shrank 5.0%.

• Personnel expense (salaries, commissions, and benefits): 55.8% of revenue, up 6.0 percentage points from a year ago
• Direct origination expense (underwriting and closing costs): 11.3% of revenue, up 4.5 percentage points from a year ago
• Other interest expense: $38.0 million, helped by a $4.1 million one-off gain on discounted bond buybacks ($42.1 million before the gain by our math)

What to watch: quarterly net loss excluding one-offs in the fourth quarter. With lending revenue set to fall further in the winter slowdown, losses will widen unless personnel costs drop sharply.

🔴 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐨 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥
The servicing portfolio — loans on which loanDepot collects monthly payments for a recurring fee and uses to win repeat business at zero marketing cost — shrank by $7.6 billion in the quarter to $115.8 billion. After selling $10 billion of Agency servicing rights in the third quarter, the lender closed the sale of another $9 billion of Government servicing rights in October.

• Refinance recapture rate (share of paying-off servicing clients kept by loanDepot): fell to 52% from 68% in Q2 and 73% in Q1
• Loans 60+ days past due: $2.37 billion, or 2.0% of the portfolio, up from 1.7% in Q2 and 1.5% a year ago
• Loans eligible for repurchase on the balance sheet: $1.50 billion, up 40.0% from December 2025
• Partner and legal disclosures: economics shared with Figure and potential cybersecurity legal settlements remain undisclosed prior to the quarterly filing

Selling $19 billion of servicing rights across the third and fourth quarters removes a steady fee stream while lower recapture and rising delinquencies weaken the remaining portfolio. What to watch: fourth-quarter servicing fee income after the October sale, which will show how much recurring revenue was given up for liquidity.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐖𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡 𝐨𝐧 𝐇𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐝
Management cited high mortgage rates, a shortage of new and existing homes for sale, and ongoing market volatility as headwinds holding back both home purchases and traditional refinancing. Those conditions kept industry-wide mortgage volume low during the summer selling season, though record homeowner equity continued to support demand for second-lien home equity lines and cash-out refinancing.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐀𝐯𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐛𝐨𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐.𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Unused credit lines that fund newly originated mortgages before they are sold rose from $1.9 billion in June and $1.8 billion a year ago. Total funding capacity held steady at $4.4 billion, while drawn warehouse debt fell 24.2% from June to $1.85 billion as loans held for sale declined.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟐𝟑𝟐.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Diluted shares of Class A and Class D stock rose 9.9% from 211.4 million a year ago and 0.3% from the second quarter as holders converted Class B and Class C shares. Including all unconverted shares, total diluted share count rose 2.1% from a year ago to 338.3 million on stock-based compensation.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐐𝟒 𝐋𝐨𝐚𝐧 𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞: $𝟒.𝟓–𝟔.𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
New. The fourth-quarter plan has funded mortgage volume dropping to a midpoint of $5.5 billion, down 22.0% from the third quarter and 31.6% from $8.04 billion a year ago. While winter seasonality normally slows home buying, the year-over-year drop shows high interest rates weighing heavily on traditional first mortgages.

𝐐𝟒 𝐏𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐰𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞: $𝟑.𝟐𝟓–𝟓.𝟐𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
New. Rate locks adjusted for expected funding probability are set to fall 24.2% from the third quarter and 41.6% from a year ago at the $4.25 billion middle of the range. Because home equity lines do not record an interest rate lock, the growing share of home equity loans depresses this figure relative to funded loans.

𝐐𝟒 𝐏𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐰𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧: 𝟒𝟐𝟓–𝟒𝟔𝟓 𝐛𝐩𝐬  ⇗ accelerating
New. The middle of the range is 4.45%, up 0.46 percentage points from the third quarter and 1.21 percentage points from 3.24% a year ago. Even with that higher margin, by our math the middle of the lock and margin ranges points to about $189 million in origination revenue, down 19.9% from a year ago.

𝐐𝟒 𝐆𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧: 𝟑𝟏𝟓–𝟑𝟓𝟓 𝐛𝐩𝐬  ⇗ accelerating
New. LoanDepot introduced an explicit outlook for its standard gain on sale margin, which divides lending revenue by funded loans rather than rate locks. The 3.35% middle of the range is up 0.17 percentage points from 3.18% in the third quarter and up 0.41 percentage points from 2.94% a year ago.

𝐐𝟒 𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐬: 𝐃𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫  ⇘ decelerating
New. Management expects total expenses to fall below the third quarter's $335.7 million, citing lower volume-driven commissions and direct lending costs alongside the expanded $25 million annualized cost-savings programme.

text:
Pope Leo XIV has delivered a challenge to Argentina's President Javier Milei that deserves to be heard far beyond Argentina. But it is not quite the attack on free-market economics that some might wish it to be.

Addressing Milei and Argentina's political leaders in Buenos Aires yesterday, Leo offered something considerably more demanding than a partisan economic programme. He reminded those exercising political authority that power has limits, that economic growth must serve the common good, and that the dignity of the human person cannot be subordinated to the demands of either the market or the state.

This is a distinction worth recovering. Catholic social teaching has never regarded economic freedom as an end in itself, but neither has it treated private enterprise, property or individual initiative as inherently suspect. The Church recognises their legitimate contribution to human flourishing while insisting that economic arrangements must be judged by their consequences for actual human beings, particularly those who are poor, vulnerable or unable to compete on equal terms.

The fundamental question is not simply whether an economy grows, but whether that growth serves the whole human person. A society may become wealthier while remaining profoundly unjust if prosperity is purchased at the expense of those least able to defend themselves. Equally, a state that claims to act in the interests of the vulnerable does not thereby acquire unlimited authority over families, communities or economic life.

What makes Leo's intervention particularly significant is that he refuses to separate economic justice from the wider Catholic understanding of human dignity. His concern for the disadvantaged belongs to the same moral vision as his defence of unborn children, the elderly, the sick and those living with disabilities. These are not competing political priorities from which Catholics may select according to their ideological preferences. They arise from the same conviction: that every human life possesses an intrinsic worth which neither governments nor markets have the authority to confer or withdraw.

There is a temptation, especially in our increasingly polarised political culture, to read every papal intervention as an endorsement of one political faction and a rebuke to another. Yet Catholic social doctrine is not a convenient collection of arguments with which to reinforce positions we already hold. It is a challenge to examine those positions against principles that precede and transcend our political loyalties.

Leo did not prescribe a particular tax regime, spending programme or economic model. Nor did he suggest that political leaders can escape moral responsibility simply by appealing to market forces. He reminded them that political authority is a form of service, economic activity has a moral purpose, and human dignity must remain the measure of both.

The Church's task is not to baptise the political Right or the political Left, but to insist upon truths that both are capable of forgetting.

That is why Leo's address matters. It is not merely a message for Javier Milei or Argentina. It is a reminder to every Catholic tempted to make political ideology the standard by which the Church's teaching is judged, rather than allowing the Church's teaching to challenge political ideology.

text:
The first primary school I went to was a C of E (Church of England) school. C of E schools are state funded, secular, and free to attend. Despite being secular, they are open to children of any background including religion, and are meant to retain a Christian characteristic. The one I attended certainly had a Christian characteristic. It was called Christ Church School, and was in St Leonards-on-Sea, Hastings. It had a large gothic church (which is still there) called Christ Church next to it. Assemblies were held in the church, where hymns were sung, and the Lord's Prayer was recited. The school itself moved to newly built premises fairly nearby, after either my first or second year at the school. My brother, who's around two years my senior, wanted to move schools, so I moved with him to the final primary school I attended, which was West St Leonards School in Hastings. This school was likely a C of E school as well, as there were morning assemblies in which hymns were sung, and although I have no clear recollection, the Lord's Prayer was likely recited on occasion. This school had a large recreational field attached to it, and two fairly large playgrounds. The secondary school (which in the US and other places is called a high school) I attended was a state school (which is free to attend and open to those within the catchment area). Fee paying private schools in the UK are also referred to as public schools, the linguistic reasoning behind this was because they were open to children from any locality. In the US, Canada, Australia and other places, a public school refers to a free to attend state funded school. The secondary school I went to was called The Grove School, and it was for all intents and purposes a fairly rough school. 
Neither of my parents are religious, but are spiritual sentient beings nonetheless. This is as true today as it was then.
As a child and as an adult, I would visit my maternal grandparents in Hove, East Sussex. Hove was then a town, but is now part of Brighton & Hove City. I remember my grandmother with fondness, especially of the times when I would visit her as a child. I remember my grandfather as being a fairly grumpy distant man, but I understand that he was someone who was ultimately able to provide for his family. They ran a successful business together, which I think mostly involved sourcing furniture for restaurants in the Brighton & Hove area. Their names were Jack and Norma Waring. Norma died aged 90 in 2016, and to the best of my recollection, Jack died around ten years earlier at the age of 88. I don't think they would have described themselves as religious, but from time to time, both Jack and Norma attended Brighton & Hove Reform synagogue, and later Brighton & Hove Progressive Synagogue. Neither of them were particularly political, and their attendance at either synagogue would have been for the community value that was offered. As a pre-adolescent child I went once with my grandmother to the Reform synagogue, and it was during Hanukkah, which was something I had not heard of before. I remember there was food, some other children there, and a talk by the Rabbi that included the story attached to the festival. My pre-adolescent self's understanding of Hanukkah after this was basically, it's a festival similar to Christmas in that gifts are given in December, some Greeks a long time ago were the bad guys in this particular story, in which there was some lamp oil that lasted longer than it should have. 
My grandparents and extended family celebrated Christmas, and with my parents and siblings, I would often spend time with them over this period.

Here are some photos of me in my younger years. 
I'm holding a baby cousin (my maternal uncle Richard's daughter) in the photo where I'm 15 years old, on Boxing Day, in Lewes, East Sussex. 

In the photo with the Boarder Collie dog, I'm standing next to my older brother Joe who's holding the dog's leash, and I was likely around five or six years old in the photo. The dog's name was Fido and he belonged to my paternal uncle Christopher, which means the photo was likely taken on the boarders of Yeovil in Somerset where Christopher lived. 

In the photo where I'm wearing my mother's lavender coloured scarf I am likely around seven or eight years old, but I don't know where the photo was taken.

The photo with the swimmers in what looks like a small lake was taken in Kyiv/Kiev, Ukraine, and I'm standing near my older brother Joe who's to the right in the photo and a nephew of my paternal uncle Philip's wife, who's to the left in the photo. I'm fairly sure the photo was taken in summer 1999, which would make me 17 years old in the photo.

It's likely that my mother Rosalind took each photo except for the one in Ukraine, as I'm quite sure she wasn't on the trip with us there.

text:
While Remembering St. Charles Borromeo
     (A) Today is the feast day of St. Charles Borromeo. He was a great Archbishop of Milan, the largest diocese in Italy.

     The Council of Trent, which had to resolve many problems, had taken place at that time. The Protestant Reformation contained heresies and denied the sacraments—rejecting the Eucharist and the true priesthood, and the council served as a Counter-Reformation.

     However, there were also internal issues within the Church that required a thorough reform. The powers of the nobility had weakened the Church, and the formation of the clergy had been greatly neglected.

     The Council lasted 18 years, under the leadership of three popes (Our Second Vatican Council lasted four years under two popes: John XXIII, who began it, and Paul VI, who continued and concluded it). A great deal of work followed the Council of Trent: many diocesan synods in Milan and in many other dioceses, partly under the influence of St Charles Borromeo, truly brought forth the fruits envisioned by the Council of Trent.

     (B) Many years after the Second Vatican Council, we must regrettably acknowledge today that it has not been sufficiently fruitful. It has been under constant attack by those who claim to be “continuing” the Council—arguing that its “reform” was not completed—while, on the other hand, there are those who suspect that the Council contains assertions contrary to the Tradition of the Church.

     Following the example of St. Charles Borromeo was the Archbishop of Kraków, who later became Pope John Paul II. He worked strenuously with his diocesan community to ensure that the Council’s documents were thoroughly understood and their teachings put into practice. Obviously, this did not happen in all the dioceses of the Church.

     Popes Paul VI, John Paul II and Benedict XVI did a great deal to ensure that the Council achieved its desired purpose, and they succeeded to a certain extent.

     Many bishops found themselves in difficulty after the Council, because they did not know how to explain to the faithful precisely what the Council had changed in the life of the Church and what it had not changed. The Holy See, under the leadership of Cardinal Ratzinger, following extensive consultations throughout the Church, drew up a “Catechism” containing the entire dogmatic, moral and liturgical doctrine of the Church, set out in a systematic order. However, the sheer volume of the “Catechism” may have put people off, and not many have actually studied it.

     (C) Forces opposed to the Council have been troubling the Church throughout these years.

     Regrettably, in these recent years we have had the supreme head of our Church who, whilst proclaiming the great validity of the Second Vatican Council, was in fact not faithful to its decrees.

     Pope Francis was certainly admirable for his kindness and his special concern for the poor and the weak. However, this kindness and predilection have lacked balance; he seemed to believe that, out of compassion for these people, one can even compromise on the truth.

     He believed that the primary danger within the Church is clericalism, and thought that through a general consultation of the People of God he could succeed in having his line of thinking approved. He was certainly a reformist. He destroyed many good things built up by his predecessors.

     He did not appreciate the entire struggle in defence of Orthodoxy waged by John Paul II and Pope Benedict XVI.

     He abolished the Synod of Bishops which had been established by Paul VI towards the end of the Second Vatican Council as a sort of continuation, miniature version, of the Council, intended to provide the Pope with counsel from the episcopate of the entire Church through their elected representatives.

     This Synod has been done away with, and in its place, something else has been created: what might be termed “a democratic consultation of the entire People of God” (See my address to the General Congregation of Cardinals prior to the conclave).

     (D) How can the Pope directly consult the entire People of God? Pope Francis said that a shepherd must have a “feel” for the scent of his sheep, but how can a Pope in Rome possess this sense? It is the bishops who can truly sense the scent of their own sheep, and they, in turn, bring this insight to the Pope so that he may see what today’s problems are and how to tackle them.

     By emphasizing the etymological meaning of the word “synod,” this Synod on Synodality has overlooked the historical reality of what synods actually are. A synod is, by definition, a matter for the bishops.

     The fact is that behind all this lay “hidden agendas”.

     After all these years of the synodal process, they have failed to get their “hidden agendas” (in fact, not so “hidden”) fulfilled. There was relentless manipulation and strict control of the process, yet it was a failure. Despite every effort to stifle genuine discussion, the objectives that the Pope evidently entrusted to the Synod Secretariat were not achieved.

     Even within the limited time for free speech in the assembly, it was evident: that Synod members rejected those objectives: changing the hierarchical constitution of the Church, ordaining women to the priesthood starting with the diaconate, the free choice of celibacy for the Roman clergy, and the sexual morality radically “updated” (?) under the L.G.B.T.Q. banner.

     As this attempt failed, the Pope then removed these “controversial” topics from the Synod and handed them over to “study groups”, the formation criteria of which were unknown. And these groups were expected to report their conclusions directly to the Pope.

     (E) That the cause of homosexuals had been one of the “hidden agendas” was highlighted by the publication of the document “Fiducia Supplicans”, which approved the blessing of same-sex couples (issued between two sessions of the ongoing Synod, without consulting the Synod participants).

     The document threatened to cause a terrible breaking up of the Church; Pope Francis and the Cardinal had to appease the public outcry with an attitude of “condescending understanding”, yet without any genuine retraction.

     That the cause of homosexuals is particularly close to Pope Francis’ heart is evident in his special favor toward Father James Martin, S.J., of “Outreach,” as well as his famous quote: “Who am I to judge?”

     And recently, something has happened which made us realize, to our horror, that the whole lengthy discourse on the synodal process is intended to provide a tool for justifying anything.

     At the end of Section D, we mentioned “study groups”. Now, the final report of Group 9 has been published, in which assuming (arbitrarily) that the synodal method is sacrosanct when it comes to the study of homosexuality, they reached the conclusion that the sexual act between a homosexual couple is a gift from God!? Is this not blasphemy? It is incredible that such a thing could appear in a publication issued by the Holy See!

     Confusion has reigned for years, but now it has reached the bottom.

     The groups are supposed to submit the results of their study to the Pope; now the Pope is Pope Leo, did he see the report before its publication? And did he give his consent?

     Everything that happens in the Church falls under the jurisdiction of the reigning Pope (he could even cut short an ongoing Ecumenical Council. There is a saying: “no Pope rules from the grave”.)

     [By the way, during the Jubilee Year, there was that “triumphal entry” into St Peter’s, which was obviously a “Pride Parade”– a true desecration of the Basilica – and yet no protest from the Holy See!?]

     (F) It is said that the doctrine of the faith does not consist solely of sexual morality. This is true; the most important thing is the love of God. Yet, no one rejects God for no reason; rather, it is always because one is drawn towards some other values—one ends up worshipping another (false) divinity.

     St Paul, in his Letter to the Romans, says that the most obvious sign of the rejection of God is precisely this sin of homosexuality.

     The enemies of God, the three enemies of our salvation are: our passions, the world and the devil. But where does the destruction of God in souls begin? Precisely with this deviation from sexual morality! For concupiscence lies within our flesh, and when indulged, it becomes an addiction, causing us to lose the power of the will. That is why even the devil says that the most important thing is to destroy the family.

     Moreover, it is not true that we insist solely on sexual morality; the question of the Church’s hierarchical structure is far more fundamental today. Jesus founded the Church upon the apostles, with Peter as their head. Now the Church must be guided by the bishops, with the Pope at their head. But the entire course of the recent synod on synodality ignores the importance of the bishops; it is no longer a true synod. By emphasising the etymological meaning of the word “synodality” as “traveling together” or “participation”, the significance of the historical reality of synods has been sidelined: synods and councils of bishops within the Church, and the synod presided over by the bishop within the diocese.

     With the conclusion of the second session of the Synod, a final document was approved, which Pope Francis has incorporated into his own magisterium. He stated that it is not strictly normative; rather, each episcopal conference is to implement it experimentally, in the manner deemed most appropriate for its own local culture. But in this way, we will end up resembling the Anglicans (no offense intended toward the Anglicans, but we are different).

     (G) The world is in a state of great confusion.

      I was not present at the recent Consistory in June, but I noted from the press that during the discussion on the question “In what kind of world are we to carry out our mission today?”, many cardinals remarked that the fundamental problem is the loss of meaning, which is why an ever-increasing number of young people are taking their own lives.

     We possess the solid doctrine that gives meaning to life, for we know that God created us for eternal life. This truth resides within the Catholic Church, but only if the Catholic Church remains faithful to the entirety of the doctrine handed down from the Apostles.

     If we now seek to accommodate the world, we betray our own mission.

     So let us put a stop to this so-called “Synod on Synodality”!

     May the Holy Father grant Cardinal Grech and Cardinal Hollerich a long vacation; he cannot entrust the governance of the Church to the Secretariat for the Synods; on the other hand, closer communion between the bishops and the Pope, between the cardinals and the Pope, is most welcome.

     People are longing for something solid. Sadly, the world is dominated by modern atheistic philosophy and nihilism, and an attitude of relativism is now permeating the Church. Let us strive to testify to the intact treasure of our faith, so as to offer hope to all of humanity.

     The Holy Father should also replace the head of the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith.

     It is well known that this cardinal has written things in the past that he would not write today.

     But most disconcerting of all is the letter Pope Francis wrote to him upon his appointment as head of the Dicastery; in that letter, the Pope assigned him a task quite different from the one traditionally entrusted to that office—no longer the defense of doctrine, but rather to encourage the theologians.

     I am old, but I believe my mind is still clear. I thank those who have formed me with the doctrine of the Church, which is a great gift that the Lord has bestowed upon so many of us. Let those who are keenly aware of the urgent need for the Church to return to the unity of the true faith, raise their voices to encourage and support the Holy Father as he undertakes this arduous task.

     Of course, we must pray intensely for the Holy Father; only Almighty God can grant him the steadfastness and prudence he needs.

“May the Lord preserve him,

and give him life,

and make him blessed upon the earth.”

Translated 6/11/2026 #synodality #synodofbishops #PopeFrancis #Jesuits #Grech #Hollerich #DicasteryfortheDoctrineoftheFaith #Jamesmartin https://t.co/g9ABYTvwzn

text:
ELYSIUM WITHDRAWALS — WHAT EVERYONE NEEDS TO UNDERSTAND BEFORE MOVING THEIR FUNDS
1H TO MAINNET 

There's been a lot of confusion about withdrawals on @Enter_Elysium  so here's a breakdown of how everything works, why withdrawals take time, and what you should be careful about

1 — DEPOSITS VS WITHDRAWALS

Moving HYPE from HyperEVM to Elysium is fast, usually taking seconds to minutes

Once your funds arrive, you're free to trade, buy, sell and interact with supported platforms

But moving HYPE back from Elysium to HyperEVM works differently

2 — WHY DO WITHDRAWALS TAKE APPROXIMATELY 5.5–7 DAYS?

Elysium is built using Arbitrum Orbit's Optimistic Rollup technology

Unlike deposits, withdrawals require a security verification process called the challenge period

The configured period is approximately 483,840 HyperEVM blocks, equivalent to roughly 5.5 days at current block times

Here's what happens behind the scenes

You request a withdrawal on Elysium
The rollup publishes a state assertion to HyperEVM
A challenge period allows invalid assertions to be disputed
Once the relevant assertion is confirmed, your withdrawal can be finalized
You may need to execute a final claim transaction to receive your HYPE on HyperEVM

IMPORTANT DETAIL

The waiting period doesn't necessarily begin the second you click withdraw

It depends on when the relevant state assertion is posted and confirmed

Also, the challenge period is measured in blocks, meaning the actual waiting time can vary

Your funds won't necessarily appear automatically when the countdown ends

3 — CAN YOU WITHDRAW FASTER?

Potentially, yes

Third-party Fast Exit providers can advance their own liquidity to users and collect the canonical withdrawal once it finalizes

Some of India's most fascinating history lies in places many of us have never even heard of.

Ranivas Mound in Kesariya, East Champaran, Bihar, has been declared an archaeological site of national importance by the Central Government.

Spread across 1.63 acres, the site will now receive greater recognition and protection under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958.

Bihar currently has 70 ASI-protected sites, while 3,686 sites across India are under the ASI's care.

For a state with such a rich historical and cultural legacy, this is an opportunity to bring more attention to Bihar's heritage. The next step should be preserving these sites, improving visitor access and helping more people discover the history that Bihar has to offer.

Bihar's history deserves to be recognised, preserved and celebrated, not just within the state, but across the country.

text:
“Don’t you get frustrated Mike when an athlete ignores your advice but listens to Dave in the FB running group?”

I get asked this lots, and in truth one that I definitely used to say yes to. 

I don’t anymore, I’ve learned that offering advice & guidance on the things to do, more than the things an athlete wants or thinks they need won’t always be received well.

There will always be a bias to hear what you want & an army of therapists & professionals happy to offer you what you want & think you need more than what is the best thing or right thing to do.

I completely understand the mentality of the athlete, they aren’t choosing to ignore me (or anyone else for that matter), it’s not personal.

The quick fix is a very tempting path.

Sometimes athletes need to get things wrong, make the mistakes that delay performance & rehab improvements before they are ready to take your advice (please don’t interpret that as we are always right, we are not!).

Sometimes they’ll take the path that looks appealing but isn’t successful & they will come back when they are ready to listen.

When this happens then I’ve had some of the best patient encounters & relationships of my career. 

Sometimes they will find another path that works for them (there’s many ways to skin the rehab & injury cat!).

It took me years to realise this though & I understand if & when therapists get frustrated. 

If it’s someone seeking advice & support then my role is to offer support & allow them to decide what they want to do.

I do get frustrated if it’s an athlete under my care who consistently or repeatedly ignores advice, after all, you came to me for help &  I’m trying my hardest to work together to help you achieve your goals. 

However, a long honest chat & understanding of the reasons they aren’t engaging often finds a resolution & the root cause is often miscommunication and assumption which are easily fixed. 

Take home: therapists, don’t get so stressed- people are allowed to do their own thing, and allowed to choose who & what they listen to.

Athletes, feel free to seek as many opinions as you want, that’s your prerogative & you should run away from anyone saying it isn’t.

⚔️🕊️ THE ELEVENTH MONTH, ELEVENTH DAY, ELEVENTH HOUR 🕊️⚔️

A Roman soldier. A divided cloak. A Benedictine monastery. And the day the guns fell silent.

November 11 is Veterans Day in America. Armistice Day in much of the world.

But long before the trenches of France, November 11 was already the feast of a soldier.

Saint Martin of Tours.

In the fourth century, Martin was serving in the Roman army when he encountered a freezing beggar outside the gates of Amiens.

He drew his sword.

Not to fight.

He cut his military cloak in two and gave half to the stranger.

That night, Martin dreamed of Christ wearing the very cloak he had given away.

"I was naked and you clothed me." (Matthew 25:36)

Martin eventually refused to take up arms again, declaring himself a soldier of Christ. According to his early biographer, he offered to stand unarmed before the enemy rather than fight. But the opposing forces sought peace before the battle began.

Martin went on to become a monk and bishop.

And here's a connection especially dear to the Benedictine tradition.

When Saint Benedict established Monte Cassino in the sixth century, he replaced a pagan shrine with a chapel dedicated to Saint Martin.

A Roman soldier's act of mercy had become part of the spiritual foundation of Western monasticism.

Then came November 11, 1918.

The eleventh month.

The eleventh day.

The eleventh hour.

After four years of catastrophic war, the guns of the Western Front fell silent.

On the feast of Saint Martin.

We don't know that the date was chosen because of the saint. But the coincidence is extraordinary.

And the symbolism is difficult to miss.

A soldier who used his sword to clothe the poor.

A soldier who laid down his weapons.

A soldier whose feast would one day coincide with the end of the Great War.

This isn't a condemnation of soldiers. The Church has always recognized the legitimacy of defending the innocent and the sacrifice of those who serve.

But it is a reminder of what peace is ultimately for.

Not merely the absence of gunfire.

The presence of charity.

🎶 "The Eleventh Month, Eleventh Day, Eleventh Hour (Saint Martin of Tours)" 

To our veterans: thank you for your service.

To the fallen: may God grant you eternal rest.

Saint Martin of Tours, patron of soldiers, pray for us.
