text:
MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body | Massachusetts Institute of Technology, ScienceDaily

MIT scientists have developed nanoparticles that reprogram immune cells directly inside the body to attack cancer and harmful immune cells, eliminating tumors and reversing liver damage in mouse experiments. The breakthrough could make powerful immune therapies dramatically simpler and less expensive while opening new possibilities for treating cancer and autoimmune diseases.

---

MIT researchers have developed a new technique that allows them to transform immune cells into cancer fighters directly inside the body, potentially making advanced treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases much easier to produce and administer.

The method focuses on natural killer (NK) cells, a type of immune cell that can be engineered to recognize and destroy harmful cells. These include cancerous T cells and T cells that mistakenly attack healthy tissue, contributing to conditions such as lymphoma and autoimmune hepatitis.

Rather than extracting immune cells from a patient and modifying them in a laboratory, the researchers use tiny particles made of fatty molecules to deliver genetic instructions directly to NK cells. These instructions, carried by messenger RNA, tell the cells to produce specialized proteins that help them identify and eliminate diseased T cells.

The resulting cells, known as CAR NK cells, could eventually be used against several different diseases. By carrying out the engineering process inside the body, the new approach could eliminate much of the time, expense, and complexity involved in manufacturing personalized immune cell therapies.

"The manufacturing challenges with CAR NK cells are significant. The idea here is you can deliver a nanoparticle that will modify your own NK cells with a CAR construct and teach them to attack tumor cells," says Daniel Anderson, a professor in MIT's Department of Chemical Engineering and a member of MIT's Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science.

Anderson is the senior author of the research, published in Nature Biotechnology. The lead authors are MIT postdoctoral researcher Yuang Chen and graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal. Robert Langer, MIT's David H. Koch Institute Professor, also contributed to the study.

Why Current Cancer Immunotherapies Are So Complex

Immune cell engineering has already transformed treatment options for certain cancers. During the past decade, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved seven cancer therapies that use genetically modified T cells, known as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells.

These treatments work by equipping T cells with specially designed receptors that recognize particular markers, or antigens, on other cells. When an engineered T cell encounters its designated target, such as a protein associated with cancer, it becomes activated and attacks the cell carrying that marker.

CAR T cell therapies have been especially effective against blood cancers arising from B cells. These include certain forms of leukemia and lymphoma, as well as multiple myeloma.

However, preparing these treatments involves several complicated steps. Doctors first collect blood from the patient and send it to a specialized facility. There, technicians separate the T cells, genetically modify them to produce the desired receptors, and grow enough engineered cells for treatment. The finished cells must then be transported back to the hospital and infused into the patient.

Natural Killer Cells Offer a Different Way to Fight Cancer

Scientists have recently been exploring whether natural killer cells could be engineered in a similar way. One important advantage is their potential to treat cancers and autoimmune conditions involving abnormal T cells.

Trying to use CAR T cells against diseased T cells creates a major problem. Because both the engineered cells and their intended targets are T cells, the modified cells may recognize and destroy one another. This unintended attack can undermine the treatment.

Natural killer cells avoid this complication because they are a different type of immune cell. They can be programmed to attack harmful T cells without triggering the same problem of engineered T cells killing each other.

"NK cells can treat these T cell malignancies -- not only T cell cancer, but also T cell autoimmune diseases," Chen says.

Producing CAR NK cells outside the body, however, still requires much of the specialized equipment, labor, and processing associated with CAR T cell manufacturing. To overcome these limitations, the MIT team investigated whether NK cells could instead be engineered "in vivo," meaning directly inside the body.

"If a patient can just get an infusion of nanoparticles, it would dramatically simplify the process and reduce costs," Anderson says.

Although researchers are actively developing CAR NK cell therapies for cancer and autoimmune disorders, none have received FDA approval.

How mRNA Nanoparticles Reprogram Immune Cells

The MIT team designed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) capable of transporting messenger RNA into natural killer cells. The mRNA carries instructions for producing a chimeric antigen receptor that directs the modified immune cell toward a specific target.

The technology can be adapted to recognize different proteins depending on the disease being treated. For example, the researchers can provide instructions for a receptor that recognizes CD19, a protein found on B cells, or CD3, a protein present on T cells, including those responsible for autoimmune attacks.

To help the nanoparticles reach the correct immune cells, the scientists covered their surfaces with antibody fragments. These fragments recognize and attach to receptors on NK cells, helping deliver the genetic instructions where they are needed.

Once inside an NK cell, the mRNA directs the production of the new receptor, giving the immune cell the ability to recognize and attack its intended target.

The researchers then tested whether this approach could efficiently reprogram NK cells and whether the resulting cells could combat cancer and autoimmune disease in mice.

Reprogrammed Immune Cells Eliminate Tumors in Mice

The initial experiments produced encouraging results. After injecting the nanoparticles into mice, the researchers successfully modified approximately 80 percent of the NK cells they were targeting.

They next investigated whether these engineered cells could attack tumors. In mice with an aggressive form of melanoma, three of the five animals treated with nanoparticles designed to direct NK cells against the cancer experienced complete remission.

The researchers also tested the technique against T cell lymphoma using humanized mice. These animals receive transfusions of human blood cells, temporarily giving them immune systems that share certain characteristics with those of humans.

In this model, the treatment produced substantial tumor destruction. After five injections of the nanoparticles, the tumors were completely eliminated.

Importantly, these results were comparable to those achieved with CAR NK cells produced through the more traditional method of collecting NK cells, modifying them outside the body, and then returning them to the animals.

This suggests that generating CAR NK cells directly inside the body could offer similar cancer-fighting capabilities while avoiding the complicated manufacturing process required by conventional cell therapies.

A Single Injection Reverses Autoimmune Liver Damage

The researchers also wanted to determine whether their technology could help treat autoimmune diseases, in which the immune system mistakenly damages healthy tissues.

They focused on autoimmune hepatitis, a condition in which abnormal T cells attack hepatocytes, the main functional cells of the liver. By designing nanoparticles that instruct NK cells to recognize these harmful T cells, the scientists tested whether they could interrupt the autoimmune response.

The treatment successfully eliminated the autoreactive T cells in mice with the disease. Even more encouragingly, the animals' damaged liver tissue healed after the harmful immune cells were removed.

These improvements occurred after just one nanoparticle injection, demonstrating the potential of the approach beyond cancer treatment.

"This study is an excellent example of the power of nano delivery systems and their ability to potentially treat cancer and other diseases," Langer says.

A New Direction for Cancer and Autoimmune Treatments

The researchers believe that reprogramming natural killer cells inside the body could eventually provide new treatment options for a much wider range of conditions.

Among the diseases they hope to target are multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, both of which can involve harmful immune responses driven by dysfunctional T cells.

Although the findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and further research will be necessary to determine whether the technique is safe and effective in humans.

If successful, the technology could make engineered immune cell treatments considerably more accessible by replacing a lengthy laboratory manufacturing process with the direct delivery of genetic instructions through nanoparticles.

Texas Templars | Regional Co-Lead & Chapter Secretary Signups

If you’d like to co-lead your region’s chapter or volunteer as chapter secretary, see the regions, roles, and how to sign up below.

If you’d like to join your local chapter as a member, I’ll make a separate post once the chapter leads are in place. Follow me if you aren’t already so you can catch that update. ✝️

I posted recently about starting the Texas Templars, and I honestly didn’t expect this many people to be interested. So I’d like to see who’s willing to help get the first chapters off the ground.

The original Knights Templar formed to protect Christian pilgrims traveling to the Holy Land during the Crusades. What I take from that history is the willingness to stand up for your faith and show up for people who need help. I want the Texas Templars to be a way for us to put our Christian faith into practice, stand with people facing persecution, and serve the country we love by starting right here in our own communities.

I’m choosing my words carefully here for obvious reasons. The work I’m talking about is peaceful, lawful, and focused on helping the American people and saving our country.

Texas is massive 😂 so I’d like to start with seven regions.

North Texas, East Texas, Central Texas, South Texas, West Texas, Gulf Coast, and Panhandle & South Plains.

I’m looking for two men to co-lead each chapter and one woman to serve as chapter secretary. I’ll go in the order DMs come in for each region and role.

Co-leads will set up and run the monthly meetings, research ways the chapter can help locally, and work with members to choose projects and follow through. Having two leads means someone can step in when the other is sick or can’t make a meeting.
Chapter secretaries will send meeting invites, take minutes of each meeting, and help coordinate the potluck. If families need help with childcare to attend, the secretary can also help see what arrangements are possible.

I’d love for the monthly meetings to be in person whenever possible. We can share a meal, pray together, and decide what we can actually do in our area. That could mean working with churches or established nonprofits to connect someone with safe housing or other support if they’re being threatened because of their faith or because they converted to Christianity.

Once a month, the co-leads and secretaries from all seven regions can meet over Zoom to compare notes, share what’s working, and make plans together. That way we stay on the same page without asking everybody to drive across Texas. We can also offer a Zoom option for local meetings when someone can’t attend in person.

If you’d like to co-lead or serve as chapter secretary, please DM me your name, email address, city or county, region, and which role you’re interested in.

Once we have the chapter leaders in place and I’ve put together a spreadsheet with their contact information, I’ll make a separate post for anyone who wants to join. I’ll list the regions so you know which chapter to pick. At that point, you can DM me your name, the region you’d like to join, and your email address. I’ll pass your information along to your chapter leads, and one of them will reach out with details about the first meeting and what to expect as a member. ✝️

And again, I’m being careful with my wording here. Part of what I want the Texas Templars to discuss is how we can uphold the principles our country was founded on, live out our Christian faith, and protect our fellow Americans through peaceful, lawful action. I think it’s time we stop just typing about the things we care about and start showing up for The American People and doing something about them.

With the passage of Amendment 87, Colorado is replacing its flat income tax with a six-tier system—raising state income taxes by an estimated $2.7 billion annually on high earners and businesses making over $500,000.

While liberals argue the $2 billion in net new revenue will fund essential services like K-12 education, affordable childcare, and housing, business leaders are warning of serious economic fallout.

Key takeaways from state business leaders and economists:

Tax Rate Spike: The top state income tax rate jumps from 4.4% to 8.4%, worsening Colorado's business tax climate ranking (which has already fallen from 9th in 2003 to 33rd).

Competitive Disadvantage: Colorado isn't just competing with high-cost states like New York or California; it's competing with neighbors like Utah, Texas, and Arizona that offer lower operating costs or no state income tax at all.

Impact on Small Businesses: Local employers will be forced to raise prices, freeze hiring, cut employee hours, or reduce jobs to offset rising costs. Life will become more unaffordable. 

Demands for ROI: Business coalitions like the Denver Metro Chamber and the Colorado Chamber of Commerce are urging state leaders to ensure this revenue is spent wisely—demanding infrastructure fixes, lower energy costs, faster permitting, and relief from additional legislative fees and regulations. Democrats have already passed legislation making these topics to be null. 

If Colorado is going to charge "premium prices" to do business, leaders argue, the state must deliver premium value to keep job creators from moving elsewhere.

🔥-take: Village Farms just delivered another quarter of real profitability and cash generation, powered by record cannabis sales and surging international exports that showcase the power of its massive, low-cost EU-GMP production platform. With the world’s largest single-site EU-GMP certified facility, expanding capacity, and a clean balance sheet, VFF is proving it can grow profitably while building durable competitive advantages that peers are paying big premiums to acquire.

🤖 ANALYSIS: 
Village Farms reported consolidated net sales of $66.9 million (essentially flat year-over-year but with record cannabis sales of $55.0 million, up 3%). International export sales jumped 75% YoY to $20.8 million—matching the prior quarter’s record—and now represent a large and growing share of the mix, supported by resilient pricing for GMP-compliant product. Consolidated adjusted EBITDA from continuing operations was $18.2 million (27% margin), while cannabis segment adjusted EBITDA was $14.7 million (27% of cannabis sales). Net income attributable to shareholders was $10.0 million or $0.08 per share—the sixth consecutive quarter of positive net income and EPS. Operating cash flow was $9.5 million, and the company closed the quarter with nearly $80 million in cash and a net cash position of $41 million.

Cannabis gross margin was 48% (down from 55% YoY), primarily due to a softer spot trim market in Canadian wholesale; management expects this to trough and begin normalizing in Q4 based on the order book and new higher-priced supply agreements. SG&A rose as the company invests for growth. Key operational highlights include maintaining a top-five Canadian market share position (with gains in convenience categories and top-10 standing across major formats), the Delta 2 expansion remaining on track (full 40 metric tonne ramp by mid-2027, taking the Delta campus to ~160 metric tonnes of dried/trimmed flower annually), the Netherlands Phase II facility now fully planted and set to contribute more meaningfully from Q4 into 2027, and early mobilization of the advanced 30-acre Monahans, Texas greenhouse for potential U.S. production. The company also exercised optionality to convert ~16 acres of the Delta 1 greenhouse to cannabis.

Overall, the results demonstrate a sustainably profitable, cash-generating business that is successfully shifting its mix toward higher-value international medical markets while retaining Canadian share and preparing significant capacity additions.

Speculation on Company Value Given the ACB Offer (Primarily EU-GMP Driven)
Organigram’s agreed offer for Aurora Cannabis values ACB at approximately C$561 million (roughly US$400 million) fully diluted, or C$7.80 per share. This was a substantial premium (93% to the unaffected price and 21% above Curaleaf’s rejected hostile bid) driven predominantly by Aurora’s EU-GMP certified manufacturing and distribution capabilities—assets that are scarce, expensive, and time-consuming to replicate, and that enable reliable access to growing, regulated European and other international medical markets. The combined entity would operate five such facilities with meaningful certified capacity, plus identified synergies exceeding C$50 million.

Village Farms positions itself as operating the world’s largest single-site EU-GMP certified cannabis facility at its Delta, British Columbia campus (with recent upgrades solidifying that claim). It is already one of the largest exporters of medical cannabis to Europe (strong position in Germany), with international export sales growing rapidly and resilient pricing relative to non-GMP supply. Capacity is expanding materially (Delta 2 + Netherlands ramp), the company is profitable with positive free cash flow dynamics and a net cash balance sheet, and it has additional optionality (Delta 1 conversion, Texas assets, Netherlands adult-use license). 

Given that ACB’s EU-GMP network commanded a ~US$400 million equity valuation (on a company that has faced more domestic margin pressure and is not as consistently profitable), Village Farms’ larger-scale, lower-cost greenhouse EU-GMP platform, proven export growth, and cleaner financial profile support the view that its strategic assets may be undervalued at a current market cap around $350 million. In a consolidating industry where EU-GMP access and scalable compliant supply are key barriers and value drivers, VFF’s footprint could attract comparable or higher strategic interest or support a higher standalone multiple as capacity comes online and international revenue scales further. Execution on the capacity ramps, margin recovery in Canada, and continued export momentum will be the key catalysts.

🗣️ MANAGEMENT COMMENTARY:
Michael DeGiglio, President and CEO:
“Our third quarter results were driven by record cannabis revenues of $55 million and approximately 43% of cannabis sales from some of the world’s most attractive and fastest growing international markets. We also delivered our sixth consecutive quarter of positive net income and EPS, clearly demonstrating the strength of our sustainably profitable and expanding global cannabis enterprise.”

“In Canada, we continue to maintain our top five market share position with continued share gains in convenience product categories and a brand portfolio that remains in the top 10 of all major product categories nationally. International export sales grew 75% year-over-year, in line with last quarter’s record, and more importantly with resilient pricing relative to non-GMP compliant areas of the supply chain. As we’ve previously discussed, we continue to expect our competitive advantage with the world’s largest single-site EU-GMP certified cannabis facility will result in continued increases in demand for our compliant production capacity, and we are looking forward to our Delta 2 expansion contributing to stronger international sales growth next year along with our entrance into multiple new European jurisdictions.”

“The year-over-year variance in our margin performance in Q3 was driven primarily by a softer spot trim market in the Canadian wholesale sales channel as compared to the prior year. We believe wholesale trim volumes and pricing reached trough levels in the Canadian wholesale channel during Q3, and we expect these conditions to begin normalizing in Q4 given the visibility of our order book in October and the commencement of new supply agreements with considerably stronger contracted pricing.”

“We’re pleased to report that our Phase II Netherlands facility is now fully planted and expected to begin contributing to stronger sales growth during Q4 and throughout 2027. Our Delta 2 expansion remains on track to reach its full production capacity by the middle of next year, positioning us for continued long-term organic sales growth through calendar year 2028. Finally, we’re actively mobilizing plans to operationalize our standalone 30-acre greenhouse in Monahans, Texas for cannabis production. Monahans is the youngest, most advanced production asset in our portfolio, and we remain very focused on pursuing all potential pathways to initiate our U.S. market entry with a commencement of production in Texas.”

“As anticipated, we delivered stronger sequential cash flow performance in Q3 as capex from our Netherlands and Delta 2 expansion projects is substantially complete. We closed the quarter with nearly $80 million in cash, and believe we’re well positioned for continued profitable growth with one of the world’s most attractive and differentiated cannabis investment platforms. We continue to evaluate additional organic and acquisitive growth investments around the globe, but will remain prudent with respect to valuation and regulatory frameworks, with a focus on profitability and long-term strategic value creation for our shareholders.”

text:
Battery-Free Sound Tags Might Actually Replace Your Smart Home Sensors | Michael Bizzaco, BGR

Smart home sensors allow you to monitor everything from leaking water and broken windows to temperature fluctuations and motion. Most sensors are DIY-friendly; you can set them up relatively quickly, and you probably won't need anything besides your smartphone for the onboarding. Unfortunately, a majority of these sensors are battery-powered, leaving you responsible for a recharge or replacement when the cells start depleting. But if the ingenuity of a Georgia Tech engineering team led by Yibo Fu is officially put into production, the future of sensor power could look very different.

Fu's team came up with a simple way of localizing home automations via ultrasonic frequencies, and they're calling this experimental platform SoundOff. Instead of using batteries, Wi-Fi receivers, and other complicated tech, Fu and his colleagues created a penny-sized metal disc with specialized notches that mounts on a 3D-printed base. The disk and base were installed near a tiny plastic tab that connected to a door, drawer, or other open-close mechanism. When you "activate" the item to which the notched disc sensor is attached, the tab strikes the metal, causing it to emit a hyper-specific, ultrasonic sound.

Ultrasonic (frequencies above 20 kilohertz) also means that human ears won't have to deal with a hodgepodge of audible tones ringing throughout a home or business. The frequency is then picked up by a microphone-equipped device, which interfaces with custom software to carry out a particular automation. No advanced AI or other robust tools required.

SoundOff offers a glimpse into a smart home future that doesn't require Bluetooth or Wi-Fi

According to Fu's team, SoundOff could literally cost just a few cents to manufacture. The engineers also went on to detail specific use cases for the technology, demonstrating how its disc-dinging tech could be beneficial for fields like geriatric care, personal fitness, and inventory systems. Fu's crew has already come up with about 1,300 unique notch sizes and placements, and each design produces a one-of-a-kind acoustic signature. Furthermore, these unique frequencies offer maybe one of the best forms of privacy known to man: decaying sound waves.

At right around the three-foot mark, ultrasonic tones rapidly disintegrate; that also means the frequencies are essentially impossible for a hacker to pick up on unless they're literally inside your home or business. Throughout their experiments, Fu and his team used a wrist-strapped Ultramic384K BLE mic connected to a Raspberry Pi Zero to detect ultrasonic frequencies. The team also says in their research paper that lower-cost microphones could potentially be used with a smartwatch; but considering the limited ultrasonic range, additional hardware development is likely required.

Should the SoundOff platform actually be picked up for full-scale production, perhaps the developers can come up with a way to utilize the mics on everyday devices like phones and smartwatches to execute automations, instead of a prototype, in-house solution that may never see the light of day beyond a laboratory. One thing's for sure: we need more resource-lite systems like SoundOff to carry out smart home automations, even if the mic device were to end up being a battery-powered add-on.

WOULD YOU READ THIS BOOK?

Three months ago, Daniel Cole left me two weeks before our wedding.

No goodbye. No explanation. Just a text at 2:14 a.m. and a loan with both our names on it.

Now he’s back.

Same smile. Same navy suit. New fiancée.

And guess who just signed the contract to plan their wedding?

Me. Chimamanda Okorie. Amanda to him, thank you very much.

The bride is Tiwa Ajayi-Williams, the sweetest heiress in Lagos, and if I walk away now, I owe her family fifty percent of a fee I’ve already spent keeping my father alive.

So I smile. I order the peonies. I pretend I don’t know the groom.

Then her brother corners me.

Oluwadamilare Ajayi-Williams. CEO. Cold as a boardroom at 8 a.m. He reads bank statements for fun, and he’s certain Daniel isn’t who he says he is.

He’s right. Daniel isn’t even his real name.

Dami’s offer is simple. Pose as his girlfriend, get close to the family, and help him expose the man who’s about to marry his sister. In return, my debts go away.

Five conditions. One signature. Absolutely no kissing.

It should be easy.

Plan the perfect wedding. Ruin it at the altar.

Except the closer I get to the truth, the more Daniel’s lies start leading back to me. Dami is looking at me like I’m the only thing he can’t put a price on.

And I’m starting to forget which part of this is fake.

text:
Everyone is watching Paris today. The more consequential table may be the one being laid in Shenzhen.

In Paris, G7 foreign ministers opened two days of talks on Monday, 9 November. Their job, as AFP put it, is to press Marco Rubio: keep any Ukraine settlement fair to Kyiv, and do not restart the war with Iran.

Germany's Johann Wadephul said it bluntly on the way in. Europe does not need "a new security architecture" and "must have a place at the table."

Canada added 38 entities and 24 individuals to its Russia sanctions list on the sidelines. Andriy Sybiga, Ukraine's foreign minister, joins on Tuesday.

That is one half of the picture.

The other half came from Donald Trump on Sunday, 8 November. Asked about next week's APEC summit in Shenzhen, on 18 and 19 November, he said: "One of the meetings will be with President Putin and President Xi, and that'll be interesting."

He listed denuclearisation and added: "We're trying to end the war in Iran."

On Monday, both capitals moved. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing is "in communication with relevant parties" about a meeting of the three presidents. He did not rule it out.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov went further, telling https://t.co/I2csK1XD5T and RIA Novosti that Russia, the US and China are exchanging proposals on a possible agenda. The meeting, he said, "will be interesting in any case."

In the same interview, Peskov said the Abu Dhabi talks starting Tuesday are trilateral: Russia and Ukraine, with US mediation. European presence there, in Moscow's framing, is a matter for Washington's own channels.

Put the two scenes side by side.

In Paris, Europe is asking for a chair. In Shenzhen, three leaders who would decide the outcome are discussing an agenda without Europe in the room at all.

That is the gap Volodymyr Zelensky warned about last month, when he said he did not want "Yalta 2, 3, 4" and a new redistribution of influence.

Of the three, Moscow wants this meeting most. Su Liuqiang of the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies told Chinese state media that Russia is the "most enthusiastic," and that an informal exchange is likelier than a structured summit.

Beijing's interest is different. Xi meets Trump bilaterally next week, their third meeting this year after Beijing in May and Washington in September. A fourth is due at the G20 in Miami. Tariffs, chips, rare earths and Taiwan are all still open.

Hosting a three-way photo costs China little and positions it as the venue where Washington and Moscow talk.

Trump's motive is the most transactional. After losing both chambers in the midterms, a stage with Xi and Putin offers a foreign-policy headline his opponents cannot block.

Iran sits in the middle of all of it. Rubio said on his way to Paris that there has been "no progress" and called some Iranian demands "outrageous and ridiculous." Brent was trading around $97.57 on Monday morning, according to the Indian Express live blog.

None of this is confirmed. No date, no format, no agenda has been published.

But the sequence is now visible. G7 in Paris today and tomorrow. Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. Shenzhen on 18 and 19 November.

Circle the 19th. If the three presidents sit down together, Europe's answer from Paris will have arrived one week too early.

Rezera Inc. ($RZRA) — Structural Record Ahead of a Proposed Nasdaq Global Market Listing

Rezera Inc. (formerly NodThera Inc.) is in registration to offer 16,666,667 common shares at $11.00–$13.00 per share (filed Nov 5–6), per SEC disclosures. At the $12.00 midpoint, gross proceeds are $200.0M and the 20,776,793 post-offering voting and non-voting common shares equal $249.3M. Bookrunners: Jefferies, TD Cowen, Cantor; lead manager: Wedbush PacGrow.

The Company's Program:
• Oral NLRP3 Inhibitor: Wholly owned ruvonoflast targets sterile inflammation with broad tissue and CNS penetration. In the 176-patient RESOLVE-1 Phase 2 trial, week-4 geometric LS-mean hsCRP fell 56.4% (150 mg QD) and 62.6% (150 mg BID), with median IL-6 down 38.2% and 62.3%.
• Phase 3 Plan: A single registrational Phase 3 trial (RELIEVE-PAD) in peripheral artery disease (PAD) is planned for H1 2027, with topline readout expected in 2028 (company estimates: ~20M U.S. PAD adults, ~$5B market opportunity).

The Four Structural Lines:

1. 100% Primary & GSK Right of First Negotiation:
• 100% Primary: All 16.67M shares (80.2% of post-offering shares after a 1-for-35.722 reverse split and preferred conversion) are sold by the company; zero insider selling.
• GSK Indication & ROFN: A GSK affiliate indicated non-binding interest in up to $25.0M at the midpoint (~10% of post-offering common). If the offering closes and GSK orders at least the lesser of 19.9% or $25.0M, GSK gets a 30-day right of first negotiation over ruvonoflast licensing/acquisition and a change of control (exclusive for ruvonoflast and post-Phase 3 M&A; non-exclusive for pre-Phase 3 M&A unless GSK uses a one-time acceleration right) plus one Clinical Advisory Board seat—with no board seat/observer, no right of first refusal, and no restriction on third-party deal terms. Ends if GSK sells >5% of its IPO shares.

2. Proceeds, Cash Burn, Debt & Dividend Waiver:
• Runway vs. Going Concern: $181.0M net proceeds ($208.9M with option) lift pro forma as adjusted cash to $214.9M (including $3.9M June 30 cash, ~$15.0M net July Series D4, and a $15.0M SVB term loan). Funds ruvonoflast through 2028 Phase 3 topline data and operations at least through Q1 2029, though not through regulatory approval or a Phase 2 topline readout of second candidate trabzanoflast at the assumed size. Operating cash burn was $17.9M in H1 2026 and $39.1M in 2025 (nil capex); without the offering, cash funds operations into January 2027 (going-concern warning).
• Debt & Dividends: Zero proceeds repay the $15.0M SVB loan (max of 6.00% or prime - 0.75%, matures June 2030). All accrued 6% cumulative preferred dividends ($50.3M at Dec 31, 2025 + $6.0M in H1 2026) are waived on conversion.

3. Share Classes & Control:
• Voting & Non-Voting Common: One vote per common share; unlisted non-voting common converts 1-for-1 up to a holder's beneficial ownership blocker. Pre-IPO holders include Novo Holdings (24.42%), Blue Owl (24.02%), F-Prime (13.14%), Sofinnova (12.06%), and 5AM Ventures (11.56%). At closing, Blue Owl swaps shares into non-voting stock to cap its voting common stake at 4.50%.

4. Corporate Structure & Lock-Up:
• Standard C-Corp: Delaware parent of Scotland's NodThera Ltd.; no Up-C or tax receivable agreement. 180-day lock-up covers officers, directors, and substantially all existing stockholders (including Blue Owl's non-voting shares).

China’s smelters are struggling with concentrate shortages, existing mines face declining grades, rising costs and operational challenges, while new copper projects can take 10–15 years to bring into production.

My thesis is that copper could sustain $6–$7/lb, with the potential to reach $8–$9/lb as structural deficits intensify toward 2030–2032. At those levels, producer margins could expand dramatically, while the economics and valuations of quality development projects could be transformed.

The market is pricing short-term macro uncertainty while I’m positioning for long-term structural scarcity.

Copper supply cannot be switched on overnight. The next generation of producers will be needed precisely when the market gets tightest.

This isn’t a short-term trade. It’s a multiyear supply-demand supercycle, and I believe copper equities are significantly undervaluing what’s coming. 🐂🚀

text:
In August 2018, a Florida judge got so tired of one defendant that he threatened to duct-tape his mouth shut. In the end the court put him in a separate room behind one-way glass. The jury could still hear him cursing.

His name is Alan McCarty Jr. He was on trial for threatening to kill a judge.

It started with his children. In 2017 he lost a custody case and decided Circuit Judge Stasia Warren was the one who took his kids away. Prosecutors said she wasn't. He called the police four times and said he would kill her. He was arrested that September in Santa Rosa County.

His trial in Daytona Beach should have been simple. It wasn't. From behind the defense table he threatened witnesses, his own lawyers and Judge Matt Foxman, who was running the trial. So they moved him next door. He watched his own trial through the glass and was let back in only to testify.

In the video below, McCarty yells, swears and refuses to stop while the court tries to keep going without him. He insults the judge, the prosecutor and his own public defender. At one point the judge said he even threatened a prosecutor's unborn child. McCarty called it a lie and claimed the judge was the one threatening his life.

The jury needed just 30 minutes to find him guilty on all four counts.

At sentencing he did it all again, from the same room behind the same glass. He made a crude sexual offer to the judge. Foxman said he declined, and added 10 more days for it. Then he gave him 20 years in state prison.

He threatened a judge because he believed she took his kids. By the end of the trial he had lost custody of them anyway.

Was Alan McCarty a father broken by losing his children, or a man who spent every minute in court proving the custody judge right?

text:
DOMINO’S PIZZA FOUNDER SOLD HIS BUGATTI TO HELP BUILD A CHURCH

He had wealth, luxury cars, private jets, and almost everything money could buy. But he eventually realized that the greatest treasure is not found on earth, but in heaven.

Tom Monaghan, the founder of Domino’s Pizza, once owned one of the rarest and most expensive cars in the world—a 1931 Bugatti Royale, which he purchased for $8.1 million.

At the height of his success, he owned the Detroit Tigers baseball team, private jets, yachts, and an impressive collection of luxury cars. By worldly standards, he had achieved almost everything a person could dream of.

But something changed in his life.

As his Catholic faith deepened, Monaghan began to realize that wealth and material possessions could never give him the lasting happiness that comes from God.

He decided to simplify his life. He sold his baseball team, his luxury possessions, and eventually Domino’s Pizza itself. Among the treasures he gave up was his beloved Bugatti Royale.

But he was not simply giving up his wealth. He was choosing to use it for something greater.

His resources helped make possible the establishment of Ave Maria University and the Catholic community of Ave Maria in Florida. At the heart of this community stands the beautiful Ave Maria Oratory, a place of worship where people gather to pray and grow in their faith.

For Monaghan, success was no longer measured by how much he owned, but by how much he could do for God and others.

His greatest desire was to reach heaven and help bring as many souls there as possible.

WHAT A BEAUTIFUL LESSON FOR ALL OF US!

There is nothing wrong with becoming successful or possessing material wealth. But we must always remember that everything we have is a gift from God, and these gifts become even more meaningful when we use them to serve Him and help others.

We may never own a Bugatti. We may never become millionaires. But each of us has something precious to offer God—our time, our talents, our resources, our kindness, and our love.

Jesus reminds us:

“For where your treasure is, there also will your heart be.” -Matthew 6:21

In the end, what matters most is not how much we accumulate in this world, but how much good we do with what God has entrusted to us.

Because the greatest success in life is not becoming rich on earth, but becoming rich in the eyes of God.

Invest not only in things that will eventually disappear, but in things that will last for eternity. ❤️🙏

Allen Iverson made $154 million in NBA salary.
By 2012 a Georgia judge was letting a jeweler pull money straight out of his bank account.
In 2030 Reebok is set to hand him $32 million anyway.

Receipts: $154,494,445 over 14 seasons, per Basketball-Reference. One MVP, one Finals trip, zero practices he was excited about.
He crossed up Jordan as a rookie. He couldn't cross up a jewelry bill.

In the video below it starts where everyone remembers him, May 2002. "We talking about practice."
Now the conversation is about checks.

Fat Joe asks him about the Reebok deal on camera. "It's 20-something years later and you're still cashing checks."
That's the only crossover that never got old.

The deal was signed in 2001, his MVP year. It was reported as $800,000 a year for life plus a $32 million trust he can't touch until he turns 55.
Reebok basically put a child lock on a legend.

The rest of the money had no lock. In 2010 a jeweler sued him over a $375,000 bill. He didn't answer, and the judgment grew to about $859,000. In January 2012 a judge let the store garnish his wages and go after his bank account.
That's a TECHNICAL foul with interest.

Fat Joe remembers the driveway: "six, seven drop-top Bentleys, all type of colors." Then he asks what kind of pressure it was, taking care of everybody.
"None," Iverson says. "That's who I am."
The jeweler had a different answer.

Everybody around him got paid first. Reebok turned out to be the only teammate who saved for him.

Hypothetical: you're 26, MVP, and a shoe company offers a lifetime deal with $32 million locked until you're 55. Sign it, or demand the cash now and take your chances with the jeweler?

text:
I was at The Palestra for Pitt vs. Penn State last night. Here are my main takeaways for each squad:

Pitt: 

1. This is Jeff Capel’s most talented roster since 23-24. The individual talent is VERY apparent, the question is whether or not Capel can get his guys to operate as a unit. Jonathan Powell, A’lahn Sumler, Jalil Bethea and Baye Ndongo are really good players that should be able to combine to create at the VERY least a top-10 ACC team. Oh, and Chase Foster, despite a down game, has the potential to have his name called in the draft at some point. At 6’9, he’s silky, patient, strong and has great mechanics + feel.  

2. Pitt actually trailed for a decent part of the first half and it was almost frustrating to watch because there was such a large gap in talent between the two squads and how severely it felt like they were underperforming — that is early November college basketball to be fair. That being said, Penn State was playing with discipline, taking good shots, getting 50/50 balls and playing as a cohesive unit. Pitt had 5 guys out there playing for seemingly 5 separate teams. 

3. Pitt’s size, or lack thereof, really, will be a huge limiting factor. Outside of Ndongo — who, to be fair, is scary good when he’s locked in — they are in trouble in the front court. Akir Souare is a tall/long body out there but offers next to nothing on the offensive end and isn’t a needle-mover on defense. Off the bench, i actually feel like Mighty is a decent option but has a pretty herky-jerky play style and still kind of needs to grow into his body despite being a senior. All this is to say, if Ndongo, who could very-well wind up on an All-ACC team, gets into foul trouble — like he did last night — Pitt is going to have a very hard time beating good teams. 

4. It’s early in the season which bodes well for the Panthers. Talent-wise, this team can absolutely make an NCAA Tournament. I know it’s early, and it’s crazy to already have a strong opinion like this, but with the construction of this roster, the trajectory and path to success feels relatively clear. Pitt needs to play as ONE and keep Ndongo out of foul trouble best as possible. If they do that, they could be dancing for the first time since 2023. 

Penn State: 

1. I really like Mike Rhoades as a coach but he has been dealt another tough hand. The funds just are not there for the basketball program — which the AD made clear. It’s unfortunate because they could absolutely be competitive, maybe even a bubble-ish team, if Rhoades had access to more resources. That being said, he has a few nice pieces. 

2. Dasonte Bowen is a solid, experienced anchor in the backcourt who plays under control and can score when Penn State needs a bucket. Ivan Juric is REALLY good and will be a problem for a lot of B1G opponents. He gets to the line whenever he wants with his physicality, timing and positioning around the rim — and converts too (9-10 last night). I imagine he will be a hot commodity in the portal after this year. Brant Byers hasn’t connected from deep efficiently yet this year but this feels like it’s inevitable. They need to find more ways to get him open; every look he got was off of a broken play or individual creation rather than a set. 

3. Penn State’s trajectory and/or path to success is not as clear. One thing was for certain: they do not have the raw talent that Pitt has. And they likely do not have the raw talent that the rest of the B1G has. Penn State’s path to conference wins will be attempting to control the pace and play in the half court while also making the best decision and taking the best shot EVERY TIME. There will be little room for error with this team. The Nittany Lions may have another long season ahead of them, but one thing they will do is compete.

Uganda is positioning its coffee sector for stronger access to the United Kingdom and Irish markets, with a focus on expanding exports, attracting investment, promoting value addition and building lasting commercial partnerships between producers and international buyers.

Government officials, diplomats and coffee industry leaders have called for deeper Uganda–UK and Ireland cooperation in the coffee sector, as a delegation of buyers, importers and specialist roasters undertakes a familiarisation mission to explore business opportunities across Uganda’s coffee value chain.

The Uganda–UK Coffee Buyers’ Familiarisation Mission, running from November 8 to 15, 2026, brings together representatives from the United Kingdom and Ireland to engage with Ugandan coffee farmers, cooperatives, processors, exporters and other industry stakeholders. The mission is organised under the theme “Uganda Arabica and Robusta: From Farm to Cup.”

Speaking during the engagement, Ambassador Steven Senabulya, Deputy Head of Mission at the Uganda High Commission in London, highlighted the importance of translating Uganda’s growing international profile into stronger commercial relationships and increased coffee exports.

He noted that the Uganda High Commission had begun strengthening engagement with the UK coffee market through initiatives such as Uganda’s participation in the London Coffee Festival in May 2025, alongside research commissioned to assess Uganda’s position and opportunities in the UK and Irish markets.

Ambassador Senabulya observed that the UK presents a significant opportunity for Ugandan coffee, with its coffee import market estimated at approximately US$1.4 billion in 2024. 

He emphasised the need to build stronger relationships with importers, roasters and distributors to improve Uganda’s market presence and increase the value derived from its coffee exports.

“The purpose of this familiarisation mission is to initiate business conversations and create meaningful partnerships between Ugandan coffee players and buyers in the UK and Ireland,” he said.

He further linked the mission to Government’s broader economic transformation agenda, noting that coffee exports, value addition and economic diplomacy remain important avenues for expanding Uganda’s export earnings, creating jobs and improving household incomes.

British High Commissioner to Uganda, Lisa Chesney MBE, welcomed the delegation and reaffirmed the United Kingdom’s commitment to strengthening commercial relations with Uganda, particularly in agriculture and the coffee sector.

She said the delegation brought together different areas of expertise, including green coffee importing, specialist roasting, retail, distribution and international market development, creating an opportunity for direct engagement with Ugandan producers and businesses.

@LisaJChesney  noted that Uganda’s coffee performance should be understood beyond export figures, emphasising the people and communities whose livelihoods depend on the sector.

“Behind these statistics are the farmers, cooperatives, women, exporters and communities who make Uganda’s coffee sector what it is,” she observed.
She cited Uganda’s export performance of approximately 8.1 million 60-kilogramme bags of coffee, valued at US$2.1 billion, in the last reporting year, describing the figures as evidence of the sector’s growing importance and potential.

The High Commissioner also encouraged greater domestic coffee consumption, pointing to the economic benefits of retaining more value within Uganda. She referenced an estimate that if just one per cent more Ugandans consumed coffee, approximately US$47 million could remain in the local economy.

Chesney also highlighted opportunities for British companies to invest in Uganda’s coffee value chain, including processing, skills development, hospitality and coffee tourism. 

She encouraged members of the delegation to use the mission to understand the quality, diversity and potential of Ugandan coffee while establishing relationships that can develop into long-term business partnerships.

President of the Uganda Coffee Federation, Robert Byaruhanga, described the UK market as a significant opportunity for Uganda, particularly given its reported consumption of approximately 103 million cups of coffee daily.
He said Uganda and the wider East African region produce coffee with distinctive qualities that deserve stronger recognition in international markets.

Byaruhanga called for increased collaboration between Ugandan producers and international buyers, noting that direct engagement would help create a better understanding of the country’s coffee and strengthen its position in the global market.

He also appreciated the organisers and stakeholders whose efforts brought the delegation to Uganda, describing the mission as an important step towards deepening Uganda–UK coffee relations.

Representing the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador  @richardkabonero , speaking on behalf of the Permanent Secretary, reaffirmed Government’s commitment to using economic and commercial diplomacy to expand trade, attract investment and create opportunities for Ugandan businesses.

He noted that Uganda and the United Kingdom share longstanding diplomatic relations founded on friendship, mutual respect and cooperation, which provide a strong foundation for expanding commercial engagement.

Ambassador Kabonero emphasised that agriculture remains a major pillar of Uganda’s economy, with coffee playing a significant role in export earnings and livelihoods. 

He said Uganda’s diplomatic missions abroad are expected to translate the country’s international relations into tangible economic outcomes.

“Our diplomacy must go beyond maintaining relationships; it must translate into trade, investment and jobs for our people,” he emphasised.

He said the familiarisation mission provides an opportunity for international buyers to engage directly with Ugandan farmers, cooperatives, processors and exporters, understand the coffee production process and identify areas for business collaboration.

The Ministry also encouraged the delegation to explore opportunities in coffee processing and value addition, which are critical to increasing the returns Uganda earns from its coffee.

Providing an overview of the sector, Gordon Katwirenabo, Assistant Commissioner for Coffee Quality Assurance and Value Addition at the Ministry of Agriculture, Animal Industry and Fisheries (MAAIF), outlined Uganda’s production capacity, export performance, quality assurance systems and investment opportunities.

He described Uganda as Africa’s second-largest coffee producer and the continent’s leading producer of Robusta coffee, with the crop supporting millions of Ugandans across the country.

Katwirenabo noted that coffee is grown in approximately 126 of Uganda’s 146 districts, with an estimated 12.5 million people directly or indirectly dependent on the sector.

He highlighted Government’s ambition to increase annual coffee production from approximately 3.5 million 60-kilogramme bags in 2017 to 20 million bags by 2030, supported by increased production, improved quality, research, farmer support and expanded market access.

He also outlined progress in strengthening traceability and compliance systems, including the registration of approximately 1.5 million coffee farmers and the mapping of 1.65 million farm plots.

These interventions, he explained, are important in preparing Uganda’s coffee sector for emerging international market requirements, particularly the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), which places greater emphasis on traceability and demonstrating that agricultural products are not linked to deforestation.

Katwirenabo identified opportunities for investment in coffee processing, roasting, packaging, commercial farming, irrigation, climate-smart agriculture and direct sourcing arrangements between Ugandan producers and international buyers.

He further pointed to the relatively low level of domestic coffee consumption as an opportunity to grow Uganda’s local market while expanding exports.

“Uganda must not only produce coffee for the international market; we must also increase local consumption, processing and value addition so that more benefits remain within our economy,” he said.

The sector, he added, has the potential to serve growing regional and continental markets, while Uganda’s diverse coffee-growing regions offer distinctive Arabica and Robusta profiles that can meet different consumer preferences.

The mission is expected to provide the visiting buyers with first-hand exposure to Uganda’s coffee production systems through engagements with farmers, cooperatives, washing stations, processors and exporters in different coffee-growing regions.

It is also intended to create opportunities for direct sourcing, business-to-business engagements, knowledge exchange and partnerships that can improve the competitiveness of Ugandan coffee in the UK and Irish markets.

The engagement builds on Uganda’s broader economic and commercial diplomacy agenda, which seeks to position the country’s products in international markets while attracting investment into productive sectors.

As the delegation continues its programme, Government and industry stakeholders are looking to convert the engagements into concrete commercial relationships, increased market access and greater value for Uganda’s coffee producers. @UKinUganda @MAAIF_Uganda @UgandaMFA

text:
'Topic' by: Vixyy Fox

Author's note: Mostly, this is for you 'new' writers, cuz the 'older more seasoned' writers, being the venerable bunch we are, will understand. 
This has everything to do with the worlds of which we write. Our minds often go back to them just to get away. 
All of the characters in this story, are actual friends of mine. Over the years, they somehow got themselves written into the Whackadoodle Inn (my choice), and their presence, like a footprint in the sand, remains. 
I have the ability of going there at any point in time, both here and there. It's what I do, cuz I'm a writer. 
And I love them all.

'Topic'

“Of course it was hot," Wirewolf near shouted, "We were in the topics after all. Things are always hot in the topics.”
“You mean ‘Tropics’,” Onic suggested, and then his fingers did a little south seas jingle on the piano. 
Wirewolf made a sour face at being corrected for the umpteenth time by the newcomer piano player. He wasn’t really sure why Miss Vixyy hired such a smartypants fellow in the first place; but that wasn’t his concern. 
They were in the dining room, and Miss Buns, who was at the table snapping beans for the evening meal, chuckled. “I do believe your goat has been got,” she told the old sailor.
“Not so,” he replied, reaching over and snagging some of the raw green beans. The Inn’s cook must certainly have been feeling generous because she didn’t even attempt to slap his paw.
The piano playing Wolf, clad in his suit vest and pants, began playing ‘Pop Goes the Weasel’, which made the Hare smile even more. “I like that song,” she said absently.
“You would,” the Inn’s gardener muttered. “It always reminds me of three buffoons running around poking and slapping at one another, and the lyrics make no sense a’tall." Looking at the piano Wolf, he asked, "What does it mean?” 
“No one is really sure,” the other Wolf replied loudly to be heard over the music, “But it certainly is a fun tune.”
When the song came to its climatic ending, Miss Buns picked up a large wooden spoon and bopped the old sailor square on the head while singing, “Pop! Goes the Weasel.”
“OW!”
“I didn’t hit you that hard,” she protested with a laugh.
“Are you then insinuating I’m Weaselly?” he asked.
“Oh heavens no! Wirewolf, you are one of the most honest creatures I know… except when you steal my cookies, or tell a sea story.”
“My stories are all true,” the Wolf protested.
“Just stretched a little bit,” the cook teased.
“But you did hit him off-topic,” the piano player added without looking up. His fingers were now flying over the keys playing ‘The Irish Washerwoman’. 
“What?” she asked.
“Off Topic,” he repeated in a louder voice. “You went from ‘hot’ to ‘bop’.”
“What’s the topic now?” Wirewolf asked.
The piano was smoothly redirected into playing the soothing tune, ‘Home, Sweet Home’. When it was done he said, “It was how hot it was on your voyage, but now it’s ‘bop’ the Wolf.”
“Durned straight it was hot,” Wirewolf told him, taking it back to the beginning. “Depending upon which voyage you’re referring to o’course. It was so hot it baked the ship until the wood was dry as a bone in the desert. We had to make sure the gunpowder was kept well below the water line just so it wouldn’t ignite and blow us all to Kingdom Come. In fact, if a mate wanted to smoke his clay pipe, all he had to do was take a match out of his pocket and hold it up to the sun, and it would spark to life.”
“But you were at sea,” Miss Buns said with a wiggle of her whiskers.
“Of course we were; and sloshing seawater over the decks just to keep the ship cool and safe from fire.”
Onic began playing ‘The Ship On Fire’, which he stopped nearly as quick as he’d started. “Forgive me asking,” he queried, “But was this in the Topic of Cancer or the Topic of Capricorn?”
“Now I know you’re having me on, cuz every sailor worth his salt knows it’s T’(r)opic, not Topic. I do believe you might have been cornfused by my salty like accent, so for that I will forgive you.”
“But it was hot in the topics?” the other Wolf asked. 
“Of course it was hot!” the gardener told him energetically, it was the ‘topics’. Sometimes trying to talk to a lubber is just…” He looked for a word and finally settled on, “Frustrating!”
The piano Wolf smiled and began playing ‘Clair de Lune’.
“Do you know ‘The Rose’?” asked a voice with a lilting accent. 
https://t.co/IORZAiKMGO
Wirewolf and Miss Buns looked to the source and found Miss Bering peeking around the corner of the dining room entrance. There was a hopeful look upon her features. The piano player, without even looking up, moved the one song smoothly into the other causing the white Fox to move completely into the room, her paws clasped together in front of her chest as she listened to a tune that took her far and away to a home she left and most likely would never return to.
From that song the musician moved into a lively jig which had both the old sailor, now standing from his chair, and the front desk vixen dancing as the cook clapped her paws in time.
“What’s all this noise?” asked the gruff voice as the swinging door to the kitchen did what it was supposed to do and swung open. A huge Pig stood there, drying his paws on a towel as he’d been giving the kitchen a good washing while the cook was absent taking care of her green beans. “A body has a hard time concentrating on chores when there is such loveliness a’play’n.”
Miss Buns patted the empty chair next to hers in invitation and, smiling, the Pig took her up on the offer. 
“Do you know ‘East of Edin’? Duroc asked. “They used to play that a lot at the boxing matches I was a part of. It always reminds me of cigar smoke and the smell of stale beer accompanied by the sound of leather hitting flesh and a whole lot of cheering and jeering.”
https://t.co/4ZJ8lm9HgH
“That’s almost disgusting,” Wirewolf told him.
“We all have the places where we came from,” the Pig told him with a wink. “You can never change that so you may as well embrace the happy memories and toss the rest, eh?”
The sailor, now wearing a sober look upon his face, nodded in agreement. “Like the time I first lost Miss Vixyy.”
“But now you’re together again,” Miss Bering told him, touching his shoulder.
I don’t have a proper drummer in attendance,” Onic told them, “But if you know the tune and wish to accompany me pounding on the table…”
And with that there came a clamor of paws on wood all keeping to the drumming needed to properly accent the notes found and sent forth from the piano.
When it was done and everyone was fully laughing, there came the sound of a throat being cleared and all eyes went to the doorway of the dining room where a small Fox with very large ears stood. There was a sudden stillness in the dining room as everyone expected to be chastised for the silliness they’d slipped into during a time when chores were to be done.
Looking to their new piano player, she asked him, “Do you know the ‘Tin Whistle Waltz’?”
“As a matter of fact,” the Wolf replied, “I do.”
https://t.co/L8ayxNacIX 
“It’s what led me to a certain sailor a long, long time ago,” she told him while looking at Wirewolf. “He was in the village square next to the fountain just sitting there playing his heart out. Neither of us could speak the other’s language, but it was that simple tune that bridged the gap between us.”
“I’d not forgotten the meeting,” the gardener confessed, “But I have long since forgotten how to play the tin whistle.”
As the waltz was struck up on the piano, Wolf bowed to Fox and asked if she would like to dance and for a moment the pair was once again young with bare feet swirling through the sands of a foreign land to a tune that needed no language to be enjoyed. 
Three and four times it was repeated and then one song melted into another and into another until the first guest of the evening arrived for a dinner that was not yet prepared.
This caused but a slight panic as Miss Buns was an excellent cook… and with music to be enjoyed along with a glass of wine, presented on the house by a most gracious innkeeper, no notice was even taken. 
I will also add that no better music was ever found in the T’(r)opics of Capricorn or Cancer than that played within the walls of The Whackadoodle Inn..

On Nov. 3, Ohio Republicans lost three statewide races with a ticket the party picked, two of them a full year before the primary. Calls for reform are rampant. Here’s what to watch for. A smart insider never opposes reform out loud. He takes it over, slows it down, and shrinks it.

He’ll announce a "renewal task force" before the grassroots can organize. He’ll concede the easy things, like posted minutes and a new liaison, while holding on to what matters: endorsements, money, central committee seats, and the rules calendar. He’ll offer jobs and chairmanships to the most capable reformers. Then he’ll wait for the 2028 filing deadline to pass.

The answer is simple. Set deadlines in public. Publish roll-call votes. Put a candidate in every empty precinct seat. Judge every "concession" against the real demand for reform.

Politicians have to earn your vote. So does the party.

The "Red Team" addendum to my recommended reform plan, which I published yesterday, is shown below. Comments welcomed. This is how the insiders will fight reform and lie about their support of it.

Some will question the benefit of publishing our plan & defensive strategy for the opposition (enemy) to read when we know they'll keep their plans & strategies double top secret. I am of the belief that we will win more support by being completely transparent than acting like the opposition (enemy). What advantage we concede by doing this will be more than compensated for in trust of our side. Plus, there will be a visible public record of the process to use as evidence if the opposition (enemy) fails to truly reform the party.

IMPORTANT: We need to quickly stand-up a committee of reformers. Contact me if you're interested. Your interest will be considered, your inclusion not guaranteed. We'll be screening ruthlessly. Apologies in advance.

text:
In 1914, Britain cut Germany’s undersea telegraph cables.

Germany still needed to communicate. That pushed messages onto radio and alternative cable routes Britain could intercept.

In 1917, Germany sent a secret proposal: if America entered the war against Germany, Mexico should join Germany’s side. In return, Germany offered financial support and backing for Mexico to reclaim Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.

The encrypted telegram went through Germany’s embassy in Washington before being forwarded to Mexico. The Berlin-to-Washington leg used American diplomatic channels.

text:
Trump's 60 Minutes interview offered an important insight into how the White House is calculating the cost of the Iran conflict.

He acknowledged that the war, alongside the rise in gasoline prices, contributed to Republican losses in the midterms. Yet when asked whether he would order the attack on Iran again, his answer was an emphatic yes. His argument is that the strategic consequences of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon will ultimately outweigh the immediate political and economic costs.

There is a significant distinction here. Trump is defending the strategic decision to enter the conflict while signalling that he has little appetite for further escalation. He said he sees no reason to intensify the war and suggested that Tehran may be close to a deal, with Qatar continuing to mediate between Washington and Tehran.

For energy markets, that leaves two very different scenarios in play. A diplomatic agreement could gradually reduce the geopolitical risk premium and improve confidence in flows through the Gulf. A breakdown in negotiations would bring the security of those flows, particularly through the Strait of Hormuz, back into focus.

The interview offered no guarantee of either outcome. But it made one thing clear: Washington is now weighing the strategic gains of its Iran campaign against the economic consequences that American consumers and voters have already begun to feel.

Europe will be in Abu Dhabi. That does not mean Europe will be at the table.

The EU says a joint team, alongside France, Germany and Britain, will attend the November 10–11 talks. Moscow says the negotiations are for Russia, Ukraine and the United States. Presence and participation are not the same thing. That distinction matters.

These talks concern Ukraine’s security guarantees and Europe’s postwar security. If European capitals are expected to provide money, weapons, sanctions enforcement or forces, they cannot be handed those obligations after Washington and Moscow settle the terms. The test is not who gets photographed in Abu Dhabi. It is whether an arrangement names who responds, with which capabilities, and when. Europe should arrive with a concrete offer: what it will fund, supply and guarantee, and on what conditions. If it is asked to carry the risks, it must help shape the deal.
