text:
$UUUU Q3 2026 earnings: Uranium prices rose, but Energy Fuels mined below its plan

Higher uranium prices made Energy Fuels' main business more profitable, while its mines produced too little ore. The company sold uranium at $88.90 a pound, a third straight quarterly increase. Chief executive Ross Bhappu tied the better margins to that price. Nine months of mining delivered 1.1 million pounds, against a two-million-pound plan.

• Revenue: $𝟐𝟗.𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (+65% from a year ago)
• Price received for uranium: $𝟖𝟖.𝟗𝟎 𝐚 𝐩𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 (+10% from last quarter)
• Net loss: $𝟓𝟐.𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 ($16.7 million a year ago)
• Full-year mining plan: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (1.1 million of at least 2.0 million pounds mined so far)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The standing case got worse, because the mining plan now needs half the year's pounds in one quarter. Two dates went backwards too: the Donald mine decision slid to December and the mill's heavy rare earth circuits lost a few months. The offset: uranium margins widened and the Korean plant sold its first alloys.

The question now is whether Energy Fuels can feed the chain it is buying. Either the mill's new circuits and the Donald mine arrive in time, or the Korean plant keeps buying material from outside suppliers at market prices. The Donald decision, promised by December, is the next test.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐔𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐨 𝟔𝟑%
Energy Fuels sells uranium concentrate to nuclear utilities under long-term contracts and into the spot market. Chief executive Ross Bhappu credited the quarter to pricing: "Higher realized uranium prices supported improved margins". Each pound sold fetched $88.90.

That price stood a tenth above the second quarter and 27% above the first, a third straight quarterly gain. Costs stayed put, because the pounds shipped came out of inventory built during earlier mill runs at about $34 each.

• Price received: $88.90 a pound, against $72.38 a year earlier
• Cost of the pounds sold: about $34, against about $54 a year earlier
• Uranium gross profit: $17.9 million on segment sales of $28.7 million

Because cost per pound barely moved, the price gain fell straight through to profit. Cost of goods sold took 38% of segment sales, against 74% a year ago. Finance chief Nate Bennett said that profit covers exploration, development and head-office costs.

What to watch: the cost of each pound sold once the mill restarts in December, because the latest Pinyon Plain ore "had a weighted average cost of approximately $23 per pound". A figure near that would widen the margin again.

🟢 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐊𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐧 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐒𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐀𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐬
Energy Fuels closed its purchase of Australian Strategic Materials on 28 August, taking over a plant in Ochang, South Korea, "which currently manufactures REE metals and alloys at commercial scale". The plant turns rare earth oxides into the neodymium-iron-boron alloy used in magnets.

September brought the first revenue from it: $0.4 million of alloy sales. Output runs at 1,300 tonnes a year, and chief executive Ross Bhappu said new furnaces and a strip caster take that to 3,600 tonnes early in 2027.

What to watch: alloy revenue in the fourth quarter, the first full quarter of ownership. Finance chief Nate Bennett expects "ASM's contributions to our financials to be limited over the near term", so a figure well above $0.4 million would mean the plant found oxide to buy.

🟢 𝐀 𝐌𝐚𝐠𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐫 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥'𝐬 𝐎𝐱𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐬
Dysprosium and terbium are the heavy rare earths that let a magnet hold its strength when it gets hot, and China supplies almost all of them. Chief executive Ross Bhappu told investors that at the White Mesa Mill in Utah "we qualified our heavy rare earth oxide production with a major global permanent magnet manufacturer".

Qualification means a buyer tested the material and accepted it for its own production line. Energy Fuels has only pilot output today, so the test shows the recipe works before the commercial circuits exist; it approved construction of those circuits in July.

What to watch: a named customer or a published price for heavy oxide. Until one appears, the qualification shows the mill can make the product but not what anyone will pay for it.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐌𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫
Energy Fuels still plans to mine 2.0 million to 2.5 million pounds of contained uranium this year. Its mines produced 385,000 pounds in the third quarter. Nine months brought 1.1 million.

By our math the final quarter needs at least 875,000 pounds, half of the year's middle figure in one quarter. Chief executive Ross Bhappu conceded that "the ore grades at Pinyon Plain came in below our expectations this quarter" and sent an overnight crew underground.

• Mined in the quarter: 385,000 pounds, against 465,000 a year earlier
• Pinyon Plain grade: 1.04%, better than 0.71% in the spring but under the 1.62% averaged in 2025
• Mined in nine months: 1.1 million pounds, 56% of the plan's lower limit

The release still calls Energy Fuels "a leading producer of rare earth elements", and Bhappu said "we delivered meaningful progress across our uranium and rare earth businesses". Finance chief Nate Bennett sounded narrower, hoping that "the additional shift in higher grades at Pinyon Plain" carries the year to the bottom of the range.

What to watch: pounds mined between October and December, published with the annual results. If the third quarter's pace holds, the year ends near 1.5 million pounds, a quarter short of the plan's lower limit.

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐚𝐬 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞
Energy Fuels funds its build-out from a holding of cash and traded securities rather than from profit. That holding came to $855.9 million at the end of September, $80.8 million less than in June, after market interest rates cut the value of the bonds inside it.

The release blamed "non-cash, unrealized mark-to-market losses on our marketable securities portfolio", which took $35.3 million off the result; interest on the same securities paid in $9.4 million of cash. Work on the two acquisitions cost a further $9 million.

• Working capital: $932.3 million, from $996.0 million in June
• Cash and securities: half of total assets, against 61% in June
• Still to spend: about $100 million on the mill's circuits, $60 million to earn into the Donald mine

Chief executive Ross Bhappu called this "an ambitious and capital-intensive plan" and listed government loans, a term loan and share sales as the sources. Australian lenders did commit money this quarter, yet Energy Fuels must still pay for VAC, the magnet maker it agreed in June to buy for about $1.9 billion in cash and shares.

What to watch: how much of the new $500 million share-sale shelf Energy Fuels uses before that deal closes. Every dollar raised there comes from existing shareholders instead of the government loans the finance team is still negotiating.

🔴 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐞𝐬
Every link in the chain Energy Fuels is assembling needs rare earth feedstock, and today it buys that material from other companies. Asked about the Korean metals plant, chief executive Ross Bhappu named the weakness himself: "sourcing the raw materials and ensuring they have adequate feed to grow that business".

Its own sources all sit in the future. Australian lenders offered "a conditional financing package from Export Finance Australia" for the Donald mine, but the investment decision moved from the third quarter to December, and first ore waits until late 2028. Vara Mada in Madagascar has no date.

What to watch: a positive Donald decision before January, and any contract naming a carbonate supplier for the mill's new circuits. Without them, both the Utah mill and the Korean plant run on material Energy Fuels does not control.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Five standing worries got no fresh numbers this quarter. Each needs one specific disclosure before it moves either way, and here is the figure to look for in each case.

• Sumter magnet dispute: the arbitration result, which can move the VAC price either way, is still out.
• Rare earth prices: no dysprosium or terbium price table, and no comment on magnet makers designing both out.
• Doing everything at once: two cross-border purchases, one building site, three mine studies, $9 million of deal cost.
• Utility contracting: Energy Fuels named no new uranium contract, and 2026 deliveries are already complete.
• Lawsuits: neither the release nor the call mentions the White Mesa or Kwale cases.

What to watch: the arbitration outcome at Sumter, because it sets what Energy Fuels finally pays for VAC and whether that South Carolina plant keeps its anchor customer.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐁𝐨𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬
Energy Fuels keeps most of its money in treasury bills and government agency bonds. Market interest rates rose during the quarter, so those bonds lost value. A $35.3 million paper loss ran through the result, about two-thirds of the net loss. Nothing left the bank, and the same portfolio paid $9.4 million of interest in cash.

𝐄𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲 𝐅𝐮𝐞𝐥𝐬 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐢𝐫𝐜𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐬
In July the company approved commercial dysprosium and terbium circuits at the White Mesa Mill, plus "a circuit to process mixed REE carbonates" bought from other mines. That second circuit matters because the mill must choose today between uranium and rare earths, and afterwards it can run both. Bhappu put next year's bill at "roughly $100 million".

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐔𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 (𝟑𝟎 𝐒𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔): 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝟐.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬  ⇗ accelerating
The stockpile grew faster while the mill stood still, reaching about 2.4 million finished and contained pounds from 2.27 million in June. Three quarters of mining went into ore piles rather than into sales. Bennett described the holding as flexibility for contract deliveries and opportunistic spot selling.

𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬: $𝟐𝟔.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Money owed by customers reached $26.9 million at the end of September, from $15.1 million in June. Receivables are revenue billed but not yet collected, and this jump ran well ahead of the quarter's sales increase. The balance has more than tripled since March.

𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐲, 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭, 𝐧𝐞𝐭: $𝟏𝟑𝟓.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Fixed assets reached $135.4 million from $74.2 million in June, as the Korean metals plant and the other assets of Australian Strategic Materials joined the balance sheet. Mineral properties added $40.6 million over the same three months. Both lines grow again as construction advances at the Utah mill.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 (𝐩𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐔𝟑𝐎𝟖): 𝟏,𝟓𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎-𝟐,𝟎𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐥𝐛𝐬  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from 1,500,000-2,000,000 lbs
Unchanged, and Bennett is aiming at the bottom of it: 1.5 million pounds. Nine months delivered 1.14 million, so by our math the fourth quarter needs about 360,000 pounds. Long-term contract deliveries for the year are finished, which leaves spot selling out of the 2.4-million-pound stockpile to close the gap.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐝 (𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐩𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐔𝟑𝐎𝟖): 𝟐,𝟎𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎-𝟐,𝟓𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐥𝐛𝐬  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from 2,000,000-2,500,000 lbs
Unchanged on paper, with the lower limit now the target. By our math October to December must yield at least 875,000 pounds, after 385,000 in the third quarter. That is half the year's middle figure in one quarter. Energy Fuels did beat its 2025 mining plan by 49% against the middle of that range, which is the one argument for patience.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐝 (𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐩𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐔𝟑𝐎𝟖): 𝟏,𝟓𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎-𝟐,𝟓𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐥𝐛𝐬  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from 1,500,000-2,500,000 lbs
Unchanged. The mill made nothing between July and September because Energy Fuels shut it for maintenance, so the year stands at the 1.7 million pounds reached in June. That already clears the lower limit. A December restart adds roughly one month of output before the year closes.

𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐫𝐮𝐧: 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐚𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝟏 𝐃𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔, 𝐫𝐮𝐧𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐐𝟏 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕  ⇄ reversing
🠆 unchanged from Q4 2026 or early 2027
Held, and now dated. Bhappu said the ore piles are deep enough to restart "probably around the 1st of December", with uranium processing into the first quarter and a switch to rare earths after that. The mill can treat up to 6 million pounds a year while the mines supply about 2 million, so it runs in campaigns.

𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐌𝐞𝐬𝐚 𝐏𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝟏𝐁/𝟏𝐂 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐃𝐲𝐬𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐛𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖; 𝐬𝐚𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐮𝐦, 𝐞𝐮𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐠𝐚𝐝𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐧 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖  ⇒ stable
🠇 cut from Terbium and dysprosium by the end of 2027; the rest by the end of 2028
Pushed back by a few months. The heavy circuits once due to finish in 2027 now carry an early-2028 date, which Bhappu repeated on the call. That lands the mill's own oxide supply for the Korean plant in the same year the Donald mine is meant to start, so neither leg arrives earlier than the other.

𝐏𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝟏𝐁/𝟏𝐂 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠: 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 $𝟏𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧, 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐢𝐧 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from $104 million in total, about a quarter of it in 2026
Held. Bhappu put next year's bill at "roughly $100 million" for the two circuits. Against $932.3 million of working capital that is affordable alone, but the Donald earn-in, with "$60 million that's remaining", and the VAC payment sit on top of it.

𝐃𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐁𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔  ⇒ stable
🠇 cut from As early as Q3 2026
Deferred again, for the fourth time in two years. Energy Fuels now points at December, helped by "a conditional financing package from Export Finance Australia" worth up to A$180 million of a proposed A$200 million loan. Building the mine then takes about 22 months, which puts the first ore in late 2028.

𝐕𝐀𝐂 𝐚𝐜𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Early 2027
Unchanged. Bhappu still expects the magnet maker to join early next year, with foreign investment approvals the main condition left. He also addressed its customer fight head on, saying Energy Fuels "knew of the Sumter customer dispute before signing the VAC acquisition agreement" and that the arbitration can move the price either way.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝?
The year's lower limit now requires about 875,000 pounds in three months, more than twice the third-quarter rate. At what Pinyon Plain grade, and at how many tonnes of ore a day, does that arithmetic work?

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐕𝐀𝐂 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧 𝐭𝐨𝐝𝐚𝐲?
Energy Fuels agreed in June to pay about $1.9 billion in cash and shares, and has still published no revenue, profit or margin for the magnet maker. Investors cannot size what the company is buying.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐰𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐜𝐢𝐫𝐜𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐬?
Fixed assets rose by $61 million in three months, but the Australian Strategic Materials purchase and construction at the Utah mill both land in that line. How much cash went into the Phase 1B and 1C circuits?

𝐖𝐡𝐨 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐊𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐧 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐥 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖?
Capacity at Ochang nearly triples by early next year, while the mill's own heavy oxide arrives in 2028. Which suppliers are under contract for the gap, at what price, and for how long?

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐥𝐞𝐟𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐥𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐧?
Bhappu said three outside firms are still running due diligence for the Office of Strategic Capital. Which conditions remain on the $725 million commitment, and how much can Energy Fuels draw before the mill's Phase 2 permits arrive?

text:
British Airways is reportedly introducing additional training for cabin crew following the viral incident in which a passenger said she was left sitting in a urine-soaked seat on a flight from Miami to London.

The passenger, Sofia, previously described being offered paper towels and a small bottle of cleaning spray after discovering the contamination, with no alternative seat available.

Now, following her formal complaint, the airline has reportedly promised to train flight attendants on how to respond when passengers discover seats contaminated with bodily fluids.

According to Sofia's account of a phone call with British Airways customer relations, the airline also apologised for its initial generic response and agreed to reimburse her flight.

The crew members involved will not face disciplinary action, she was told.

Sofia subsequently praised the airline's customer relations team for taking her complaint seriously, describing its response as a significant improvement on what happened onboard.

The training commitment raises an obvious question: why wasn't there already a satisfactory procedure for dealing with a passenger being asked to sit in a contaminated seat?

The airline has not publicly detailed the proposed training programme.

text:
You don't have to rank for every service you offer. 

When I take on a client, the first thing we talk about is: 

what is your main revenue driver? 

What do you want more of? 

What's the goal here? 

What do we want your Google Business Profile to appear for when people are in search looking for a specific service?

Say you're a vehicle wrapping company. 

Are there certain makes or certain vehicle types that you want a lot of? 

Do you really like doing trucks?

Do you like wrapping boats a lot? 

Is that one of your main revenue driving sources? 

Maybe there's a service you're getting a lot of leads for, but you don't want. You're tired of doing tents, so you want to rank more for the wraps, because this is where you make the majority of your revenue. 

Then we come up with a plan, and we set up a campaign to start ranking more for the higher revenue generating sources. 

Or maybe you're in Florida and you want to do more boat wraps. 

Maybe that's a higher ticket item for you. Then we would target that.

The profile first. 

Your primary category needs to best match your number one revenue generating source. 

It should not be one of your secondary sources of revenue. 

If you offer pressure washing or some other secondary service, but that is not your primary source of revenue, then that needs to be a secondary category, or this is a great opportunity to get a second Google Business Profile. 

We do not want to be fighting for two different sources of revenue on one profile. 

Then list the services, with keyword variations by vehicle type and by vehicle make, and two to three sentences behind each.

Then the money page. 

The whole point of a money page is to target a very specific keyword, a very specific service. 

Say you want to get into boat wraps. 

You create a money page specifically for boat wraps, to target anybody searching in Google for boat wraps. 

A little keyword research first: how do people actually search for this service? 

Do they type boat wraps, boat wrapping company, boat wraps near me? 

Then competitor research. 

Do we have any competitors for boat wraps, and what are they doing to their pages that we need to start doing to ours? 

Where is the delta, the difference of our page compared to theirs? 

Why are they ranking higher than us? 

Then we apply it, backlinks or more on page optimization, to get our page ranking higher than theirs.

A blog is not a money page. 

That's informational traffic, and that's not what we want if we're trying to sell a couple thousand dollar wrap. 

The whole purpose of blog content is to add relevance, to add authority, and to add geographic relevance. 

Then we take all of this blog content and link from it to the boat wraps page, our money page. 

The page we want ranking first whenever someone searches boat wraps or boat wrap company near me.

text:
THE GIRL WHO ASKED GOD WHERE LOVE HAD GONE.

There once lived a little girl who believed love was the most beautiful thing in creation.

She believed it lived in her family's arms, in friendships, and in the hearts of those who promised never to leave.

And so, she loved.

She loved without suspicion, never imagining that not every heart knew how to protect what it had been given.

But life was not gentle with her.

The hands she reached for wounded her. The voices she trusted deceived her. Those who promised protection became those she needed protection from.

Still, she loved.

The years passed, the girl became a woman.

She wandered through life searching for the love she once believed in.

She sought it in family, only to discover blood did not always mean belonging.

She sought it in friendship, only to learn loyalty was not always returned.

She sought it in lovers, offering her heart to those who admired its warmth but not its worth.

Each time her heart broke, she gathered its pieces and continued walking.

She watched people preach love while practising cruelty, watched promises dissolve into silence, watched kindness mistaken for weakness and forgiveness for permission.

And a question grew within her soul.

Where has all the love gone?

One evening, weary from searching, she stood beneath a silent sky.

She fell to her knees and lifted her face towards heaven.

"God, I have searched for love my entire life."

Her voice trembled.

"I searched for it in those You placed around me. In arms that should have protected me, friendships that should have cherished me, and hearts that promised never to break mine."

Tears fell upon the earth.

"I have given love despite cruelty, forgiveness despite betrayal, and compassion to those who never considered my suffering."

She lowered her head.

"Tell me, Father, where is the love?"

In the stillness, God answered.

"IN YOU, MY CHILD."

The woman looked up.

"In me, Lord? But I have spent my life searching for it."

And God said,

"You believed that because others could not give you love, love itself was absent."

He continued,

"When they wounded you, did you not still recognise the suffering of others?

When they deceived you, did you not continue to value truth?

When they abandoned you, did you not understand the importance of remaining?

When they showed you cruelty, did you not still choose compassion?"

The woman wept.

"Yes, Father."

And God answered,

"Then tell Me, where do you believe that love came from?"

She remained silent.

God spoke once more.

"You searched for My love in others, forgetting I had already placed it within you.

You mistook their inability to love you for the absence of love itself.

But the love you offered, the mercy you extended, the tenderness you preserved despite every reason to surrender it..

THAT WAS THE LOVE YOU WERE SEARCHING FOR.

Not because suffering made you worthy, but because you were worthy long before it began.

You need not allow others to wound you to prove your love is real.

My child, you were never required to destroy yourself to demonstrate the love I placed within you."

The woman placed her hand upon her heart.

For the first time, she understood.

She had spent her life searching for something she believed the world had stolen.

Yet beneath every scar, beyond every betrayal, through every darkness, something sacred remained.

The love within her had survived.

As she rose, she asked God one final question.

"Then why, Father, did I spend so many years searching?"

And God replied,

"My child, you were looking for love to recognise you, when you had yet to recognise the love within yourself."

From that day, she no longer measured love by the hearts that failed to give it.

Another person's inability to love was never proof that love did not exist.

FOR THE WORLD HAD SHOWN HER MANY THINGS THAT LOVE WAS NOT.

GOD HAD SHOWN HER WHERE LOVE HAD ALWAYS BEEN.
WITHIN HER. 🙏🤍

"The kingdom of God is within you."  Luke 17:21

text:
Five Lessons from a Losing School Board Candidate

As some of you might know, I ran for the Indianapolis school board this year. If you didn't know, it's because I deliberately kept that political work on other social media channels. And I intend to keep it that way, other than to acknowledge that this was not an especially good year to run as an Independent in a district that is 80 percent Democrat—even against three Democratic opponents.

But I mention the race now because I came away with several observations from the campaign trail that seem worth sharing, particularly with my friends in the school reform community.

I acknowledge that these observations are anecdotal. But they were far too prominent to ignore, and I think they offer some important warning signs.

Here you go, in no particular order…

The public is genuinely clueless about school funding. And we haven't made it easy for them to become informed.

My local district spends, at minimum, $22,000 per student. That's the number I used in my campaign because it was the lowest of three different published figures, ranging from $22,000 in the district's own budget to as high as $31,000 in federal reporting, with state figures falling somewhere in between.

But most people simply didn't believe the number.

Chalkbeat even included a disclaimer in my candidate profile saying they couldn't confirm the figure, despite my having provided three sources supporting that amount or more!

And among those who did believe it, many struggled to contextualize the number—or simply responded reflexively that the schools "need it!"

Okay. Maybe they do need more than HALF A MILLION DOLLARS for every classroom of 25 students. Granted, that money supports much more than the classroom itself. But wouldn't it be nice to have some understanding of where all that money goes?

And why, with that level of funding, can't we pay teachers more? Why is ANY teacher still spending personal funds on classroom supplies?

I've seen polling suggesting that much of the public, including many teachers, believes schools spend only around $5,000 per student.

That level of misunderstanding represents a failure of the media, policymakers and those of us working to improve schools. And, frankly, it's also a failure of teachers unions, which have done a remarkably poor job of translating available education funding into better teacher compensation.

"Cuts" to school funding remain a powerful rallying cry—even when the reality is more complicated.

Indiana lawmakers have enacted property tax reforms that limit the growth in revenues schools and other local governments had anticipated. But limits on projected growth are typically portrayed as actual funding cuts.

That distinction matters.

The resulting controversy helped fuel an extraordinary round of school operating referenda, with 27 of 39 proposals passing statewide. That included the Indianapolis referendum, which, for the first time, will share proceeds with charter schools.

That last point might seem to contradict my next observation. Except that charter schools were themselves frequently blamed for the need for the referendum.

Of course, plenty of blame also fell on Indiana's Republican-led legislature, which has been repeatedly accused of "starving" urban districts like Indianapolis.

Yet even as IPS has lost enrollment over the years, its overall funding has often remained steady or increased—meaning that per-pupil funding has continued to rise.

And still, the narrative that urban schools are being systematically defunded remains remarkably powerful.

All of this points to a growing need for policymakers—and, I would argue, the media!—to do a much better job of reporting PER-PUPIL funding levels, distinguishing actual cuts from reductions in anticipated growth and examining how much funding genuinely reaches classrooms.

The charter school brand is in trouble.

Yes, I know. Charter schools have always been polarizing. I've been involved in these battles since 1995, so none of that is news to me.

But Indianapolis is a city where more students now attend charter schools than attend the traditional district, and where multiple studies have found stronger academic outcomes among charter students.

You might think that would make the charter school brand somewhat less controversial.

Apparently not.

Especially among some of the educated, politically engaged voters I encountered, the word "charter" seemed almost toxic. You would have thought every charter school in Indianapolis had been named after our current president. (None has, of course.)

This was one of the more surprising and troubling observations from the campaign. It suggests that even where charter schools have become a major part of the educational landscape, the political narrative surrounding them may be moving in the opposite direction.

There's much more I could say about this, but I'll save some of that for another day.

Academic performance seemed not to matter much.

I've grown accustomed to the familiar explanations for poor academic performance in urban districts: poverty, student demographics, special education needs, language barriers and so forth.

But this time, academic performance itself almost seemed like a dead issue.

And that was genuinely strange to me.

In the final days of the campaign, I raised concerns about the district's low participation in career and technical education. And that actually seemed to get some attention.

But the fact that roughly one-quarter of third graders weren't reading proficiently, or that approximately 80 percent of students weren't meeting certain state academic benchmarks? Those numbers seemed almost accepted as inevitable.

The winning candidate rarely discussed academics beyond emphasizing the importance of reading. Another candidate suggested that academics were fine and would largely take care of themselves if families would simply stop leaving the district.

In a district facing such serious academic challenges, that apparent lack of urgency was confounding.

And for those of us who believe that academic outcomes should be central to public education, it ought to be deeply concerning.

The definition of "grassroots" can be remarkably selective.

One of the more frustrating aspects of the campaign was watching the teachers union and a relatively small group of politically active parents and community members establish themselves as the district's "real grassroots."

Their influence was unmistakable. Voters embraced their slate cards, and the media frequently reinforced their grassroots credentials.

Yet the network supporting my campaign included parents and students who, demographically and experientially, looked much more like the families actually served by the district.

Our coalition, however, was routinely dismissed as a "charter group."

Meanwhile, a self-described Parent Council, composed largely of middle-class white women in a district serving a student population that is roughly 80 percent minority, was readily accepted as the authentic grassroots voice.

To be clear, those parents have every right to organize, advocate and influence elections. And the winning candidate also enjoyed support from several left-wing activist organizations, including the Democratic Socialists of America, whose members may well have represented a genuine grassroots political movement.

But a successful political organization is not necessarily representative of the families whose children attend the schools.

And that distinction seemed largely lost in the public conversation.

So what does all of this mean?

There are certainly more observations I could share. But these five stood out most, and I think they deserve some serious reflection from those of us who have spent years—or decades—working to improve public education.

We can continue to debate school funding, charter schools, accountability and academic performance among ourselves. But if voters don't understand the funding, distrust the educational options, aren't especially motivated by academic results and look elsewhere for their political cues, we have a much larger challenge than any particular school board election.

For whatever may be learned from a losing school board candidate, I hope these observations offer something useful.

And perhaps the most important lesson is this: If we want education reform to succeed, we need to understand not only what makes schools better, but what actually persuades the public to demand better schools.

Ukraine has much more to offer America than we sometimes realize. 🇺🇦🇺🇸

And I believe it’s time we talked more about what we can build together.

Last week, I had the privilege of joining the U.S.–Ukraine Trade and Investment delegation in Washington, D.C., organized through the Congressional Office for International Leadership (COIL) and its Open World program.

I participated in a roundtable at the Library of Congress alongside representatives of the U.S. Department of State, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), the Ukrainian diplomatic community, and congressional offices from both parties.

We also met with the U.S. Helsinki Commission to discuss strengthening economic cooperation between our countries.

My central message was simple:

Ukraine is not just a country that needs support. Ukraine is a partner capable of creating real economic and technological value for the United States.

We deeply appreciate America's support. And one of the best ways Ukrainian entrepreneurs can reciprocate is by doing what we know best: building businesses, developing technologies, investing, and creating jobs.

This is a two-way street.

Ukrainian engineering expertise, combined with American capital, industrial capabilities, and market opportunities, can create something much bigger than either could achieve alone.

At DroneUA, we have accumulated experience across more than 3 million hectares of agricultural drone spraying operations in Ukraine.

Through Futurology, we are bringing that expertise to the United States, developing partnerships and investing in American manufacturing capabilities. Our journey has also been recognized as a Success Story by the U.S. Department of Commerce.

Real businesses. Real investments. American jobs. Measurable results.

Special thanks to COIL, the Open World program, and Lewis Madanick for their longstanding commitment to building bridges between our countries.

This program is particularly meaningful to our family. I'm an Open World alumnus, and my wife, Oleksandra Afanasieva, who has been involved with the program since 2008, is leading this year's delegation.

I'm incredibly proud of her and the outstanding Ukrainian professionals continuing their journey to Charlotte and Asheville, North Carolina.

Shared values brought our countries closer. Shared investment, opportunities, and success will make that partnership stronger for generations.

text:
Michael Crichton's ER made Warner Bros more than $3.5 billion, his estate says, and a clause he signed in 1994 now keeps the studio in court over The Pitt.

1994. Crichton signs the ER deal. No sequels or spinoffs without his consent.

December 2022. Warner writes to his widow that it will respect the estate's approval rights, the complaint says.

April 11, 2023. A "best and final" offer arrives at 5:30 p.m., due the same night. The estate refuses.

November 4, 2026. A California appeals court lets the case go forward against the studio and drops the claims against Noah Wyle and producer John Wells.

Next comes a jury trial in Los Angeles, unless the two sides settle, AV Club reports.

In the video below, Crichton sits with Charlie Rose in 2007 talking about gene patents. ER never comes up. Owning something, he says, works "just as if it was a piece of land" that others can be kept off. The line sits at the end of a long hepatitis C example, easy to skip.

This is my reading; he never said it about ER. His contract paid $7,500 an episode for the "Created by" credit, the complaint says, and he still treated the right to say no as the bigger asset. Writers often trade that kind of veto for a bigger check. Crichton kept his, and the case now turns on it.

The case for the estate: the appeals court wrote of "clear and numerous similarities" between the shows, from the pace to the young doctor fresh out of medical school. Both are set in a busy emergency room.

The case for Warner: the studio calls The Pitt "an entirely original series." It says the claims have no merit and that it will defend its position as the case proceeds.

Should a 1994 signature still decide what a hospital drama can be in 2026, or should it end with the man who signed it?

text:
Vance Wants to End the Iran War. But a Failed Meeting Could Bring the Region Closer to Another Escalation

The prospect of another diplomatic meeting involving Vice President JD Vance, this time with Rezaei, is an important development. But I would be very careful about reading too much into it.

Following the earlier contacts, the letter to Iran's leadership, and now the possibility of a direct meeting, Tehran can hardly ignore the message: Vance appears genuinely determined to bring this war to an end.

And there are good reasons for him to do so. Ending the conflict would serve American interests, ease the economic and political pressure on the administration, and offer Republicans an opportunity to move beyond a war that has become increasingly costly.

But wanting to end a war and being prepared to make the compromises necessary to end it are two very different things.

First, Washington should understand that Rezaei is not Delcy Rodríguez. Anyone who believes that identifying a senior figure within the Iranian establishment creates an opportunity to bypass the leadership or persuade Tehran to abandon its fundamental positions is making a serious mistake.

Rezaei is deeply rooted in the Islamic Republic's political and security establishment. Even if he has the authority to negotiate, that does not mean he has either the mandate or the desire to fundamentally change Iran's position. He is not an alternative to the regime, and Washington should not expect him to deliver an Iranian surrender simply because the United States is willing to engage with him.

More importantly, Iran's leadership has made its position clear. Tehran is not prepared to abandon its fundamental demands, particularly regarding the Strait of Hormuz, the maritime restrictions and the economic measures imposed on Iran. From the Iranian perspective, these issues must be addressed before meaningful nuclear negotiations can begin.

And this is where the real challenge lies. The proposed meeting would be a meaningful indication that both sides are searching for a political way out. It would also demonstrate Vance's personal commitment to ending the confrontation. That matters, especially given the deep distrust between Washington and Tehran.

But we have been here before. As the Islamabad experience demonstrated, a high-level meeting, however important, cannot substitute for an agreement on the fundamental issues dividing the two sides.

If Washington arrives with essentially the same position, demanding that Iran first reverse its measures in Hormuz while offering no meaningful movement on the restrictions and guarantees Tehran considers essential, I see little reason to expect a breakthrough.

The United States does not necessarily have to accept every Iranian demand. But it must be prepared to explore a different sequence of reciprocal steps, one that gives Tehran a credible reason to move forward without appearing to surrender.

That could involve a phased arrangement addressing freedom of navigation, maritime restrictions, economic measures and guarantees against renewed hostilities, with nuclear negotiations following on an agreed timetable.

There is also a crucial question about Washington itself: Does Vance have Trump's backing to explore such compromises, or is he being sent to test Iranian flexibility without any corresponding change in American policy?

For Tehran, that distinction is essential. The Iranian leadership will not make major concessions simply because it believes Vance wants peace. It needs to believe that any understanding can actually be delivered and sustained by the administration.

And this brings me to what I consider the most dangerous aspect of the proposed meeting.A failed meeting could be worse than no meeting at all.

If Vance and Rezaei meet and fail to bridge the gaps, Trump could conclude that diplomacy has been exhausted and that renewed military pressure is the only remaining option. Tehran, meanwhile, could interpret the failure as further evidence that Washington is not genuinely prepared to negotiate on terms Iran considers acceptable.

Such an outcome would strengthen those within the Iranian leadership who believe that only continued resistance and escalation can force American concessions.

We could then find ourselves in a particularly dangerous situation: both sides enter the meeting hoping to find a way out, only to emerge more convinced that the other side understands nothing but force.

And after everything that has happened during this war, another round of escalation would not necessarily resemble the previous ones. Iran has demonstrated its willingness to impose significant economic costs through Hormuz and attacks on regional infrastructure. Washington may believe it can conduct another limited military operation, but Tehran could conclude that a much stronger response is necessary to restore deterrence.

That is how a diplomatic failure could become the starting point for a much broader confrontation.

The bottom line is that a Vance–Rezaei meeting, if it takes place, would be a significant diplomatic step and an important indication of Vance's determination to end the war. But unless Washington is willing to reconsider its approach to Hormuz and the broader economic restrictions, the meeting is unlikely to produce a breakthrough.

I believe Vance genuinely wants to end this conflict. But his personal commitment, important as it is, cannot overcome the fundamental disagreements between Washington and Tehran without a corresponding change in American policy.

While the United States and Europe have spent years arming one side, imposing sweeping sanctions, and lecturing the world on “rules based order,” it is Prime Minister Narendra Modi who has just secured a concrete diplomatic opening on the single issue that actually affects hundreds of millions of people: unblocking Black Sea grain corridors.​

Zelenskyy’s own statement after the call makes the contrast unmistakable.

He confirmed that India is ready to mediate food corridors precisely because New Delhi talks to both Moscow and Kyiv without the ideological hostility that has defined Western policy.

Modi has repeatedly told Putin, as Zelenskyy himself acknowledged, that the war must end.

That is not rhetoric; it is the practical advantage of a country that never joined the sanctions regime, never supplied weapons, and therefore retains leverage with both capitals.​

The West’s approach has been the opposite.

Sanctions on Russian fertilisers and shipping, combined with the destruction of port infrastructure, have driven global food prices higher and hit developing nations hardest. 

Europe and the United States continue to prioritise military packages over any serious mechanism that would allow Ukrainian grain and Russian fertiliser to move freely.

The result is prolonged suffering for Ukrainian farmers, Russian exporters, and food importing countries alike.

India’s offer of mediation cuts through that failure. It treats food security as a shared interest rather than a propaganda tool.

This is why Zelenskyy is now looking to New Delhi ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks. 

India does not need to choose sides to deliver results.

It can speak to Moscow about de-escalation in the Black Sea and to Kyiv about the economic necessity of open export routes.

That is the difference between performative solidarity and actual diplomacy.

While Washington and Brussels keep funding the battlefield, Modi is positioning India to open the corridors that feed the world.

That is not neutrality for its own sake; it is the only posture that has any chance of producing an outcome both Ukraine and Russia can live with.

text:
"US ​President Donald Trump will meet the prime minister of key mediator Qatar on Monday as efforts to end the Iran war ramp up following last week's ‌midterm elections, though senior US and Gulf officials cast doubt on the chances of an imminent deal.

More than eight months into the conflict he launched alongside Israel on February 28, Trump has played down the likelihood of major warfare restarting soon but remains unwilling to accept an existing Iranian truce plan.

Mutual attacks continue, with the US striking Iran's Qeshm island overnight, according to Iranian state media, and Iran attacking tankers in the Gulf and ​Strait of Hormuz this month while its Yemeni Houthi allies have hit Saudi Arabia.

DIPLOMATIC MOVES
Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, who is both prime minister and foreign minister of ​Qatar, will meet Trump and Vice President JD Vance in Washington later on Monday after having visited Tehran last week.

Iran's proposal to end ⁠the war involves an end to the US blockade of its ports, the lifting of some sanctions and a halt to bombing in return for Tehran stopping its own blockade ​of the Strait of Hormuz, with talks on its nuclear programme and other sanctions to follow.
The US has repeatedly rejected that plan, which Iran has said could be condensed to a ​two-day timeframe, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio describing Tehran's conditions on Sunday as "outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic".

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei defended the plan on Monday as the most reasonable offer on the table.

Senior US Republicans including Vance have blamed their party's losses in last week's elections on the Iran war, but despite growing domestic political pressure to end the conflict, Rubio said he did not believe ​a diplomatic breakthrough was imminent.
A senior United Arab Emirates official, Anwar Gargash, echoed that view on Monday, saying a comprehensive political settlement between the US and Iran appeared difficult.

Vance, who led the negotiations for a short-lived truce in June, ‌will also ⁠meet Al-Thani, whose country has been a prime mediator since early in the war, conveying messages between the sides and proposing ways to bridge their differences.

Anxiety over the war has pervaded the region for months and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday he had told Trump that Ankara did not want to see a new escalation.

MILITARY ACTION
Sunday ​night's strikes on Qeshm island did not impact ​vital infrastructure or services, a provincial ⁠official told Iran's semi-official Fars news agency on Monday. The US has not commented on the Iranian media reports.
A senior Iranian source told Reuters that US strikes were targeting Iranian radar systems serving both air defence and ship navigation, as well as bases for missile launchers ​and mine-laying systems.

Attacks on tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz ramped up sharply in October and have continued at the ​highest rate since the ⁠start of the war, figures from international maritime agencies showed last week.
Iran, which typically does not acknowledge striking vessels that report being hit by projectiles, said on Sunday a tanker had hit a mine east of the Strait of Hormuz.
A state television reporter said on Monday that 11 tankers had been "disabled" over the past 10 days.
The war has triggered a global energy shortage, prompted Iranian ⁠strikes on Gulf ​Arab countries, spilled over into a major Israeli offensive in Lebanon during the spring and summer and reignited ​Yemen's long-frozen civil war.
On Sunday Yemen's Iran-allied Houthi group said it had struck an office building of Saudi state oil company Aramco in Riyadh. The attack blew out windows across several floors of a building in the city's financial district. The ​Energy Ministry acknowledged damage from an attempted attack on the building without assigning responsibility."

text:
Trump Is Still President. Washington Is Already Moving Without Him

The Jensen Huang affair is exposing how little control Trump may have over the files, leaks and investigations surrounding his own allies.

The Jensen Huang scandal begins with an affair. Its political meaning begins somewhere else: inside the US government.

Donald Trump had already been briefed on intelligence concerning Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman whom US officials reportedly assessed to have been recruited by Chinese intelligence. He chose not to escalate the matter.

Then the intelligence left the classified world.

It reached the press. Huang’s private relationship became public. Nvidia’s independent directors opened an investigation. Three Republican House committee chairmen asked Huang to appear for a joint closed-door briefing on November 18.

Trump publicly defended him.

The story kept moving.

That sequence deserves more attention than the affair itself.

Intelligence does not enter a newspaper by accident. Someone with access to the material, or to people who had been briefed on it, decided that a judgment sitting inside the national-security system should acquire a public life.

The source remains hidden. The act does not.

Someone decided that Trump’s decision to leave the matter alone would not be the last word.

That alone changes the meaning of the case.

It also raises a second problem, one that has been strangely absent from much of the coverage: intelligence files are not repositories of revealed truth.

They contain intercepted fragments, human reporting, foreign liaison material, source judgments, analytical assumptions and sometimes information that later proves wrong. The US intelligence community’s own standards require analysts to distinguish collected information from their own judgments and to state the confidence and uncertainty attached to major assessments. Even a high-confidence judgment is not the same thing as proof.

Those qualifications rarely travel as well as the allegation.

Inside an intelligence product, a claim can carry caveats about sourcing, corroboration and confidence.

Once it reaches the public domain, the caveats shrink. The allegation survives.

That should make Huang’s case far more uncomfortable for the business figures around Trump.

They know which contracts they signed.

They know which campaigns they funded, which regulators they lobbied, which officials they met and which government programmes their companies benefited from.

Those records can be anticipated.

An intelligence file is different.

A foreign contact may have been under surveillance. A conversation may have been collected because somebody else was the target. An executive’s name may have appeared in a report generated for an investigation he never knew existed. Separate fragments can remain scattered across databases for years until somebody asks a new question.

Section 702 offers one obvious example of the underlying mechanism. It targets non-Americans abroad, but US-person communications can be incidentally acquired when those people communicate with foreign targets. The government maintains rules governing how such material is retained, queried and disseminated.

A CEO can prepare for a subpoena.

He cannot prepare for a file he does not know exists.

So the question becomes more unsettling than What does Washington know?

What does Washington think it knows about me?

And who, at some future political moment, might decide to make that judgment public?

Huang gives that fear a concrete shape.

A private relationship entered an intelligence narrative. That narrative entered the media. Congress picked it up. Nvidia’s board then had its own obligations to investors and the company.

The underlying material did not need to become a criminal case.

It became politically usable.

That possibility reaches well beyond China.

Huang enters the story through intelligence, export controls and Beijing. Elon Musk enters through a different door. He spent heavily to preserve Republican power in the midterms while his companies maintain extensive commercial relationships with the federal government. Democrats preparing to take control of Congress have already discussed scrutiny of his DOGE role and of corporate relationships with the Trump administration.

Another executive may face procurement questions.

Another may face scrutiny over a federal project, tax treatment, a regulatory decision or business involving people around the president.

The exposure changes from person to person.

The concentration of private wealth, political loyalty and public power is what makes the network combustible.

And Huang’s case adds one feature that contracts and campaign disclosures do not: some of the relevant material may already exist outside the subject’s knowledge.

That matters even more because Trump is fighting his own state.

Reuters reported days before the midterms that intelligence sharing across the US government had fractured during his second term. Relations between the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence deteriorated sharply. The CIA stopped co-authoring some National Intelligence Council assessments. Some intelligence flows to Congress were temporarily halted. Analysts described an environment in which producing judgments that conflicted with White House views had become increasingly fraught.

This conflict is larger than China.

Trump has spent years arguing that parts of the intelligence, law-enforcement and administrative establishment used state power against him. His second administration has tried to assert much tighter political control over those institutions.

Inside that struggle sits a bureaucracy with its own memories, professional judgments, grievances and ideas about where institutional responsibility ends.

That is the environment in which the Huang information surfaced.

One possible reading is obvious enough to deserve serious attention: disclosure itself can become a form of policy intervention.

An official who believes the president is ignoring a national-security risk does not need to win an argument in the Oval Office if the material can instead reach a journalist.

Publication changes the arena.

The White House must respond.

Congress can demand answers.

A company board may have to act.

The political cost of doing nothing rises immediately.

For officials deeply hostile to Trump, the same mechanism can serve a wider purpose. It can constrain the president without first defeating him inside the administration.

No central command is required.

One institution preserves information. Someone with access discloses part of it. A journalist publishes. A Republican national-security hawk has his own reason to respond. Months later, a Democratic chairman can inherit the same trail and pursue it for entirely different reasons.

Different motives. Same direction of pressure.

That may prove harder for Trump to manage than a single organised opponent.

He can fire an official.

He can replace an agency head.

He can denounce a committee.

He cannot easily erase information already dispersed across institutions, nor can he guarantee that everyone holding it accepts his judgment about what deserves to disappear.

This is why the timing of the Huang affair matters.

Trump is still president.

Republicans still hold the relevant House committee gavels.

The men asking Huang to appear on November 18 are Republicans, not incoming Democratic chairmen. Nvidia’s board moved while Trump was publicly defending its CEO.

The machinery is already in motion before Democrats take control.

After January, they inherit it.

Democratic lawmakers are openly preparing investigations involving Musk, senior Trump officials and corporate America. Committee control will give them staffs, document demands and subpoena authority. More importantly, they will inherit whatever information, unfinished inquiries and institutional suspicions already exist.

They do not have to start with a blank page.

November 18 makes the contradiction unusually visible.

Trump expects to be in China for the APEC leaders’ summit and says he expects to meet Xi Jinping. On the same day, three Republican committee chairmen have asked Huang to sit behind closed doors in Washington.

In China, Trump will exercise the power of the presidency at its highest level. He can bargain over trade, technology and the broader political relationship with Beijing.

Back in Washington, an issue he had already chosen not to escalate will still be alive.

One scene shows presidential power.

The other shows how far that power now reaches.

For Trump’s business allies, the questions are becoming difficult to avoid.

What has the government recorded about them?

How reliable is it?

Who controls it?

And who might decide, at the right political moment, that it should no longer remain secret?

Trump may not know the answers either.

He remains president.

The people around him are already learning that this may no longer be enough.

text:
Jason Rathje came by @spc on Friday to meet with our founders, share a bit about his career building within the government as an engineer and researcher, and offer his experience on what needs to get built, how, and how that gets done. This perspective was particularly helpful for our deep tech founders.  

Unrelatedly, I often think: if the investments he made in the government organizations he’s created were for equity, he probably would have had a track record better than most venture firms.  After building two programs in the government that have accelerated investment and innovation in frontier technology, he most recently joined WebAI as president of the public sector and also sits on the board of @elroyair 

There are very few people, in my mind, who have had as much of an impact on driving U.S. innovation as Jason has. He has one of the most unique perspectives as someone who has worked on the technology, the buying process, the early funding path, the industrial capital behind production, and now the challenge of taking a company’s product to government customers.  

At SPC, that experience gave him a particularly helpful and insightful answer to the dilemma founders building at the frontier have: build what the government cannot yet imagine, but do not confuse showing it an invention with getting that invention deployed.  While doing his PhD at Stanford, he studied how government programs were effective at funding new technology. What he learned was that, at the time, Silicon Valley and the military often had a cultural or political divide. He became obsessed with understanding how the government could actually adapt its programs to accelerate company growth.  To him, SBIR’s goal was to grow and strengthen the economy and help companies that start off small become really big. Through his research, he discovered that the program wasn’t doing that. This led him to build two programs in the government that deployed more dollars into innovation and technology over the last nearly decade, via AFWerx and the Department of Defense’s Office of Strategic Capital.  

The Office has the sole focus of investing in industries that were ultimately beneath the national security system, including everything from supply chain and manufacturing—not just military products. He left the government to go back to building, and believes that every American is right to own their own artificial intelligence. 

In order to be resilient, we should not depend entirely on central infrastructure or closed models.  

He shared a lot of insight and specific perspectives on what it looks like to successfully sell into the government, and we can't wait to have him back.

A representative for Megaspeed said the company was conducting an internal investigation into allegations of chip diversion and had repeatedly offered to cooperate with the U.S. government but that those offers had gone unanswered.

The United States began investigating Megaspeed and Ms. Huang in 2024, after the company started importing billions of dollars’ worth of advanced Nvidia A.I. equipment into Malaysia. Megaspeed had been planning and constructing data centers around Southeast Asia to serve Chinese clients, including Alibaba, the Chinese tech giant. While that behavior is legal, U.S. officials were concerned that some of the Nvidia chips the company had bought were illegally routed into China.

In August 2025, officials at the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security who were pursuing the case received an email from Mr. Teter, the general counsel of Nvidia, people familiar with the incident said. In a message to the agents, Mr. Teter said that Mr. Kessler had given him permission to reach out about the case.

A Commerce Department official said that Nvidia had contacted the employees directly to request a meeting with one of them. When the employees declined the meeting, Mr. Teter responded to the employees by saying he was unsure what the issue was because Mr. Kessler had said Nvidia could communicate with the bureau’s employees.

The employees forwarded the email chain to Mr. Kessler. Hours later, Mr. Kessler responded, saying they should continue to handle the case strictly by the book, the official said.

Mr. Kessler did not order his employees to divulge information to Nvidia, and he did not weigh in with the agents on what meetings to take or what information to divulge, that official said.

text:
In 2015, I built an AI that detects early cancer.

It’s still running across hundreds of hospitals in the US today.

It was the most fulfilling work of my life, and I was building in AI years before everyone called it “AI”.

Building in AI then was a dream.

Now It feels like we’ve taken a turn for the worse.

It started when i was in undergrad.

I built my first company: AI models that made the political data transparent to voters.

At 21, I was offered six figures for it, but the buyers wanted to use it for reasons I couldn't ethically support.

So we turned down the offer and shut down the company instead.

In 2014, I moved into deep learning research on language models, for the Intelligence Community and Goldman Sachs.

Then HCA Healthcare came to us.

They put me in a competition against 10 people from IBM Watson. It was just me and the tools I’d built.

Our job was to build an AI model that can catch the cancer that slips through the cracks in hospitals.

It was the most intense 30 days of my life. Multiple all nighters.

My models won. That turned into a $5M deal, and later its own company, Azra AI.

Then the world caught on.

ChatGPT and Claude arrived, and AI costs exploded.

Building in AI in 2015 felt novel.

We were using it to find cancer tumours and save lives.

Now the biggest tech companies have turned AI into a money extraction machine.

That’s when I decided to make a change.

We raised $8.5M to build a better future for AI.

On Wednesday, we’re launching Rayline.

AI shouldn’t be locked inside a few labs’ models, prices and clouds. It should be open, transparent and decentralized.

More on Wednesday.

text:
Few people in China have heard of Transsion Holdings, but hundreds of millions of people across the Global South use its phones.

The firm, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has risen from obscurity to become a dominant player in Africa, where it makes nearly half of all phones bought on the continent every year, beating competition from Samsung, Apple, and domestic Chinese giants like Xiaomi and Huawei Technologies. It also holds more than a 10% share of the Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern markets.

Transsion’s rise has been all the more impressive given its humble origins: unlike many of its rivals, it hasn’t benefited from massive funding or market-leading technology.

Instead, it has built a global business almost from scratch — a decades-long journey spanning Shenzhen’s knock-off electronics markets, scrappy networks of African “suitcase entrepreneurs,” and years of careful, locally targeted innovation.

Lu Miao, a media anthropologist and assistant professor at Hong Kong’s Lingnan University, charts this fascinating tale in her book “The Transsion Approach: Translating Chinese Mobile Technology in Africa.”

Based on years of research, it explores the secrets to the company’s success in the Global South — and how its strategy offers an alternative to the “blitzscaling” model favored by many tech startups in both Silicon Valley and China.

In this interview, Lu talks to Sixth Tone and Zhang Lin, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire whose research focuses on tech innovation, about the Transsion story and what it teaches us about global technology flows.

Read more: https://t.co/wHd0LdAfts

If you're considering a B2B creator partnership on LinkedIn, here's how to evaluate the person before you spend anything:

Start with audience fit, not follower count. Read the comments under their posts. Look at job titles, industries, and companies. A smaller audience of relevant decision-makers can be more useful than a large following with little connection to your offer.

Check credibility. Do they have real experience in the category, or are they summarizing trends they barely understand? Look for specific examples and evidence of the work they describe.

Look at consistency. Someone who posts about one area of expertise every week builds clearer authority than someone bouncing between unrelated topics. In B2B, depth often beats volume.

Evaluate engagement quality. A few serious comments from decision-makers can matter more than hundreds of generic reactions. Look for questions, disagreements, shared experiences.

Finally, watch how they handle sponsored work. Clear disclosure, good judgment, and natural fit matter. If sponsored posts feel forced, examine the response before assuming the partnership will work.

More on planning a focused creator-partnership test:

text:
Fastest-growing industries to launch an AI offer into (by the numbers):

I train business owners, corporate teams, governments and universities on AI.

The offers that land are the ones built for one industry.

Here's the full breakdown + the prompt I'd run on each:

INDUSTRY 1: Behavioral health practices

- More practitioners means more intake, scheduling, reminders and follow-ups
- First offer to test: AI front-desk setup (forms, reminders, FAQs) plus patient-education content, never clinical work
- Offices of mental health practitioners: projected +27.6% jobs, 2025-35 (BLS)
- Run it: "I need to identify business opportunities in AI and behavioral health practices..."

INDUSTRY 2: Therapy and rehab clinics

- Booking, intake, insurance paperwork, patient handouts
- First offer to test: AI-written patient handouts and a booking/FAQ assistant
- PT, OT, speech therapy and audiology offices: projected +25.4%, about 130,600 new jobs, 2025-35 (BLS)
- Run it: "...in AI and physical therapy clinics..."

For both clinics: check patient-privacy rules before touching patient data.

INDUSTRY 3: Elder and disability care

- Big teams, constant scheduling, new hires to train
- First offer to test: AI-built onboarding and training for new aides
- Projected to add 625,400 jobs, the most new jobs of any industry, 2025-35 (BLS)
- Run it: "...in AI and home care agencies..."

INDUSTRY 4: Solar and clean-energy installers

- Small installers live on quotes, permits, follow-ups and customer questions
- First offer to test: an AI quote-and-follow-up system plus local marketing content
- Solar, wind and geothermal power are projected to be the fastest-growing industries. Solar power generation: projected +152.9%, and solar PV installers +36.5%, 2025-35 (BLS)
- Run it: "...in AI and residential solar installers..."

INDUSTRY 5: Construction and the trades

- AI use is rising fastest in construction, not tech
- The office industries started high, so the room to grow is in the trades. As of May 2026, information (39.7%) and finance (33.9%) businesses led AI use, vs. a 19.8% average (Census Bureau survey)
- First offer to test: an "AI office in a box" for one trade (quotes, emails, scheduling, phones, marketing)
- Run it: "...in AI and roofing contractors..."

INDUSTRY 6: Battery and electrical manufacturing

- New plants mean new hires who need training fast
- First offer to test: AI training workshops for plant and office teams
- A top-10 fastest-growing industry: projected +25.9%, about 45,500 new jobs, 2025-35 (BLS)
- Run it: "...in AI and electrical equipment manufacturing..."

HOW TO PICK YOURS:

- Shortlist two industries from this list
- Run my market-research prompt on each (it's in my quote post)
- Take the top opportunity and test one offer with one business

Job growth tells you where the work is coming.

The prompt tells you where people are already paying.

Pick one industry. Run the prompt. Build for that one.

She was a teenager when 12 men lined up in front of her on a prison set. She says she gave in. The pay was $3,500.

Her name is Belladonna. Born Michelle Sinclair. Raised Mormon in Salt Lake City, second of seven kids. Her father was a retired Air Force captain and a former bishop.

In 1999 she moved to Los Angeles and shot her first scene. She was promised $1,000. The director offered $600 more for one extra act.

Then came the prison set. An agent and a director talked her into a rough group scene with 12 men. The price was $3,500. Her own words to the reporter: "I didn't handle the pressure well; I gave in."

Look at the pay ladder. $1,000 for the first day. $600 on top for going further. $3,500 for the scene with the most men and the least control.

The same story has a second number. She claims she earned about $100,000 in her first year. That is her figure, not an audited one.

She stayed in the industry until 2012. Then she posted on Twitter that she was no longer interested in having sex on camera. Two years later she was in mainstream films, including Inherent Vice.

She also says nobody forced her. That she could have said no. The reporter who wrote it down describes a woman who spent years numb and smoking after scenes.

So the numbers tell two stories at once. Prices went up as the scenes got rougher. And she kept saying yes at the new price.

The ABC segment where she talks about it is below.

Was this an industry that paid more for what hurt most, or a choice made with the price tag in front of her?

text:
Keep it simple young man.

Before you launch a cold-email campaign, research accounts and launch offer-led messages:

Scraping for research: 

Start with the homepage, About page, services + products, pricing, case studies, locations, careers, and recent news. 

Then turn what you find into columns you can actually use to write humanized, offer-led copy for each row inside of the table.

- Products + services. 

What do people pay them for? 

“Mobile repair for Class 8 trucks” tells you more than “automotive services.”

- Main buyers. 

Who buys it? 

Look at the product pages and who shows up in the case studies. 

A fleet manager buying maintenance has a different problem from an owner-operator who needs a truck fixed today.

- Years in business. 

Find the founding year or a statement like “serving Ohio since 1998.” 

Keep the source beside it.

- Where they operate. 

Pull the service area so you know what geography your offer needs to cover.

- Likely marketing channels. 

Look for location pages, a referral program, recent LinkedIn posts, or other signs of how they bring in customers. Save what you saw and mark what you’re assuming.

- Estimated ACV. 

What’s a typical annual contract worth? 

Use published prices, packages, or a deal size you can point to. If they sell one-off jobs, estimate the job value.

- Estimated LTV. 

What might a customer be worth over the relationship? 

Use a range if you have evidence on repeat purchases or retention. Otherwise leave it blank.

- Reason to reach out now. 

A new location, a new service, a hire. 

Save the date and the line that supports it.

A shop that makes its money on recurring fleet maintenance is getting a different offer from me than a guy doing one-off roadside repairs. 

That’s what all this research is for.

Pull the pages with curl or JavaScript fetch(). 

Use Cheerio to get the text out of the HTML or parse it right into each columns rows.

If the content only shows up after JavaScript runs, use Playwright for that page. 

A direct HTTP pull has no scraping vendor fee. 

Search for contacts at each account, most relevant titles to your offer, we aim for 2-3 per account.

Do one table run properly yourself through your harness and then turn it into a function you can run on the next wave of tables.

- Gemini 3.5 Flash for the first pass. 

Give it the cleaned pages and tell it to fill the factual columns. You’re doing the same extraction over and over, so give it a tight list of fields and make it show the line it pulled each fact from.

- DeepSeek V4.1 for deciding which accounts are worth an email. 

Give it the extracted fields, your buyer criteria and the offer. Have it pick fit, skip or review and show which fact drove the decision.

- GPT-6 Luna for the copy pass. 

Give it the accounts that made the cut, the recipient’s role, the relevant facts and what you’re actually offering. That’s the part I’d spend more time judging by hand because it’s what the buyer is going to read.

Give each agent a budget, a focused task, and its own rules. 

Score 25 rows before you run 1,000s.

Flywheel what you didn't like back into the engine. 

Look at what you paid per row you’d actually send and send the weird ones to review.

If the account does mobile Class 8 repair around Columbus and you’ve already mapped the fleets, write it like this.

-

Jess, saw you do mobile Class 8 repairs around Columbus.

We put together a list of fleet yards nearby that you don’t already service. 

You can have your team pitch them for repairs and ongoing maintenance.

Want me to send over a few along with a message they can use?

-

We’re using our own product in-house starting today. 

This thing is a beast, fully agentic, used only through your harness, UI to see the work (not do the work), MCP and API with unlimited rows, tables, HTTP and API connections, leverage all the new AI tools all while your agents do the work so you don't need to know how to functionize a run or do repeat work with natural language.

Site research, HTTP calls, research columns and saved functions all run through the same MCP.

Donald Trump must take a lot of blame for his miscalculations. It was always clear if he didn’t get the price of gas and food down, he’d be sitting in the White House looking for Band Aids.
