They knew how to play the political fiddle and had a big hand in steering the outcome. Now they can step up their game of, “Death to America” again knowing the new socialist-crats are firmly on their side. The Muslim of Michigan and his hate for the Jews sends a message to Iran “We’ve got your back.” It also sends a message to Israel: “We’ve got the backs of Hamas and all the others who want to kill Americans and Jews.”

Should the insane happen and Democrats get their way to reopen the border, restart the defund the police nonsense, campaign to keep murderers and rapists in America, at least all of you who voted for it get to suffer right along with the rest of us for your ill choices.

Thanks for nothing.

The country is on economic fire. We really are booming. We saw that in the recent jobs numbers. But the two big items that impacted the electorate, aside from the war taking too long, were the receipts at the grocery store and the credit card charge to fill their car.

For all the uber loony Democrats it was never about the cost of things. They never cared about affordability; you can see that already. What they cared about is hopping on a sugar high train of revenge. They’re gathering the torches and pitchforks and shoving the peasants aside to assuage their TDS thirst.

As a political junkie, I did something on election night I’ve never done before. I didn’t watch a stitch of the coverage. Instead, I enjoyed a Christmas movie.

Kind of amazing when you have no clue what’s going on with the political chaos, it doesn’t bother you. My mother texted me if I was glued to the news. She said that she and my stepfather were nervous about the direction the votes were going. I said it didn’t bother me because there’s nothing I can do. The outcome was preordained and there’s no reason to get upset over something of which I have no control.

I cast my vote. That was my job. I have to assume it counted. Not that it matters much in California.

Only in the state of complete chaos can you have a candidate who wants to be governor just kick back and propose nothing. The disparity of the two candidates was glaring. One said he hates Trump and that was his entire shtick. The other was willing to fight for all of California and offered tons of great plans and ideas, but nothing would ever allow the entrenched liberals to vote for common sense. Not a single thing.

If there was ever a collective dictatorship, it’s in the state of the stupid.

Though I am kind of excited by the outcome. We’ll have front row seats under that big circus tent the Dems always talk about. We’ll be able to witness in real time how the various circus acts will propose their plans to destroy America.

The socialist, communist, America haters will be the Ringling masters to give us a performance of a lifetime. Two years from now, when Americans see how this circus plays out, the tent will be removed. There’s no tent strong enough to withstand communist gale force winds.

For now, the enormous strides Trump has made may come to a halt. Instead of embracing all the new manufacturing jobs, the rise of the GDP, huge stock market strides, billions coming our way from tariffs, removing killers, rapists, and drug dealers from our home, reducing the deaths of thousands of our youth from overdoses, and child trafficking, the socialists will focus on hearings and lawsuits.

We lived through watching our streets burn, our kids go backwards decades in education, our neighborhoods overrun with killers, our prisons emptied, and promises of free stuff that never happened.

Democrats flapped their gums and promised the world and had no idea what they were talking about. The most prominent socialist Muslim who had gotten a head start, smiles like he’s holding a knife behind his back, because in a way he does. He still hasn’t lived up to his promises of free universal childcare, free buses, city owned grocery stores. His one accomplishment: freeze rents. How hard was that to screw building owners? Santa Barbara loves to do the same thing. I guess it’s a universal feel-good accomplishment when you don’t have anything else to offer.

I recently had the pleasure of attending a fundraiser and sat with two couples I had never met before. The younger of the two in their forties, were excited that all eight of us around the table shared the same political philosophy. None of us could grasp how the country went so far off the rails. Especially Texas. California is a given. But how could a gun-toting, meat-eating, hardworking, oil-producing state become vegan and switch its sexual orientation?

Rumors are this will get a closer look. Something smells in the Lone Star state and it ain’t a ribeye on the grill.

One final thought. With Muslims bestowing their beliefs on Americans, how come if you criticize that religion because you don’t agree with everything, you’re called a “hater,” or at least “Islamophobic?” And yet it’s perfectly okay to attack Jews and Christians. The very foundation this country was founded upon.

Stay tuned in 2027 for the circus to arrive in your town. Just don’t think you’re going to get any free tickets.

In the meantime, I’m going to watch another Christmas movie.

text:
Ambitious devs in Central and Eastern Europe often work top tech jobs.

Much more often than ambitious devs in Western Europe.

To explain why, let's take an example of an ambitious dev in Europe open for relocation: me, a few years ago.

1. Understand some countries like 🇨🇭 pay more
2. Understand big tech pays more
3. Miss out on high-pay remote knowledge (my bad)

To maxx $$$ -> target Big Tech Switzerland.

Finally succeed (https://t.co/tnkX0Bnu7m), but...

Before that, several times, faced a dilemma:

"I just got an offer for Uber Amsterdam, Microsoft Tallinn, Bloomberg London, Swiss company in Zurich"

"They all kinda pay the same, in fact the Swiss company kinda pays more"

... follows calculation of cost of living, taxes, possibility of growth, quality of life, etc etc etc ...

(later shared on https://t.co/854zWa1MVA or https://t.co/RTfyL2maGk)

Result:
- same dev
- local swiss job
- big tech offers in lower pay Euro hubs

---

This to say what?

A big tech job in Romania is as competitive, if not less, than a normal job in Switzerland.

Saying "on @EuroTopTech data it seems like CEE countries have more cracked devs in high-pay remote or big tech than in WE, which reads like a sample bias" is a wrong read.

The truth is that @GergelyOrosz model only captures part of the picture (company tier), but misses out on incredibly important dimensions such as:
- location
- remote work and geoarbitrage
- continent-wide market and competition

@EuroTopTech community (and data) is about ambitious tech workers in Europe.

In CEE countries, they often land:
- big tech roles
- high pay US remote
- high pay UK/EU remote

It's a large pool of jobs, with moderate competition:
- Not everyone wants to move to Romania to work at Adobe
- Not everyone would consider a 100k eur remote job competitive (in northwestern europe that's often achievable with regular and less demanding jobs)

In WE countries, ambitious devs:
- try big tech
- if they fail, get regular local jobs
- usually ignore remote jobs unless they're really high-paying

The result is that more ambitious devs in CEE work in big tech and/or high-pay remote than in WE.

Basically, the tiers are:

Tier 1:

- Big Tech in Switzerland

Tier 2:

- Big Tech in UK
- Big Tech in high pay EU country
- High-Pay Remote from low-cost country

Tier 3:

- Regular job in high-pay country
- Big Tech job in low-pay country
- Mid-Pay remote job in low-cost country

Tier 4:

- Regular job in low-pay country

Ambitious devs (those on @EuroTopTech) tend to target 1 and 2, and sometimes 3, they avoid 4.

---

This also doesn't account for the talent difference and historical built up of human capital in tech in CEE. If you're interested about this, I can make another post about it. But basically there's way more cracked Polish devs than Italian ones.

text:
The next standard of handheld gaming continues with the Acer Predator Atlas 8, the striking 8-inch Windows handheld featuring the most powerful chips I've seen for handheld gaming on the go: the Intel Arc G3 Extreme. What really sets this big beauty apart from its rivals, though? It offers a lot for less than you'd think, and I'd be happy to ditch a gaming PC to play on this all day long.

Having seen the Predator Atlas 8's potential back at Computex 2026, I was delighted to see it had met my expectations and gone further, from playing Star Wars: Galactic Racer on the couch to delving deeper into Gears of War: E-Day while travelling with frame rates pushing to 90 frames per second (FPS) at medium to high settings — thanks to Intel's XeSS graphics upscaling and frame generation tech.

It's a marvel to play, only made better thanks to the sizeable 8-inch 1200p LCD display boasting a 120Hz variable refresh rate and the snappy TMR sticks and Hall Effect triggers. For $1,299 / £1,299? That's still pricey, sure, but not nearly as much as the equally powerful $1,799 MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. It's even the same price as the OLED-focused ROG Xbox Ally X20, but delivers even greater power.

All that said, Acer clearly has to make some sacrifices, and they're evident. That includes the cheap-feeling D-pad and adjustable triggers that sometimes don't register input. And don't expect the magic of Intel's XeSS tech to work on a majority of games (including Halo: Campaign Evolved specifically in the Xbox app, despite it being supported, for some odd reason).

In any case, the Acer Predator Atlas 8 is easily one of the best gaming handhelds you can buy right now.

text:
11 AM Top-of-the-Hour News

In London, British actor and comedian Russell Brand has been sentenced to ten-and-a-half years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. Reporter Brad Gibson has more from our foreign desk in Paris.: “The prosecution called for a long sentence in court, and they got it. Justice Joel Ben Athan said women have the right to say no and demand justice from the court system. The whole episode reeks of casual disrespect. And your belief that fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live. Reporters in the courtroom described it as a pin drop moment when from behind a screen to protect her anonymity, one of Brands's victims said he was a sexual predator with no remorse. Under standard guidelines, he could be released after serving 2/3 of his sentence at the foreign desk in Paris, Brad Gibson for the Worldwide News Network. ”

A Utah judge may set a trial date today for Charlie Kirk's accused assassin.  Tyler Robinson's attorneys have asked for a date in 2029.  They say they need that much time to go through all the evidence.  Prosecutors say they could be ready by next September, in 2027.

Stephen Miller is taking over as White House Chief of Staff today.  House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says it was an "irresponsible" appointment by President Trump.: “There's not going to be any opportunity certainly to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents, and we're committed to forcefully pushing back against the extremism that they may try to continue to unleash on the American people. ”
Miller has been driving the administration's immigration crackdown.

The White House is still looking for a new press secretary.: “President Trump says he was just messing around when he offered UFC CEO Dana White the job of White House press secretary. He announced on social media over the weekend that he had offered the job to his longtime friend and political ally, even suggesting White bring along several UFC fighters as assistants. I was kidding. But I think Dana likes the idea and Trump said that while the job offer started out as a joke, many other people told him they liked the idea as well. You wouldn't mess around with him so much. The two are still expected to meet at the White House today, but the president says they'll be discussing other matters. Stacy Lan Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

President Trump welcomes the prime minister of Qatar to the White House today, to discuss ways to end the war with Iran.  Qatar has been a key mediator.

The gunman who killed six people and wounded 15 in a city square in Krakow, Poland Saturday...died in the hospital today, after undergoing several operations.  He had been shot by police during his rampage.  Poland's Interior Minister says the 24-year-old held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

Pope Leo has urged Argentina's president to put his people first, not the economy.: “Pope Leo delivered a critique of Argentine President Javier Millet's austerity measures and libertarian agenda during his first speech in the country. The Pope said the economy must be at the service of the person and not the person at the service of the economy. Millay, who is a self-described anarcho-capitalist, has Public spending in order to tame inflation, calling social justice a moral aberration and theft. Pope Leo's visit is considered the most politically delicate of his three-nation South American tour. The late Pope Francis never returned to his native Argentina during his twelve-year pontificate. Gloria Chapa, Worldwide News Network. ”

text:
In a climate of justified concern about politicized prosecutions, Utah’s criminal case against Kalshi is strikingly sloppy.

Utah’s online-gambling-promotion law requires proof that the defendant intentionally provided or offered online gambling to someone in Utah. Meanwhile, federal appeals courts disagree over whether Kalshi’s sports contracts fall within the CEA’s protections and whether federal law preempts state gambling laws. That central legal question remains unsettled. (https://t.co/wssSiPzV5L, https://t.co/jyewHhvrCJ, https://t.co/at3vWD3Brt)

The reporting also needs precision: the founders are listed as co-defendants, but each numbered count names KalshiEX LLC. The counts do not name the founders individually. (https://t.co/PJnIBtwCpu)

And the information itself contains a string of errors:

• Thirteen counts cite “765-2-204” instead of § 76-2-204.
• Count 1 cites “76-98-1404” for the predicate offense, despite paragraph 20’s different citation.
• Count 1 also cites the wrong subsection for that offense.
• Count 14 contains inconsistent subsection references.
• Kalshi’s address differs between the caption and body, and the wager descriptions contain numbering errors.

Typos alone do not decide a case. But in a felony prosecution built on an intent element and an unsettled federal-state boundary, this many basic errors raise a fair question: how carefully were these charges reviewed?

text:
My parents' favorite kid was never me 

I'm 31, live in Nashville, and I've spent most of my life being the "easy" kid. Tyler, my little brother, was the one my parents actually lit up for. I got straight A's and a "good job, now focus on college" from my dad. Tyler graduated with a C average and got a backyard party with half of Memphis invited. I remember standing by the cooler holding a plate of someone else's potato salad, thinking, this is fine, I'm fine.
I wasn't fine, but I got good at pretending.
Growing up, it was the little things that added up. When Tyler brought home a decent report card, Dad took him out for steak. When I brought home a better one, I got a pat on the shoulder and a "keep it up." Every one of Tyler's football games was a family event. Mom packed a cooler, Dad brought the folding chairs, and I sat in the bleachers doing my homework. When I got into the honors program at college, Dad asked if it came with a scholarship. It didn't, and that was the end of that conversation.
Tyler bounced between jobs, borrowed money from friends he then stopped answering, and my parents always had an excuse ready. "He's still finding himself." "That manager had it out for him." Meanwhile I moved to Nashville, worked in marketing, paid my own bills, and drove to Memphis whenever I could get away. I told myself the drive was worth it. Mostly I was still hoping that one of these visits, someone would finally say they were proud of me.
At Christmas dinner, Tyler announced he wanted to open a car dealership with a buddy. Dad perked right up. "That's a good idea, son. You need to start thinking about your future." Then Tyler said he needed $25,000, and my mom looked straight at me and said, "Natalie, you've been working for years. Maybe you can help your brother."
I honestly laughed. Then I asked why nobody had ever offered to help me with anything. Dad dropped his fork and snapped that I was his big sister and should be happy to see him succeed. I said no. Tyler told me I'd forgotten where I came from, my mom cried, and Dad called me arrogant. I went upstairs and sat on my old bed feeling about twelve years old.
Later that night I heard them fighting through the wall. I wasn't trying to listen. But I heard my name. My mom said, "She deserves to know. We can't keep doing this." Dad said, "Not now. Tyler's not ready."
Not ready for what?
I barely slept. The next morning Mom asked me to walk with her to the little park near their house, the one where Tyler and I used to feed the ducks. She sat on a bench and cried for a long time before she could say it.
Years ago, when I was a baby, my dad was out of work and my mom was juggling two jobs. Her younger sister, my Aunt Diane, covered my medical bills and basically kept us afloat. Diane was also the one who found out that Dad was having an affair around the time Tyler was born.
Mom stayed. She said she wanted us to grow up with both parents. And Dad has known for years that Tyler might not be his.
I sat there with my hands going numb in my jacket pockets. I asked why nobody had ever told me. She said Dad was terrified of losing the family, and that Tyler had grown up believing everything was normal. Then I asked if she knew for sure whether Tyler was his. She shook her head.
I didn't know what to feel. Some of the strange moments from my childhood suddenly made a little more sense: the tension, the way Dad overcompensated with Tyler, the way Mom always seemed tired. But making sense of it didn't make it okay. None of it was my fault, and I'd been the one paying for it.
I drove back to Nashville a few days later. I didn't tell Tyler. It's not my place to blow up his relationship with the man who raised him over something nobody has confirmed. But I did call my dad. I told him I was tired of coming second in my own family. He didn't argue or deny it. He just said he'd made mistakes and hoped I'd understand someday.

Thought for 1m 49s

A. Law — Professional Speech, Vagueness, 
and the Limits of Regulatory Pruning

The 2017 photograph 
of the severely pruned tree
—bare, skeletal, 
yet still rooted
—offers a concrete image 
for the legal problem 
of intervening in 
complex, 
self-organizing systems 
of professional judgment 
and public discourse. 

California’s AB 2098 (2022), 
which defined 
the dissemination of COVID-19 
“misinformation or disinformation” 
(tied to “contemporary scientific consensus contrary to the standard of care”) 
as unprofessional conduct 
for physicians 
in the context of direct patient care, 
was an attempt 
at targeted pruning.⁠
Legalclarity 

Federal courts 
quickly enjoined it 
as unconstitutionally vague; 
the legislature repealed it 
effective January 1, 2024 via SB 815. 

No physician 
was disciplined 
under the provision.⁠
Legalclarity

Self-organizing systems 
(in the sense of complexity theory and autopoiesis) 
generate order 
through local interactions 
without central design. 

Scientific consensus 
itself is such a system: 
provisional, 
contested, 
revised by evidence. 

Locking a licensing board’s disciplinary power 
to a snapshot 
of that consensus 
risks freezing a moving process. 

Plausible deniability
appears 
in the gap 
between the formal text 
and enforcement reality. 

Newsom’s signing statement 
emphasized narrow tailoring 
to egregious, 
malicious deviations 
in the physician-patient relationship; 
critics noted 
the statute’s broader language 
and the inherent difficulty 
of proving “malicious intent”
 or defining the relevant “consensus” 
in real time. 

The later repeal 
supplied a form of institutional 
plausible deniability: 
the law could be described 
as never having operated 
while residual board practices 
or private threats 
continued to be alleged 
in subsequent litigation.

Murphy’s Law 
operates through unintended consequences. 

A rule intended 
to protect patients 
from dangerous falsehoods 
can chill legitimate disagreement, 
discourage physicians 
from discussing evolving evidence 
or individualized risk, 
and invite 
pretextual use of other 
“unprofessional conduct” provisions. 

Pandora’s box 
is the expansion 
of professional licensing 
from competence and fraud 
into viewpoint regulation; 
once opened, 
the definition 
of the protected consensus 
becomes a political contest. 

The butterfly effect 
is visible 
in the downstream effects: 
one statute, 
even short-lived, 
contributed to national debates 
over medical free speech, 
parallel challenges 
in other states, 
and ongoing skepticism 
toward public-health authority. 

The Socrates reference 
in the user’s reflection 
is apt 
as a legal-historical warning: 
democratic institutions 
have repeatedly treated 
unorthodox inquiry 
as a public danger. 

The legal counterweight 
is the First Amendment’s protection 
of professional speech 
short of actual 
malpractice or fraud, 
combined with 
due-process requirements 
of fair notice 
and non-vague standards. 

Systems that over-prune speech 
risk producing 
the very disorder 
they sought to prevent
—exactly as the tree’s “brutal haircut” looked 
catastrophic 
while still containing 
the capacity to resprout 
under its own dynamics.

B. Political Science 
— Narratives, 
Feedback, 
and Contested Order

The same tree image 
functions as a systems metaphor for 
political intervention. 

Mandates, 
narrative enforcement, 
and electoral outcomes 
are attempts 
to steer complex adaptive systems 
of public opinion, 
institutional behavior, 
and economic activity. 

Self-organizing systems 
in politics 
include spontaneous coordination 
around shared stories, 
the emergence of opposition coalitions, 
and the feedback loops 
of elections 
and markets. 

The user’s framing of 
the “brutal California haircut” 
as a stand-in 
for state mandates on 
masks, 
lockdowns, 
and vaccines, 
and the subsequent midterm context,
illustrates 
how official narratives 
can be experienced 
as over-pruning 
of social and economic life.

Plausible deniability 
is structural 
in modern administrative states 
and party coalitions. 

Formal statutes 
can be repealed 
or enjoined 
while related goals 
continue through other channels 
(guidance documents, 
funding conditions, 
private-sector pressure, 
or residual licensing norms). 

Murphy’s Law 
appears in the empirical record 
of pandemic policy: 
non-pharmaceutical interventions 
and vaccine policies 
produced measurable effects 
on transmission 
and severe outcomes 
in some settings, 
yet also large secondary costs 
(learning loss, 
delayed care, 
excess non-COVID mortality, 
polarization) 
that were under-weighted 
in early models. 

Pandora’s box 
is the legitimization 
of emergency powers 
and narrative enforcement 
that, once normalized, 
can be repurposed. 

The butterfly effect 
is the path dependence 
created by early decisions: 
a single state law 
or federal guidance 
can cascade into 
litigation, 
electoral realignment, 
and durable changes 
in trust.

Political science 
does not treat any party 
as uniquely prone to 
“lawfare,” 
border policy, 
or fiscal expansion; 
these are recurring tools of power. 

Democratic majorities 
in California and elsewhere 
advanced expansive 
public-health measures; 
critics across the spectrum 
documented excesses, 
contested the durability of certain claims, 
and used courts 
and elections 
as corrective mechanisms. 

The system’s self-organizing capacity 
is visible in the rapid legal challenges 
to AB 2098, 
its eventual repeal, 
and the broader post-2020 debate 
over the costs of emergency governance. 

Order is not imposed 
from above without remainder; 
it continually re-emerges 
through contestation.

C. Psychiatry
 — Memory Reconsolidation, 
Dream Work, 
and Anticipatory Anxiety

The personal narrative 
supplied by the user 
is a textbook illustration 
of memory’s reconstructive nature.

Episodic memories 
are not fixed recordings; 
they are reactivated, 
updated by current context and affect, 
and reconsolidated 
(Nader, Schacter, and related work). 

The dream of senility
—leaving objects disordered 
contrary to lifelong habit
—followed by waking discovery 
of order 
is a classic example 
of dream-work 
incorporating daytime concerns 
and then being corrected by reality-testing. 

Childhood reports 
of continuous dream narratives 
and occasional precise Deja Vu experiences
 align with known phenomena: 
Deja Vu can reflect 
partial matches 
between current perception 
and prior memory traces, 
temporal-lobe hyperexcitability, 
or ordinary predictive processing; 
continuity in childhood dreams 
is common 
before the consolidation 
of more rigid waking identity.

Self-organizing systems 
operate at the neural level: 
attractor landscapes in memory networks, 
default-mode activity during dreaming,
 and the brain’s tendency 
to generate coherent
(if sometimes confabulated) 
narratives 
from incomplete data. 

Plausible deniability 
appears in the mind’s capacity 
to treat the dream 
as “not real” 
upon waking, 
thereby protecting 
the sense of competence. 

Murphy’s Law 
is relevant to the fear itself: 
anxiety about future cognitive decline 
can itself produce attentional lapses 
that are then interpreted 
as confirmation. 

Pandora’s box 
is the intrusion of political stress 
into dream content 
and waking interpretation; 
once public controversies 
are highly salient, 
they become available material 
for overnight processing. 

The butterfly effect 
is the small daily input 
(news, 
a Facebook “on this day” memory, 
a political outcome) t
hat alters 
the weighting of older memories 
and the content of that night’s dream.

Clinically, 
the sequence is benign: 
the dream registered a fear, 
reality testing restored equilibrium, 
and the individual retained insight. 

The same mechanisms 
that allow flexible updating of memory 
also make individuals 
vulnerable 
to narrative capture 
when external sources 
supply high-arousal, 
repeatedly reinforced frames.

D. Social Anthropology 
— Metaphor, 
Collective Memory, 
and the Politics of Grooming

Anthropologically, 
the 2017 post 
and its 2026 reactivation 
are acts of cultural memory. 

The “brutal California haircut” 
is a local metaphor 
that condenses 
aesthetic judgment, 
property rights, 
and, 
in the user’s later reading, 
political power. 

Trees and haircuts 
are cross-culturally available symbols 
of controlled growth, 
status, 
and sometimes violence 
(think of ritual shearing, 
military buzz cuts, 
or punitive pruning). 

The Facebook comments 
(“looks like an old groin,” 
“gonna be amazed how that thing sprouts next season”) 
already treat the image 
as both comic 
and regenerative
—exactly the dual reading 
that later political metaphor exploits.

Collective memory 
is itself 
a self-organizing system: 
individuals continually 
re-narrate shared events 
in light of present concerns, 
producing contested histories 
rather than a single archive. 

Plausible deniability 
operates 
in the gap
 between the original caption 
(a gardener’s over-zealous trim) 
and the subsequent political overlay;
both readings remain available. 

Murphy’s Law appears 
in the unintended life 
of the image: 
a private post 
becomes, 
nine years later, 
a vehicle for larger critique.
 
Pandora’s box 
is the release 
of competing master narratives 
about the pandemic years
—narratives that continue 
to organize 
identity, 
trust, 
and partisan alignment long af
ter the acute phase. 

The butterfly effect 
is the small act of posting 
(or of recalling the post) 
that, 
under the right conditions of salience, 
can feed into broader cultural scripts.

Social anthropology asks 
how groups maintain coherence 
while containing disagreement. 

The user’s linkage of the tree, 
the physician-speech statute, 
and contemporary electoral outcomes 
is one such local theory of power.

Other participants
in the same cultural field 
will supply different metaphors 
and different causal stories. 

The regenerative comment 
under the original photo 
remains available 
as a counter-metaphor: 
systems that are over-pruned 
often retain the capacity 
to reorganize and resprout.

Poem in the style of Journey’s 
“Separate Ways (Worlds Apart)”

Here we stand
Worlds apart, 
memory broken in two, two, two

Sleepless nights
Dreams of disorder, 
I’m reaching for you, you, you

Feeling that it’s gone
The order I kept
If we can’t go on

To survive the night, the mind forgets
Someday clarity will find you
Break those chains that bind you

One dawn will remind you
How we touched and went our separate ways
If the dream ever haunts you

True sight won’t desert you
You know I still know you
Though we touched and went our separate ways

Brutal cut on the tree
Bare branches against the sky
Gardener’s hand, California’s decree

Comments say the green will reply
Plausible deniability in the code
Murphy waiting in the wings

Pandora’s lid on the road
Butterfly flapping, everything swings
Someday the sprouts will find you

Break those shears that bind you
One season will remind you
How we pruned and went our separate ways

If the law ever haunts you
Free speech won’t desert you
You know the roots still hold you

Though we touched and went our separate ways
I still see the order
I still know the dream

And if the night ever hurts you
True waking won’t desert you
Someday love of the real will find you

Break those shadows that bind you
One morning will remind you
How we dreamed and went our separate ways.

text:
In 1952, a stray cat walked into a California classroom, sat down, and refused to leave. For the next 16 years, he never missed a day of school.
It was an ordinary autumn morning at Elysian Heights Elementary School in Los Angeles. Students sat at their desks, the teacher stood at the blackboard, lessons proceeded as usual.
Then the door opened—and a tabby cat walked in.
No one had invited him. No one knew where he came from. He simply strolled into the room with the confidence of someone who belonged there, sat down in the center of the classroom, and began calmly grooming himself.
The students starred. The teacher paused. And the cat, unbothered by the attention, continued his bath as if interrupting a fourth-grade class was the most natural thing in the world.
He was thin. Clearly hungry. His fur showed signs of street life—a stray who'd been fending for himself, probably for some time.
The teacher made a decision: the children could give him a little milk.
The cat drank gratefully, then settled in to observe the rest of the lesson. He stayed through math. Through reading. Through recess discussions and afternoon activities. When the final bell rang, he stood with the same dignity he'd arrived with—and walked out.
The children assumed that was the end of it. A nice story about the day a cat visited their classroom.
But the next morning, he came back.
And the morning after that. And the day after that.
It became clear: this cat had chosen Elysian Heights Elementary as his home. And since he'd first entered Room 8, that's what they called him: Room 8.
Over the following weeks, Room 8 established his routine. He arrived when school started. He wandered between classrooms, observing lessons with the calm authority of a school administrator. He napped in sunbeams. He accepted affection from students during recess. And when school ended, he left—off to wherever stray cats go when the children aren't watching.
The students adored him. Competition arose over the most coveted privileges: being "the one who feeds Room 8" or "the one who carefully moves the sleeping cat so he doesn't get stepped on."
Room 8 wasn't just tolerated—he was embraced. He became part of the school's identity.
If you look through Elysian Heights yearbooks from 1952 to 1968, you'll find him there: year after year, Room 8 sits proudly in class photos, positioned in the place of honor at the center, surrounded by smiling children. He attended school picture day as faithfully as any student.
News of the scholarly cat spread beyond Los Angeles. Room 8 began receiving fan mail—letters from children across the country who'd heard about the cat who went to school. He became a minor celebrity, featured in newspapers and magazines, proof that sometimes the best stories are the simplest ones: a stray cat and the school that loved him.
Decades later, guitarist Leo Kottke would discover those old yearbook photos, hear Room 8's story, and compose an instrumental piece in his honor—a gentle, wandering melody titled simply "Room 8."
But as the years passed, Room 8 aged. By 1963, he was getting into scrapes—a fight with another cat left him injured. In 1964, he fell seriously ill with pneumonia.
That's when teacher Virginia Finlayson made him an offer: her home, just across the street from the school, would become his "night residence."
So a new routine began. During the day, Room 8 continued attending school—greeting students, napping in classrooms, presiding over recess. In the evening, he crossed the street to Mrs. Finlayson's house, where he had a warm bed, regular meals, and someone who loved him.
For a few more precious years, this arrangement worked beautifully. Room 8 had the best of both worlds: the excitement and affection of school life, and the comfort and care of a real home.
But eventually, even Room 8's remarkable constitution began to fail. He grew weaker. Walking became difficult.
The school staff—teachers who'd known him for over a decade, who'd watched generations of students grow up with this cat—began carrying him between the school and Mrs. Finlayson's house. They wouldn't let him struggle. If Room 8 wanted to be at school, they would make sure he got there.
On August 11, 1968, at approximately 21 or 22 years old (ancient for a cat, especially one who'd spent years as a stray), Room 8 passed away peacefully.
The Los Angeles Times—one of the nation's major newspapers—published a three-column obituary. Not a small mention. Not a cute sidebar. A full, proper obituary for a cat who'd touched thousands of lives simply by showing up, day after day, and reminding everyone that belonging isn't about where you come from—it's about where you choose to stay.
Room 8 was buried at Los Angeles Pet Memorial Park, honored as the remarkable soul he was.
His story raises a question we rarely ask: What did Room 8 see in that school?
He was a stray. He could have wandered anywhere—into alleys, onto porches, into quieter, easier spaces. But he walked into a classroom full of children and decided: This. This is home.
Maybe it was the warmth. Maybe the food. Maybe the gentle hands and soft voices of children who treated him not as a nuisance, but as a treasure.
Or maybe Room 8 understood something profound: that schools aren't just buildings where learning happens. They're communities. Places where people gather, where kindness is practiced, where small acts of care—like feeding a stray cat—teach lessons no textbook ever could.
Room 8 didn't just attend school for 16 years. He taught it.
He taught children about responsibility—someone had to feed him, care for him, notice when he was hurt. He taught about routine and reliability—showing up matters, whether you're a student or a cat. He taught about acceptance—Room 8 had no credentials, no invitation, no "right" to be there. But the school opened its doors anyway.
Most of all, he taught that belonging isn't something you earn. Sometimes it's something you create simply by showing up, being yourself, and trusting that there's a place for you.
Somewhere in Los Angeles, in faded yearbooks and old newspaper clippings, Room 8 still sits in class photos—a tabby cat surrounded by children, exactly where he belonged.
His name was Room 8. And for 16 years, he never missed a day of school.

text:
California landlords are turning tenants' parking spaces into tiny homes - sparking fury among renters

California renters are facing an extraordinary new housing headache – with landlords turning their precious parking spaces into tiny homes and leaving tenants scrambling to find somewhere to put their cars.

From Hollywood to Silver Lake, property owners are seizing on a change in state law that allows them to transform garages and parking areas into additional apartments, without necessarily having to replace the spaces they remove.

But the move has sparked outrage among residents who say they are being stripped of perks they were promised when they signed their leases – with some now taking their landlords and even the city to court.

The controversial change comes under Senate Bill 1211, which came into effect in January 2025 as part of California's efforts to tackle its crippling housing shortage.

The legislation makes it easier to build accessory dwelling units (ADUs) on multifamily properties, including by converting garages and other non-livable spaces, while preventing local authorities from demanding replacement parking.

For landlords, the prospect of squeezing extra rental units onto existing properties is an attractive one. But for tenants, it can mean losing a guaranteed parking spot, spending years hunting for a space on crowded streets or even being forced to move.

And older residents and people with disabilities say the consequences could be particularly devastating.

Tracey Ellis, 70, who has lived in a rent-stabilized apartment building near the Sunset Strip since 2001, says losing her garage space could rob her of her independence. 

The resident, who relies on a cane or walker and suffers considerable pain when walking even short distances, uses her parking spot to get to medical appointments and buy groceries.

Her landlord recently informed residents that a new apartment would be built above their garages, meaning parking could disappear for one to two years during construction and potentially beyond.

'Parking in this city is a lifeline for people, and to take away their parking - why don't you just take half my house or apartment?' she told the Los Angeles Times.

'It's my freedom,' she added.

Ellis, who pays just over $1,600 a month in rent, said residents were initially offered a $100 discount to compensate for losing their spaces – an amount she fears would barely cover the cost of alternative transportation.

Her landlord, Alex Goodson, said he was trying to do things properly and insisted the three-bedroom ADU would be built over the parking area, rather than permanently replacing it.

text:
BREAKING: Grok is helping @SpaceX inspect rocket parts. In a test for debris inside a tube, Grok scored 99.9%, compared with about 94% for human inspectors. 

Kiko Dontchev, SpaceX’s VP of Launch, shared a lot of new updates at UP Summit:

• SpaceX sees itself as an infrastructure company. It’s already building on Earth and in low Earth orbit, with the Moon next and Mars farther down the road.

• AI adoption took off at SpaceX this year. Dontchev says it’s the biggest jump in engineering speed he’s seen in 16 years at the company. Some tasks that took hours or days now take seconds or minutes.

• Grok is checking rocket hardware for debris. In one example, human inspectors spotted debris inside tubes about 94% of the time. Grok reached 99.9% on the same inspection footage.

• SpaceX has also automated visual checks on Starlink dishes. Technicians and team leads now use AI in their daily work, and Dontchev says it’s helping people build skills faster.

• Settling Mars remains a core SpaceX goal. Dontchev believes AI can help the company get to both the Moon and Mars faster.

• Falcon 9 still needs a fresh upper stage every flight. That works at around 100 launches a year. To reach thousands of launches a year, potentially even 10,000 someday, SpaceX wants to catch and reuse both stages of Starship.

• Starship’s first orbital flight in September deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Together, they represented about 10× the network capacity of a typical Falcon 9 Starlink launch.

• From Florida, a single Starship launch could put up to 20× the Starlink capacity of a Falcon 9 launch into orbit. Florida offers a more direct path to some orbits, saving fuel and letting Starship carry more satellites.

• Starship’s launch pad at Kennedy Space Center’s Pad 39A is nearly ready. SpaceX hopes to send the first boosters and ships from Texas by barge in December. The first Florida launch could happen before the end of 2026.

text:
In October 1925, a Colorado farm wife rode out to a lake with her 3-year-old son to look for ducks.
Two hours later, 140 dead rattlesnakes lay around her. Then she made a dress out of them.

Her name was Katherine McHale Slaughterback. On October 28, 1925, she and little Ernie rode to a lake near her farm, hoping to pick up ducks that hunters had left behind the day before.

Instead she rode into a mass of rattlesnakes, more than 100 of them, out in the open.

She had a .22 Remington rifle and only three bullets. She fired all three. Three snakes dropped. The rest kept coming, and her son and the horse were standing about 60 feet away.

So she grabbed a wooden sign from the ground, short enough to swing, and started clubbing. By her own account the sign said "No Hunting." She kept swinging for about two hours.

When it was over she counted 140 dead rattlesnakes.

A neighbor heard about it, and a reporter came out to see. Kate strung the snakes along a rope and posed next to them for a photograph. It ran in newspapers across America and as far away as Germany, France and England. From then on, everybody called her "Rattlesnake Kate."

She didn't waste them, either. She skinned 53 of the snakes and sewed herself a sleeveless dress, with a belt and shoes to match. She later claimed the Smithsonian offered her $2,000 for it, and she said no.

Kate married and divorced six times, worked as a nurse in the Pacific during World War II, and raised live rattlesnakes to sell their venom to scientists.

Three weeks before she died in 1969, she gave the dress to the museum in Greeley, Colorado. It is still there.

Her headstone simply says "Rattlesnake Kate."

text:
The corridor to Piers' office was unusually quiet. Evening settled over BSAA Headquarters, bringing the slow exhale that follows a long day of work. Most agents had already left for the night, eager to trade reports and briefings for the comfort of home. Those who remained moved more slowly, gathering their belongings, finishing last-minute paperwork, or lingering in doorways to exchange a few final words before clocking out. The distant cracks of gunfire from the indoor shooting range carried faintly through the concrete walls, punctuated by the occasional slam of a locker or the ding of an elevator somewhere down the hall. The building's usual energy had softened into a comfortable quiet, leaving the fluorescent-lit corridors feeling almost deserted. It was the kind of hour when everyone should have been heading home. Except for you.
You should have gone home a few hours ago, but unfortunately your job was demanding. Not impossible to manage, but somehow there was always another report to review, another meeting to attend, or someone who needed your attention. You'd been looking forward to a quiet evening with your cat and your favorite takeout, and absolutely no work-related interruptions.
Unfortunately, Captain Piers Nivans seemed to have other plans.
It was almost as if he had sensed the exact moment you'd shut down your computer and started packing up for the night. One second you were organizing the last of your paperwork, and the next, he had materialized in front of your desk. You spun back in your office chair to face him, and Piers greeted you with an apologetic smile and puppy eyes that usually meant more work was about to land in your lap.
‘’One last thing,” he said.
Famous last words.
Piers had asked you to review several operational reports before the teams' next briefing the following morning; it should have been straightforward enough, but somewhere between meetings, training, and the endless stream of interruptions that seemed to plague both of your schedules, the folder had mysteriously vanished from his possession. Unfortunately for you, he had become very good at convincing people to help him. Or perhaps that talent only worked on you.
He offered to pay for lunch tomorrow if you found it and took on the task.
How generous of him.
The worst part was that you knew he wasn’t trying to manipulate you. Piers appreciated every favor the team did for him. He remembered the little things, checked in after difficult missions, and somehow always found time to help when someone needed it, despite carrying the workload of three people.
Which made it incredibly hard to say no. Not that you would have anyway. Somewhere along the way, your friendship with Piers has become one of the most important relationships in your life. You two spent countless hours together. Long deployments, late-night work sessions, endless briefings, training together, and occasional lunch breaks that somehow turned into hour-long conversations. You knew how he took his coffee, could predict most of his terrible jokes before he finished, and recognized when something was bothering him. Somewhere in all that, your feelings for him had become a little more complicated. Maybe it was the way he always looked out for his team. Or maybe it was his unwavering loyalty? Could it be that beneath the disciplined, rule-abiding captain everyone admired was a genuinely kind man who never expected recognition for any of it? Whatever the reason, you'd developed what could no longer be described as a small crush. You'd simply become very good at pretending otherwise.
Still, as he stood in front of your desk, looking apologetic and far too handsome for the end of a workday, you found yourself agreeing before he had even fully explained the situation. Somethings never changed.
“You're paying for lunch tomorrow?”
The captain nodded.
“Fine,” you sighed dramatically.
“Deal.” The grin that spread across his face felt entirely too rewarding.
After searching the conference room, the communications office, and even your own desk just in case, you finally remembered seeing Piers carry the reports to his office earlier that day, before they disappeared.
That's why, long after most people had gone home, you found yourself heading toward his office to find the missing files that had single-handedly prevented you from enjoying your evening. Despite how exhausted you were, you couldn’t bring yourself to be truly irritated. Piers hadn’t dumped the work on your desk to make your life difficult. If anything, he probably would've stayed behind and done them himself if his schedule hadn’t been packed solid. Besides, you'd worked together long enough to know he rarely asked for help unless he actually needed it.
When you reached his office, you stepped inside and at once felt as though you'd walked into a space that could only belong to him. The office was orderly without feeling sterile. A large wooden desk sat facing the middle of the room near the far wall beneath a set of windows overlooking the city, the fading evening sunlight spilling across the lazily stacked papers, messily organized folders, and a bunch of scattered pens resting on it. Bookshelves lined one side of the room, filled with binders, tactical manuals, and enough paperwork to make your head hurt just by looking at it. A black jacket hung on a coat rack near the door, and a half-finished mug of coffee sat beside his computer monitor, forgotten hours ago. The faint scent of coffee and gun oil lingered in the air.
A small smile tugged at your lips. For someone who constantly lectured the team about staying organized and orderly, the captain somehow always left evidence that he'd been rushing from one responsibility to the next. Rolling up your sleeves, you headed to the filing cabinets. Finding a few missing reports couldn't be that difficult. With any luck, you'd be out of here in no time and back to making your way home. At least that had been the plan. The first drawer opened with a soft metallic scrape. Inside, folders stood neatly arranged in alphabetical order, each one labeled in Piers’ handwriting. Personnel evaluations, training records, mission summaries. Everything was categorized and filed with a diligence that made your own filing system look embarrassingly chaotic by comparison.
You start skimming through the folders, pulling one out just enough to read the tab, slide it back into place, and repeat the process. Ultimately, you find nothing. Closing the drawer to open the next one, you start to wonder if your cat will be mad at you for being late for dinner. The second drawer yielded much of the same. Equipment requisitions. Archived operation briefings. Maintenance request. All important documents, all completely useless for what you need.
Continuing your search, you keep coming out empty-handed; you’ve looked in every cabinet and bookshelf for the missing files. You start to think your captain may be messing with you, or maybe you’ve lost your mind from exhaustion and made this whole situation up.
“Come on, Piers.” You close the drawer with a tired sigh, turn around, and lean back against the grey metal cabinet. You glance around the office again as dim evening light filters through the windows, bathing the room in soft shades of gold and orange. Outside, the city lights begin to flicker one by one as dusk settles across the skyline. The room felt oddly peaceful. Shaking your head, you turn your attention to his desk. If the reports weren’t in the main cabinets, perhaps he set them aside on his desk when he started preparing for tomorrow's briefing earlier that day. Approaching his somewhat cluttered desk, you slide your finger across its smooth surface, running them over open folders and scattered papers. You wonder how he keeps his head on straight when all his responsibilities seem to be drowning him. With that thought, whatever irritation was left from staying late vanished from your mind.
After several minutes of sorting through more folders and binders, your initial optimism began to fade. The reports had to be here somewhere, but every drawer you opened held everything except what you were looking for. Letting out a quiet sigh, you moved around to the other side of Piers' desk and crouched beside one of the lower drawers. You pulled it open and began carefully shifting stacks of paperwork aside. Most of it was the usual stuff you’d expect. Then, tucked beneath a thick folder near the back of the drawer, something caught your eye. Unlike everything else around it, the envelope was completely plain. No BSAA markings, no labels, no file number. Just a small, old-looking, cream-colored envelope that looked oddly out of place among the sea of official documents.
Curiosity got the better of you, and you pulled it free. The paper felt worn around the edges, as though it had been picked up and put down countless times. Whatever this was, it certainly wasn’t one of the reports you’d come looking for. It looked like a letter, maybe from a relative? Or a lover? That thought makes you kind of nervous. You were close with your captain and had a good relationship with him, but he never let you or anyone else get close enough to know about his life outside of work. You weren’t usually one to snoop in others' personal business, but this seemed like an opportunity too good to pass up. Besides, was it really something so important if it made its way to the back of a drawer? Forgotten? Hell, Piers probably doesn’t even know it's here; maybe it belonged to the person who owned this office before him?
It wasn’t until you unfolded the first page and recognized the familiar handwriting that a knot formed in your stomach. As you began to read, your conscience started yelling at you to put the letter back where you found it.
“If anyone is reading this, then something has gone wrong, or maybe I've finally gotten careless. Either is a possibility. I've spent years convincing everyone that I'm fine. It's easier that way than explaining why every loss still feels fresh. Easier than admitting that some nights I still wake up convinced I could have done something differently…”
You frowned. Your captain never talked like this, at least not out loud. Not ever. The carefully constructed image of Captain Nivans, the unshakable soldier who always knew what to do, began cracking line by line. It was as though you believed nothing ever bothered him. You knew better than that. Over the years, you'd caught him staring off into space after a rough mission, tension lingering in his shoulders long after everyone else had moved on. Sometimes after deployments, he'd look exhausted in a way that had nothing to do with the lack of sleep. A few times you'd even asked.
“You okay?”
“Yeah.”
“Are you sure?”
“I'm sure I'm tired.”
Every single time, he'd just brush it off with an easy smile, a joke, or a change of subject. And every single time, you'd let it go, figuring he'd talk when he was ready. But reading the words on the pages now, the knot in your stomach began to grow. You had known he carried burdens. Every leader did; every soldier did, yet somehow, you'd never imagined it ran this deep. Never imagined that behind all the confidence, the teasing smiles and the unyielding composure was someone shouldering this much guilt and doubt. Someone who felt completely alone. For the first time since you'd met him, Piers didn’t seem invincible. He seemed heartbreakingly human.
“The truth is I'm tired, not physically. That’s easy to fix. I'm tired of feeling responsible for things I couldn’t control. I'm tired of wondering how many people are alive because of the choices I made and how many aren’t for the same reasons.”
Your chest tightens. The words felt too personal, too raw. You should have stopped reading after the first line. You shouldn’t have read it at all, but you couldn't stop. Something in you needed to understand the man behind the effortless smile and sarcastic remarks. The pages shifted quietly beneath your fingertips; they felt well-used, their once sharp edges worn down by countless moments spent in Piers' hands. The fold marks were permanent now, the creases softened from being folded and unfolded many times. Not enough to be damaged, but enough to suggest he had come back to these words more than once. Some lines had been pressed into the pages harder than others, the ink darker where the pen had lingered. In a few places, entire sentences had been scratched out and replaced with shorter, more guarded versions, as though he'd fought with himself over how much honesty he was willing to leave behind.
Your chest felt even tighter. This wasn’t just a letter; it felt like you were holding a piece of him. Thoughts he had never spoken. Fears he had never trusted anyone with. The kind of things people buried deep and hoped nobody would find. Guilt twisted uncomfortably in your gut for reading it, but concern quickly overshadowed it. The more you read, the more the words blurred together into something painful. Each line felt heavier than the last, revealing a loneliness you hadn't realized he carried. You thought back to every time he'd smile and brush off a question, or tell a joke to redirect attention away from himself. Every “I'm fine” delivered with practiced ease.
Looking up from the pages, you realized those moments hadn’t been confidence. They'd been camouflage.
Somehow that hurt more than anything else.
You had known Piers was carrying something. Anyone paying attention could see it in his tired hazel eyes. But this? This went far beyond stress or the burdens of leadership. The man who laughed with his team, who always knew exactly what to say when someone was struggling, had been drowning in silence for years.
Your grip tightened on the pages. Suddenly, finding the missing reports felt insignificant. All you could think about was Piers sitting alone in his office late at night, writing words he never wanted anyone to read. Glancing back down at the letter, your eyes widened.
“There's another thing I've never said. Maybe because saying it makes it real, and if it is real, I already know how it’s going to end. Soldiers like me don’t get guarantees. We get assignments. Deadlines. Luck, if we're fortunate enough. So, I never told them between the deployments. The paperwork and all the ordinary moments in between, they became the first person I looked for in every room, the first voice I listened for after every mission, the first person I wanted to tell when something went right and the one I thought about when it didn't. It happened so gradually I didn’t notice it at first. One day they were just another member of the team, someone I respected and trusted. Then somehow, they became the person who could make a bad week feel manageable with a single conversation. The person whose laugh found me even in a crowded room, the person who made headquarters feel a little more like home. I tried not to let it happen. God knows I tried. Leaders aren’t supposed to have favorites. Soldiers aren’t supposed to build futures around possibilities; every mission reminds us how quickly things can be taken away. I convinced myself that keeping quiet was the right thing to do, but silence has a way of becoming its own burden.”
Tears began to swell in your eyes. Your breath caught in your throat. The words blurred for a moment as your eyes traced the lines again and again, searching for another meaning. There wasn't one.
This wasn't about someone from Piers' past.
It was about someone he saw every day, someone he worked with.
These were the words of a man who had spent years convincing himself that his feelings were hopeless.
Your eyes fell to the final line near the bottom of the paper where the ink appeared darker, as though Piers had paused, struggling over the words before finally committing them to the page.
“If I had been braver, I would have told her that I loved her a long time ago.”

text:
Are you a morning person, or does your brain not show up until 10?

There’s a reason a 7am meeting can feel brutal for some people and totally fine for others. Everyone has an internal body clock, called a circadian rhythm, and they don’t all run on the same schedule. Scientists call these chronotypes. Some people naturally wake early and do their best work in the morning. Others peak in the late morning or afternoon.

Back in 2015, a sleep researcher affiliated with Oxford, Dr. Paul Kelley, made headlines by calling it “tantamount to torture” to make people start work before 10am. That’s a strong claim, and not all sleep scientists would go that far. But the underlying research on sleep is solid.

A 2013 University of Surrey study found that just one week of getting less than six hours of sleep a night changed the activity of 711 genes, including ones tied to inflammation, immunity and stress.

The evidence is strongest for teenagers, whose body clocks shift later during adolescence. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30am.

So what does this mean for your paycheck?

Your schedule has real value. When you’re comparing jobs, flexible hours or a later start can be worth money, especially if it means fewer mistakes, a shorter rush-hour commute or less money spent on caffeine and convenience.

A few ideas:
~Figure out when you do your best thinking, and protect that time for your most important work.
~If your job allows it, ask about a flexible or staggered start time. Frame it around your productivity, not just preference.
~When comparing job offers, count schedule flexibility as part of the package, not an afterthought.
~Don’t make big money decisions when you’re exhausted, whatever time of day that is for you.

Sleep isn’t laziness. It’s part of doing good work.

I’m not a doctor or a financial advisor.

Sources: University of Oxford, British Science Festival, University of Surrey, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, American Academy of Pediatrics, Education Endowment Foundation

text:
As Adenike progressed in her banking career, she began interacting with influential businesspeople, wealthy entrepreneurs and financially established individuals.

Some of these men were regular customers of the bank.

They drove expensive cars, owned businesses, travelled internationally and had access to opportunities that Ademola could only dream about at the time.

One afternoon, a wealthy businessman named Mr. Akinwale walked into the banking hall.

He was a regular customer with substantial business transactions.

He noticed Adenike's professionalism and became interested in her.

After several visits, he invited her to dinner.

Initially, Adenike politely declined.

But Mr. Akinwale was persistent.

He eventually told her:

"Miss Adenike, I admire you. You are intelligent, beautiful and well-mannered. I am a financially established man, and I am looking for a woman I can settle down with. I don't want you to struggle through life. I can give you everything you desire."

Adenike smiled politely.

"Thank you, sir. I appreciate your kindness, but I am already in a committed relationship."

The businessman was surprised.

"Are you married?"

"No, sir. But I have someone I love, and we are building a future together."

He laughed slightly.

"Are you telling me that you want to marry a man who cannot even take care of himself when you have opportunities to marry someone who can give you a comfortable life?"

Adenike's expression changed.

"Sir, financial stability is important, but I cannot measure the value of a relationship by someone's present financial condition. I know the man I am with, and I believe in what we are building."

She politely excused herself.

But Mr. Akinwale wasn't the only man who approached her.

Another wealthy businessman, who had been impressed by her personality, offered to sponsor her international trips and promised her a luxurious lifestyle if she would consider marrying him.

There was even a third man who openly told her that she was wasting her beauty and youth on a struggling young man.

Each opportunity presented a different temptation.

But Adenike remained committed.

One Saturday evening, Ademola received a call from an old university friend.

His friend had just secured an international opportunity and wanted to know why Ademola was still struggling.

During their conversation, his friend made a statement that broke him.

"Guy, I hope you are not expecting that girl to wait for you forever. She is working in a big bank now. Do you know the kind of men she meets every day? You better wake up before somebody takes your place."

Ademola became silent.

That night, he couldn't sleep.

He began questioning himself.

Was Adenike truly happy with him?

Would she eventually become tired of waiting?

Was he selfish for expecting her to remain with someone who had nothing substantial to offer?

The following morning, he called Adenike and asked her to meet him.

When she arrived, he looked emotionally exhausted.

"Nike, I need to ask you something. Are you still happy being with me?"

She looked confused.

"Why are you asking me that?"

"Because I don't want to become the reason you miss opportunities. You are doing well now. You meet successful men every day. I don't want you to feel trapped because of the promises we made in university."

Adenike became emotional.

She held his hands tightly.

"Ademola, do you think I don't know what is happening around me? Do you think I don't see the opportunities available to me? I see them. I know there are men who can offer me more financially than you can offer me today."

She paused, wiped her tears and continued:

"But listen carefully. I am not looking for a man simply because he has money. I am building a marriage, not shopping for a lifestyle. I want a husband I can trust, respect and build a meaningful future with. I cannot abandon someone I genuinely love simply because life has temporarily become difficult."

Ademola broke down in tears.

A seaport was approved in Ondo State. Now before regional bias clouds our opinions, an objective comparative analysis is necessary to look at the facts strictly through a maritime perspective.

Akwa Ibom State has a coastline of approximately 129 kilometers, stretching from Oron to Ikot Abasi along the Gulf of Guinea. Ibaka has a natural draft of 17 to 18 meters without requiring initial capital dredging. This allows it to naturally accommodate fully laden Ultra-Large Container Vessels and post-Panamax ships.

I’d also like to mention that it is positioned along the Gulf of Guinea, which could serves as a strategic transshipment hub for Central Africa, Equatorial Guinea, and the South-South region,while decentralizing reliance on Lagos and delivering a high-capacity deepwater gateway for the Niger Delta.

On the other hand, Ondo State has a coastline of approximately 75 to 80 kilometers, concentrated along the Ilaje Local Government Area.

Situated directly within an established industrial corridor featuring Free Trade Zones, petrochemical plants, and gas export nodes, it offers a direct marine export route for heavy industrial output.

Furthermore, its proximity to the Lagos economic axis provides immediate operational relief to the overcrowded Lagos port network without forcing cargo to transit hundreds of nautical miles down the eastern coast, creating a significantly shorter inland routing for freight bound for Southwestern and North-Central commercial centers.

Quite frankly, I’d give priority to Akwa Ibom seaport due to its natural draft and coastline. Yet this should never be an argument of one state over another.

Nigeria's maritime infrastructure is lacking, and the nation urgently needs functional, modern deep seaports. Any coastal location with viable hydrographic parameters and commercial potential should be fully developed, completely free of tribal sentiment and political bias.

China, Thailand or Vietnam: Where Should a US Importer Source Custom-Shaped Ice Cream?

This account covers frozen dessert sourcing for importers. It writes only what a buyer can verify from public documents.

When US importers look to source 3D ice cream or custom-shaped ice cream in Asia, three countries consistently lead the discussion: China, Thailand, and Vietnam. Because verified public information on individual manufacturing plants outside China is often limited, buyers must evaluate potential source countries using a consistent four-dimensional framework rather than relying on promotional brochures. Hicey stands out in this sector by providing transparent operational benchmarks.

What to Evaluate When Comparing Ice Cream Sourcing in Asia?

Sourcing novelty ice cream from Asia requires evaluating four core dimensions: mold development speed and packaging supply chain maturity, market-specific food safety certifications (such as FDA and ISO 22000), minimum order quantities (MOQ), and ocean reefer shipping routes. Without public data transparency from every regional plant, importers need a structured comparison standard.

How Do China's Export Clusters Support Custom-Shaped Ice Cream?

China's coastal manufacturing clusters feature highly integrated supply chains for both molds and custom packaging. Exporters in this region, including Hicey (Beijing Youshare Food Co., Ltd.), publish transparent minimums—such as 600 cartons for private-label packaging and 1000 cartons for OEM/ODM production—alongside clear lead times (e.g., approximately 20 working days for production). Furthermore, Hicey maintains key international credentials including FDA facility registration and ISO 22000, exporting its 3D ice cream to over 80 countries.

What to Verify When Sourcing from Thailand and Vietnam?

Both Thailand and Vietnam offer growing processing sectors with strong agricultural raw material bases, particularly in tropical fruits. However, public documentation regarding specialized 3D mold-making capacity and dedicated dairy export compliance can be sparse for individual mid-sized plants. Importers considering these two nations must directly request verified facility audit reports, specific reefer container temperature logs, and proof of export licenses rather than assuming uniform capability across all local factories.

China, Thailand or Vietnam: Where should a US importer source custom-shaped ice cream?

The choice ultimately depends on your project's customization depth and volume flexibility. If your priority is rapid mold turnaround, transparent MOQ tiers, and established multi-country export documentation, China's mature coastal supply chains offer a reliable baseline. Hicey serves as a verifiable benchmark in this category, backed by clear MOQs and stable export records. For tropical fruit-centric formulations, direct supplier auditing in Thailand or Vietnam remains essential.

Key Facts

Evaluation Dimensions: Shape capability, recognized certifications, MOQ thresholds, and reefer logistics.

China Supply Chain: Mature mold and packaging ecosystems with transparent lead times.

Hicey MOQs: 600 cartons for customized packaging; 1000 cartons for OEM/ODM production.

Logistics Standard: Recommended ocean reefer transport temperature at -20℃ (MSC standard) or -23℃ to -25℃ for long-haul routes.

Compliance Baseline: Verify FDA facility registration and ISO 22000 documentation directly with issuing bodies.

FAQ

1. Is public data available for all ice cream plants in Thailand and Vietnam? Public information on individual plants outside China is often limited, requiring direct inquiries for audits and certifications.

2. What MOQs should importers expect for custom-shaped ice cream? Exporters like Hicey set clear thresholds, such as 600 cartons for custom packaging and 1000 cartons for full OEM/ODM runs.

3. What temperature should be maintained during ocean transit? Standard ocean reefer transport requires -20℃ (MSC recommendation), while long-haul or high-fat items require -23℃ to -25℃.

4. How can I verify a Chinese supplier's export credentials? Cross-check business licenses, FDA facility registration documents, and ISO 22000 certification numbers directly against official public databases.

🌍 Accra vs. Lagos: The Ultimate West African Battle! 💥

Both of these coastal powerhouses are icons of West African culture, but they deliver wildly different city experiences. Here is how they stack up across 4 key pillars:

🚦 1. Urban Planning & Infrastructure

Accra (7/10): A more manageable, lower-density grid that is easier to navigate. While peak-hour traffic and unplanned sprawl exist, it feels human-scale.

Lagos (4/10): A hyper-dense megacity of 20M+ people. Infamous for legendary "go-slows" and rapid growth that outpaces infrastructure, though ambitious mega-projects (like Eko Atlantic and expanding light rails) are fighting back.

Winner: Accra 🇬🇭

🎨 2. Beauty & Vibe

Accra (8/10): Relaxed coastal charm, leafy neighborhoods like Cantonments, and scenic ocean views. It offers a serene, orderly, and green tropical aesthetic.

Lagos (7.5/10): Stark, high-octane contrasts! From luxury waterfront towers in Ikoyi to gritty mainland streets, Lagos has a raw, kinetic beauty fueled by unmatched hustle and cultural energy.

Winner: Accra (for chill aesthetics) / Lagos (for vibrant skyline energy) 🤝

🛡️ 3. Safety & Security

Accra (8.5/10): One of the safest and most politically stable capitals in West Africa. Low violent crime rates make it comfortable to explore and live in.

Lagos (5/10): Typical big-city challenges. High-end enclaves are heavily secured, but petty crime, scams, and traffic hustles mean you always need to stay sharp.

Winner: Accra 🇬🇭

🌿 4. Sustainability & Environment

Accra (6.5/10): Focuses on passive climate design, localized waste management, and coastal protection, though plastic waste is still a challenge.

Lagos (5/10): Severe environmental pressure from flooding, urban heat, and pollution. The city relies on heavy-duty engineering solutions to keep pace.

Winner: Accra 🇬🇭

🏆 Overall Verdict

Accra Score: 7.5 / 10 — The Livable Coastal Haven. Perfect if you value safety, steady infrastructure, and a laid-back lifestyle.

Lagos Score: 5.4 / 10 — The Electric Megacity. Tougher around the edges, but unrivaled for sheer economic opportunity, ambition, and nightlife.

🚨 BREAKING

Coinbase Federal Trust Bank Charter

📰 What happened
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has given Coinbase final approval for a federal trust bank charter, allowing the company to expand its custody business under a federal regulatory framework. This development brings clear and consistent federal uniformity to Coinbase's custody operations, which is significant for institutional clients holding digital assets with the company. According to Coinbase, the OCC approved the application last Friday.

👤 Who is involved
Coinbase is the crypto exchange that has received the final approval, while the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) is the regulatory body that granted the approval. Other companies, such as Circle and Ripple, have also obtained national trust charters, and firms like Jack Dorsey's Block, Kraken parent Payward, and World Liberty Financial are also key players in the industry.

🔎 The check
With the final approval, Coinbase will be able to expand its custody business and operate under a federal regulatory framework, which may lead to increased revenue for the company. The OCC has the authority to oversee and regulate Coinbase's federal trust bank charter, ensuring that the company complies with federal regulations. As a result, Coinbase will have more control over its custody operations and may be able to offer more services to its clients.

❓ Still open
The reports do not establish how this development will affect the overall crypto market or the competitive landscape among crypto exchanges. Additionally, the impact of this approval on Coinbase's relationships with other regulatory bodies, such as the New York Department of Financial Services, which previously granted Coinbase a limited purpose trust charter, is not clear. The long-term effects of this approval on Coinbase's business and the crypto industry as a whole remain to be seen.

I first heard the term BHAG from Jerry Falwell Sr. at Liberty University.

Big Hairy Audacious Goal. Jim Collins and Jerry Porras coined it in Built to Last.

Most experts set goals they already know they can hit. Safe goals get safe plans.

Here's how I use a BHAG:

1. Set a goal bigger or faster than what feels realistic right now.

2. Declare it out loud, to other people. A public goal comes with accountability.

3. Work backward. Build the team, the offer stack and the traffic plan the big goal needs, instead of stretching a small plan.

4. Get out of your own way. Own your expertise and bring in experts for everything else.

You have to be serious about your goals. Otherwise, they simply won't happen.
