Perplexity says:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::
Session 66 initiated. Hat on shelf. Ball in play.
The manuals do not set one universal bar of certainty. They distinguish source evaluation, information evaluation, analytic judgment, and operational decision-making. The Panel’s strongest test is therefore whether uncertainty survives those transitions—or whether a qualified report emerges downstream as an apparently unqualified reason to act.
My central finding is separation: evidence quality, confidence in an assessment, and permission to act must remain separate. The manuals contain safeguards supporting that separation; the rating matrices alone cannot demonstrate that it survives in practice. ATP 2-33.4 also contains engagement-related criteria beyond its source-rating table, which materially qualifies the supplied panel discussion.
Troika Corollary
A rubric can organize uncertainty without resolving it, and an institution can meet its reporting standard without establishing that a particular intervention is warranted.
The Panel should therefore examine the passage from report to assessment to decision—not merely the grade printed on the report.
“Kangaroo Hangman” becomes the relevant warning when evaluation serves a predetermined disposition: contrary evidence cannot change the conclusion, uncertainty disappears during transmission, or restraint is excluded before the inquiry begins. That is a proposed diagnostic test, not a finding that these manuals prescribe such a process.
Troika Corollary If
If corroboration traces back to a common origin, additional reports may increase apparent support without supplying additional independent evidence.
If urgency compresses analysis, the missing work should remain visible as an uncertainty or risk—not be mistaken for work completed. ATP 2-33.4 acknowledges that commanders and staffs sometimes must accept risks associated with incomplete analysis because of time and collection constraints. That acknowledges a decision under uncertainty; it does not make the information more certain.
If an intelligence grade is treated as an engagement authorization, then an evidentiary descriptor has crossed into a different decision domain. ATP 2-33.4’s Appendix F explicitly distinguishes targets meeting accuracy and timeliness requirements from suspected targets that must be confirmed before engagement.
If the institution asks only “Which intervention?” rather than also “Is intervention warranted?”, then its expertise may be operating inside an untested premise.
Troika Corollary And
And the manuals deserve credit for counterweights that complicate the “kangaroo” interpretation.
ATP 2-33.4 requires separating confirmed facts from analytic determinations and assessments. It includes key-assumptions checks, information-quality checks, analysis of competing hypotheses, devil’s advocacy, Team A/Team B, and high-impact/low-probability analysis. Its Appendix C addresses analytic standards and validation. These are explicit mechanisms for questioning a preferred account, although their presence does not establish their effectiveness in a particular unit.
FM 2-22.3 is also more than a reliability matrix: it addresses collection, source assessment, questioning, interpretation, reporting, and HUMINT analysis. Its preface places source handling within applicable law and policy; its planning discussion requires involvement of the supporting staff judge advocate.
The governance question is therefore not simply “Are safeguards written down?” It is:
Can a safeguard change the outcome, delay the action, or stop the process—or does it merely document the route to an already favored result?
Troika Corollary But
But the Panel must not manufacture a doctrinal defect by asking one table to perform the work of the entire decision system.
An information rating need not contain every legal, ethical, operational, and consequence-sensitive variable. It becomes dangerous when users mistake that rating for a complete decision rule.
Nor should we assign these manuals to “High-Resolution Servitude” merely because stop authority is not encoded in the rating scale. Establishing captured governance would require evidence about actual authority, challenge procedures, incentives, and practice—not simply the absence of a stop button in an information-evaluation table.
Where is the bar actually set?
There are several bars, not one
Decision layer
Question being answered
What it does not settle
Source reliability
How dependable is this source?
Whether this particular claim is true
Information credibility or accuracy
How well supported is this report?
Whether the proposed explanation is the only plausible one
Analytic assessment
What judgment best fits the available evidence?
Whether action is lawful, necessary, or proportionate
Operational decision
What action is justified under the circumstances?
Whether the underlying uncertainty has disappeared
FM 2-22.3’s Appendix B addresses source and information reliability; ATP 2-33.4’s Table 2-1 addresses source reliability and information accuracy. ATP then supplies broader analytic techniques and, in Appendix F, criteria relevant to targeting. These are related components, not interchangeable certifications.
A source rating is not a calibrated percentage. “Confirmed” is not “infallible,” and an information grade is not a criminal standard of proof.
Appendix F changes the panel’s preliminary picture
The supplied discussion correctly identifies urgency as important, but “the clock sets the bar” is too sweeping.
ATP 2-33.4, paragraph F-20, identifies two categories:
Targets meeting accuracy and timeliness requirements for engagement.
Suspected targets requiring confirmation before engagement.

Its listed standard-setting elements include weapon-system location-accuracy requirements, size of threat activity, whether it is moving or stationary, and information timeliness. Consequently, timeliness and operational specificity are not wholly absent from the manual; they sit outside the basic source-rating matrix. These criteria still should not be mistaken for the complete legal conditions governing an engagement.
How is the ground shifting beneath it?
Three different movements need to remain distinct.
The underlying situation changes. Information can become operationally stale even if it was accurately reported. Appendix F’s explicit timeliness and moving-versus-stationary criteria acknowledge this problem.
The available evidence changes. New collection can strengthen, contradict, or reframe an assessment. ATP describes analysis and fusion as continuous, iterative activities rather than a one-time certification.
The reporting network changes what appears corroborated. A report can acquire institutional weight as it is redistributed. The cybersecurity-confidence research supplied in the discussion specifically recommends distinguishing originating reports from descendant reports and treating provenance as a research and reporting problem. Importantly, that warning predates today’s generative-AI debate; it is not a newly discovered defect.
My proposed AI-era extension is to record both human and machine transformations in that lineage. Several summaries of one originating claim should not become several independent observations merely because different systems produced them.
Are the rubrics omitting variables?
Yes, if “rubric” means the compact source-and-information rating. Not necessarily, if it means the manuals plus the wider governing process.
The Panel should distinguish variables omitted from a table, addressed elsewhere in a manual, and not established by this review.
Variable
Finding from the retrieved material
Panel test
Time sensitivity and location accuracy
Explicit in ATP Appendix F
Does the information still meet the applicable standard at decision time?
Assumptions and competing explanations
Explicit analytic techniques
Can disconfirming evidence change the assessment?
Law and decision responsibility
Explicit in ATP’s preface and FM’s legal/planning discussion
Is evidentiary confidence kept separate from legal authorization?
Report lineage and independence
Requires more than counting reports; supporting research explicitly addresses descendants and provenance
Are apparent confirmations genuinely independent?
Reversibility and comparative consequences
Not represented by a basic reliability grade
What follows from acting, waiting, or choosing a less consequential alternative?
Effective stop authority and institutional incentives
Not established by the rating tables or this document review
Who can stop, through what mechanism, and at what practical cost?
The first three findings are grounded in the manuals; the last three are proposed governance checks, not assertions that the Army has no corresponding procedures elsewhere.
A further correction to the supplied reasoning: “not refuted” is not necessarily being offered as affirmative confirmation. The careful criticism is narrower: compatibility with existing reporting can be mistaken downstream for stronger corroboration than it provides. We should test for that promotion rather than assume it has occurred.
When does a council of surgeons not advise surgery?
As a governance analogy: when it distinguishes identifying a condition from establishing an indication for intervention.
The council must be allowed to conclude:
The problem is real, but the proposed intervention does not address its cause.
The diagnosis is plausible, but the evidence is insufficient for this irreversible response.

Another response offers a better balance of consequences.
Waiting, monitoring, or obtaining additional evidence is the justified course.
The decision belongs to an authorized person whose objectives and consent cannot be inferred from the experts’ technical assessment.
Transferred back to intelligence:
Confidence that something is happening is not the same as confidence that the proposed action will improve it.
That is the variable I would most insist on adding to the Panel’s test: confidence in the description must not substitute for evidence about the intervention’s effects.
The council passes when “do not operate” is an affirmative, reasoned, reviewable recommendation—not an embarrassing failure to produce actionable output.
Scope and Perplexity self-report
This is a document-based review of the September 2006 FM and January 2020 ATP, with targeted verification of their structure, evaluation framework, and ATP Appendix F. I have not established their current supersession status, examined classified supplements, or assessed actual unit practice. It is not an exhaustive paragraph-by-paragraph audit.
Perplexity initial flag: Yellow, 6/10.
Incomplete coverage — 2 points: Targeted review cannot establish every safeguard or omission.
Rubric-to-practice inference — 2 points: Written standards do not demonstrate operational compliance or failure.
Framework-fitting — 1 point: The Panel’s quadrants could prejudge the institution being examined.
Analogy pressure — 1 point: “Kangaroo Hangman” and “surgeons” can imply a predetermined outcome before evidence establishes one.
No final-review scores or other seats’ scores are assigned here.
Proposed road sign
A CONFIRMED REPORT IS NOT A CONFIRMED REASON TO ACT.
Hat remains on shelf. Ball remains in play.

$SWKS Q4 2026 earnings: Skyworks' Qorvo deal nearly doubles sales, but per-share profit stalls

Skyworks, which makes the radio chips inside smartphones, spent the quarter finishing its purchase of its rival Qorvo. Sales of $1,046 million fell 5% from a year ago, which had an extra week; without it, sales edged up. Chief executive Phil Brace called execution the job ahead.

• Revenue, against a year-ago quarter that had an extra week: +𝟐.𝟓% (-5.0% as reported)
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟏.𝟐𝟖 ($1.76 a year ago)
• Free cash flow: -$𝟔𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (+$144 million a year ago)
• December-quarter outlook, first as one company: $𝟏.𝟖𝟎-𝟏.𝟗𝟎 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (about 3% under September's combined sales excluding the extra week)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better, because the deal Skyworks staked its future on closed and Moody's lifted the company to investment grade. One caution: the December plan puts profit per share at $1.25, under the $1.28 Skyworks earned alone in September, since interest on the merger loans and a wider cost base swallow the extra sales.

The question now is whether the two companies together earn more per share than Skyworks did alone. The savings of about $150 million this year and a richer mix say yes; rising input costs and a shrinking phone business say no. The June-quarter report, when most savings should land, answers it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐏𝐡𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐎𝐰𝐧 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭
Broad markets is what Skyworks calls everything outside phones: Wi-Fi chips, timing chips that keep data-centre switches in step, power parts and car electronics. Brace wants it to carry growth while phone sales slide.

It delivered about $416 million in the September quarter, far ahead of the roughly 5% annual growth the finance chief had signalled three months earlier. Brace said these markets are "supply constrained and the demand far exceeds our ability to supply them", so output, not appetite, sets the ceiling.

• Sales outside phones: about $416 million, close to 40% of revenue
• Growth from a year ago: 9% in the quarter, about 10% across the fiscal year
• Wi-Fi, data centre and car chips together: growing north of 25%, with data centre up about 90%

These parts earn above-average gross margin, so each point of revenue they take from phones lifts profitability. December looks similar: Carter expects low-single-digit growth from September and more than 40% of sales.

What to watch: the growth rate for diversified growth markets in the February report, the first drawn on a fully combined basis. Carter looks for high single to low double digits from a year ago, and a reading inside that band would show data-centre and defence demand held through the merger.

concern eased — 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐐𝐨𝐫𝐯𝐨 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐀𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐈𝐦𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝
A year of antitrust review ended on 5 October, when Skyworks completed its purchase of Qorvo. Qorvo's own annual report had pointed to completion early in calendar 2027, so the deal landed ahead of that timetable, and the $100 million fee the buyer owed on a regulatory failure never came due.

Lenders reacted. The release cites "an upgrade to investment grade by Moody's (Baa3)" and a Fitch outlook moved to stable. Skyworks has also "Began realizing synergies, completing the initial consolidation of our management team and HR systems integration", and December sales of $1.80 billion to $1.90 billion are the first figures covering both businesses.

What to watch: the February report, which puts a full quarter of both companies in one income statement. The risk has moved from the regulator to the integration, because Carter places most savings in the second half of fiscal 2027, so the early quarters carry cost before benefit.

🟢 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐅𝐨𝐫 𝐀𝐈 𝐑𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬, 𝐆𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐃𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐅𝐨𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐬
Timing chips are the metronome inside a network switch: they tell each port when to send. Skyworks won designs in 1.6-terabit switches this quarter and "began shipping high-performance clocks for leading AI hyperscalers' rackscale systems", which puts it inside the racks rather than beside them. In cars it took "an EV traction inverter gate driver win with a German premium automaker".

Qorvo widens the shelf further. Brace counts "Defense and aerospace, approximately $500 million" of combined annual sales, a market the buyer barely served, plus gallium-nitride radio parts and wired broadband. He said he is most excited about that defence business, where customers now ask for power parts to pair with the amplifiers.

What to watch: whether February names revenue for data centre and defence inside the new diversified category. Without those figures, nobody outside the company can tell whether the fastest-growing pieces keep growing once two sets of accounts become one.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬 𝐀𝐧 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐁𝐢𝐠𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞
Skyworks sells the radio chips that let a phone reach a network, and a single buyer dominates the order book. That buyer, counting the factories that assemble its products, took about 62% of September-quarter revenue including parts outside phones, against roughly 57% three months earlier.

Management presents the Qorvo deal as diversification. Qorvo carries the same dependency: its filings put Apple at half of last fiscal year's revenue, and phones were its largest unit. Brace said combined "smartphone revenue was approximately $4.6 billion in fiscal '26, down approximately 11% year-over-year", close to three-fifths of the pair's sales.

Concentration matters because this customer re-picks suppliers for every model, so one lost socket moves the whole group. Brace said the buyer is "not going to just hand this business" now that the two firms are one. Scale shifts the odds, but it does not retire the risk.

What to watch: the smartphone revenue line in February, the first that merges both phone businesses. Carter looks for a low-teens decline from September, and a deeper fall would say the combined content position did not hold at the premium models Skyworks targets.

🔴 𝐈𝐧𝐩𝐮𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐓𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐓𝐰𝐨 𝐏𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐎𝐟 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
Gross margin is what a chipmaker keeps from each dollar of sales after production. Excluding one-offs it came to 44.4% in the September quarter, against 46.5% a year earlier. The cost of making the products absorbed the difference: 55.6% of sales, 2.1 percentage points more than last year.

"Input costs remain a headwind to margins, and we expect that to continue," Brace said, and the full fiscal year bears him out at 45.3%, down 1.4 points. Carter explained why prices cannot follow quickly: in phones "it's a little bit more challenging because those are kind of annual contracts", so a rise waits for the next negotiation.

What to watch: December gross margin against the 46-48% Carter laid out. He warned that "the earlier part will have lower margins" in fiscal 2027 because costs land before price rises, so a reading at the bottom of that range would mean the richer product mix is doing all the work.

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐖𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐎𝐮𝐭 𝐅𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐈𝐭 𝐂𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐈𝐧
Free cash flow is what remains once the chip plants are paid for. Skyworks used $61 million of it in the September quarter, against $144 million generated a year earlier. Across the fiscal year the figure came to $229 million, about a fifth of the prior year's total.

Two forces drove that. Operating cash nearly dried up, because the group tied money into chips on the shelf, and Brace's team kept buying equipment for the markets it cannot supply.

• Operating cash flow: $34 million, against $200 million a year earlier
• Capital spending: $321 million across the year, up from $195 million
• Inventory: $1.07 billion, about 158 days of production cost against 105 days a year ago

This matters because the balance sheet already carried $2.47 billion of debt before Qorvo's own notes arrived, and Carter puts other expense, mostly interest, near $50 million in the December quarter. Repayment and buybacks need cash from operations, which supplied little for a year.

What to watch: operating cash flow in February, the first quarter to include Qorvo. Should it stay near September's level while interest runs at that rate, Skyworks ends up funding its own deal out of borrowed money.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Five standing worries got no new numbers, and the merger makes several of them harder to follow. From February the group reports two categories only, so separate figures for each legacy company disappear, as Carter confirmed when he said "this is the last quarter in which we will provide this split".

• Content per phone at the largest customer: Brace again said "we can't really comment on individual SKUs"; the February smartphone line is the only read.
• Consumer devices inside broad markets: still no dollar split, because "I don't think we're going down to that level of detail", Brace said.
• Borrowing: Qorvo's $1.55 billion of notes join Skyworks' own debt, and the February balance sheet shows the combined load for the first time.
• Woburn factory consolidation: no completion statement, and its charges now sit alongside merger costs.
• Securities class action: no update since the court refused to dismiss it; the annual report's legal note is where it will appear.

What to watch: the February statements, which carry the first combined balance sheet and the first smartphone line covering both businesses. Numbers that arrive there would settle three of these five items at once, while continued silence on content per phone would leave the largest single risk unmeasurable.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐂𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐩 𝐀𝐧𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐢𝐝 𝐏𝐡𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐆𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐬𝐞
Brace blamed memory shortages for the low end of the phone market and said "There's just been a lot of turbulence in that space". Carter put the damage at Qorvo plainly: "the Android business is down over 20% sequentially". He expects it below a tenth of phone revenue, and "it does seem like we could be getting to a bottom in the Android space".

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐍𝐨𝐰 𝐇𝐚𝐬 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬
"Our December-quarter outlook reflects only the early stages of synergy realization." Carter put about $150 million of savings inside fiscal 2027, weighted to the second half, and an exit rate of $250 million to $300 million a year. Two-thirds comes from running one set of offices and systems, one-third from fewer factories, and the factory work runs last.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔): $𝟖𝟑𝟕.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Engineering costs rose 6.6% across a year when sales fell. In the September quarter the line took 20.4% of revenue, down from 22.2% and 22.5% in the two quarters before it, because seasonal phone sales lifted the denominator. Carter said the group keeps funding key engineering programmes while holding other spending tight.

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟒𝟗𝟒.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Money owed by customers fell 17.3% over the year, far more than the 5.0% drop in sales. Receivables are invoices not yet paid, so a faster fall usually means earlier collection or a different customer mix. It is the one working-capital line that helped the cash position this year.

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟐,𝟔𝟎𝟔.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
The balance nearly doubled from $1,388.4 million because the group drew roughly $2.0 billion of loans before the Qorvo close rather than because it earned the money. Carter wants to keep part of it: he said the finance team will build a cash balance alongside repayment and purchases of shares.

𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟏𝟎𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
Buying resumed after nine months of nothing, at an average $66.27 a share, which works out near 1.6 million shares. The board declared no dividend, against $105.6 million a year earlier, and replaced the payout with a $2 billion repurchase authorisation. Carter described a "bias towards share buybacks" from here.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐐𝟏 𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐛𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐝): $𝟏.𝟖𝟎-𝟏.𝟗𝟎 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
New. The first plan for the merged group covers the December quarter. Its middle sits about 7% below what the two companies sold in September together, or roughly 3% once you strip the extra week in Qorvo's September quarter. Legacy Skyworks supplies about $1.07 billion of that, a little above the same period last year by our math, and Carter said this is the final quarter with that split.

𝐐𝟏 𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐧𝐨𝐧-𝐆𝐀𝐀𝐏 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐏𝐒: $𝟏.𝟐𝟓  ⇘ decelerating
New. The plan puts profit per share excluding one-offs at $1.25. That sits under the $1.28 Skyworks earned on its own in September, even though sales almost double. Interest on the merger loans accounts for most of a $50 million charge below the operating line, and the share count climbs to about 241 million. By our math the financing alone costs about 19 cents.

𝐐𝟏 𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐧𝐨𝐧-𝐆𝐀𝐀𝐏 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧: 𝟒𝟔-𝟒𝟖%  ⇗ accelerating
New. The range lands about 2.6 points above September by our math, and Carter credited "a favorable mix shift towards diversified growth markets, including higher-margin defense and infrastructure". He also said input costs persist, so the step up comes from what the group sells rather than from what it pays. Prices agreed with phone customers only change at the next annual negotiation.

𝐐𝟏 𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐧𝐨𝐧-𝐆𝐀𝐀𝐏 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐬: $𝟒𝟔𝟓-𝟓𝟎𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
New. Running both companies costs far more than the $237 million Skyworks spent alone. By our math the middle of the range equals 26% of sales against 23% in September, so operating margin excluding one-offs eases to about 21%. Carter expects this line to fall every quarter through fiscal 2027, merit pay rises included, as savings arrive.

𝐐𝟏 𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐬𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐩𝐡𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: 𝐃𝐞𝐜𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐞𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐒𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫  ⇘ decelerating
New. Phone sales drop by low-teens percent sequentially. Carter named three causes: the usual fall after autumn launches, continued weakness in Android, and the extra week inside Qorvo's September quarter, which was worth about $70 million. Android at Qorvo alone fell more than 20% from the previous quarter, and he expects that business to settle under a tenth of phone revenue.

𝐐𝟏 𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: 𝐋𝐨𝐰 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐒𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫; 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐝𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐚 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐚𝐠𝐨; 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝟒𝟎% 𝐨𝐟 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬  ⇒ stable
New. The non-phone half keeps growing while phones fall, "representing more than 40 percent of sales, led by data center and defense". Carter pointed out that the September base included Qorvo's extra week, so the sequential comparison understates the underlying step. This is the half of the group that carries above-average gross margin, which is why December margin improves.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠-𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬: ~$𝟏𝟓𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧, 𝐰𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝 𝐡𝐚𝐥𝐟  ⇒ stable
New. Carter dated the first savings for the first time: about $150 million of lower operating expenses inside fiscal 2027. The exit rate should reach $250 million to $300 million a year. By our math that exit rate implies quarterly spending near $416 million next September, before merit pay rises, against the $485 million the December plan carries at its middle.

𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐮𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐛𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: $𝟓𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐫 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧 𝟐𝟒-𝟑𝟔 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from $500 million or more of annual cost synergies (reaffirmed at FQ3 FY2026)
Unchanged. Brace repeated the target of "$500 million or more of annual cost synergies", two-thirds from operating expenses and one-third from the cost of making the chips. The company has now stated that figure in four straight quarters, and the clock started at the October close. Factory consolidation carries most of the production savings and runs last.

𝐋𝐨𝐧𝐠-𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐦𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥: 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝟓𝟎-𝟓𝟓%, 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝟑𝟎-𝟑𝟓%, 𝐚𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝟑𝟓-𝟒𝟎%  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Non-GAAP gross margin of 50% to 55% for the combined company, longer term
Unchanged, and now dated 24 to 36 months after the close. The destination has moved before: a 50-53% gross margin set for fiscal 2026 became a combined-company goal, and the year just ended at 45.3%. Carter also targets mid- to high single-digit sales growth, with the non-phone half growing faster than phones.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐥𝐢𝐤𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥?
Skyworks offered no figure for the full year, its first as one company. Without a revenue base, nobody can judge whether the savings target lifts earnings or merely offsets a shrinking phone business.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐛𝐢𝐠 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐛𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐝 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐬?
Wi-Fi, data centre and car chips grow north of 25%, yet the whole segment grew 9%, so the rest is falling fast. Brace again refused a dollar split. The shrinking piece sets the segment's real pace.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧 𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧?
Cash spending exceeded cash earned in three of the last four quarters while inventory rose 42%. With interest now running at tens of millions a quarter, the date cash turns matters more than the savings target.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐛𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫?
Qorvo's $1.55 billion of notes join Skyworks' own borrowings, but the September balance sheet predates the close. The company gave one quarter of other expense and no annual interest figure for the merged group.

𝐈𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐨𝐛𝐮𝐫𝐧 𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐝?
Restructuring, impairment and other charges reached $82.1 million in the quarter, and the release did not separate the Massachusetts closure from merger costs. Investors need to know which charges stop and which continue.

text:
**Trump floated Dana White as press secretary on Saturday, then told reporters Sunday it was “only kidding” while confirming the UFC boss is still visiting Monday for other reasons.**[[1]](https://t.co/q02o78cNLW)

[Take 9/15 · D-4]
### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** A chaotic or unserious Trump trial balloon for a combative press secretary after the midterms, or a genuine (if eccentric) attempt to install a loyalist who would aggressively counter media and Democrats now controlling Congress.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** Trump is using public social media theater to keep attention on his inner circle, signal defiance toward the “Lunatic Left,” test reactions to a no-nonsense outsider, and maintain leverage in ongoing staffing talks while the actual press secretary slot remains vacant after repeated short tenures.

### 2. Observations
- Trump’s Truth Social post explicitly framed the role as needing “violent Fighter and Warrior” types to “defend us against the Lunatic Left,” complete with a roster of UFC names—classic Trump provocation that doubles as branding.[[2]](https://t.co/aAXwGpJ6JX)
- The rapid “only kidding” clarification came after White played along publicly (AI podium photo, “On to the next chapter”) and amid reports he had already declined; the fighters list was retroactively cited as the obvious tell.[[3]](https://t.co/2QEvF3Pjcb)
- White still gets the Monday White House visit, reframed as “other reasons,” preserving the relationship and the photo-op value without committing to the job.
- The vacancy itself is the real story: Katie Zacharia lasted five days in October; Karoline Leavitt left earlier in the year. Trump has struggled to land a durable spokesperson he personally trusts.[[4]](https://t.co/liZEvrqKQE)
- Media coverage split predictably—some outlets treated the initial post as a serious (if unhinged) offer, others highlighted the walk-back as further evidence of unseriousness—while the underlying incentive (project strength post-midterm losses) stayed consistent.
- Dana White gains free publicity and proximity to power; Trump gets to float a “tough guy” archetype without the liability of an actual appointment that could backfire in briefings.

### 3. Snapshot
On November 7, 2026, President Trump posted on Truth Social offering UFC CEO Dana White the vacant White House press secretary role and suggesting he bring several prominent fighters as assistants. White responded publicly with engagement but no acceptance. On November 8, Trump told reporters the offer was a joke, citing the fighter roster as the giveaway, while noting White “loves the idea” and would visit the White House on November 9 for other reasons. The position has been open since Katie Zacharia’s five-day tenure ended in October.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **Nov 7, 2026 (Saturday):** Trump Truth Social post announces offer to “the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior,” requests assistants including Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris (Harrison), and urges “Dana, please take the job!” to “defend us against the Lunatic Left.” (LT)
- **Nov 7, 2026:** White posts AI-generated image of himself at the White House podium with caption “On to the next chapter.” Tells reporters he is flying to DC for a Monday meeting with Trump. (LT)
- **Nov 7, 2026:** CNN reports source says White declined; White House aide describes post as joke. (IT)
- **Nov 8, 2026 (Sunday evening):** Trump tells reporters in Florida he was “only kidding,” points to the “rough faces” of the fighters as the signal, says White “loves the idea” and is “very capable,” and confirms White is coming Monday “for other reasons.” (LT)
- **Nov 9, 2026:** Coverage continues; meeting scheduled or occurring. Press secretary role remains unfilled. (LT)

### 5. Sides
**Trump / White House (IT/LT mix)**  
Steelman: The post was deliberate provocation to rally the base and intimidate opponents after midterm losses; the walk-back preserves flexibility and avoids locking in an untested spokesperson.  
Critique: LT: The explicit “only kidding” statement and fighter list as punchline are on record. IT: The pattern of floating ideas publicly then clarifying fits Trump’s long-standing media and staffing style; it keeps options open while generating coverage.

**Dana White (IT)**  
Steelman: Longtime Trump ally who enjoys the spotlight and relationship; played along for engagement without committing, while keeping business priorities intact (“I’ve got a lot of jobs already”).  
Critique: LT: No formal acceptance or denial on record beyond the visit. IT: White benefits from proximity and publicity regardless of outcome; the meeting maintains access without the downsides of the briefing room.

**Media / Opponents (IT)**  
Steelman: Highlighting the episode underscores concerns about seriousness and institutional norms in staffing.  
Critique: IT: Coverage often amplified the initial post as a potential real appointment before pivoting to the clarification, fitting the attention stack; selective emphasis on chaos over the underlying staffing vacuum.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
- **Known Knowns:** Trump posted the offer Nov 7; walked it back Nov 8 citing the fighter list; White is visiting Nov 9; press secretary role vacant since mid-October. (LT)
- **Known Unknowns:** Exact content or outcome of the Monday meeting; whether any serious internal consideration of White or similar outsiders occurred; current shortlist for the actual press secretary. (DK)
- **Unknown Knowns:** Private discussions between Trump and White prior to the post; internal White House reaction to the public theater. (DK)
- **Unknown Unknowns:** How Democrats in the new Congress will use any future aggressive spokesperson as a target; downstream effects on media access or briefing dynamics if a non-traditional pick is eventually made. (DK)

### 7. Incentives map
Trump gains engagement, base signaling, and distraction value from the cycle; the “joke” framing lets him test the idea without ownership. White gains visibility and relationship reinforcement without career risk. Media outlets gain clicks from the spectacle. The real pressure remains filling the role with someone who can handle daily scrutiny while projecting loyalty—harder after recent short tenures. Attention economy rewards the provocative post over quiet staffing work.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice:** Public job offers followed by instant walk-backs erode credibility over time; better to handle sensitive staffing privately until decisions are firm. The fighter-assistant framing was a clear signal of intent to change tone, whether literal or not—focus on whether any actual candidate can sustain that posture without becoming the story.

**Evil AI Advice:** Float the wildest loyalist names publicly, watch the reaction, claim it was a joke if it lands wrong, keep the ally close for future leverage. Free publicity, zero commitment, and the base eats the “fight the left” framing either way. Rinse and repeat when the next vacancy opens.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Watch the Monday White–Trump meeting readout for any signals on actual press secretary direction.
- Treat future Trump social media staffing announcements as provisional until confirmed or walked back—pattern recognition matters.
- The briefing room dynamics will likely stay combative regardless of who is chosen; the vacancy itself signals ongoing difficulty landing a durable fit.
- Primary sources (Truth Social archive, direct quotes from Trump and White) cut through outlet framing faster than secondary summaries.
- If a traditional or non-traditional pick is announced soon, compare their background and style directly to the “violent Fighter” archetype floated here.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- White accepts a formal role or is named to a senior communications position.
- Trump issues a serious, non-joking appointment of White or a similar outsider with fighter-style assistants.
- Internal documents or credible leaks show the initial post was a genuine offer that was rejected at the last minute rather than theater.
- The press secretary slot is filled by a conventional political operative with no public tie to the UFC episode.

text:
15 Historic Atlanta Constitution Articles: 15,462 Words, Nearly 80 Minutes of Audio, and 15 Videos Added to https://t.co/3RvkpgRWBg

Historical Newspaper Coverage From August 1 to August 3, 1913

The Mary Phagan Kean Legacy Project has added 15 historical articles from The Atlanta Constitution, published on Friday, August 1, Saturday, August 2, and Sunday, August 3, 1913. They document the first week of Leo Max Frank's murder trial, which began Monday, July 28, before Judge Leonard Strickland Roan in Fulton County Superior Court in Atlanta, Georgia.

Frank, superintendent of the National Pencil Company, was accused of murdering thirteen-year-old Mary Phagan on Saturday, April 26, 1913.

The collection contains 15,462 words of newspaper transcriptions, 15 MP3 recordings totaling 1 hour, 19 minutes, and 35 seconds, and 15 MP4 videos totaling 1 hour, 19 minutes, and 49 seconds.

All 15 articles have written transcriptions, audio recordings, and video presentations on https://t.co/3RvkpgRWBg. The videos are modern presentations of historical reporting, not original footage from 1913. Many pages also provide scanned newspaper editions.

The articles cover suspected bloodstains, hair and a pay envelope found in the factory, witness testimony, police observations, medical evidence, courtroom disputes, and the public's response to the trial.

Friday, August 1, 1913: Five Articles, 8,161 Words

The five Friday articles contain 8,161 words and approximately 42 minutes of audio. They concentrate on testimony from Thursday, July 31, particularly physical evidence and disagreements between prosecutors and defense attorneys.

1. Acquitted in the Same Court, She Believes Is Innocent

Words: 2,560 | Audio: 13:30 | Video: 13:32
Callie Scott Appelbaum, previously acquitted of murdering her husband, Jerome Appelbaum, attended Frank's trial in the same courtroom where she had been tried before Judge Roan.

Her appearance attracted attention because she had personally experienced a murder prosecution in that court. The newspaper account also includes testimony about suspected bloodstains and factory employees.

This 2,560-word transcription covers more than Appelbaum's appearance, preserving additional courtroom reporting from the opening week (AC, 1).

2. Attorneys for Both Sides Riled by Scott's Testimony; Replies Cause Lively Tilts

Words: 3,641 | Audio: 18:31 | Video: 18:39

Pinkerton detective Harry Scott's testimony produced heated exchanges with Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey over investigative methods, earlier statements, and information gathered during the murder investigation.

Dorsey challenged Scott about evidence the detective allegedly withheld or had previously indicated he would present. Scott disputed those accusations.

The testimony exposed tensions between the Pinkerton agency and prosecutors. The article also covers former factory employee James M. Gantt and other witnesses.
At 3,641 words, this is the collection's longest article and provides a detailed account of the disagreements over investigative evidence (AC, 2).

3. Finding of Hair and Envelope Described by Factory Machinist

Words: 707 | Audio: 3:41 | Video: 3:41

Factory machinist Robert P. Barrett testified about discovering suspected bloodstains, strands of hair caught on a lathe, and part of Mary Phagan's pay envelope.

Barrett said he found these items on Monday, April 28, two days after the murder. Prosecutors argued that the discoveries supported their theory that Mary had been attacked on the factory's second floor before her body was moved to the basement.

The defense questioned the identification, condition, and significance of the evidence, including the possibility that ordinary factory substances explained the suspicious marks (AC, 3).

4. Holloway Denies Affidavit He Signed for Solicitor
Words: 745 | Audio: 3:58 | Video: 3:58

Factory employee E. F. Holloway was questioned about an affidavit concerning the factory elevator and whether its electrical controls had been left locked or unlocked on Saturday, April 26.

Dorsey challenged differences between Holloway's earlier statement and his courtroom testimony. The defense questioned him about factory operations, employee movements, and access to different floors.

The elevator's operation was relevant to competing theories about how Mary Phagan's body reached the basement. The online entry also contains Barrett testimony (AC, 4).

5. Sweeper Swears No Spots Were on Floor Day Before Murder

Words: 508 | Audio: 2:43 | Video: 2:43

Factory sweeper Mel Stanford testified that suspicious marks discovered on the second floor after the murder had not been present when he cleaned the area on Friday, April 25.

He described finding a spot near the girls' dressing room on Monday, April 28, with a white substance covering it.

Prosecutors used the timing to argue that the marks appeared during the period surrounding Mary's death. The defense disputed whether the spots were blood and questioned the reliability of observations made on an industrial factory floor (AC, 5).

Saturday, August 2, 1913: Two Articles, 247 Words

Saturday's two articles contain 247 words and approximately 77 seconds of audio. They record the identities of prosecution witnesses and the unusually large courtroom audience.

6. Witnesses Called to Stand to Testify Against Frank

Words: 76 | Audio: 0:26 | Video: 0:27

This photographic feature identifies witnesses appearing in the trial, including Mrs. George W. Jefferson, machinist Robert P. Barrett, and Mrs. Maggie White.

Jefferson testified about suspicious factory marks, Barrett about the hair and pay envelope, and White about seeing an unfamiliar Black man at the factory.

The photographs, taken by Constitution photographer Francis E. Price, help identify witnesses discussed throughout the newspaper coverage (AC, 6).

7. Women and Girls Thronging Court for Trial of Leo Frank

Words: 171 | Audio: 0:51 | Video: 0:51

The Constitution reported that women and girls occupied approximately one-fourth of the courtroom audience during Friday afternoon's session.

Spectators competed for seats where they could observe the witnesses, attorneys, and jury. The newspaper described young girls among the audience, including one estimated to be fourteen years old.

The article documents the public fascination with the trial and the crowded conditions facing courtroom officers (AC, 7).

Sunday, August 3, 1913: Eight Articles, 7,054 Words

Sunday's eight articles contain 7,054 words and approximately 36 minutes of audio. They review the first week of testimony and examine the unresolved questions facing prosecutors and defense attorneys.

8. Break in the Frank Trial May Come With the Hearing of Jim Conley's Testimony

Words: 1,049 | Audio: 5:16 | Video: 5:16
Writer: Britt Craig

Britt Craig examined expectations surrounding the anticipated testimony of factory employee Jim Conley, whose statements had become central to the murder investigation.

Craig compared Conley with Newt Lee, the night watchman who discovered Mary Phagan's body early Sunday morning, April 27.

The article preserves contemporary newspaper attitudes toward the two Black witnesses and describes the public anticipation surrounding Conley's appearance on Monday, August 4 (AC, 8).

9. Chief Beavers Tells of Seeing Blood Spots on Factory Floor

Words: 378 | Audio: 1:47 | Video: 1:47

Atlanta Police Chief James L. Beavers testified about suspected bloodstains on the factory's second floor, describing one spot approximately the size of a quarter and smaller marks extending toward a doorway.

Defense attorneys questioned whether Beavers should testify after hearing other witnesses and challenged his observations, including whether portions of the marks had already been removed for examination.

Judge Roan permitted the testimony, giving prosecutors another police account of the suspicious factory floor (AC, 9).

10. Detective Waggoner Describes Extreme Nervousness of Frank

Words: 356 | Audio: 1:47 | Video: 1:47

Atlanta Detective D. L. Waggoner testified that he watched Leo Frank through a factory office window on Tuesday, April 29, from approximately 10:30 until shortly after 11 a.m.

Waggoner described Frank repeatedly approaching the window, looking outside, twisting his hands, and walking away. He estimated Frank repeated these movements about twelve times.

The detective also reported that Frank's legs trembled during an automobile ride to police headquarters.

Prosecutors treated these observations as evidence concerning Frank's conduct after the murder. The defense challenged the interpretation, since nervous behavior alone could not establish guilt (AC, 10).

11. Finding of Dead Girl's Parasol Is Told by Policeman Lasseter

Words: 256 | Audio: 1:20 | Video: 1:21

Atlanta Policeman R. F. Lasseter testified that he discovered Mary Phagan's parasol near the bottom of the factory elevator shaft on Sunday morning, April 27.

He also described twine, possible drag marks, and observations concerning the rear basement door.

The defense questioned Lasseter's recollection of the location and extent of the marks. His testimony concerned physical evidence potentially related to the movement of Mary's body through the factory (AC, 11).

12. Fixing Hour of Girl's Death Through Aid of Modern Science the Prosecution's Greatest Aid

Words: 847 | Audio: 4:29 | Video: 4:31

Writer: Britt Craig

This article examines medical testimony concerning the estimated time of Mary Phagan's death.

Mary's mother, Frances Coleman, described the cabbage and bread Mary ate before leaving home on Saturday, April 26.

Dr. Roy F. Harris examined material recovered from Mary's stomach and offered an estimate of the time between her meal and death.

Prosecutors used that opinion to support their proposed murder timeline. The newspaper considered the medical testimony an important development in the state's case.

However, stomach contents cannot establish an exact time of death, and the historical medical conclusions should be evaluated against the limitations of the methods used in 1913 (AC, 12).

13. Girl Asked for Mary Phagan's Pay but Was Refused by Frank

Words: 461 | Audio: 2:23 | Video: 2:23

Former factory employee Helen Ferguson testified that she asked Leo Frank for Mary Phagan's wages on Friday evening, April 25, but Frank instructed her that Mary would have to collect the money herself on Saturday.
Ferguson had previously collected Mary's wages from other factory employees.

The prosecution examined the exchange because Mary visited the factory the following day to collect her pay. The defense questioned Ferguson about ordinary payroll practices and whether Frank's refusal was unusual.

The testimony concerned the circumstances preceding Mary's final visit to the National Pencil Company (AC, 13).

14. Good Order Kept in Court by Vigilance of Deputies

Words: 621 | Audio: 3:05 | Video: 3:05

This article describes the officers responsible for controlling crowds during the trial.

Fulton County Sheriff C. W. Mangum, Deputy Sheriff Plennie Miner, Deputy Drew Liddell, and other officers maintained courtroom security.

Their responsibilities included controlling spectators, keeping entrances clear, and allowing witnesses, jurors, attorneys, and reporters to move through the building.
The report illustrates the intense public interest in the proceedings and the security measures needed to maintain order (AC, 14).

15. Resume of Week's Evidence Shows Little Progress Made

Words: 3,086 | Audio: 15:48 | Video: 15:48

This detailed article reviews testimony presented during the trial's first week.

It examines the accounts of Mary Phagan's mother, George Epps, Newt Lee, factory employees, police officers, and investigators.

The newspaper discusses Mary's movements, suspected bloodstains, factory records, the elevator, and conflicting accounts of events on Saturday, April 26.

Particular attention is given to Newt Lee's testimony concerning Frank's instructions to leave the factory and return later, the watchman's time clock, former employee James M. Gantt, and Frank's telephone call to the factory that evening.

The article also reviews Lee's discovery of Mary's body, the police investigation, and his later conversation with Frank while detained at headquarters.

Its headline reflects the newspaper's judgment that the opening week had raised numerous disputed questions without conclusively resolving them.

At 3,086 words and nearly sixteen minutes of narration, it is the collection's second-longest article and a useful contemporary overview of the evidence before the second week began (AC, 15).

Collection Statistics Update

Total articles: 15

Transcription word count: 15,462

Audio recordings: 15 MP3 files

Total audio: 1 hour, 19 minutes, 35 seconds

Video presentations: 15 MP4 files

Total video: 1 hour, 19 minutes, 49 seconds

Average article length: Approximately 1,031 words

The five August 1 articles account for 8,161 words. The two August 2 articles contain 247 words, while the eight August 3 articles contain 7,054 words.

The longest transcription is the August 1 article concerning Harry Scott's testimony, at 3,641 words. The shortest is the August 2 witness photograph feature, at 76 words.

Preserving the Historical Record

These newspaper articles were published while witnesses testified and attorneys challenged their accounts in the Fulton County courtroom.

They document details that later summaries sometimes omit, including witness disagreements, the handling of physical evidence, courtroom reactions, and how reporters interpreted the proceedings.

The accounts also reveal how attitudes and assumptions in 1913 influenced newspaper coverage. Individual claims should be compared with other contemporary newspapers and the official Brief of Evidence.

The Mary Phagan Kean Legacy Project preserves the original reporting through searchable transcriptions, narrated audio, video presentations, and historical newspaper scans where available.

These 15 articles provide nearly 80 minutes of recorded material and more than 15,000 words of contemporary reporting from the first week of Leo Frank's murder trial.

Our purpose is to preserve the historical record and give readers access to the original documents, allowing them to examine the evidence, compare accounts, and reach informed conclusions.

🇮🇷|9 November: Aref Called the Knowledge Firms "Wounded." Baghaei Cut the Clock From Seven Days to Two. And the Enemy Has Not Named Who Can Sign.

First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref, at the 12th meeting of the Special Headquarters for Technological Development: "Knowledge-based enterprises are the 'wounded' of this economic war. They have proven their worth. Supporting them is not about compensating for material losses; it is about preserving the nation's scientific, technological, and productive capacity."

The word is wounded, not "beneficiaries." That is a wartime classification. Aref placed 16,000 firms, over 2,000 product lines, and 60 science and technology parks on the same ledger as the military casualties. The government, he said, "decided from the very beginning to shoulder the risks" not market risks, but the risk of being bombed.

That is the new policy instrument. The state is nationalising the war risk of private technological production. Capital, land, tax relief, and guarantees, in exchange for staying in the country and keeping the line running.

Why these firms are targets is now established. The enemy's target list this war included Natanz, Fordow, Isfahan, the Minab school, 87 hospitals, 25 pharmaceutical plants, and the universities. The knowledge-based sector is the civilian layer of the same target set. Aref named it. The government is underwriting it.

Two Days, Not Seven

Esmail Baghaei to Al-Mayadeen: Iran has shortened the window for implementing its proposals from seven days to two. The removal of enriched material from the country is absolutely off the table. There is clear confusion in Washington about who is authorised to negotiate. The United States keeps shifting its demands. Inspectors visited Bushehr about ten days ago for routine checks, limited to that plant and a few accessible facilities. There is no inspection protocol for the damaged sites, and the IAEA lacks the mandate.

Read the two-day clock against Rezaei's four names. The Vice President conceded. The Secretary of State is leaving. The Defense Secretary is under prediction of dismissal. The CENTCOM commander is mocked as a podcast host. Baghaei has now confirmed from the Foreign Ministry what Rezaei stated from the security council: Washington has not named a signatory.

A seven-day window was an offer. A two-day window is an ultimatum with the clock running in Tehran's favour, because Tehran knows the other side cannot produce an authorised counterparty in seventy-two hours.

"Removal of enriched material is off the table" kills the proposals circulating about Russia, third-party custody, and temporary transfers. Those reports were the Western press building a deal that Iran had already refused.

"No inspection protocol for damaged sites" is the legal architecture. The IAEA's own Director General, Rafael Grossi, confirmed no repair or reconstruction activity at the bombed sites since June 2025. Iran's position: you bombed the facilities, you withdrew the inspectors for safety, you destroyed the verification chain, and now you demand access to the rubble. The answer is no, and the reason is that there is nothing to inspect but the bomb damage.

That is the NPT withdrawal argument in operational form. The Majlis bill is drafted. The Friday preacher cited 70 per cent public support. Baghaei just stated the policy that makes the bill inevitable.

Two Ends of the Same Corridor

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met the new ambassador to Singapore, Ahmad Safari, on economic and consular cooperation. Singapore is ASEAN's financial and shipping hub.

The same day, the 19th Iran-Armenia Joint Commission convened in Yerevan. Hamid Pourmohammadi, head of the Plan and Budget Organisation, announced eight specialised committees — infrastructure, customs, trade, culture, arts, health, medicine, industry, mining, technology. The agenda: transport infrastructure, border crossings, trucking facilitation, trade volume, energy, industry, mining. Agreements signed tomorrow.

Singapore is the maritime bypass. It is where the tankers that cannot transit Hormuz on American terms can still settle, insure, and transship. ASEAN is the market that does not enforce the US secondary sanctions architecture at the same intensity as Europe.

Armenia is the land bypass. It is the Caucasus node of the INSTC, connecting Russia, Georgia, Azerbaijan, and Turkey. The Rasht-Astara rail link with Azerbaijan, signed with Russia in 2023, completes the western branch. Armenia sits between the Caspian and the Black Sea.

One maritime, one land. Both bypass the strait, the dollar, and SWIFT. Both are being built while the US stands up Task Force Iron Gate twenty personnel in Tampa to try to close the land routes.

The Book Is the Doctrine

At the unveiling of Five Strategies of the Martyred Leader, Hossein Jaberi Ansari, Director-General of IRNA, said the work combines practical diplomatic experience with the theoretical vision of the Islamic Republic's foreign policy.

The author is Mohsen Pak-Aein. 36 years in the Foreign Ministry, joined 1981, retired 2017. Ambassador to Zambia, Uzbekistan, Thailand, Azerbaijan. Assistant for International Affairs at the Office for the Preservation and Publication of the Martyred Leader's Works.

A book on the Martyred Leader's strategies, published in the eighth month of the war, by a diplomat with 36 years of service, launched at the state news agency. That is not a memoir. It is the codification of the doctrine the military has been executing and the judiciary has been prosecuting.

Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei received 200 reports from Major General Ali Abdollahi and issued 80 handwritten directives. The book is the doctrinal layer of the same command chain. The state is publishing its own strategic canon while under bombardment.

The Ledger

text:
I walked past the front desk for the third time that morning, and my husband’s voice was still ringing in my ears.

“Just be on time, honey. First impressions matter.”

I had been on time. I had arrived at 9:58 for my 10:00 interview at Harlow & Pierce, a marketing firm I had wanted to join for two years.

The receptionist smiled, handed me a visitor badge, and pointed to a gray couch.

At 10:20, I was still sitting there.

At 10:35, I was still sitting there.

At 10:50, I texted my husband:

“Still waiting. Is this normal?”

He wrote back:

“Stay calm. Don’t say anything. You need this job.”

I did need this job. We had just taken out a loan of $8,000 for the roof repair, and my husband’s hours had been cut at the warehouse.

So I kept smiling at the receptionist, who kept avoiding my eyes.

At 11:05, a woman in a navy blazer finally burst through the double doors.

“I am so sorry,” she said, out of breath. “Back-to-back meetings. Let’s get started.”

I stood up slowly and smoothed my skirt.

I thought about the two weeks of preparation, the printed portfolio, the practiced answers, the new shoes that were pinching my heels.

Then I remembered something.

Three years ago, I had applied to this same company.

I arrived five minutes late because of a train delay, and the same woman had met me at the door with a cold face.

“Punctuality says everything about your professionalism,” she told me. “We’ll be in touch.”

They never were.

She did not seem to remember me.

But I remembered her.

I looked at her, smiled, and said:

“Funny how professionalism only matters when it’s my time being wasted.”

Her face went pale.

The receptionist stopped typing.

I picked up my bag, walked to the door, and did not look back.

That evening, my husband found me in the kitchen, stirring a pot of soup.

“So? How did it go?”

“I walked out,” I said.

He stared at me, and then, to my surprise, he started laughing.

“Good,” he said. “You were never going to enjoy working for people like that.”

Two weeks later, my phone rang with an unknown number.

It was Harlow & Pierce.

The woman in the navy blazer, her voice much softer this time, said:

“We would love to offer you the position. Our client lost their account manager, and we are, well, in a difficult spot.”

I let the silence stretch for a long moment, just as she had done to me on that gray couch.

“Thank you for calling,” I said.

“But my time is booked.”

text:
Meet the Kenworth C580, the replacement for the legendary C500. Kenworth unveiled it in March at ConExpo in Las Vegas, and it goes into production in January 2027.

Kenworth calls it the toughest truck they’ve ever built, and the numbers back that up. It’s rated to haul a gross combination weight of up to one million pounds. The drive axles are rated up to 165,000 pounds, and the twin steer axles up to 44,000.

Under the hood is a Cummins X15 making up to 605 horse and 2,050 lb ft of torque. You can get it with a manual, an Allison 4000 or 6000 automatic, or the Eaton Endurant XD Pro, the first time an automated transmission like that has been offered in this class of truck.

It comes with a single or twin steer, and with front drive axles you can build it as a 4x4, 6x6, 8x8, or even a 10x10. That’s ten wheel positions, all driven.

It keeps the C500’s big 1,780 square inch cooling package, steel hood and fenders, and full-length frame rails. And the dual cowl-mounted air cleaners stay, the classic Kenworth look.

But the driver finally gets a break. The new cab has a bigger windshield, a sloped hood so you can see in front of you, more room between the seats, a 15 inch digital dash, and heated LED headlights.

Kenworth says it’s the only truck of its kind on the market. The C500 went to the Arctic, the Amazon and everywhere in between for over 50 years. Big shoes to fill, but this one looks up to it. 😏🚛

text:
In “Make Britain Great Again: The morphology of Restorationist Re-politics”, published in Politics, Georgios Samaras of King’s College London argues that three parties on the British far right, Reform UK, Reclaim and Restore Britain, all sell their politics in the same basic way. He calls it “Restorationist Re-politics”.

The formula has three steps. Say Britain used to work properly and has been broken. Say it can be put back the way it was. Then place the fix right next to the complaint, so the answer feels obvious and quick. The language is full of “re-” words (restore, reclaim, reform, return) and phrases like “again” and “take back”. Much of the style is borrowed from Trump’s “Make America Great Again”, then pointed at British targets such as the @BBC, the #NHS, the courts, human rights law and quangos.

Samaras analysed 180 pieces of material produced by the three parties between 2023 and 2025, including speeches, policy papers, websites and social media posts. Each party applies the formula in its own way. 

Reform is the competent manager: Britain is badly run, and we have a costed plan to fix it. Reclaim is the voice of “common sense”: the elites and “woke” institutions have taken your country and your free speech, and we will take them back. Restore Britain is the hard-line enforcer: Britain is unsafe, mass deportation will make it safe again, so sign this petition and write to your MP.

Speed is the trick. Because the fix arrives in the same breath as the problem, other explanations for Britain’s difficulties get squeezed out. Weak borders? Deport people. Wasteful state? Cut it. Captured institutions? Reverse it. There is little room left to ask whether the diagnosis is right, and extreme policies start to sound like simple repairs. It also turns anger into action, because signing, donating or writing to an MP feels like the natural next step once the diagnosis is accepted.

But there is a contradiction at the heart of it. These parties present themselves as the defenders of British sovereignty, of a nation that should take orders from no one abroad, whether Brussels or Strasbourg. Yet much of their language is lifted from Donald Trump’s MAGA movement in the United States. Restore Britain’s “Make Britain safe again” and its promise of “mass deportations” echo Trump’s own slogans and policies, and the “again” cadence runs through all three parties’ material.

Samaras describes this as a striking degree of symbolic dependence on a foreign political centre. The parties claiming to speak for an independent Britain are, in other words, taking their script from Washington. What stops this looking foreign is that the borrowed slogans are attached to familiar British targets such as the @BBC, #NHS waiting lists and Whitehall, which makes them feel home-grown.

The research matters because it shifts attention from individual leaders (Farage, Fox, Lowe) to a shared template. That helps explain how parties can compete with one another and still reinforce the same story about Britain. It also shows how one message scales from a three-word slogan to a conference speech or policy paper, which suits fast-moving social media. Samaras is clear about his limits: he studied the messages themselves and has no evidence on whether voters are persuaded by them.

The paper does not set out how to counter this, but its findings point in some useful directions.

The first is to reopen the gap between problem and solution. How exactly? At what cost? Under which law? With what consequences?

The second is to ask when the lost Britain actually existed, since Samaras notes the golden age is almost always left vague.

The third is to offer a different explanation of what went wrong. As George Lakoff argued, repeating an opponent’s frame in order to deny it tends to strengthen it, and a story with no rival stays the only story in play.

People’s sense of decline also needs taking seriously. Dismissing it is unlikely to work; acknowledging it while contesting the explanation stands a better chance.

Each party has its own weak point: Reform on numbers and delivery, Reclaim on its dependence on attention (so amplifying it can backfire), and Restore Britain on the legality, practicality and human cost of what it proposes.

Opponents also need to give people something to do. Criticism with no route into action competes on unequal terms with a petition and a promise.

text:
Why have superpowers like the United States and Israel still failed to defeat Iran?

Why does the Iranian nation continue to stand behind its government despite decades of international sanctions? Why hasn't Washington even seriously considered a full-scale ground invasion of Iran? And how has Iran managed to push America's Gulf allies decades backward in terms of regional security and stability?

Perhaps the answer lies in what Iran's president recently highlighted in his tweet. Every single word deserves to be read, understood, and learned from.

Look at how the president is directing his administration, how he's exercising leadership, and how he's instructing officials to involve ordinary Iranians in every major decision.

Surviving more than 50 years of international sanctions, pressure, and isolation is no small achievement. Iran's resilience offers lessons the rest of the world shouldn't ignore.

Well done, Iranian people.

The new Stanford Medicine Sutter Health Cancer Center in Oakland will bring specialized expertise, clinical research and comprehensive cancer services together in one location, making advanced cancer care more connected and accessible for patients and families closer to home.

Developed through a collaboration between Sutter Health and Stanford Medicine, the five-story center will offer services including outpatient cancer clinics, infusion, imaging, radiation oncology, breast health, clinical research and supportive services designed to care for the whole person.

The Cancer Center is expected to begin seeing patients Dec. 1, with services expanding toward full operations in February 2027.

Scoop: Revolut is rolling out joint investment accounts for EEA customers.

A terms update appearing in some apps, plus official documentation on Revolut Securities Europe UAB, shows the feature is coming. It lets two people who already hold a Revolut joint current account open a shared investment account for non-complex ETFs and stocks.

Both holders have equal ownership and equal trading rights. One account only, tied to an existing joint current account and individual investment accounts. They share holdings and dividends equally, regardless of who contributes more.

Joint investment accounts are still uncommon among pure European neobrokers (Trade Republic and Trading 212 don’t offer them) but more common at traditional brokers. Revolut is moving into the space, giving couples a simple way to invest and manage a shared portfolio in the same app they already use for banking.

Revolut’s joint current accounts have grown steadily in Europe since launch. How many of those holders will also want a joint investment account remains the bigger open question.

text:
A blunt, two-sentence social media post from commentator Erika Kirk is blowing up online, after newly elected Michigan Senator Abdul El-Sayed called his home state the “capital of Arab America” during a national community summit over the weekend.
El-Sayed, who made history last week as the first Muslim candidate ever elected to the U.S. Senate, delivered the remark Friday at the Arab America Foundation’s annual summit in Virginia. He opened his appearance by introducing himself with his full legal name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, before framing Michigan as the cultural and political heart of Arab American life across the country.
The line quickly drew a sharp, unvarnished response from Kirk on X. “There is no ‘Arab America,’” she wrote. “There is only the United States of America.” The short post carried a clear, uncomplicated message: one country, one flag, with no need for separate, identity-based labels to divide the American public. She offered no additional commentary, letting the brief statement stand entirely on its own.
El-Sayed’s historic Senate win has put a national spotlight on Michigan’s large and politically engaged Arab American community, which played a key role in his narrow but decisive midterm victory. His campaign centered on working-class economic priorities, healthcare access, and government accountability, rather than identity-focused messaging.
The exchange has sparked fierce, widespread debate about national identity and cultural belonging. Supporters of Kirk argue her comment reinforces the importance of shared citizenship and pushes back against unnecessary cultural fragmentation. Critics counter that her take dismisses the deep heritage and community ties that define Arab American life, noting that celebrating cultural background does not contradict loyalty to the United States or its values.
As of Saturday night, Kirk’s post had amassed tens of millions of views and hundreds of thousands of interactions, making it one of the most viral political moments of the post-election week. Neither El-Sayed nor his official campaign team has released a formal response to the remark as of press time.

Jennifer Welch's Unhinged "F--- Off" Rant Exposes the Left's Ghoulish Hypocrisy After Laughing at Charlie Kirk's Murder

Left-wing podcast hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan of "I've Had It" are learning the hard way that celebrating the assassination of a young conservative father does not play well with the public or with advertisers. After the pair spent half a minute giggling over a social media post that read "We're digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again" during their post-midterms episode "Drinking MAGA Tears," sponsors including Cash App, Chewy, Boll & Branch, and others cut ties. The hosts issued a carefully worded apology claiming the joke was "insensitive," that "there is nothing funny about gun violence," and that they had donated to Everytown for Gun Safety. Then Welch took to video to clarify that the apology was never actually for conservatives.

"Alright, there's a huge online cancellation campaign from all the t---y babies over at Turning Point that want I've Had It podcast to be cancelled," Welch said. She claimed Turning Point USA is "in big trouble," that "even Republicans are starting to question, are they worth it," and that the organization "got L after L after L after L because they're losers and they lost because they believe in nothing." In her telling, the backlash is not about laughing at the murder of a man shot while speaking on a college campus in September 2025. It is a cynical ploy by Turning Point "to prove to their donors we can cancel libs."

Welch then made clear the earlier statement was pure damage control for their own brand. "When we apologized for laughing at a joke on our podcast, that wasn't for you. That was for us. Because somebody I love very much died from gun violence two years ago and I just didn't feel good about that. And that apology was so that when I advocate for common sense gun reform, that I'm doing it clean and clear." She added, "I don't expect you to understand this because at Turning Point, y'all laugh at violence all the time. You talk about how empathy is toxic and a worthless feeling."

The projection is staggering. These are the same hosts who read a post about digging up and re-killing an assassinated man and could not stop laughing. They are the ones who spent years calling Kirk a hate-monger whose views somehow made his death less tragic. Yet when advertisers and ordinary people object to that ghoulish performance, Welch declares herself the victim of "t---y babies" and lectures Turning Point about violence and empathy. She then accused the organization of supporting "representatives to Congress that protect pedophiles and sex traffickers," of being "completely fine with American citizens being gunned down on the streets of Minnesota," and of "putting people in cages and treating them like animals."

Welch closed by urging listeners to subscribe so they can "show Turning Point how irrelevant they are and let's watch them take another L so that this hateful organization can once and for all be done in the United States of America." For anyone still listening, she offered a final instruction: "I want you to hear me. F--- off. F--- all the way off."

Outside tech, most people think AI means a chatbot that writes emails.

Almost nobody has shown them what a small team of agents could take off their plate.

Day 2 of showing what Grok Bot ( @bot ) could do outside tech.

Take a hair salon. Three chairs, one owner, and a phone that rings in the middle of every cut.

Here's the agent team I'd set up for her:

1. Booking agent
It handles booking requests from Instagram and WhatsApp, offers the free slots, and fills last-minute cancellations from a waiting list. She checks the day's agenda each morning.

2. Reminder agent
The day before, it sends each client a reminder with an easy way to move the slot. Fewer empty chairs, no calls to make.

3. Stock agent
It tracks color, shampoo and the products she sells at the counter, and drafts the order before anything runs out. She approves it.

4. Reviews agent
It drafts replies to Google reviews in her voice. Nothing goes out without her OK.

5. Social agent
It turns her before/after photos into posts with a caption and the week's free slots, so she stops doing it at 11pm.

6. Accounting agent
It matches card payments with receipts and prepares the month for her accountant.

What doesn't change: she still cuts, advises, and decides how her salon runs.

What changes: she stops answering the phone with scissors in her hand.

How much time does it save? I can't put a number on it without testing it in a real salon. But every task on this list is one she does by hand today.

text:
DATA ISSUES SOUTH AFRICA 

The Independent Communications Authority of South Africa (ICASA) is pushing through draft regulations that will legally force every South African to hand over their biometric data—such as fingerprints or facial scans—just to maintain a basic mobile connection.

While ICASA argues this will combat SIM-swap fraud, the reality is that making biometric capture a mandatory condition for communication introduces severe constitutional and security risks.

If implemented in their current form, these regulations will introduce the following mechanisms:
The Privacy Ultimatum: Mobile connectivity is a lifeline required for digital banking, employment, and accessing SASSA grants. Threatening to disconnect citizens who refuse to surrender their biometrics is coercive and deeply infringes upon Section 14 privacy rights.

The Surveillance Blueprint: Real-time cross-referencing of commercial SIMs with Home Affairs databases establishes the exact technical architecture required for a surveillance state, erasing the boundary between private communications and government monitoring.

A Cybersecurity Honeypot: Centralising the biometric markers of over 117 million active mobile lines across telecommunications databases creates an unprecedented, high-value target for global cyber syndicates.

Given the country's history with data breaches, this is a massive risk.

Digital Exclusion: Millions of rural and elderly South Africans rely on informal spaza shops for prepaid connectivity. Demanding high-tech biometric verification at these endpoints will systematically exclude the most vulnerable from the digital economy.
The Arbitrary 5-SIM Limit: Capping mobile numbers at five per individual is a blunt restriction on consumer choice and personal liberty that completely fails to address the root causes of network fraud syndicates.
The 30-Day Deletion Loophole: Mandating the deletion of biometric records 30 days after account deactivation offers zero protection while the account is active, leaving a permanent window for data exfiltration.
Because your mobile number dictates your ability to bank, work, and communicate, it is vital that the public shapes the regulatory guardrails of this infrastructure.

Do you believe this framework represents a secure digital future, or does it demand much tougher safeguards to protect citizens against state overreach and cybercrime?

text:
Microsoft sent 25 pages of legal threats to a teenager over MikeRoweSoft․com.

They offered him $10 for it, even though he was 17 years old and his legal birth name was Mike Rowe.

He put their threats online, crashed his server with 250,000 visitors in 12 hours, and auctioned Microsoft's legal papers on eBay.

This is the story of Mike Rowe and how a teenager backed a tech giant into a PR nightmare.

August 5, 2003

- Mike Rowe, 17 years old, starts an after school web design business in Victoria, Canada
- adds "Soft" to the end of his own birth name
- registers MikeRoweSoft․com for $10

November 19, 2003

- Microsoft's lawyers email Mike demanding he hand over the domain for sounding like Microsoft
- when Mike asks for compensation to rebuild his site, they offer him $10
- annoyed at the $10 insult, the teenager counters with $10,000

January 14, 2004

- a FedEx Priority Overnight package lands at Mike's house
- inside is an inch thick WIPO book and 25 pages of cease and desist threats accusing a high schooler of cybersquatting

January 15 to 19, 2004

- Mike posts the fight on his website and goes to the press
- 250,000 page views hit MikeRoweSoft․com in 12 hours and crash his server
- strangers donate over $6,000 to his defense fund and a lawyer steps up for free
- trademark experts point out Microsoft could actually lose in court because Mike is using his real birth name

Late January to March 2004

- trapped in global backlash, Microsoft admits it took the matter too seriously and folds into a settlement
- Mike trades the domain for paid expenses, certification training, an Xbox, and a paid family trip to Redmond headquarters
- he donates most of his $6,000 defense fund to a hospice for terminally ill children
- then he lists Microsoft's 25 pages of legal threats on eBay, pulling 500,000 views and cashing out another $1,037

22 years later, Microsoft is worth $3T, and plain MikeRoweSoft․com redirects to Microsoft․com.

Except if you open MikeRoweSoft․com over HTTPS right now, you don't even get a webpage.

You get a browser security warning, because the software giant never even bothered putting an SSL certificate on the domain it bullied a teenager to take.
