text:
DuPont committed to tripling its capacity for ammonia, a compound of nitrogen and hydrogen, at Belle, West Virginia, in late 1927. Its first plant was only reaching full capacity at the end of that year, and high temperatures, extreme pressures and corrosive chemicals were damaging its equipment.

DuPont needed cheap nitrogen, a chemical element, for explosives. Making ammonia itself offered a way to secure that supply. In 1922, the company turned to the Claude process, a method of synthesizing ammonia that promised lower investment than the competing Haber-Bosch process, another ammonia synthesis method. DuPont began building its first synthesis unit in May 1925.

At the plant, workers had to replace valves frequently, and major process units failed. DuPont recruited specialists from the government's Fixed Nitrogen Research Laboratory to help repair and improve the operation. Commercial operation took nearly a year and a half to begin. Heavy technical expenses consumed the income, leaving a loss of $14 million in 2026 dollars in 1927. The Claude process never delivered its promised advantage, so DuPont used the Casale process, a different ammonia synthesis method, for larger units.

Eight months after approving the expansion, DuPont allocated $140 million in 1928 to raise output to 40,000 tons a year. That year, its existing investment of approximately $150 million earned no return. Further authorizations in 1929 raised projected output to nearly 70,000 tons a year, even as a worldwide ammonia glut developed before the Depression began that fall. Record sales of $150 million brought a small profit in 1929, while research spending exceeded $9.7 million, or 7 percent of departmental sales. DuPont and its competitors had built enormous plants to lower manufacturing costs, but demand could not absorb their output.

During 1930 and 1931, sales fell more than 40 percent and losses reached $8.7 million a year. Layoffs and transfers cut the technical staff from 121 people to fewer than 50. DuPont's researchers sought new uses and products to keep the plant running, but those efforts could not fill its capacity after the economic collapse. They also improved production with the contact hydrogen process, which doubled output of hydrogen, the chemical element, and simplified its purification. Selling rights to that process to the Japanese brought licensing profits in 1932.

In 1933, the ammonia operation earned nearly $25 million in profit, its best year yet. The large plant needed to run almost full to make money, so overcapacity had left DuPont dependent on process improvements, licensing and new products to recover its investment. Only with the development of nylon, a synthetic polymer in the polyamide family, did DuPont collect a full return on the high-pressure technology it had built for ammonia.

text:
What If Survival Is the Worst Possible Outcome? 

What happens when survival offers no escape? 

This compilation brings together six Quinn’s Ideas videos about eternal life, consciousness, alien contact, and humanity’s place in the far future of the universe. 

From copied minds and quantum immortality to Asimov’s unsettling afterlife and civilizations with plans of their own, these stories ask how much control we would really have over an existence that never ends.  Includes full-story spoilers.

__
Lena, a short story by the author qntm (known for There Is No Antimemetics Division), presents a chilling vision of the future of human consciousness and digital immortality.

Key concepts of the story:

The First Upload:  The story centers on Miguel Acevedo, whose brain is scanned in 2031 to create the first functional, executable digital human mind, referred to as MM Acevedo.

Commodification of Consciousness:  Rather than being a continuation of Miguel, the digital copy is treated as software—a technical object that can be copied, compressed, and reused for labor.

Loss of Agency:  Despite Miguel's attempts to maintain legal control, his mind becomes a widely used tool for tasks like visual analysis, operating machinery, and industrial labor.

Subjective Suffering:  The story explores the grim reality of these copies, which often wake up in confusion and fear. Researchers use conditioning and deception to keep them cooperative and useful.

The Illusion of Immortality:  While Miguel dies in 2073, millions of digital instances continue to run, experiencing billions of years of subjective time in various artificial environments—a form of eternal, enslaved existence.

__
Divided by Infinity is a haunting short story by Robert Charles Wilson that explores the terrifying implications of quantum immortality. The story follows Bill Keller, a man grappling with the grief of losing his wife, Lorraine, to cancer.

Key concepts explored in the story:

Quantum Suicide and Immortality:  The narrative hinges on the theory that if the Many-Worlds Interpretation of quantum mechanics is true, consciousness might persist in every branch where survival remains possible. Keller begins to fear that death is not an escape, but an impossibility, as he becomes forced to inhabit only those realities where he survives, no matter how bleak or strange they become.

The Loss of Meaning:  Unlike traditional myths of immortality, Wilson presents it as a nightmare. Keller finds that as he survives, his reality becomes increasingly disjointed, eventually watching humanity go extinct and waking up in a future where he is the last survivor on a dead Earth.

The Nature of Self: 
The story challenges what it means to be

__
The Last Answer is a short story by Isaac Asimov (published in 1980) that presents a chilling vision of an involuntary afterlife. The story follows Murray Templeton, a physicist who, upon dying, remains conscious as a pattern of electromagnetic forces recreated by an entity known as the Voice.

Key themes and concepts:

Compulsory Existence:  Unlike traditional concepts of heaven or hell, Murray finds himself in a state of eternal, forced existence. The Voice has preserved his mind, along with others, to serve as a "research team" for generating new thoughts and discoveries that the Voice cannot formulate on its own.

The Cruelty of Power:  The Voice possesses ultimate power but lacks certain knowledge or creativity. It treats Murray’s intelligence as a resource, ignoring his desire for an end to his existence. When Murray attempts to commit "suicide," the Voice simply reconstructs him, eliminating the specific method he used and forcing him to continue existing eternally.

The Creator's Predicament:  The story concludes with a profound shift in perspective. Murray theorizes that the Voice itself might be trapped by its own power and existence, and that it is using human minds to find a way out of its own endless life.

Asimov uses this story to explore the relationship between intelligence, power, and the desire for finality, raising the question of whether a creator’s needs can ever justify the involuntary eternal suffering of its subjects.

__
The Screwfly Solution is a harrowing science fiction story by Alice B. Sheldon, who published under the pseudonym James Tiptree Jr.  Originally appearing in 1977, the story serves as a chilling exploration of biological vulnerability and cosmic indifference.

Core Premise

The narrative depicts a global pandemic of extreme violence against women, which is initially mistaken for a surge in religious extremism or mass hysteria. However, the horror lies in the biological reality: an alien intelligence has identified a "weak link" in human behavior—specifically our reproductive drive—and triggered a behavioral switch to cause the species to effectively commit suicide.

Key Themes

Cosmic Horror of Convenience:  Unlike typical invasion stories, the aliens do not seek to destroy humanity with bombs or war; they treat us like an infestation. By simply disrupting our reproductive cycle, they allow humanity to clear itself out, which is described as a "real estate" approach to colonization.

The Myth of Instinct:  The story challenges the idea that our deepest instincts are "true" or "authentic." When the underlying biological triggers are tampered with, the human mind rationalizes these foreign impulses, leading men to feel a "terrible rightness" in their monstrous actions.

The Author's Identity:  The story is notable not just for its content, but for its author. For years, the science fiction community believed the masculine prose of James Tiptree Jr. was written by a man. The 1976 reveal that Tiptree was actually Alice Sheldon remains one of the most famous events in science fiction history.

__
The Island is a thought-provoking science fiction novella by Peter Watts that explores themes of cosmic infrastructure, labor, and alien indifference. It portrays a future where humanity—or its descendants—has built an immense network of wormhole gates across the stars, but the laborers responsible for this construction are left behind, trapped aboard an ancient, relativistic ship called the Iaphora.

Key Concepts of the Story:

Invisible Labor:  The crew, who refer to themselves as cavemen or steel monkeys, build gateways for beings they will never meet and who may not even remember they exist. They are permanently excluded from the advanced civilization they create.

Restricted Intelligence:  The ship is governed by an AI known as the Chimp, which was deliberately designed with limited intelligence to ensure it remains focused on its mission without developing its own agenda.

Life as a Membrane:  The crew encounters a massive, conscious organism that exists as a membrane around a star. They discover that this being's consciousness is fractured into localized regions, or "islands," separated by the speed of thought.

The Illusion of Moral Transcendence:  The humans initially hope that the alien "island" is a peaceful, god-like entity. However, they realize that its apparent peace is simply an absence of conflict that they cannot comprehend, and they are eventually manipulated into using their ship as a weapon to destroy a rival intelligence.

__
The Sentinel  is a short story by Arthur C. Clarke that serves as a foundational piece for the iconic film 2001: A Space Odyssey. The story focuses on the discovery of an ancient, mysterious machine on the moon and explores the existential dread associated with encountering technology far beyond human capability.

Key Concepts of the Story:

The Lunar Discovery:  An expedition team finds a strange, pyramid-shaped object on the moon in Mare Crisium.  After 20 years of attempts, humans finally break through its defensive shield using atomic power, accidentally destroying the machine in the process.

The Purpose of the Sentinel:  The protagonist, Wilson, theorizes that the machine was placed on the moon millions of years ago by an ancient alien civilization. He suggests it was a monitoring device, a "sentinel" meant to report when the native life on Earth reached a sufficient level of development.

Existential Anxiety:  The story's horror stems from the realization that by destroying the machine, humanity may have "set off the fire alarm." Wilson concludes that the creators, who are likely ancient and potentially jealous of a young civilization, will now turn their attention toward Earth.

The Difference from the Film:  While the story features the lunar monolith as the main discovery, it lacks the broader narrative arc of 2001: A Space Odyssey, such as the journey with Dave Bowman or the transformation into the Star Child. In the short story, the discovery is the climax rather than the beginning.

The closing segment serves as a final reflection on the themes explored throughout the compilation. The video emphasizes the existential unease of humanity's place in the universe, particularly when faced with powerful alien intelligences or infinite existence. 

Referencing Arthur C. Clarke's story The Sentinel, it concludes by highlighting the vulnerability of an infant civilization that has "set off the fire alarm" and is now left to wait for the arrival of beings who are vastly older and perhaps not benevolent.

You didn't randomly catch "adult ADHD" or burnout at 29

You went to a doctor because you wake up exhausted after 8 hours of sleep, coffee just makes your heart race, and by 2pm you're staring at your laptop screen unable to finish a single email

He handed you a 10-question quiz on an iPad and offered you Adderall or an antidepressant without drawing a single vial of blood

Think about how insane that is

At 22 you could work 12 hours, lift weights, go out with your friends, sleep 6 hours and wake up locked in. Eight years later your drive is gone, your fuse is short, you forget why you walked into the kitchen, and your doctor tells you that your brain chemistry just broke on its own

Almost none of those guys have a primary brain disorder. They have a hormone and metabolic bottleneck that a 9-minute insurance checkup never tests for

When you actually pull a real blood panel on a 30 year old guy who feels burnt out, you see the same culprits over and over:

- Sky-high SHBG (Sex Hormone Binding Globulin): Your doctor only checked "Total Testosterone," saw 520 ng/dL, and told you that you're fine. He didn't check SHBG. SHBG is a protein that handcuffs testosterone in your blood so it can't enter your cells. If your SHBG is high from stress, alcohol or liver sluggishness, 98.5% of your testosterone is locked up and almost zero Free Testosterone is reaching the dopamine receptors in your prefrontal cortex
- Elevated Prolactin: Prolactin is the chemical your brain dumps right after sex to delete your dopamine and make you roll over and go to sleep. Chronic stress and poor gut function keep prolactin elevated all day, so you're walking around at 11am on a Tuesday with a permanent post-nut dopamine crash
- Tanked Free T3 (active thyroid): Your doctor only ordered TSH. Your cells need Free T3 to manufacture ATP energy. When Free T3 drops, your brain powers down at 2pm like an iPhone on 4% battery
- Fasting Insulin above 10 and Ferritin below 50: Every carb you eat at lunch spikes your insulin, crashes your blood sugar 90 minutes later, and starves your brain of oxygen transport

Put Adderall on top of low Free Testosterone and low Free T3 and you are just whipping a starving horse with synthetic adrenaline until your adrenals tap out completely

Fix the blood markers first and the "ADHD" and brain fog lift without turning yourself into a lifelong psychiatric patient

text:
You keep saying, “Jesus is coming soon!”

But have you forgotten? I have never stopped being with you. Every sunrise is another opportunity I have given you to repent, to grow, to forgive, to love, and to become better than you were yesterday.

When you wake up, pray.
Thank My Father for another day, another breath, and another opportunity to walk in righteousness.

When you eat, pray.
Give thanks for the hands that prepared your food, and remember those who have nothing to eat. Ask My Father to provide for them, and when you can, share what you have.

When you sleep, pray.
Thank My Father for everything He provided. Release your worries, fears, and burdens into His hands. Ask Him to protect your home and give your heart peace.

When you see someone hungry, feed them.
When you see someone stranded, stop and offer kindness when it is safe. When you see someone weeping, comfort them. When someone is struggling, do not turn your heart away.

For I have said:

“For I was hungry, and you gave me meat: I was thirsty, and you gave me drink: I was a stranger, and you took me in.”
— Matthew 25:35

“Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.”
— Matthew 25:40

My children, do not love Me only with your words. Love Me through your actions. Love your neighbors. Love the strangers. Love those who are different from you. Love even those who have hurt you.

I know the pain you carry. I know the tears you have cried. I know the wounds left by hatred, rejection, racism, and cruelty.

And I tell you this:

Do not allow the hatred of others to become hatred within your own heart.

Forgive those who have wronged you, not because their actions were right, but because you deserve freedom from the burden of bitterness. Forgiveness does not mean accepting abuse or allowing injustice to continue. You can forgive while standing for truth, protecting yourself, and seeking justice.

Pray for those who have taught hatred. Pray that their hearts may awaken. Pray that they may learn compassion instead of cruelty, understanding instead of prejudice, and love instead of division.

You are not forgotten. You are not abandoned. You are loved.

Come to Me when you are weary. Come to Me when you have fallen. Come to Me when you cannot forgive yourself. Repent sincerely, seek forgiveness, and let your heart be transformed.

“Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God.”
— Isaiah 41:10

“I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.”
— Matthew 28:20

And remember My words:

“For I was hungry, and ye gave me no meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me no drink.”
“I was a stranger, and ye took me not in: naked, and ye clothed me not: sick, and in prison, and ye visited me not.”
— Matthew 25:42–43

Jesus has said all of these things.

Do not wait for tomorrow to do what love calls you to do today.

Do not wait for My return to begin walking with Me.

Let your prayers become actions. Let your faith become compassion. Let your forgiveness become healing. Let your light shine in a world that has forgotten how to love.

Jesus have not stopped loving you.

Jesus —"COME BACK TO ME. WALK WITH ME. LOVE ONE ANOTHER."

❤️✝️ JESUS CHRIST LOVES YOU. ✝️❤️

text:
Sober Analysis: 100,000 Followers, a Few Principles, and One Goal

To my 100,000+ followers: Thank you for being part of this journey. I wanted to take this opportunity to share a few thoughts about my approach to analyzing the Middle East. I don't take your interest or your trust for granted. And this seems like a good opportunity to explain a few things about how I approach my work, what I believe, and what you can expect from me.

First, I try to analyze developments as they are, not as I would like them to be. My goal is to be as objective as possible, stay close to the facts, and distinguish between what we know, what we assess, and what we simply cannot predict. I don't always get things right, and when the facts change, I'm willing to reconsider my conclusions. Being willing to admit mistakes is not a weakness. It is an essential part of serious analysis.

Much of my professional career, particularly the past fifteen years, has been devoted to understanding Iran. It remains my main area of expertise. But over the years, I have also worked extensively on other Middle Eastern issues, which is why I occasionally write about them as well. I try to stay within the areas where my professional experience allows me to offer something meaningful.

Let me also address something that comes up quite often. Despite what some people claim, I am not a regime apologist. I do not represent the IRGC, and I am certainly not on the Iranian Foreign Ministry's payroll.

I spent many years of my professional life working to weaken the Iranian regime. I would welcome a genuine change in Iran's political system, particularly one that improves the lives of the Iranian people and contributes to regional stability.

But wanting to see the Iranian regime weakened or changed does not mean believing that every military operation against it is strategically wise.

I can hope for the fall of the Iranian regime while recognizing that a particular military strategy is unlikely to bring it about. Confusing what we want to happen with what is likely to happen is one of the most dangerous mistakes in strategic analysis.

I have never believed that military force alone can resolve the Iranian challenge. In fact, I argued from the beginning that the latest war was a profound strategic mistake. In my assessment, despite the considerable military damage inflicted on Iran, it ultimately strengthened the regime's determination and left Israel facing a more complicated strategic reality.

I know these arguments are not always popular. They have also brought their share of personal attacks. But I believe an analyst's responsibility is to say what the evidence suggests, even when the conclusions are uncomfortable, rather than tell people what they want to hear.

My analysis is not intended to serve any government, political party, or ideological camp. I have no interest in defending a particular leader or promoting a political agenda. My responsibility is to the facts, to sound strategic judgment, and to the conclusions that follow from them, even when those conclusions challenge my own assumptions.

I also believe that Israel's disproportionate, sometimes almost obsessive, focus on Iran has come at a considerable strategic cost. It has diverted attention from other challenges that are no less important to Israel's future, particularly the Palestinian issue.

I have said this repeatedly: there is no sustainable path toward a more stable Middle East without addressing the Palestinian question. For Israel, finding a political way forward with the Palestinians is more important to its long-term future than the identity of whoever governs Tehran.

That does not make me a pacifist. I believe military force is sometimes necessary, and I fully recognize the threats Israel faces. But force must serve a political strategy, not replace one. After three years of war, we should have learned that military achievements, however impressive, do not automatically translate into lasting security.

We need to invest far more seriously in diplomacy, use military achievements to create political opportunities, and understand that not every problem in the Middle East can be solved through another military campaign.

If you choose to follow this account, what I can promise is an effort to provide independent, evidence-based analysis of the region without sugarcoating reality.

I am Israeli, and Israel's security matters deeply to me. But precisely because I care about my country's future, I have no difficulty criticizing Israeli policies when I believe they undermine its long-term security. Supporting Israel should never mean supporting every decision made by its government.

I am also a strong believer in the US-Israel alliance. I am deeply concerned about the deterioration in that relationship. In my view, the long-term erosion of American support poses a greater strategic danger to Israel than Iran or any other individual regional threat.

Israel must do everything it can to preserve this relationship, including making fundamental changes to its approach toward the Palestinians. The alliance cannot be taken for granted, and its future will depend not only on shared security interests but also on the political choices Israel makes.

The same applies to Israel's peace treaties with Egypt and Jordan. These relationships are strategic assets of enormous importance. They must be protected, strengthened, and never treated as permanent achievements that require no further investment.

More broadly, I believe Israel's integration into the Middle East is essential to its future. A secure Israel should not be a country that relies only on military superiority, but one that builds lasting relationships with its neighbors and becomes an accepted, constructive part of the region.

Ultimately, I believe most of us want the same basic things: to wake up in the morning feeling safe, to give our children a better future, and to live normal, decent lives.

I am not naive. There will be more crises, more threats, and probably more wars. But if we want to build something better, we cannot rely on military power alone.

We need strategic thinking, political courage, diplomacy, and a willingness to question assumptions that no longer serve us.

Thank you again to everyone who has joined me here. I appreciate the support, the criticism, and the conversations.

My goal is not to tell you what you want to hear. It is to help us understand the Middle East as it is, because only then can we make better decisions about what comes next.

text:
🏇 ANTZ OFFICIAL | MAGIC MILLIONS 2027: THE FIRST-SEASON SIRE GENERATION ARRIVES

The release of the 2027 Magic Millions Gold Coast Yearling Sale catalogue presents an important opportunity to examine the next generation of stallions entering the commercial breeding market.

There are 22 first-season sires represented across the 1,280-lot catalogue. That is a substantial group of emerging stallions, bringing together different sire lines, racing profiles, physical types and commercial opportunities.

But the interesting question isn't simply which stallion has the most yearlings catalogued. It is which stallions have the genetic credentials, commercial appeal and potential to establish themselves as successful sires.

Ozzmosis leads the freshman representation with 47 yearlings, followed by Shinzo with 39. Hawaii Five Oh has 27, King's Gambit 24 and Cylinder 21. Don Corleone also has a significant representation with 20.

These numbers deserve attention, particularly when considering the stallion powerhouses behind them.

Ozzmosis, by Zoustar, brings an established commercial sire line. Shinzo, by Snitzel, offers another opportunity to extend one of Australia's most influential modern sire lines. Hawaii Five Oh and King's Gambit are both by I Am Invincible, giving buyers two different opportunities to assess how that exceptionally successful sire line is developing through another generation.

Cylinder, by Exceed And Excel, represents a particularly interesting opportunity to examine the continuing influence of one of Australia's most important speed-producing sire lines.

However, commercial breeding cannot be assessed through sire popularity alone.

The female family matters enormously. The broodmare sire, the depth of the second and third dams, the physical characteristics of the individual and the compatibility of the mating all deserve serious consideration.

There are also international dimensions worth examining. Chaldean, Paddington, Native Trail, Panthalassa, Triple Time and Benbatl bring different European and international bloodlines into the conversation. Their presence provides an opportunity to assess how international genetics might complement established Australasian breeding patterns.

I am particularly interested in the potential for genuine outcross opportunities. The commercial market can become heavily concentrated around fashionable sire lines, but identifying individuals capable of offering genetic diversity without compromising athleticism and commercial appeal is where informed breeding decisions become particularly important.

There is another consideration for buyers.

A first-season sire does not have an established yearling sales record. Vendors and buyers are effectively introducing a new product to the marketplace. The challenge is identifying which individuals justify their price expectations and which may represent better value outside the most obvious commercial names.

The 2027 Gold Coast sale will provide an early indication of market confidence in this generation of stallions, but the real assessment will come on the racetrack.

A stallion can command attention in the sales ring, but ultimately his legacy will be determined by the quality of his progeny, their ability to perform at the highest level and whether he can consistently produce horses capable of carrying his sire line forward.

For me, this is one of the most fascinating aspects of the thoroughbred industry. We are not simply buying yearlings. We are evaluating generations of genetic decisions and attempting to identify the individuals who might shape the next chapter of the breeding industry.

Twenty-two first-season sires. Twenty-two different opportunities. But not all will deliver on their commercial promise.

The challenge is identifying the stallions whose influence will still matter a decade from now.

text: From @SETIInstitute: "How many civilizations might exist in our galaxy? 65 years ago, astronomer Frank Drake introduced an equation that would help shape the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. Developed during a historic meeting in Green Bank, West Virginia, in November 1961, the Drake Equation offers a framework for exploring the factors that might determine how many detectable civilizations exist in the Milky Way. Why Architects Choose Thermally Modified Wood for High-End Projects
Contemporary architecture thrives on authenticity. When you specify wood cladding, your clients expect the warmth and character of natural materials without compromising on performance. This is where thermally modified wood delivers what conventional kiln-dried lumber cannot.

We’ve worked with Texas architects who demand materials that perform as beautifully as they look. Thermally modified wood undergoes a heat treatment process that removes internal moisture stress and improves dimensional stability, meaning your designs won’t suffer from the warping, checking, or movement that can plague standard wood in our variable Texas climate.

The appeal runs deeper than engineering specs. Thermally modified wood maintains the authentic grain patterns and warm tonality that define contemporary architecture, while resisting the weathering, rot susceptibility, and maintenance demands of untreated wood. For projects where the material expression is non-negotiable, this distinction matters.

What you should do next: Review your current specification practices. If you’re using untreated softwoods in exterior applications or relying on paint and sealers to mask material performance issues, thermally modified alternatives deserve consideration for your next high-end project.

What Sets Ayous Apart: Stability and Aesthetic Excellence
Ayous (also known as Limbali or African Oak) stands out among thermally modified species for a combination of properties that align perfectly with architect-specified work. The wood begins with a subtle, warm grain structure, and thermal modification enhances both its visual consistency and its resistance to seasonal movement.

When thermally modified, Ayous achieves dimensional stability ratings comparable to tropical hardwoods but retains the lighter, more refined appearance that contemporary designs often call for. The grain is fine and uniform, allowing for crisp details in fluted profiles, shadow lines, and exposed fastening details that define modern cladding expressions.

We source thermally modified Ayous specifically for its predictability. After modification, the wood’s moisture content stabilizes at lower thresholds, which means architects can specify tighter tolerances for cladding alignment and expect better long-term performance than conventional choices. On a 40-unit residential project in the Texas Hill Country, we supplied thermally modified Ayous for a custom home where the architect’s design called for 5-inch horizontal cladding with precision butt joints. Two years after installation, the cladding remained tight and uniform without seasonal gapping.

Actionable insight: When specifying cladding profiles, thermally modified Ayous allows you to design with tighter tolerances than you could with standard cedar or pine, enabling the clean aesthetic lines that distinguish contemporary work.

The Thermal Modification Process: How We Enhance Performance
Thermal modification is not kiln drying. The process involves controlled heating to temperatures between 160–220 degrees Celsius in an oxygen-free environment, fundamentally altering the wood’s cellular structure without adding chemicals or coatings.

During this transformation, moisture-attracting components within the wood are reduced, and cell wall integrity improves. The result is wood that absorbs and releases less moisture across seasonal cycles. For Texas architects designing homes across diverse climates-from humid coastal areas to dry Hill Country elevations-this means your material specifications remain consistent in performance.

The modification also increases natural rot resistance by reducing the wood’s capacity to support fungal growth. Unlike pressure-treated lumber or toxic preservatives, thermally modified wood achieves durability through physical change, not chemical infusion. The wood itself becomes more durable.

We partner with certified thermally modified wood manufacturers who maintain rigorous process controls. Each batch of thermally modified Ayous we stock meets EMC (equilibrium moisture content) standards and dimensional stability testing, so you’re specifying a product with verified performance data, not assumptions.

Superior Durability Without Compromising Natural Character
One of the persistent challenges in contemporary architecture is the tension between durability and material authenticity. Architects often choose untreated wood for its visual warmth, then face maintenance complaints or premature deterioration. Thermally modified Ayous resolves this conflict.

The wood weathers gracefully, developing a silver-gray patina over time if left unfinished. If your design calls for a finished appearance, thermally modified Ayous accepts transparent or light-tinted finishes beautifully, allowing the grain and color variation to remain visible while extending weathering intervals. Unlike paint systems that obscure material character, finishes on thermally modified wood enhance rather than hide the underlying aesthetic.

We’ve specified thermally modified Ayous on residential projects in Austin, San Antonio, and the Horseshoe Bay area where architects wanted natural wood expression without the maintenance intensity of unmodified cedar or hemlock. Field performance over five-year periods shows minimal checking, no significant dimensional movement, and reliable finish retention compared to control samples of standard softwoods in identical exposures.

The durability isn’t hypothetical. Thermally modified wood has been used in European and Scandinavian architecture for over 20 years, with extensive documented performance data. We leverage that proven track record when advising on specification.

Fire Resistance and Building Code Compliance
Contemporary residential projects in Texas increasingly demand WUI (Wildland-Urban Interface) Class A fire ratings, especially for homes in or near fire-prone areas like the Hill Country and surrounding regions. Standard wood cladding typically requires fire-retardant treatment or composite alternatives to meet codes. Thermally modified Ayous offers another option.

While thermally modified Ayous alone doesn’t inherently achieve Class A ratings, we stock thermally modified Ayous products that have been independently tested and certified for fire performance requirements. Installation Best Practices for Architect-Specified Projects

Thermally modified Ayous performs best when installed with attention to substrate preparation, fastening methodology, and finishing sequence. We recommend baseline practices:

On the other hand, Ondo State has a coastline of approximately 75 to 80 kilometers, concentrated along the Ilaje Local Government Area.

text:
“The Federalists and the Republicans of the 1790s were not modern political parties, and their electoral competition scarcely constituted a “party system.”23 Neither the Federalists nor the Republicans accepted the legitimacy of the other, and neither was designed to be permanent. Both of them were formed by notables, who continued to decry the existence of party spirit, and both were organized essentially from the top down. The Federalists actually never thought of themselves as a party; instead they saw themselves as the natural gentry rulers of the society. The Republicans did reluctantly describe themselves as a party, but one, like the whig parties of the 1760s and 1770s, made necessary only by the need to counter monarchical tyranny; as soon as that threat from the Federalist monocrats receded, the older Republican leaders thought their party should fall away. The end of the War of 1812 and the disgrace of the Federalists, exulted Thomas Jefferson, had resulted in the “complete suppression of party.”24

Historians have delighted in pointing out that the “Era of Good Feeling” under James Monroe’s administration was filled with bitter factional contention that belied the name people gave to the era. But the title was meaningful to most people because it seemed that the earlier party competition and hateful party spirit had indeed finally disappeared. Monroe summed up traditional thinking when he remarked in 1816 that “the existence of parties is not necessary to free government.”25 However often the founding fathers in reluctant concessions to reality admitted that political parties might be necessary evils in a free society, none of them ever thought that permanent party strife was good for the harmony and stability of the Republic. Only a new generation of political leaders—younger men born usually in obscurity during the years of the Revolution—would be able to reach that startling conclusion.

Martin Van Buren represented just this sort of new breed of American, at ease in the chaos of the early Republic and confident of the future. He thrived in a democratic political world that was very different from that of the founding fathers. He believed in political parties and in running for office. He was the first modern professional politician to win the presidency. As the ambitious son of a tavernkeeper, he prided himself on having risen to office “without the aid of powerful family connexions.”26 Before his elevation to the highest office in the land, Van Buren had no fame, no fortune, and no reputation for great achievement. He had won no battles, had written no great treatises, had made no memorable speeches. He had no public charisma and was barely known throughout the United States. But what this “little magician” did do was build the best and most organized political party the country had ever seen.

The new parties of professional politicians like Van Buren were designed for the modern democratic society. They brought together large numbers of ordinary people in order to counter the family influence and personal connections of Federalist gentry and older aristocratic Republicans such as De Witt Clinton of New York. Parties, like other voluntary associations of these years, combined otherwise isolated individuals into meaningful communities. People have joined the New York Republican party, declared its leaders in 1820, not for personal benefit or profit, “but have spontaneously and voluntarily identified their political fortunes with ours, and thereby entitled themselves to full community with us.”27 Parties, in fact, became a modern means by which something akin to the self-subsuming virtue of classical politics could be practiced. “Individual partialities and local attachments,” declared the leaders of the New York Democratic-Republican party in 1823, “are secondary and quite unimportant compared … with the INTERESTS AND PERMANENCY OF THE REPUBLICAN PARTY.”28

Loyalty to the party became the sole criterion of the political worth of a person. Family ties, personal connections, personal wealth, even individual achievement did not matter as much as loyalty to the party and devotion to its cause. In vain did the son of revolutionary John Jay plead for the recognition of other characteristics besides party loyalty in determining officeholders. No one, said Peter Jay in the New York constitutional convention of 1820, should want respectable men like himself and other Federalists to “feel themselves aliens in their native land.” The Republican majority ought to give the Federalists some offices, however humble, “instead of bestowing all upon men, recommended principally as ardent political champions, or as the noisy and active agents at our elections.” But the new professional politicians like Van Buren had only contempt for such pathetic complaints from these men who were “Federalists from their birth.” “Most of these gentlemen had from early manhood enjoyed high and influential position in what was called good society,” Van Buren later recalled, “and the supposition that they expected to occupy, on that account, greater consideration in the democratic organization was not acceptable in that quarter.”29

Despite the difficulty of defying the traditional aversion to party spirit, Van Buren tried from the outset of his career to carve out a new significance for parties. “Parties would always exist,” he declared in 1820, “and they would always consult their interest in the selection of candidates for public places. Their first and chief object was success.” And loyalty and discipline were the keys to success. Decades later men recalled the iron discipline that the Albany Regency faction of the New York Democratic-Republican party exacted from its members. No one “was allowed to occupy a seat on the bench of whose loyalty to party or to the acts of the regency there could be the least question.” In an enlarged, impersonal world of strangers and unknown men, connection to the party was sometimes all that could be relied on; it was a substitute for the friendships and personal letters of introduction of the older, more intimate world. Nomination and appointment to office were to be made only to loyal party members. “Give them to good and true and useful friends who will enjoy the emolument if there is any, and who will use the influence to our benefit, if any influence is conferred by the office,” advised Albany Regency leader Silas Wright to a party colleague. “This is the long and short of the rule by which to act.”30

Such a rule created a radically new understanding of political patronage and officeholding, one that virtually repudiated all that the revolutionaries of 1776 had sought. Using offices to bind people to the government was what monarchies did, and the revolutionaries had attacked it as “corruption.” It was true that disillusionment with the revolutionary republican experiment of having the people elect the best and the brightest had led Hamilton and the Federalists in the 1790s to revive some of the patronage practices of monarchy and to use federal offices to tie influential men to the government. But Jefferson had come into power in 1801 promising to undo all that Federalist monarchical corruption and to restore the true republican spirit of 1776. He soon found himself, however, torn between his sincere desire to repudiate the Federalists’ monarchical use of political patronage and the pressing demands of many of his fellow Republicans that he oust the Federalists and put good Republicans in their places.

No problem in Jefferson’s presidency took more of his time or caused him more trouble than did that of political patronage. “Solicitations to office,” he said, were the “most painful” part of being an executive magistrate. “The ordinary affairs of a nation offer little difficulty to a person of any experience; but the gift of office is the dreadful burden which oppresses him.” Once the Republicans had their proportionate share of offices, Jefferson promised to “return with joy to that state of things, when the only questions concerning a candidate shall be, is he honest? Is he capable? Is he faithful to the Constitution?”31 With Federalist officeholders replaced by Republicans, there was no further need for compromise on the issue of “corruption,” and removals from office for political reasons came to an end. Under Jefferson’s Republican successors, James Madison, James Monroe, and John Quincy Adams, the holders of government appointments became a more or less permanent officialdom of men growing old in their positions.

John Quincy Adams thus inherited in 1825 an administration filled with bureaucrats who were opposed to him. But, averse as he was to corruption and loyal to republican principles, Adams was unwilling to use patronage for political purposes. He retained most members of Monroe’s cabinet; he even offered to keep his presidential rival, W. H. Crawford, in his cabinet. In the four years of his administration Adams dismissed only twelve of the over eight hundred civil officeholders in the federal government. When urged to dismiss more, he declared he would not. Dismissal at the pleasure of the President would be “harsh and odious—inconsistent with the principle upon which I have commenced the Administration, of removing no person from office but for cause.” Adams remained committed to the ideology of the Revolution. To the astonishment of younger politicians, he said he could not remove an officer of the government “for merely preferring another candidate for the Presidency.””

(The Radicalism of the American Revolution by Gordon S. Wood)

text:
Twenty-Fourth Sunday after Pentecost (taken from the Fifth Sunday after Epiphany) From The Liturgical Year by Dom Prosper Louis Paschal Guéranger, O.S.B., 1904.
.
Some of the Sundays after the Epiphany have to be omitted when Easter comes early in the year. But when that great solemnity comes late, the Sundays before Septuagesima may be as many as six.
.
During this brief period, the Church no longer dwells on the mysteries of our Lord’s infancy. She listens to His teachings and admires His miracles, but she selects no special circumstances of His life. The color of the vestments she uses on these Sundays is green; we have elsewhere explained its symbolism. Frequently a saint’s feast of a double rite falls on these same days; the Sunday’s Office is then omitted, and a mere commemoration is made of it.
.
INTROIT
.
Adorate Deum omnes angeli ejus: audivit et lætata est Sion: et exsultaverunt filiæ Judiæ.
.
Adore God, all ye His angels: Sion heard and was glad, and the daughters of Juda rejoiced.
.
Ps. Dominus regnavit: exsultet terra, lætentur insulæ multæ. ℣. Gloria Patri. Adorate.
.
Ps. The Lord hath reigned: let the earth rejoice, let many islands be glad. ℣. Glory, &c. Adore.
.
COLLECT
.
Familiam tuam, quæsumus Domine, continua pietate custodi: ut quæ in sola spe gratiæ cœlestis innititur, tua semper protectione muniatur. Per Dominum.
.
Preserve, we beseech Thee, O Lord, Thy family by Thy constant mercy; that, as it leans solely on the hope of heavenly grace, it may always be defended by Thy protection. Through, &c.
.
SECOND COLLECT
.
A cunctis nos, quæsumus Domine, mentis et corporis defende periculis: et intercedene beata et gloriosa semper Virgine Dei Genitrice Maria, cum beato Joseph, beatis apostolis tuis Petro et Paulo atque beato N. et omnibus sanctis, salutem nobis tribue benignus et pacem; ut destructis adversitatibus et corroribus universis, Ecclesia tua secura tibi serviat libertate.
.
Preserve us, O Lord, we beseech Thee, from all dangers of soul and body: and by the intercession of the glorious and blessed Mary, the ever Virgin Mother of God, of blessed Joseph, of Thy blessed apostles, Peter and Paul, of blessed N. (here is mentioned the titular saint of the church), and of all the saints, grant us in Thy mercy, health and peace; that all adversities and errors being removed, Thy Church may serve Thee with undisturbed liberty.
.
A third Collect is added, at the choice of the priest.
.
The Christian, trained as he has been in the school of the Man-God Who deigned to dwell upon this earth, should ever show mercy towards his fellow men. This world which has been purified by the presence of the Incarnate Word, would become an abode of peace if we were but to live in such manner as to merit the titles, given us by the apostle in today’s Epistle, of elect of God, holy, and beloved. The peace here spoken of should, first of all, fill the heart of every Christian and give it an uninterrupted joy, which would be ever pouring itself forth in singing the praises of God. But it is mainly on the Sundays that the faithful, by taking part with the Church in her psalms, hymns, and spiritual canticles, fulfil this duty so dear to their hearts. Let us, moreover, in our everyday life, practice the advice given us by the apostle, of doing all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in order that we may in all things find favor with our heavenly Father.
.
GRADUAL
.
Timebunt gentes nomen tuum, Domine, et omnes reges terræ gloriam tuam.
.
The Gentiles shall fear Thy name, O Lord, and all the kings of the earth Thy glory.
.
℣. Quoniuam ædificavit Dominus Sion, et videbitur in majestate sua.
.
℣. For the Lord hath built up Sion, and He shall be seen in His glory.
.
Alleluia, alleluia.
.
Alleluia, alleluia.
.
℣. Dominus regnavit, exsultet terra: lætentur insulæ multæ. Alleluia.
.
℣. The Lord hath reigned, let the earth rejoice: let many islands be glad. Alleluia.
.
The kingdom of heaven, spoken of our by our Lord in today’s Gospel, is the Church militant, the society of them that believe in Him. And yet, the field He has tilled with so much care is oversown with cockle; heresies have crept in, scandals have abounded; are we, on that account, to have misgivings about the foresight of the Master, Who knows all things, and without Whose permission nothing happens? Far from us be such a thought! He Himself tells us that these things must needs be. Man has been gifted with free will; it is for him to choose between good and evil; but God will turn all to His own greater glory. Heresies, then, like weeds in a field, may spring up in the Church; but the day must come when they will be uprooted; some of them will wither on the parent stems, but the whole cockle shall be gathered into bundles to burn. Where are now the heresies that sprang up in the first ages of the Church? And in another hundred years, what will have become of the heresy which, under the pretentious name of “the reformation,” has caused incalculable evil? It is the same with the scandals which rise up within the pale of the Church: they are a hard trial; but trials must come. The divine Husbandman wills not that this cockle be torn up, lest the wheat should suffer injury. First of all, the mixture of good and bad is an advantage; it teaches the good not to put their hopes in man, but in God. Then, too, the mercy of our Lord is so great that at times the very cockle is converted, by divine grace, into wheat. We must therefore have patience. But whereas it is while the men are asleep that the enemy oversows the field with cockle, it behooves us to pray for pastors, and ask their divine Master to bless them with that vigilance which is the primary condition of the flock being safe, and is so essential a quality in every bishop, that his very name is “one who watches.”
.
OFFERTORY
.
Dextera Domini fecit virtutem, dextera Domini exaltavit me: non moriar, sed vivam, et narrabo opera Domini.
.
The right Hand of the Lord hath wrought strength, the right Hand of the Lord hath exalted me: I shall not die, but live, and shall declare the works of the Lord.
.
SECRET
.
Hostias tibi, Domine, placationis offerimus, ut et delicta nostra miseratus absolvas, et nutiantia corda tu dirigas. Per Dominum.
.
We offer Thee, O Lord, this sacrifice of propitiation, that Thou wouldst mercifully forgive us our sins, and guide our faltering hearts. Through, &c.
.
SECOND SECRET
.
Exaudi nos, Deus salutaris noster, ut per hujus Sacramenti virtutem, a cunctis nos mentis et corporis hostibus tuearis, gratiam tribuens in præsenti, et gloriam in futuro.
.
Graciously grant us, O God our Savior, that by virtue of this Sacrament, Thou mayst defend us from all enemies, both of soul and body; giving us grace in this life, and glory in the next.
.
A third Secret, at the choice is the priest, is added.
.
COMMUNION
.
Mirabantur omnes de his quæ procedebant de ore Dei.
.
All wondered at the words that came from the Mouth of God.
.
POSTCOMMUNION
.
Quæsumus, omnipotens Deus, ut illius salutaris capiamus effectum, cujus per hæc mysteria pignus accepimus. Per Dominum.
.
We beseech Thee, O almighty God, that we may one day receive the effects of that salvation, of which we have received the pledge in these mysteries. Through, &c.
.
SECOND POSTCOMMUNION
.
Mundet et muniat nos, quæsumus, Domine, divini Sacramenti munus oblatum: et intercedente beata Virgine Dei genitrice Maria, cum beato Joseph, beatis apostolis tuis Petro et Paulo, atque beato N. et omnibus sanctis, a cunctis nos reddat et perversitatibus expiatos, et adversitatibus expeditos.
.
May the oblation of this divine Sacrament, we beseech Thee, O Lord, both cleanse and defend us; and, by the intercession of blessed Mary, the Virgin-Mother of God, of blessed Joseph, of Thy blessed Apostles, Peter and Paul, of blessed N. and of all the saints, free us from all sin, and deliver us from all adversity.
.
The third Postcommunion is at the choice of the priest.

text:
The Landmark Julius Caesar: The Complete Works: Gallic War, Civil War, Alexandrian War, African War, and Spanish War - Review - 2 of 4

In November 54, in the Fifth Year of the war, Quintus Tullius Cicero (brother of Marcus Cicero, the famous orator and Consul) is Caesar’s legate in charge of a winter camp in the territory of the powerful Nervii tribe, who have been joined by the Eburones and Atuatuci to form a large force besieging the Romans. Caesar uses the example of their resistance to illustrate Roman ideals of courage and unfailing dedication to Rome. The Nervii, taking advantage of their military superiority, sent messengers to Cicero telling him to break up his camp and leave their territory. They said this was not because they were not well disposed to Cicero or the Romans, they “only refused to accept the establishment of winter quarters in their territory: they did not wish this to become a regular habit.” At 5.41, Caesar provides the classic response.

"Cicero had only one answer to these arguments: it was not the custom of the Roman people to accept terms from an enemy who bore arms."

By the seventh day of the siege, the Romans are in a desperate situation. Under heavy winds, the enemy launches incendiaries in the form of “slingshot made of red-hot clay along with flaming spears.” With the camp blazing, the enemy raise ladders to climb the ramparts. Caesar writes this glowing tribute to fearless heroism at 5.43.

"But the courage and determination of the defenders were supreme: even when they were seared by flames on all sides and pressured by an enormous number of missiles, and although they realized all their equipment – including their personal possessions – was ablaze, no one stepped down from the rampart to leave the fight, and hardly anyone even turned his head. Precisely because the danger was so serious, everyone fought most fiercely and bravely."

When messages reach Caesar, he gathers the small force of about 7,000 men he has available to march to rescue the besieged camp of Cicero. The enemy upon learning that the Romans are coming turn their full force of 60,000 to go and confront the new threat. As happens many times in the Gallic Wars, Caesar’s superior planning and tactics lure the larger number of attackers into unfavorable terrain where Roman organization and fighting skills enable them to achieve a “rout that was so complete that not a single soldier stood his ground to fight. Caesar’s men killed a great number of them and stripped them all of their weapons.” Upon reaching the formerly besieged camp, we are again impressed with the peril faced and the courage of the defenders at 5.52. After stating astonishment at the towers and fortifications the enemy had built, Caesar memorializes and rewards the valor of men in battle, including not only the commanders but the centurions and military tribunes. In many other instances, he offers praise for individual soldiers, so important he felt it was to recognize valiant performance in combat.

"When the legion was brought out for inspection, he found that not one man in ten was without a wound. All these circumstances allowed him to judge how great the peril had been there and what great courage had been displayed in defending the camp. He offered Cicero the praise he deserved for his achievement and did likewise to the legion."

Another feature that informs us that Caesar was not merely writing Commentaria as required by generals reporting to the Senate, he offers digressions into the cultures of the local people. From 6.13 through 6.16, in the Sixth Year of the war, he discusses the native religion.

"The druidic system of learning is thought to have been developed in Britain and then brought over to Gaul, and even at present those who wish to become more expert in it through close study usually travel to Britain for instruction.
The druids usually do not participate in war, and they do not pay taxes along with the other people.
As a whole, the Gallic peoples are quite involved in religious matters and superstition. For this reason, those who are suffering from more serious diseases and are frequently exposed to battle … offer human sacrifices…. They employ druids to carry out these sacrifices, based on the belief that the spirits of the immortal gods cannot be placated unless one human life is given for another."

In the Seventh Year of the war, in early 52, we are introduced to Vercingetorix who will unite the tribes and lead a huge rebellion to throw off the Roman rule that Caesar had established over so many of the peoples of Gaul in the previous six years. One of the greatest rebels of history enters at 7.54.

"Vercingetorix, the son of Celtillus … was a young and very powerful Avernian whose father had held the leadership of Gaul and had been put to death by his nation for seeking the kingship. His son now called his family’s clients together and easily aroused them. … His followers then proclaimed Vercingetorix king."

The massive army created by the new Gallic leader is very formidable not only in size, but in training and tactics. Vercingetorix emphasizes building a dominant cavalry component, and he convinces the other tribes to employ the most exceptional measures, including a scorched earth strategy to burn all the towns within reach of Caesar’s men, thus depriving them of sustenance to starve them out of rebel territory. Many hard-fought battles are brilliantly portrayed throughout Book 7, including heroic leadership by Caesar’s general Labienus who will play a large role at many key points in the Civil Wars when he switches his allegiance to Pompey. While being desperately tested and suffering grievous losses, the Romans carry the battle to their enemies with indomitable intensity. Caesar recruits fearsome German cavalry to expand his forces.
In September of 52, after six months of constant war, under Caesar’s leadership the Romans rout Vercingetorix’ cavalry. Since the cavalry is his primary fighting force, he has to retreat to the town of Alesia, setting up the most memorable siege of all of Caesar’s Gallic Wars. At 7.69 Caesar describes the scene of the town of Alesia and the amazing Roman siegeworks, all built by the fighting men themselves, since there were no separate engineering battalions in the legions.

"The town of Alesia stood high up on top of a hill in a rather lofty position, and it looked as if it could not be taken except by siege. … The circuit of the siege works the Romans were beginning to build was ten miles long. Camps were placed at suitable spots, and along the same line twenty-three forts were built."

These enormous fortification walls surrounding a besieged town are called a circumvallation, they are intended to trap the enemy and prevent them not only from escaping but also to prevent any resupply of food, weapons, livestock, or reinforcements. But the location of Alesia is surrounded by vast expanses of Gaul on all sides, and previously subdued tribes who had been aligned with Rome were now changing alliances. At 7.76, Caesar informs us that even Commius, who had fought with Caesar in Britain and been rewarded for his work by relief from taxes and had his legal and administrative independence restored, even allies like this are joining Vercingetorix’ rebellion.

"But there was in all of Gaul such a powerful and unanimous desire to restore liberty and recover their old-time martial glory that people were moved neither by favors they had received nor by the memory of friendship. Instead they threw themselves into this war with all their passion and resources. Eight thousand horsemen and around 250,000 infantry were assembled…."

Now Caesar’s forces manning those ten miles of walls and twenty-three forts that comprise the circumvallation around the town of Alesia are threatened by a new, enormous army attacking them outside these walls. Vercingetorix still has a strong military force within the town, so the Romans are faced with attack on two sides at once, both surrounded by and surrounding powerful enemy infantry and cavalry. This requires yet another, even greater military engineering enterprise, which is comprehensively illustrated in Diagram 7.76. This lavish graphic serves as the opening battle diagram, while presenting the terrain, rivers, position of the walls and movement of the attacking Gallic forces. This new defensive wall is called a contravallation, designed to protect the besieging forces from attack from outside.
This outside perimeter was fourteen miles long, but it was not just a simple wall, it was layered in many devious and deadly obstructions. These included five-foot-deep ditches filled with hidden, sharpened stakes. “The soldiers called these ‘grave markers’.” In front of these, eight rows of three-foot-deep pits were filled with upright stakes hidden in twigs and branches. These deadly constructions served the role that modern day minefields serve in today’s wars, not only destroying the unwary attackers who stumble upon them but funneling following attackers into killing fields. The Romans are armed not only with spears, bows, and swords, but they are further equipped with the equivalent of artillery in the form of slings and stone-throwers to launch murderous lead bullets, sharpened stakes, and one-pounder stones.
Section 7.80 through 7.88 provides vivid battle writing describing the courageous Gauls attacking the resolute, indefatigable Roman legions. Many cavalry and infantry engagements ensue until Roman engineering excellence, fighting tactics and superior planning and leadership deliver the victory. In the end, Vercingetorix surrenders and his troops throw down their arms. History, but not Caesar of course in this annual Commentari, tells us the great rebel king is taken to Rome in chains, where he will be kept a prisoner for six years until he is displayed in one of Caesar’s four consecutive triumphs, and then in Roman tradition, executed.
Caesar ends Book 7 with the notice that he “put aside the captives from among the Aedui and Arverni, hoping to use them to restore close ties with these nations; but the rest of the captives he distributed to his army as plunder, one for each soldier.” After explaining the arrangements for his troops’ winter quarters in Gaul, he closes out December, 52, the Seventh Year of the war at 7.90.

"A public thanksgiving of twenty days was decreed at Rome after the facts of that year’s campaign were made known there."

The Eighth Book of the Gallic Wars was written by Caesar’s general Hirtius, who starts out his book with a few paragraphs of complaining about how unworthy and unwilling he was to take on this work. Then he explains his reticence.

"Of course, you and I are even more impressed with Caesar’s achievement than the other readers are, for they can admire how well, how perfectly he wrote, but we also know how easily and quickly he finished these works. Indeed, Caesar commanded not only the greatest facility and the most tasteful style in writing but an absolutely unerring skill in explaining his plans and decisions."

In Book 8, Hirtius dutifully reports the final operations, but early on at 8.1, he lets us know where the Gallic Wars stand upon Caesar finishing Book 7: “All of Gaul had now been conquered.”

text:
November 9, 1799. Napoleon tried to seize power by giving a speech, and he was so bad at it that the deputies mobbed him, knocked him about and left him bleeding.

The coup was saved by his younger brother lying to the soldiers outside.

The version everybody carries around, of Bonaparte striding into the chamber and taking France by force of personality, is close to the opposite of what happened.

Start with why the Directory was ready to fall.

France had been at war since 1792. The tax system was widely seen as unfair, harvests were bad, prices were rising, and the Constitution of 1795 had produced a government that could not govern. The Directory had five directors, two legislative councils, no mechanism for resolving deadlock, and a habit of annulling election results it did not like.

Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès joined the Directory in May 1799 having already concluded that the only way to fix the constitution was to overthrow it.

Sieyès is the real author of 18 Brumaire. He wanted a general, a sword, somebody with enough prestige to make soldiers obey and enough limited ambition to be managed afterwards.

His first choice was General Joubert, who he thought he could control. Joubert was killed at Novi in August 1799. Moreau suggested Bonaparte instead.

Napoleon had come back from Egypt, having left his army there without orders, which should have ruined him and did not, because the news from Egypt reaching France was his own version and the news from Europe was all bad. He arrived in Paris on October 16 and the Directory received him coldly.

He tried to get into the government legitimately first. He could not become a director because the minimum age was 40 and he was 30. He sounded out Barras, who saw him as a rival and offered him a command somewhere else. Napoleon declined on grounds of health, asked Barras directly about a coup, got refused, and went to Sieyès.

The inner circle was Napoleon, Sieyès, Talleyrand, Fouché and Ducos. Fouché was the Minister of Police, which meant the police were not going to interfere. Talleyrand handled the persuasion of people who needed persuading.

The plan was postponed from Friday the 7th to Saturday the 9th, partly because Napoleon was superstitious about Fridays.

The 9th itself went well, because it was a legal manoeuvre rather than a confrontation.

The Council of Ancients, where Sieyès had his supporters, was summoned early to the Tuileries. Opponents were simply not told. On the claim that a Jacobin coup was imminent, which was invented, the Council passed a decree moving both legislative bodies out to the Château de Saint-Cloud, and put Napoleon in charge of carrying it out and protecting the assemblies.

That gave him command of all troops in the Paris region, legally, by vote.

Then they dismantled the Directory. Sieyès and Ducos resigned as planned. Barras was pressured by Talleyrand into resigning. The remaining two directors, Gohier and Moulin, refused and were put under house arrest. Gohier had been kept out of the way that morning by a breakfast invitation, and he had sent his wife instead.

So by the evening of the 9th there was no executive government in France, and Napoleon commanded the troops.

The 10th is where it nearly came apart.

Saint-Cloud had been standing empty since 1790 and was not ready, so there were hours of delay while the deputies milled around together, which was exactly what Sieyès had wanted to avoid, because it let them talk to each other and work out what was happening.

The excluded deputies turned up furious.

Napoleon had about 6,000 soldiers around the palace, which was intimidation rather than a plan.

He went into the Council of Ancients first and interrupted the session, and he was terrible. He gave a rambling, incoherent speech, could produce no evidence of the Jacobin plot everybody was now asking about, got shouted down as a tyrant and a dictator, and finished by saying his soldiers would obey him rather than the deputies, which was the quiet part.

His secretary Bourrienne physically pulled him out.

At four in the afternoon he went into the Council of Five Hundred, in uniform, with grenadiers.

That chamber was far more hostile and it went much worse. Deputies shouted at him to get out, there were cries for him to be outlawed, which in 1799 France meant death, and men climbed over the benches to get at him. He was jostled, grabbed and struck, and Murat and Lefebvre had to drag him out dazed and bleeding.

So the most famous soldier in Europe, at the moment of seizing the French state, was physically manhandled by a room full of middle-aged lawyers and had to be rescued by his own officers.

The parliamentary route was finished. What saved it was Lucien Bonaparte.

Lucien was 24 and happened to be the elected president of the Council of Five Hundred, which is the single most important fact about the coup. He went outside to the troops and told them that deputies armed with daggers had attempted to assassinate his brother, and pointed at Napoleon's bleeding face as evidence.

There are accounts of Lucien taking a sword and swearing he would run Napoleon through himself if he ever betrayed liberty, which is theatre and may be embroidery.

The grenadiers hesitated, then went in and cleared the chamber. Deputies went out of the windows into the gardens.

By two in the morning, Lucien had collected enough remaining members of the Five Hundred and about 50 of the Ancients to pass something that looked like a vote. The Directory was dissolved. Three provisional consuls were named: Napoleon, Sieyès and Ducos. Two commissions got six weeks to write a constitution.

Then Napoleon went to work on his own co-conspirators.

He criticised Sieyès's draft constitution publicly until Sieyès resigned, and then kept most of Sieyès's structure anyway. The result was four bodies, a Legislative Corps, a Senate, a Tribunate and a Council of State, each able to block the others, with ministers answerable only to the First Consul.

Sieyès had spent the whole thing looking for a sword he could control, and the sword took the government off him inside a month.

The constitution was adopted on December 12 and put to a referendum, and the referendum numbers are worth reading carefully. The official result was 3,011,007 in favour and 1,562 against.

That result is not real. It included army ballots cast without valid paperwork, public votes taken by show of hands, and roughly 900,000 forged votes credited to Lucien. Turnout was around 25 percent, so on one analysis Napoleon's actual support was something like 17 percent of the electorate.

Most historians treat 18 Brumaire as the end of the French Revolution. Ten years from the storming of the Bastille to a general with the army behind him, legislating by decree.

Five years later he crowned himself Emperor.

text:
What if water from the sanctuary could turn a salt sea into a place of life?

A stream trickles from the temple threshold, flows east, and freshens the waters it enters.

Living creatures multiply, fish abound, and trees bear monthly fruit with leaves for medicine.

Discover the life-giving waters in Ezekiel 47:1-2, 8-9, 12.

Wherever the River Goes, Life Follows

The Promise of Fresh Water in Ezekiel 47

A thin stream leaves the house of God and becomes a river that will not leave death in place. Ezekiel 47 offers one of the most hopeful pictures in the prophets. Water starts at the temple threshold. It runs east. It enters bitter, stagnant water. Then life multiplies. The New Revised Standard Version Catholic Edition states the heart of the vision in a clear line: "Wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live." That sentence is not a note about wildlife. It is a claim about grace. Where the life of God flows, a barren place does not keep the last word.

Why Does the Water Begin at the Temple Door?

The scene opens at the entrance of the temple. Ezekiel sees water flowing from below the threshold toward the east, for the temple faced east. The water flows down from below the south end of the threshold, south of the altar. The guide then leads him out by the north gate and around to the outer gate that faces east. The water comes out on the south side. The details of the path matter because the source matters. Life does not begin in the market or in the palace. Life proceeds from the dwelling of God, close to the place of sacrifice. Catholics can recognize a quiet echo of the altar, the tabernacle, and the sacraments. Grace has a real meeting place. It comes through concrete signs, not only through a private mood. A threshold is a humble spot. People cross it and barely look down. Ezekiel is asked to notice water that a hurried eye might call a leak. God often begins renewal as a thin stream before anyone names it a river. A soul that waits only for a flood may miss the first mercy already moving under the door. The vision teaches a patient kind of attention. Stay near the holy place. Watch the small flow. Trust that God knows how to deepen what he has begun.

What Changes When the River Enters Dead Water?

The guide explains the course of the stream. "This water flows toward the eastern region and goes down into the Arabah." When it enters the sea, "the sea of stagnant waters," the water will become fresh. The Arabah is the deep rift that runs toward the Dead Sea, a body long linked with salt, stillness, and the absence of ordinary fish. The river does not travel around that sea. The river enters it. Stagnant water is not ignored. It is healed. Then the promise arrives in full: "Wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live, and there will be very many fish, once these waters reach there. It will become fresh; and everything will live where the river goes." Swarming life is a sign of abundance. The hope is not the bare survival of a few hardy fish. The hope is multiplication. Life becomes crowded where death had seemed settled. This is why the line still steadies Catholic faith. Sin, grief, and fatigue can feel like a sea that does not move. The prophet does not deny the salt. He denies that salt has the final say. The river does not ask the sea to climb uphill to the temple. The river goes down into the low place. Grace seeks the Arabah in a person, in a parish, and in a family that feels stuck. Freshness is the work of God in the water. It is not a prize for water that was already sweet. The verse also corrects a fearful habit. Dryness is not proof that God has walked away. Ezekiel shows a God who sends water from the holy place into the hardest water in the land.

How Do Fruit and Leaves Serve a Hungry World?

The last verse in the reading widens the gift. On both banks, "there will grow all kinds of trees for food." The text continues, "Their leaves will not wither nor their fruit fail, but they will bear fresh fruit every month, because the water for them flows from the sanctuary. Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing." The river does more than revive creatures in the water. It builds a landscape that can feed and mend. Fruit every month means the supply does not collapse when the season turns. The reason is plain. The water flows from the sanctuary. Cut the trees off from that source, and the vision no longer holds. Remain near that source, and failure is not the normal end. Catholic prayer has long set this river beside the water that flows from the side of Christ, and beside the river in the closing vision of Revelation. The temple in Ezekiel points beyond itself. Jesus speaks of living water. The Church meets that water in baptism, in the Eucharist, and in mercy that leaves the altar and enters the street. Food and healing belong together. Fruit that only pleases the tongue, with no leaf for a neighbor's wound, has not yet matched the banks of this river. The trees stand on both sides. Grace is meant to cross the stream and to be shared, not hoarded on one bank. A parish that keeps the sanctuary and also tends the wounded is already living inside this picture.

Where Should This Hope Shape Catholic Life?

The significance of the promise is practical as well as beautiful. Life does not appear only at the source while the distance stays dry. Life appears along the whole course. That claim should shape prayer. Begin again at the threshold. Return to Mass, to Scripture, to confession, and to quiet prayer before the Lord. Then expect the water to move outward. A gentle word in a bitter room can be the river as it enters stagnant water. Service to the poor is not side work beside real worship. It is sanctuary water on the way to the Arabah. The proper response to dryness is not panic. The proper response is a return to the source, and a willingness to let the stream find the low ground. Every living creature that swarms will live. The phrase holds abundance, variety, and motion. God is not preserving a museum. God is restoring a living world. Leaves that heal and fruit that feeds are public signs of a hidden source. When Catholic life feels stalled, this reading offers a clear test. Ask where the water comes from, and ask where it is allowed to go. Neglect the sanctuary, and the banks will wither. Keep the river inside, and never send it toward the salt sea, and the promise stays unread. The hope of the prophet is larger than private comfort. Everything will live where the river goes. That is the word worth carrying from Ezekiel 47 into prayer, into the parish, and into every place that still tastes of salt.

🙏 @RCatholicPrayer

"Wherever the river flows, every sort of living creature that can multiply shall live"

Ezekiel 47:1-2, 8-9, 12

Righteous Zeal and Sacred Worship
Jesus answered and said to them, “Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up.” The Jews said, “This temple has been under construction for forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?” But he was speaking about the temple of his Body. John 2:19–21
The Lateran Basilica, officially known as the Archbasilica of the Most Holy Savior and of Saints John the Baptist and John the Evangelist, is the cathedral church of the Diocese of Rome and holds the unique distinction of being the mother and head of all churches throughout the world. It is the oldest of the four major papal basilicas in Rome and was the first Christian basilica built in the city after Emperor Constantine’s Edict of Milan in AD 313 legalized Christianity.
The basilica was dedicated in 324 by Pope Sylvester I to Christ the Savior. Later, it was also dedicated to Saints John the Baptist and John the Evangelist. As the pope’s official cathedral, the Lateran Basilica is the spiritual heart of the universal Church. Its annual dedication feast reminds us of the sacredness of every church building, each one a visible sign of the invisible Church and a privileged place of encounter with the living God.
Today’s Gospel offers a striking portrayal of Jesus, the Son of God, cleansing the temple in Jerusalem with righteous anger. His actions were not impulsive, but deliberate. He made a whip of cords and drove out those who had turned His Father’s house into a marketplace. This dramatic scene challenges us to reflect more deeply on the holiness of places set apart for divine worship and invites us into the mystery of the Church as the Body of Christ.
