text:
First, Jesus’ actions reveal the sacred character of our churches. By honoring the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica, we honor every church consecrated for the worship of God. Our churches are not to be marketplaces, theaters, or social halls. At their center is the altar and the tabernacle—places where the divine Presence dwells among us. In these sacred spaces, we listen to the Word of God, offer our lives to Christ, and are spiritually renewed to bring His presence into the world.
Jesus’ cleansing of the Jerusalem Temple also reminds us that our souls are now the true temples of God—the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit and tabernacles of the Most High. Just as our Lord was filled with zeal to cleanse the Temple, so too is He continually moved to purify our souls, calling each of us to repentance and conversion. When considering our own need for cleansing and purification, it’s helpful to ponder Jesus’ zeal in the Temple, seeing Him desiring to cleanse us with the same zeal.
Though this divine purification is personal, it is also ecclesial and communal. The Church, as the Mystical Body of Christ, must always be renewed and transformed. Throughout history, the Church as an institution has strayed from the path of holiness through the sins of her members. When this has happened, God has raised up saints to serve as prophetic voices, calling the members of the Church on earth to holiness, cleansing, and fidelity.
The Church’s cleansing, as well as our own, is not always met with open arms. When the religious leaders confronted Jesus as He cleansed the Jerusalem Temple, He spoke a mysterious prophecy: “Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up.” Though misunderstood at the time, He was speaking of His own Body—the true and eternal Temple. Today, He continues to speak those words about His Body, the Church, and about each of us, who are members of that Body through grace. We must die in and with Him so that we will rise renewed as saints and as the holy and spotless Bride of Christ.
Reflect today on the sacredness of your own soul. Ask our Lord to cleanse whatever needs purifying and to raise you up in holiness, so that you may become a more perfect temple of His presence in the world. Pray also for your parish church and the Church universal. With zeal, pray for the purification necessary to make every member of the Church true temples of God.
Most zealous Lord, Your righteous anger is not directed at me or at any member of Your Church, but at the sin and defilement that hinder us from offering You pure and holy worship. Please cleanse me and every member of Your Mystical Body, that we may radiate Your divine presence more fully in this world and draw all people to Yourself. Jesus, I trust in You.

Year 4            

Chapter 20

---
The meeting room near Dumbledore’s office was wide and bright, with tall windows that caught the morning light. It was clearly meant for photography. The other champions were already there. Krum stood with Karkaroff, who gave Lyra and Harry a short, cool nod. Cedric stood beside Dumbledore and offered Harry an encouraging smile; Dumbledore’s eyes twinkled. Madame Maxime’s expression was distinctly unimpressed. Fleur watched Harry with open intensity. He felt the faint, slippery tug of her presence and tightened his grip on Lyra’s hand until it faded. Ludo Bagman sat near a witch in magenta robes, beaming as if the entire morning had been arranged for his benefit.

Bagman rose the moment he saw them. “Harry! There you are! Wonderful, wonderful—come in, come in!”

The witch in magenta moved with him, photographer already in tow. She extended a hand and a bright, professional smile.

“Rita Skeeter, Daily Prophet. I was hoping for a few words with you, Harry—just to add a bit of color to the article.”

Lyra’s smile was warm, elegant, and immediate. “Why aren’t you interviewing the other champions, Miss Skeeter?”

Rita’s smile widened, affable. “Well, Harry is the most unexpected! And he’s already famous—”

“Then an interview may be on the table,” Lyra said, still pleasant. “At a time of his choosing.”

“Why not now?”

“Potter is much too busy today. You’ll need to make an appointment. I’m sure my father can arrange it.”

“But you’re clearly so close to Harry. Can’t I just ask you directly?”

Lyra’s smile remained genteel. “So sorry, Rita, but as you know, I’m an heiress. My school workload is just as heavy as Potter’s, if not more so. And we have a lot to do.”

“Surely just a few minutes is all I would need! After all, you don’t want your relationship with Potter being presented to the world in a bad way, do you? By some hack journalist only after sensation?”

“Whatever kind of relationship are you talking about, Rita?” Lyra’s smile sharpened at the edges. “And whatever have you been hearing?”

Rita actually took a small step back. “Ah, well… you know, I do hear things from time to time. Just doing my job.”

“Really? Well, remember the Goblin Rule of Acquisition 190: Hear all, trust nothing.”

“Yes, of course, but… wouldn’t you prefer to control the narrative on how this comes out? There are rumors flying about already. Don’t you want to set the record straight?”

Lyra hummed, considering, then glanced at Harry. “I suppose that is a good point.” She turned the charming smile back on Rita. “And thankfully we have a trustworthy reporter here. What do you say, Potter? It’s your choice how you want to proceed.”

The speed of the exchange had left Harry slightly behind. He knew Rita Skeeter’s name. She had written several unpleasant pieces about Arthur Weasley. Lyra, however, looked entirely at ease. She squeezed his hand once, a small, questioning pressure.

He nodded, slow. “I suppose we could do that.”

“Wonderful!” Rita brightened. “Perhaps in private—”

“I will be with Potter in every interview,” Lyra said, all smiles. “I am assisting him in the Triwizard, after all.”

“Perfectly acceptable, yes!”

Bagman clapped his hands together, delighted by the entire exchange. Cedric caught Harry’s eye across the room and gave a small, sympathetic shrug. Fleur’s gaze lingered a moment longer before she turned back toward Madame Maxime. Harry kept Lyra’s hand in his and decided, firmly, that he was glad she had come.

The photoshoot went fairly well. Each champion was photographed with their headmaster beneath a banner of their school and house, then together as a group. Rita kept trying to position Harry at the front. Lyra countered, calmly, that every champion should have a turn in the center. Dumbledore agreed. Rita allowed it with visible reluctance.

Harry watched Lyra work and felt a quiet, unexpected admiration. She had been nasty and unpleasant to him and others for years, but when she chose to be, she could be sweet, charming, and entirely in command of a room. Part of him liked it. He was not entirely sure why.

At last Bagman laughed and shook each champion’s hand in turn.

“Good show, good show! This will be a Triwizard—or Quadwizard—to remember! Won’t it, Headmaster?”

“Quite.” Dumbledore was still smiling, but the expression looked a little brittle at the edges.

Rita moved forward, quill already in hand. “So… since I’m here, would there be time for an interview with Harry, Lyra?”

Lyra’s smile was bright. “But of course. Let’s just walk over here and arrange the details. I won’t be a moment, Harry.”

She led Rita a short distance away, out of easy earshot. Harry turned to Dumbledore. The headmaster moved with him toward the far corner of the room. Only then did Harry speak, voice low.

“Headmaster? Have you found anything yet?”

Dumbledore glanced toward Rita. The ordinary noise of the room seemed to dampen around them.

“Not as yet, Harry. I do apologize for that. We’ve only had a day to work on it.”

“O-oh. I guess that makes sense. Sorry.”

“Not at all.” Dumbledore’s smile was gentle. “We want answers just as badly as you do. We’re trying to find them. For the moment, I suggest you stay focused. Your friends will help you, and so will the professors. You just need to ask.”

“Thank you, Professor.”

“Don’t mention it. I do wish I could have given you a quiet year, Harry.”

“Yeah, well…” Harry shrugged. “I’m starting to think that’s not an option for me.”

Dumbledore’s smile turned wry and a little sad. “Perhaps. But it hasn’t been all bad, has it?”

Harry glanced across the room. Lyra was still speaking with Rita, posture easy, one hand lightly gesturing. He flushed and smiled, small.

“No.”

“That’s the best way to see things.”

The ambient sound of the room returned just as Lyra and Rita walked back to them.

“Potter,” Lyra said, “Rita wants to do an interview with you. I will be with you at all times… and she’ll be using a quill I choose.”

“Why, Lyra!” Rita’s smile was bright and slightly strained. “Don’t you trust me?”

“I trust you a bit more than I would trust any other reporter, Rita.” Lyra’s smile never wavered. Rita winced, just a fraction. “But it is still your choice, Potter.”

Harry glanced at Dumbledore. The headmaster’s eyes twinkled and offered nothing more. Harry looked back at Lyra and Rita, then nodded slowly.

“All right. Let’s do this.”

Rita headed out, her photographer lingering a moment longer before following. Harry and Lyra went after her. Rita spotted a broom closet along the corridor and brightened.

“Aha! How about in here—?”

Lyra’s smirk was tiny and precise. “Rita, I am sure you’re very familiar with the broom closets at Hogwarts, but we would prefer something more open.”

Harry stared. Rita looked briefly shocked, then recovered.

“Yes, well—”

“Empty classroom, over there.” Lyra’s tone left no room for argument.

They went. The classroom was full of unused desks and chairs. Harry pulled two over for himself and Lyra. Rita took her own and sat facing them. Lyra handed her a quill. Rita set to writing at once.

“So, Harry. How did you get your name into the Goblet?”

“I didn’t. Someone else did.”

“Do you know who?”

He shrugged. “Well, a former supporter of Voldemort’s—” He caught their winces and coughed. “I mean, You-Know-Who is my best guess.”

“Now, Harry, he’s been gone a long time—”

“And his supporters are still around.” A note of irritation slipped through. Lyra squeezed his hand. He settled.

Rita noticed.

“And what about You-Know-Who? What are your feelings towards him?”

Harry blinked. The question was bizarre and infuriating. He kept his temper and answered with sarcasm.

“I mean… he’s trying to kill me. He killed my family. How should I feel about that?”

Lyra squeezed his hand again. He drew a breath.

“Let’s stick to the present time, Rita, shall we?” Lyra said.

Rita’s eyes lit. “Of course! Tell me: is Lyra Malfoy your girlfriend now?”

“Ah, well… y-yes. Yes, she is.”

“Weren’t you rivals before?”

“We were…”

Lyra’s smirk was small. “Still are. Once we get back to Quidditch, I’m going to defeat you.”

Harry’s eyes narrowed before he caught the tiny wink. For a moment Rita did not seem to register it.

“Oh, I don’t think so. You never have before.”

“Things do change, Potter.” She smirked. “Maybe you’ll slip up.”

“That’s the only way you might win. Might.”

She flushed and huffed, nose in the air. “Or maybe I’ll just get better than you.”

“Not a chance.”

“You’re so sure?”

“Yes, I am…”

They had leaned closer without quite meaning to. Rita’s quill moved furiously. Lyra laughed, soft.

“Well, let’s get you through the Triwizard first, shall we? One step at a time.”

“I…” He nodded, feeling slightly stupid. “Yeah, I guess so…”

“Oh, you two have such marvelous chemistry!” Rita beamed. “Tell me, how did your father react when he found out?”

Lyra’s smile was wide and perfect. “He couldn’t have been happier for us.”

She handled most of the rest of the interview after that, Harry chiming in only when needed. When the bells rang, they both stood.

“You’ll have to excuse us, Rita. Class calls.”

“Of course, of course! Wonderful interview! Thank you so much! And best of luck, Harry, Lyra!”

She left in a rush of magenta. Lyra waved her wand and sealed the door. She sighed, sat, and rubbed her temple.

“That woman is exhausting.”

Harry sat beside her and nodded. “Yeah… still… are you sure about giving her… all those details?”

“Better we give her something like this than let her make up whatever she wants. She’s done that to my father a few times—made up stories and innuendos just close enough to the truth to not be grounds for libel. She’s all about sensation and drama.”

“Still…”

“It is better to make sure she prints only what we want than to let her run roughshod over your reputation. Especially in this situation.” She huffed. “I’m just trying to help.”

He took her hand and met her eyes. “You are. You are. I’m just… I’ve never thought about publicity before. And, well… I’m glad you’re around to help me.”

She smiled. “You’d better be…”

He shrugged, slow. “And, well… I’m not exactly used to you being so… nice.”

Her smile softened. Something more vulnerable showed through. “…That’s what family does, Harry. If… if you’re courting me, one day we’ll be family. And… is there anything you wouldn’t do for… for family?”

For a moment his thoughts went to the Dursleys. Nothing good lived there. Then they moved on—to the Weasleys, Hermione, Sirius, Remus, Hagrid. And Lyra. His own smile softened.

“No. No, there isn’t.”

A moment passed. Lyra sighed.

“We are both very late for class.”

Harry chuckled.

“Yeah, we are. But I’m sure they’ll understand.”

The great holy martyr Theodore the Recruit was a soldier in the city of Amaseia in Pontus (modern day Turkey) on the coast of the Black Sea, under the command of the Praepositus (regimental commander) Brincus. Theodore was ordered to offer sacrifices to idols, but he proclaimed his faith in Christ the Savior in a loud voice. Brincus gave him a few days to think it over, during which time Theodore prayed.

They charged him with setting a pagan temple on fire, and threw him into prison to be starved to death. The Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him there, comforting and encouraging him. Brought to the governor, Theodore boldly and fearlessly confessed his faith, for which he was subjected to new torments and condemned to burning. Theodore climbed onto the fire without hesitation and with prayer, and gave up his holy soul to God. He died in 306 AD.

Unharmed by the fire, his body was buried in the city of Euchaita. His relics were afterwards transferred to Constantinople, to a church dedicated to him. His head is in Italy in the city of Gaeto.

Fifty years after Theodore’s death, the emperor Julian the Apostate, who had tried every means to restore pagan customs within the Roman empire, noticed that Christians were accustomed to sanctify the first week of Lent before Pascha by fasting and prayer. The cruel despot ordered the prefect of Constantinople to sprinkle all the food in the market with the blood of victims sacrificed to idols, so that it was impossible for any of the city's residents to escape the taint of idolatry.

But the Lord did not abandon his faithful people. He sent his servant Theodore, who appeared in a vision to Archbishop Eudoxius to foil the machinations of the tyrant. He ordered that no Christian was to buy the food then presented in the markets, but rather to eat cooked wheat with honey instead, that they already had at their homes. Thus, through the intervention of the Holy Martyr Theodore, the Christians kept pure from the defilement of idolatry.

From grok:

SpaceX’s Crew-9 launched on September 28, 2024 (still under the Biden administration), with only two crew members (Nick Hague and Aleksandr Gorbunov) and two empty seats reserved for Wilmore and Williams. That same Crew Dragon Freedom later brought them home. They undocked from the ISS and splashed down off Florida on March 18, 2025—after Biden left office on January 20, 2025, and during the Trump administration. Their total stay was about 286 days.

Musk has claimed he offered the Biden administration an earlier dedicated Dragon rescue that Biden refused for political reasons. There is no documented evidence that Biden asked Musk or SpaceX for a special rescue. SpaceX then worked with NASA and formulated a technical decision in August 2024 to use the already-scheduled SpaceX Crew-9 vehicle rather than risk Starliner or fly a dedicated extra mission.

SpaceX brought them home after Biden left office, under a plan Musk and NASA had set in motion in 2024. Although claims of deliberate political abandonment lack official supporting evidence from NASA, Musk has personally stated that he really did not want SpaceX help even though the astronauts were stranded.

text:
Content warning: readers should know this post is about the 1913 murder of 13-year-old Mary Phagan.

On Sunday, November 9, 1913, 113 years ago, The Atlanta Constitution ran a feature by Britt Craig on Page 9, Column 1: "A Dead Hero Is The Poorest Sort Of A Husband; Boots Rogers, Hero Extraordinary, Learns Lesson."

Mary Anne Phagan, 13, was murdered at the National Pencil Company in Atlanta on Saturday, April 26, 1913. A Fulton County jury convicted Leo Max Frank, the factory superintendent, on Monday, August 25, 1913. Judge Leonard Strickland Roan of the Fulton County Superior Court denied him a new trial on Friday, October 31, 1913, and the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the conviction on Tuesday, February 17, 1914.

W. W. "Boots" Rogers was a Fulton County motorcycle policeman. Early on Sunday, April 27, 1913, he drove the detectives to Frank's home and then took Frank to the undertaker's to see Mary's body and on to the factory. He testified for the State. The paper's photo caption shows him "with detectives with whom he worked on the Phagan murder mystery." The story says he resigned from the force to marry Miss Louise Petty.

The defense version, 1913 and modern: Frank's nervousness that morning was normal for any man woken by police.

The prosecution's answer at the time: Rogers and the detectives described Frank as nervous and trembling that morning, before anyone had accused him.

Our modern rebuttal: Rogers had no stake in the case. He was a policeman who drove the car, saw what he saw, and swore to it.

Forever 13 and Never forgotten.

#MaryPhagan #LeoFrank

Appendix: Full article transcript

The Atlanta Constitution,
Sunday, November 9, 1913,
PAGE 9, COLUMN 1.

A Dead Hero Is The Poorest Sort Of A Husband; Boots Rogers, Hero Extraordinary, Learns Lesson

Photos by Francis E. Price.

Upper picture: Boots Rogers, at extreme right, standing beside automobile with detectives with whom he worked on the Phagan murder mystery.

Lower illustrations: Rogers at time of the Frank trial, his daughter, Louise, and his wife, who formerly was Miss Louise Petty.

By Britt Craig.

The little clock ticked impatiently between the statue of the market girl and the boy with the fishing rod on the mantelpiece. The folding doors were closed, and the shades came plumb down to the sill.

W. W. (Boots) Rogers got down on one knee in appropriate attitude of humbleness on the flower-bordered carpet of a north-side parlor not so awfully long ago and said to the maiden, who blushed and fidgeted on the sofa:

Howd you like to get married?

It wasnt so eloquent as the proposal in the third act of Lovers. You and I, but it amply conveyed its fullest meaning. It was with some difficulty that the blushing maiden stammered this reply:

Sure, Boots, just as soon as you quit being a policeman.

She could have told the humble swain at her feet that she must deign his proposal because of an earlier offer which she had accepted from the Earl of Denmark, and Boots would have been no more surprised. He jumped to his feet, flicked the dust from his knees.

Then this:

But why quit the police force?

Oh, just because.

But thats purely a womans reason and its ridiculous.

The maidens nose tilted skyward and she pouted, which isnt unnatural in maidens even in those who are receiving proposals of marriage. Considering the fact that but a moment previously a very worthy young man had entreated her to become his bride, she was legally, probably, unquestionably entitled to pout, or most anything else.

WOMANS REASON IS GOOD ENOUGH.

Well, I guess if a woman decides mans wife, she has a perfect right to give any kind of reason she wants, womans reason or not. And besides, I guess a womans reason is as good as anybodys, I do.

Very well.

Resignedly. Have it your way. But dont think for a minute that when I turn in my resignation purely on the grounds of Because, that the chief will accept it without investigation. We have some kind of system even in the county police department, you know.

But the chief doesnt have to know anything about it. You just quit and be done with it.

Great! You ought to be in politics. You could just do things and be done with them.

All right, thenhave if your own way. Remember, young man, I dont have to marry until I get good and ready.

Now, listen, Louise, you dont understand. Being a policemans honorable I know that And upright I know that, also.

It pays well And I know that.

Theres nothing disgraceful about it.

But, its not that; its none of those. Youre just a great big fool when youre in uniform, and youd do most anything on earth and try to get away with it. I dont want them to bring in my husband a corpse the first week were married.

Hes got to be aliveabsolutely aliveand I positively refuse to have any other kind.

LIVE COWARDS V. DEAD HEROES.

See, Boots; Id rather have a live coward than a dead hero. Live cowards can make some kind of a husband, at least an excuse for one, but dead heroes dont make anything but widowsandorphans.

Oh! Now, youre snowing right. (This with elation.) Im beginning to catch your drift.

I knew you would. You see. I didnt want to tell you until you made me. I was afraid youd get the swellhead. Its so easy.

But Im no heroI dont get in danger. Im just a plain, ordinary policemana county policeman, at that. You women ought to stop readin novels.

But, Boots, what about that time the negro shot at you at the oil mill?

Oh, I forgot that.

And the time you drove that automobile at that crowd of burglars?

That, too. My memorys bad here lately.

Also the time you jumped off your motorcycle into that crazy automobile?

You dont expect me to remember everything?

And that time your automobile ran off the bridge?

Oh, I remember that occasionally.

Now, listen!

I wouldnt mind you being a policeman, dear, if a policeman didnt have to police like they do. To tell the truth, I think you look good in uniformespecially the one you wore last summer. But, as I said just now, my husbands got to be perfectly alive with good prospects of staying so for a good, long time.

I get you!

Then, are you going to quit?

Are you going to marry me?

Curtain.

A WOMANS BECAUSE, THATS ALL Twenty-four hours later, Chief Zack Rowan, in his office at county police headquarters, receives a resignation from one of his motorcycle staff, for which he cannot account. There are no grounds to it, no reasons, nothing.

Except Because.

Thats all.

Next Sunday the society columns announce the engagement of Miss Louise Petty to Mr. W. W. Rogers.

Which brings on more talk.

During his several years service as motorcycle patrolman with the county police department. Rogers gained the wide distinction of the nerviest and most daring man on Chief Rowans staff. Many have been the times the chief has gone out of his way to bestow praise upon the dauntless youth who grazed death so frequently that he was on speaking terms with it.

The career of Boots has been entertainingly varied. He served as a sharpshooter in the Philippines, as sailor on a man-o-warsman and as a private detective. Finally, as county policeman. The God of Fate, who seems to be partial, more or less, to the courageous has been good to him. He is still this side of thirty without a gray hair in his dome.

It was during the famous Buckeye oil mill barricade that Rogers won his first laurels of heroism.

A negro desperado, wild and drug-crazed, who had slain four of his race in the Backeye plant, had sought refuge in the loft of a vacant dwelling out near Pittsburgh, the scene of the famous riots of several years ago.

With pockets overloaded with ammunition, a repeating Winchester and revolver at his service, he pumped lead on defiance in the faces of the two mounted policemen who just reached the spot. An emergency call for reserves was sent to headquarters of both county and city police departments.

Rogers and three other motorcycle men were sent from the county force. Arriving at the negros stronghold, they were met by an auto filled with reserves sent from police headquarters on Decatur street. In the machine was Detective George Bullard, who since has been promoted to sergeancy.

EVERY BULLET SANG A FUNERAL NOTE.

George evinced no hesitation in attempting to rush the negros fort alone. He barely realized his mistake in time. As his foot reached the front doorsteps of the barricaded dwelling house, a bullet sang through his hat, while others played a funeral roll about his feet.

The detective jumped for shelter with an exclamation that had something to do with the futility of such generous warning, when one shotprobably the one that went through his hatwould have been a Lords sufficiency. George prudently turned his footsteps toward a considerate oak tree and the job over to whichever applicant who might be braveor foo lishenough to tackle the black brute and his bullets.

Its up to some unmarried guy, he said. My endowment policy wont permit it.

Rogers was standing behind the automobile that had brought the men from the city headquarters, blazing away at the shattered plane from which protruded the outlaws gun, verbally and pistolly trying to consign the hapless negro to every kind of eternity from fire and brimstone to a hereafter of nakedness in the frozen arctic.

After the unfortunate gentleman behind the barricade had been doomed to Hell, Hull, Halifax and all intermediate points, Boots emerged from behind the machine, his ammunition and profanity at low ebb.

Ill get you, you blasted blister on a snakes skin. Getcha head back in at hole.

This from behind several trees as Rogers skirted the yard and reached the building in a precipitation of bullets.

Thank God, the poor fool isnt married.

BOOTS EMERGES WITH THE SHIVERING SMOKE.

When boots emerged, he dragged a shivering negro by the collar. All the outlaw desperation and bravado were gone. His Winchester and revolver upstairs with his ammunition. All he now had were a set of chattering teeth and a prayer for mercy.

Rogers had caught him unawares through the trapdoor that enters into the loft. And, even a desperado, as desperate as they may sometimes get, isnt going to start something when the drops staring him in the face.

Its like turning your four perfectly good sevens over to a royal flush when the jokerbless his heart, even though he is untrue at timesis completely out of the deck and over in the discarded strips.

That placed the first feather in the Rogers cap for police duty.

Then, there was the time he drove four policemen and a helpless police reporter into perfect hail of burglars bullets out on the north side at an hour of night when all respectable folks are supposed to be in bed. He had charge of Chief Rowans car, at the time, and was loafing with the big machine down at police headquarters.

It was about 3 a. m. when a message came over the telephone that burglars were robbing a store out near Pryor street and Georgia avenue. Rogers offered to carry the reserve men out in the chiefs car, which stood outside at the curb. Three motorcycle men, a captain and police reporter for a morning newspaper jumped in.

As the car neared the scene of burglarization, Rogers cut out his engine and lights and coasted down the slope. Barely had he reached sight of the building than two menlookouts stationed on the corneropened fire, Policeman Anderson, who sat on the front seat, was first to return the shots.

NEVER SIT ON A RED LAMP.

Captain Mayo and Policeman Watson, sitting in the tonneau, also opened up. The reporterunarmed, his revolver having fallen prey to the sign of the three ballsdid the only logical thing he could expected to do under the circumstances. Which was climbing over the back of the tonneau and sitting upon the red lamp. There are scars, yet. What more could you expect of an enterprising red lamp?

The two lookouts were augmented by three others who came from the building. Fire from five burglars is generally supposed to be enough to repulse three ordinary men, and, undoubtedly would have repulsed three perfectly good policemen on this particular occasion, had it not been for Rogers, who threw in his engine and drove the car directly into the fusillade.

The burglars probably took fright more at the onrushing automobile than they did at the pistols. They scattered in all directions, ducking into a big touring car that stood, engine running on the shadowy side of the street. The car was off before Rogers could swerve into the center of the road. A few shots were exchanged, but the burglars had escaped before pursuit was possible.

Also, there was the time Rogers, unassisted, unaided, unabetted, leaped from his motorcycle into the driving seat of a runaway automobile, saving the life of a wild and hysterical gentleman and $1,500 worth of 1910 model automobile.

Boots was patrolling his beat along Paces Ferry road, a favorite route for speed-fiends who have money enough to pay for the gasoline and sufficient lightness of the head to take the risk. Jerry M. Fields, a resident of north Georgia, who owned a car that went quite cranky at times, was bowling along at a goodly pace on his way home.

ROGERS SPRINGS OUT AN AUTO HERO.

Something went wrong with his engine. Either that or Mr. Fields lost his head and absolute control of said engine. Evidently the latter, as Rogers afterwards said he found no difficulty in shoving in the clutch and using the emergency brake. Anyway, the car dashed down the river hill like an anti out of an equal rights convention.

The machine shot by Rogers on his motorcycle. He speeded up, overtaking the runaway near the river bridge. While both machines were running at a dizzy rate the policeman left his motorcycle, clung to the tonneau of the swaying automobile and crawled to the steering wheel. In a moment the car was at a standstill.

Returning to town, Rogers could find but few who would believe the story of this late heroism.

However, he had a badly bent and battered motorcycle for substantiation and the business card of Jerry M. Fields, Jackson County, with a cordial invitation to call around whenever in the vicinity.

And, there have been many other times, including the incident when he toppled over a bridge at Peachtree creek trying to outrun a speeding automobile that outdid the law by at least twenty excess miles an hour. They had to fish him out and parts of his motor are still in the creek.

Then he fell in love. And what love cant do, it behooveth no man to undertake. In the words of Boots:

A guysome guyscan do most anything and get away with it, but when it comes to trying to outdo love and a woman, there isnt a chancea bit of a chance.

By the way, Rogers is now doing office worktame, but safe and compensating.

References

The Atlanta Constitution. (1913, November 9). A dead hero is the poorest sort of a husband; Boots Rogers, hero extraordinary, learns lesson (p. 9, col. 1). https://t.co/3RvkpgRoLI. https://t.co/T3fC63i3X4

text:
Got a letter from Citizens? Don't let a default pick your insurer.

Citizens, the state-created insurer of last resort, now covers about 217,000 policies. In 2023 it covered roughly 1.4 million. Much of that shrinking has come through "takeouts," where private insurers approved by the Office of Insurance Regulation offer to assume selected Citizens policies. The commissioner expects more policyholders to leave in the coming months.

If you are in the December round, the date to know is Dec. 4. That is the policyholder choice deadline on Citizens' published 2026 calendar for the Dec. 15 takeout.

Here is the part people miss. According to that calendar, if no choice is registered by the deadline, Citizens assigns the policy to one of the takeout companies that selected it. If more than one company selected it, the policy goes to the one with the lowest estimated premium.

Lowest estimated premium is a reasonable way to break a tie. It is not a review of your home, your deductible, or your budget. Only you and your agent can do that.

Your packet should include coverage worksheets and estimated premiums for Citizens and for each offer. Lay them side by side and read past the price:

The hurricane deductible, and what it would mean in actual dollars.
The dwelling limit. Would it rebuild the house, not just buy it back?
Any endorsements added, changed, or missing.
The company itself: its financial condition and its license, which you can confirm through the regulator.

Florida law also has rules about when a takeout offer still lets you stay with Citizens, generally tied to how the offer's premium compares with Citizens' renewal premium. How those rules apply depends on your policy, so ask your agent or Citizens directly.

Agents register the choice in Citizens' system. Do not wait until deadline day to call.

Leaving Citizens can be a good outcome. Staying can be too. Either one should be a decision you made, not something that happened because the mail sat on the counter.

text:
I asked grok, and he gave me this theological answer that wraps together about four different answers for four different questions. Darn he is thorough.

According to Catholic theology, the blessing of meals (and the accompanying Sign of the Cross) is a sacramental rather than a sacrament. Sacramentals do not confer sanctifying grace *ex opere operato* in the manner of the sacraments. Their efficacy derives from the intercession of the Church and the disposition of the person who uses them (*ex opere operantis*). The *Catechism of the Catholic Church* teaches that they “prepare us to receive grace and dispose us to cooperate with it” (CCC 1670), and that blessings of meals are among the foremost sacramentals (CCC 1671).[](<https://t.co/tzF2tyUz46>)

For a baptized person, the spiritual fruits of the practice are more fully efficacious when the individual is in a state of grace (that is, not in mortal sin) and acts with faith and devotion. Mortal sin constitutes an obstacle that diminishes or impedes the reception of the graces associated with sacramentals. In proportion to one’s disposition, sacramentals can assist in the remission of venial sins and temporal punishment, as noted by St. Thomas Aquinas and traditional teaching. The ordinary meal blessing is an invocative prayer (asking God to bless the persons and the gifts), which the baptized may and should offer in virtue of their share in the common priesthood (CCC 1669). It is not a constitutive blessing reserved to ordained ministers.[](<https://t.co/tzF2tyUz46>)

In the specific case of an unbaptized person or catechumen, the act remains spiritually beneficial and is encouraged. Canon law provides that blessings may be given to catechumens (Canon 1170). A sincere prayer of thanksgiving and the Sign of the Cross, performed in faith, is a good work to which God can respond, disposing the person toward the grace of baptism. It does not, however, possess the same sacramental efficacy as when performed by one already in the state of grace through baptism. The original poster’s practice is therefore consistent with Catholic encouragement of such devotion among seekers, without requiring prior baptism for its basic value as prayer.

text:
Muhammad Iqbal the Jurist: On the 149th Anniversary of His Birth
Prof. Dr. Ergin Ergül · 9 November 2026. Akademik Akıl.
In a story Muhammad Iqbal tells in Rumūz-i Bīkhudī, an architect from Khujand builds a mosque on the orders of Sultan Murad. The mosque does not please the sultan. In his anger, he draws his dagger and cuts off the architect’s hand. The architect goes before the qadi and recounts the wrong done to him. The qadi recalls the Qur’anic verse on qiṣāṣ, the law of equal retribution. He declares that a slave is no less than a free man and that the sultan’s blood cannot be held more precious than the architect’s. At these words, Sultan Murad rolls up his sleeve and holds out his hand. The architect forgives the sultan. The story expresses the idea of equality before the law in these lines:
The sultan’s blood is no richer in colour, and no finer, than the architect’s.
Before the Qur’an, slave and master are equal; there is no difference between the reed mat and the silken divan.
Article 10 of Türkiye’s 1982 Constitution provides that no privilege shall be granted to any individual, family, group or class. Iqbal stages this principle as a courtroom scene. The qadi reminds the sultan of the rule of qiṣāṣ, undeterred by the rank of the man before him. And it is the architect, whose hand was cut off, who forgives the sultan.
The poet who wrote this story was born on 9 November 1877 in Sialkot, in the Punjab. His father, Nur Muhammad, was a tailor. Though he had received no formal schooling, he could read books in Persian and Urdu and sought to attend the gatherings of scholars. Pakistan observes 9 November as Iqbal Day; its status as a public holiday, withdrawn in 2015, was restored in 2022. In Türkiye we know Iqbal chiefly for his devotion to Rumi and his reflections on the self, and his name is often mentioned alongside that of Mehmet Âkif Ersoy. His twenty-six years at the Bar, however, are seldom remembered. On the 149th anniversary of his birth, I would like to look again at what Iqbal wrote about law.
From Lincoln’s Inn to the Courts of Lahore
While reading philosophy at Cambridge, Iqbal also enrolled at Lincoln’s Inn in London. According to the Inn’s archives, he was admitted on 6 November 1905. He passed the bar examinations in 1907 and was called to the Bar on 1 July 1908 on the proposal of Sir Frederick Pollock, the eminent jurist of the day. Back in Lahore, he took on both civil and criminal cases and remained in practice until 1934. In his 560-page book Qanoon Dan Iqbal, the Pakistani lawyer Zafar Ali Raja examines 103 judgments in cases Iqbal handled. The book, published in Lahore by Jamhoori Publications, brings together these judgments as reported in law journals. By Raja’s count, more than half were decided in favour of Iqbal’s clients. The call to will and effort in Asrār-i Khudī should therefore also be read as the voice of a lawyer who listened to clients, prepared case files and earned his living at the Bar. His experience of the courts also shaped what he wrote about law.
The Ruler, Too, Is Bound by Law
Iqbal carries the idea of equality in the Sultan Murad story into his writings on government. In his 1908 essay “Political Thought in Islam”, he explains Sunni legal thought, drawing on al-Māwardī. He reports that the ruler enjoys no privilege before the law and may be sued and criticised. He considers together the ruler’s coming to office by election, his duty to discharge the obligations of that office, and his removal should he act unlawfully. Years later, in his lectures on religious thought, he expressly rejects the idea of a state headed by “a representative of God on earth who can always screen his despotic will behind his supposed infallibility”.
Justice and Mercy
In the notebook he began keeping in 1910 and called Stray Reflections, Iqbal warns that justice may be sacrificed in the name of mercy. In my years as a judge, I often saw this tension in the courtroom. In showing understanding for one party’s hardship, a judge may lose sight of the other party’s rights. The debtor’s poverty may eclipse the creditor’s right, just as the defendant’s tears may eclipse the victim’s. A judge may take a person’s circumstances into account within the discretion the law confers; a discretionary reduction of sentence, the deferral of the pronouncement of judgment and the suspension of a sentence are examples. The judge grounds that discretion in specific reasons. The judge remains attentive to the human situation but rests the decision on the rule and the evidence.
In the same notebook, Iqbal describes the legacy of the Muslim jurists as “a complete system of law”. In a note on democracy, he warns that the urge to legislate can blur the distinction between “the illegal” and “the wrong”. When a society tries to outlaw every wrong, its laws multiply and become entangled with one another. The sphere governed by morality, custom and professional rules steadily shrinks. The distinction matters most when legislation changes frequently, omnibus laws proliferate and every new problem is met with a new prohibition. A jurist who asks whether a rule is in force must also ask, separately, whether it is just.
Ijtihad and Legal Education
Iqbal’s most enduring contribution to legal thought lies in what he wrote about ijtihād, the exercise of independent legal reasoning. The sixth lecture of The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam is entitled “The Principle of Movement in the Structure of Islam”. There Iqbal sees life as a process of continuous creation: “each generation, guided but unhampered by the work of its predecessors, should be permitted to solve its own problems.” He likewise regards as “perfectly justified” the demand of a generation seeking to reconsider the foundational principles of Islamic law in the light of the conditions of modern life.
For Iqbal, interpretation needs a yardstick. In assessing how a rule operates, he keeps in view the five objectives identified by al-Shāṭibī: the protection of religion, life, intellect, property and lineage. In the Punjab, some women who had no other way to end their marriages were being driven to apostasy, since apostasy was held to dissolve a marriage. Iqbal asks whether applying the rule in this way truly serves the protection of religion.
Iqbal sees ijtihādas a collective undertaking. In a piece quoted by his son Javid Iqbal, he says that a jurist capable of interpreting legal principles to meet the needs of the age has yet to emerge. Given the scale of the task, he thinks it will take more than one person and at least a century. He entrusts ijtihād to legislative assemblies and wants those versed in religious learning to work there alongside those who understand law and society. He attaches particular importance to legal education: “The only effective remedy for the possibilities of erroneous interpretations is to reform the present system of legal education in Muhammadan countries.” He wants legislators to receive an education that brings classical Islamic jurisprudence together with modern legal science. In a letter to Aligarh, he calls the revival of an old-style faculty of Islamic studies “entirely useless”. The real aim, in his view, is to raise a generation of scholars capable of independent and creative thought.
The attention he gives Türkiye in the same lecture holds particular meaning for Turkish readers. On 3 March 1924, the Grand National Assembly passed Law No. 431, abolishing the office of the caliphate and stating in the law itself that the caliphate was already inherent in the concepts of government and republic. Iqbal reads the Turkish position as an exercise in ijtihād. In his account, Türkiye concluded that, in keeping with the spirit of Islam, the office of the caliphate or imamate could be vested in a body of persons or an elected assembly. He then says: “Personally, I believe the Turkish view is perfectly sound.” He does not endorse every aspect of the Turkish experience. In Jāvīd Nāma, he worries that the Turks are severing their ties with their past and turning exclusively towards the West, and on family law he parts company with Ziya Gökalp. His readiness to commend the decisions of a country he felt close to while still subjecting them to criticism is a lesson in method for anyone working in comparative law.
Rights and Duties in Hard Times
Iqbal considers what it means to respect the rights of others under extreme pressure in “The Siege of Edirne”, a poem in Bāng-i Darā. Its subject is the city defended by Şükrü Pasha during the Balkan War. When famine takes hold in the besieged city, there is a proposal to seize the food of its non-Muslim residents. After the religious scholars object, the proposal is dropped. What strikes Iqbal is not only the city’s power of resistance but its respect for the rights of others even in its darkest hour. Emergency powers, too, have limits. Article 15 of the Constitution allows the exercise of fundamental rights and freedoms to be partially or entirely suspended in times of war, mobilisation or a state of emergency, provided that obligations under international law are not violated and the measures do not exceed what the situation requires. The scene Iqbal describes still raises an old question in the law of war: how are the rights of civilians to be protected under siege?
Iqbal does not belittle rights, but he considers them together with responsibilities. He puts it in a single sentence in Stray Reflections: “True political life begins not with the claiming of rights, but with the doing of duties.” The sentence reminds us that rights can be safeguarded only among people who know their duties. Iqbal approaches democracy with the same care. In one of his early writings, he says that the basic principle laid down by the Qur’an is election. In Zarb-i Kalīm, published in 1936, he satirises a form of government that counts votes without weighing them. He accepts election as a principle and also questions the quality of elections. At a time when many countries are once again debating the relationship between electoral legitimacy and the rule of law, it is worth noting that both positions find a place in the work of one writer.
Never Delegating One’s Judgement
What Iqbal says in his early notes about owning a large library speaks today to jurists who use artificial intelligence. For Iqbal, owning a large library and knowing its books does not in itself show that a person can think for himself; it shows that he has the means to draw on the thinking of others. Today, software can produce a pleading, a report summary or a draft judgment in seconds. In 2023, in Mata v. Avianca, the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York fined lawyers who had cited non-existent decisions, and similar sanctions have since been imposed by courts in several countries. Verifying that a cited decision exists and says what it is cited for is the jurist’s own responsibility.
The most personal lesson Iqbal the jurist leaves us is his intellectual independence. Soon after returning from Europe, he gave up his post teaching philosophy at Government College, convinced that government service would prevent him from expressing his views freely. Some of his remarks about the government were considered so harsh that he was passed over for the judgeship of the Lahore High Court that had earlier been offered to him. When he accepted a knighthood in 1923, a friend feared that he would now be beholden to the British government. Iqbal wrote back that no power on earth could stop him from speaking the truth. When Sir Akbar Hydari, the prime minister of Hyderabad, sent him a cheque for a thousand rupees, Iqbal sensed that it was being offered as a favour and sent it back. The Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct place independence first among their values and set standards for accepting gifts. Iqbal’s conduct shows how independence shapes a jurist’s everyday decisions.
In his years at the Bar, Iqbal took on only a few cases at a time and was content to earn enough to live on for a month or two. His biographers relate that he lived in straitened circumstances even in his final years, when his fame was at its height. Hence the name “the poorest knight”. Even when his poems were being translated into European languages and he had become a celebrated figure in Lahore, his door remained open to anyone who wished to see him. He died in Lahore on 21 April 1938 and was buried beside the Badshahi Mosque. Each year on 9 November, Pakistan’s Iqbal Day ceremonies begin with the changing of the guard at his tomb.

text:
A little-known omega-6 fat called DGLA appears to be a weak spot for the damaged cells that build up in our bodies as we age.

As we get older, some damaged cells stop dividing but never die off, a state called senescence, and they linger in tissues while releasing inflammatory signals. Some of the strongest evidence that they matter came from a 2016 study in Nature, which found that clearing them from normal mice extended median lifespan and slowed the age-related decline of the kidneys, heart and fat tissue.

DGLA is rare in food, so your body builds it from GLA, an omega-6 fat concentrated in a few seed oils. Borage seed oil is the richest source at roughly a fifth to a quarter of its fat, black currant seed oil provides about a sixth, and evening primrose oil a little under a tenth. The body quickly converts GLA into DGLA, and because the next enzyme in the chain works slowly, much of it stays as DGLA and is used to make compounds such as prostaglandin E1 that are generally linked to calmer inflammation. In a controlled trial of 64 healthy adults, four weeks of borage oil raised blood DGLA by about half in some people and more than doubled it in others, depending on which version of the FADS1 gene they carried.

The new study in Cell shows why senescent cells avoid this fat. They keep DGLA unusually low because it can trigger ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death in which the fats in a cell's membrane oxidize until it breaks apart, something earlier work had already shown in worms and human cancer cells. When the researchers restored DGLA, senescent cells died this way while healthy cells were largely spared. In old mice, five days of oral DGLA lowered markers of senescence in fat and liver, and the males developed less liver scarring. In 185 Finnish adults with obesity, people carrying a FADS1 variant that keeps DGLA higher had lower levels of a senescence marker in their fat tissue.

Because most of this evidence comes from cells and mice, and the human finding is a genetic association rather than a trial, nobody has yet shown that GLA oils or DGLA clear senescent cells in people. DGLA also increased liver fat in the mice, and human observational studies have linked higher blood DGLA to fatty liver and type 2 diabetes, so more is not automatically better. The study's senior author is also an inventor on patents covering this use. What the work offers is a clear, testable explanation of how one nutrient could shape aging biology, which is a reason to watch for human trials rather than to start supplementing.

Sources: Kuehnemann et al., Cell, 2026; Baker et al., Nature, 2016; Perez et al., Developmental Cell, 2020; Mustonen and Nieminen, International Journal of Molecular Sciences, 2023; Sergeant et al., American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 2020.

text:
For 7 years Tyler Perry put on the same play and lost money every time. He ended up homeless in Atlanta, sleeping in a car the repo man was trying to take. On March 12, 1998 he gave it one last try. Sold out.
Today he owns a 330-acre studio and Forbes says he's worth $1 billion. All because he didn't quit.

In the video below he tells it himself, in his 2022 commencement speech to Emory University's graduating class in Atlanta, from the empty theater to the night it finally sold out.

He had moved to Atlanta with one play he'd written himself.

He worked jobs, saved, and rented the 14th Street Playhouse.

He expected 1,200 people over the weekend.

30 came. For 6 shows.

Someone in the crowd wanted to invest. He tried again. Nothing.

Someone else invested. He tried again. Nothing.

7 years. Different cities. Same play.

He ended up on the streets of Atlanta, sleeping in a car he was hiding from the repo man.

His mother had the answer: go to the phone company, make $300 or $400 a week, get benefits, let the play go.

He decided she was right. He was done.

Then a promoter offered to back it one more time. He had no money for ads, just people who trusted him to pay later.

March 12, 1998. Sold out. Then two more sold-out nights at the Fox Theatre.

Then came the movies.

Diary of a Mad Black Woman, 2005. Made for $5.5 million. Took $50 million.

Madea Goes to Jail, 2009. $90 million.

Boo! A Madea Halloween, 2016. $73 million.

The Madea films alone have taken more than $660 million at the US box office.

In 2020 Forbes named him a billionaire. His studio sits on a former army base he bought in Atlanta.

Would you have taken the $300 a week, or tried for year 8?

text:
2027: EBONYI TARGETS 80% VOTES FOR TINUBU-SHETTIMA TICKET
......As Betta Edu, APC PCC Women’s Directorate take First Lady’s mobilisation to 171 ward leaders

The Ebonyi State Government has pledged 80 per cent of the state’s votes for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and Vice-President Kashim Shettima in the 2027 presidential election, citing federal government projects and interventions.

Governor Francis Nwifuru gave the assurance at an All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council rally in Abakaliki on Monday, declaring that the ruling party had consolidated its political foothold across the state.

According to the reported 2026 INEC voter register, Ebonyi has 1,828,056 registered voters, with the 80 per cent target translating to approximately 1.46 million votes across the state’s 13 local government areas and 171 electoral wards.

Nwifuru said the Tinubu administration had strengthened the APC’s political standing in Ebonyi through appointments, infrastructure and development initiatives.

He cited the appointment of former Governor Dave Umahi as Minister of Works, federal road projects, the proposed aviation college, the Army Training Depot and the growing number of beneficiaries of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) as key interventions that had boosted the party’s support.

“Eighty per cent of our votes is assured. This is an APC state,” the governor said.

The pledge came as Dr Betta Edu and the APC PCC Directorate of Women Mobilisation intensified grassroots engagements on behalf of the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, across the state.

The mobilisation drive followed the First Lady’s stakeholder engagement in Abakaliki on Sunday, where she was represented by Edu and the Women’s Directorate in visits to markets and hospitals to support women traders and vulnerable residents.

During the outreach, market women received business support, while patients were offered assistance as part of efforts to extend the Renewed Hope Agenda to communities and households.

The engagement was subsequently extended to women leaders and stakeholders across Ebonyi’s 171 electoral wards, with Edu and the Directorate urging women to sustain their participation in the political process and mobilise support for the Tinubu-Shettima ticket.

The Women’s Directorate said the ward-level engagement was aimed at strengthening the APC’s grassroots structures, taking the message of the Renewed Hope Agenda to households, markets and communities, and securing a decisive victory for the ruling party in 2027.

text:
Red Sox legend Curt Schilling put more than $50 million of his own money into a video game company. Rhode Island taxpayers backed it with $75 million more. Two years later it was bankrupt

In the video below, Schilling pushing past reporters after the state of Rhode Island came after him

He won three World Series. He pitched the 2004 ALCS with a bleeding ankle, the famous bloody sock

After baseball he started 38 Studios, a game studio in Massachusetts. He wanted to build the next World of Warcraft

In 2010 Rhode Island wanted the jobs. The state offered a $75 million loan guarantee if he moved the company there. He did

Here's the catch. With a state guarantee, the people buying the bonds barely had to check the company's finances. If it failed, the state would cover them

In 2012 the studio released its first game, Kingdoms of Amalur. Reports said it sold over 1 million copies, still not nearly enough

Within months the money ran out. Paychecks bounced. About 400 people lost their jobs overnight, many without warning

Schilling went on TV and said he was "tapped out"

"I put in just north of $50 million." He got none of it back

"This was my decision to do this and I failed"

The lawsuits dragged on until 2017

He lost his fortune. The state lost its bet. The 400 employees lost the most

Who deserves the blame here: Schilling, or the politicians who handed him $75 million?

The following is a brain dump about the reaction to the state of College Football, do with that what you will: 

I hate to break it to all of the martyrs leading the College Football outrage, but networks have been calling the shots long before any of this (or even back when the CFP began). CC Notre Dame. 

The moment Texas and Oklahoma were moved to boost the SEC TV value, this was the obvious outcome. 

The purposely-ignored point in all of this is that College Football hasn’t been this watchable and exciting in a long time. Week-to-week has been absolute appointment television. 

That point isn’t just for the P4, but honestly across the FBS. (Who saw Troy beating JMU coming?) The PAC-12 has had wild games (Fresno State had Boise St beat till the end, Oregon State’s insane offense, ect). 

Yes, we have now officially entered the period of college football disruption that we have been literally talking about for years (@DSmithShow was all over it, we’ve had extensive conversations with @cannonhartman about it). 

College football is not dead, and claiming it’s dead diminishes the incredible work these student athletes put in every single week. Work that most of you never take into account when sitting and judging every moment of a game based on your own rooting/gambling interests. 

Every program and conference across the board offers so much value, but the structure will need to change to make sure that value is maximized, and these next few seasons will likely be very frustrating for all of us before that part is accounted for.

text:
The omission of Pakistan from Tehran's announced exemptions is notable, especially given shared borders and regional proximity. Tehran's declared criteria behind the list explain why certain nations were included, as well as where Pakistan fits into that dynamic:
​1. The Realpolitik Behind the Exemptions
​Iranian officials explicitly framed these exemptions around immediate, transactional leverage:  
​China: To secure vital political backing from a permanent UN Security Council member and maintain its main buyer for crude exports.  
​India: Specifically tied to maintaining essential trade corridors for medical and pharmaceutical imports into Iran.  
​Qatar & Iraq: Granted under "mutual interests" and shared regional, energy, and border dynamics.
​2. Pakistan's Geopolitics & Neutrality
​U.S. & Gulf Alignment: Pakistan maintains strategic security ties with both the United States and Gulf Arab partners (particularly Saudi Arabia). Tehran often views Islamabad's balancing act as leaning too close to Washington during active conflicts.
​Border & Security Friction: Periodic cross-border tension in Balochistan continues to complicate bilateral relations, preventing the sort of seamless economic integration seen with neighbors like Iraq.
​Lack of Direct Leverage: Unlike China (diplomatic shelter/oil buyer) or India (critical supplies), Pakistan does not currently offer Tehran a unique trade or diplomatic bargaining chip that warrants explicit military-transit concessions.
​3. Practical Impact on Pakistan
​Pakistan imports significant quantities of liquefied natural gas (LNG) and refined oil passing through the Persian Gulf. By leaving Pakistan off the explicit exemption list, Tehran effectively maintains leverage over Pakistani-flagged or bound shipping, keeping Islamabad under pressure to maintain strict neutrality in the broader West Asian conflict.

China extended its suspension of an additional 24% tariff on U.S. goods for two months, giving exporters more breathing room while keeping a 10% tariff in place. The extension takes effect November 10 at 1:01 p.m. Beijing time.

The decision preserves part of the trade truce as President Donald Trump (@realDonaldTrump) and Chinese President Xi Jinping prepare for another meeting later this month. China linked the extension to agreements reached during the leaders' September summit in Washington.

Shipping companies also received a reprieve. Beijing extended its pause on special port fees for U.S.-linked vessels through January 10, 2027, and kept an investigation into shipping and shipbuilding supply-chain security suspended during that period. Those measures affect a separate set of costs from tariffs on imported merchandise.

A broader package remains unfinished. The two countries have discussed about $60 billion in reciprocal tariff reductions, including roughly $17 billion in U.S. agricultural products that China imported in 2024. The suspension does not mean that package has been finalized.

Beijing also said it would watch Washington's next moves on Section 301 tariffs and adjust its response as necessary. For businesses planning shipments and purchases, the announcement offers a defined period of greater predictability. 

The longer-term cost of U.S.-China trade still depends on whether the temporary pause leads to a broader agreement.

Professor Mahmoud Sadri, a sociologist at Texas Woman’s University, and I have co-authored an article in Etemad, Tehran’s reformist-leaning daily (November 8, 2026), on a paradox of the US midterms: Democrats’ gains could open the door to diplomacy with Iran—or raise the risk of military escalation.

The weeks before the new Congress convenes deserve particular attention. Despite the Republicans’ electoral setback, Trump retains substantial presidential authority.

Our argument goes beyond Trump’s immediate choices. Drawing on Robert Putnam’s two-level games framework, we explain why an agreement between Washington and Tehran must also be politically defensible in both countries. The normalization of US–Vietnam relations in 1995 offers a useful historical parallel.

Rather than wait for a comprehensive settlement, we propose limited, reciprocal and verifiable steps on humanitarian issues, preventing unintended military clashes and maritime security. Genuinely independent academic, scientific, medical and civil-society ties could help build broader support for cooperation.

Democratic opposition to war should not be mistaken for acceptance of Tehran’s policies. Nor would portraying an agreement as Washington’s humiliation help sustain it.

Ultimately, the test of diplomacy is whether it reduces the risk of war, establishes credible commitments and advances the welfare of the Iranian people.

Full article (in Persian; English title translated): “An Opportunity for Diplomacy with a Fragmented America”

text:
Russia and Ukraine are set to begin a new round of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi. This time, the agenda could draw European governments and NATO into direct negotiations with Moscow. For the first time since Istanbul in 2022, Washington has put Russia’s own post-war security explicitly on the table alongside guarantees for Ukraine. We explain the formats Washington is proposing for wider talks on European security. The US appears to want European governments and NATO to do much of the bargaining with Moscow while it keeps a watchful eye.

European governments want a say in any settlement that affects their security. Many are wary, though, of being asked to negotiate directly with Moscow over NATO’s military posture and Ukraine’s choice of alliances. Moscow sees those issues as part of the war’s ‘root causes’ and wants concrete commitments before signing a settlement.

In the new R.Politik Bulletin, I look at how Russia approaches the talks, what agendas are on the table and what the Kremlin still thinks Trump can deliver, especially after the midterms.

I also look at why Putin’s Africa summit matters to officials and businesses competing for influence in Moscow. At home, Mishustin has reassigned responsibility for public finances and digital policy, while the Finance Ministry’s pension plan raises questions about who gets to decide how household savings are invested. And the prosecution of regional Communists is testing how much protection the party’s long-standing accommodation with the Kremlin still offers.

R.Politik Bulletin No. 19 (193) is available at https://t.co/6FU4ieMsEp

Iran's Araghchi Says Israel Is Dragging US Governments Into Endless Wars
TEHRAN: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Monday that Americans are tired of Israel pushing US administrations into prolonged wars, reacting to President Donald Trump's interview on CBS's "60 Minutes."
Sharing a clip of the interview on X, Araghchi wrote that the US president "clearly acknowledges" that the vast majority of Americans are fed up with Israel, but seemingly does not understand why. He added that people in the region feel the same way.
In the interview with journalist Ross Douthat, Trump discussed the Republican losses in last week's midterm elections. He said voters disliked the war and rising gasoline prices, and that there was unusually strong resentment toward Israel. He also cited candidate popularity and campaign issues as factors.
Trump defended the decision to take military action against Iran, saying he would "strongly" do it again because Tehran cannot be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon. He claimed US strikes had badly damaged Iran's nuclear capability. He said Washington and Tehran had been close to a deal before the elections, but that he does not currently want to escalate the war. Araghchi said mediation efforts have slowed in recent days and need more time to resume.
According to CBS, Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate, with Republicans losing more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats; some races remain undecided.
Araghchi's claim about American attitudes is his political assessment, and Trump offered no polling or figures in the interview to support it. Analysts differ on what drove the election result. Tensions remain high after US and Israeli military action against Iran, which disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and oil supplies, pushing up global fuel prices.

text:
In late 1969, a father handed scissors to his ten-year-old daughter and asked her to help him commit a felony that could send him to prison for the rest of his life.

The office was dark except for the faint green glow of a Xerox machine. Daniel Ellsberg, 38, fed page after page through the feeder. Each sheet carried the stamp TOP SECRET—each copy a federal crime under the Espionage Act. He was not a radical. He was a Harvard PhD economist, a former Marine officer who had served in Vietnam, a senior Pentagon analyst who had helped shape U.S. strategy. He had held the highest security clearances in the country. He had believed in the mission.

Then he read 7,000 pages that shattered every belief he held.

The documents—later known as the Pentagon Papers—were a classified, 47-volume study commissioned by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara. They traced American involvement in Vietnam from World War II through 1968. The conclusion was devastating and consistent: four consecutive presidents—Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson—had privately concluded the war was unwinnable yet continued escalating it. They sent hundreds of thousands of young Americans into combat knowing victory was impossible—to avoid the political cost of admitting defeat.

By 1969 more than 40,000 U.S. troops were dead. The public was told progress was being made, that the light at the end of the tunnel was visible. The papers proved it was a lie maintained across administrations.

Ellsberg faced a stark choice: protect his career, his freedom, his family—or expose the truth.

He chose truth.

Copying 7,000 pages alone at night was slow, nerve-racking work. Every passing car outside could be the FBI. Every paper jam risked discovery. The penalty was severe: life in federal prison. He had already tried official channels. He approached six senators and several congressmen, begging them to release the documents legally through the Congressional Record. Every one refused.

So he decided to go public.

He brought his children into the room.

Robert was 13. Mary was 10. Robert ran the Xerox machine—feeding pages, collating stacks. Mary sat on the floor with scissors, carefully cutting the words TOP SECRET off each photocopy so the stolen documents would not be immediately identifiable as classified. Ellsberg later explained: “I expected to be in prison very shortly. I wanted them to know their father was doing something in a calm, sober way that I thought had to be done.”

He told Robert directly: this will probably put me in prison. He wanted his children to understand that conscience sometimes demands sacrifice. That doing the right thing is not always safe. That a parent’s greatest legacy is not wealth or status—but moral courage.

In March 1971 he gave the papers to The New York Times. On June 13, 1971, the Times published the first installment. The Nixon administration erupted. For the first time in American history, the government sought a prior restraint order to silence a newspaper before publication. A federal judge granted a temporary injunction. The Times stopped publishing.

Ellsberg responded by giving copies to The Washington Post. When they were blocked, he gave them to the Boston Globe. Then more outlets. The truth spread faster than the government could contain it.

Nixon did not just want the leak stopped. He wanted Ellsberg destroyed.

He formed a secret White House unit called “the Plumbers.” They broke into the office of Ellsberg’s psychiatrist, searching for compromising material to discredit him. They found nothing—but the break-in was a felony. The Justice Department charged Ellsberg with espionage, theft, and conspiracy. He faced 115 years in prison.

The trial began in 1973 in Los Angeles. Prosecutors painted him as a traitor who endangered national security. Then the government’s misconduct began to surface.

The psychiatrist break-in became public. Illegal wiretaps were revealed. Prosecutorial abuse emerged. Most shockingly: Nixon had offered the trial judge the directorship of the FBI—while the trial was under way. Blatant judicial tampering.

On May 11, 1973, the judge dismissed all charges with prejudice, citing “improper government conduct.”

Daniel Ellsberg walked free.

The Pentagon Papers did not end the war overnight. But they changed everything. They confirmed what millions suspected: the government had lied for decades about a war that killed more than 58,000 Americans and millions of Vietnamese. Public opposition surged. Congress began cutting funding. The war that could not be ended politically was ended by exposure.

There was one more consequence Nixon never foresaw.

The same Plumbers who burglarized Ellsberg’s psychiatrist later broke into the Democratic National Committee headquarters at the Watergate complex. Nixon’s obsession with destroying Daniel Ellsberg set in motion the scandal that destroyed his presidency.

Ellsberg lived to 92, dying on June 16, 2023. He spent the rest of his life as an antiwar activist, whistleblower advocate, and lecturer. He never regretted his choice. He never stopped speaking truth to power.

His children grew up understanding something profound: that citizenship sometimes requires courage. That doing the right thing is not always safe. That a father’s greatest legacy is not wealth or status—but moral courage.

In late 1969 he was simply a father in a borrowed office after midnight, feeding classified pages into a Xerox machine while his 13-year-old son collated and his 10-year-old daughter sat cross-legged on the floor with scissors, cutting TOP SECRET off copies.

He could have stayed silent. Kept his clearances. Protected his career.
Instead he handed scissors to his daughter and told her to start cutting.

Because sometimes the most patriotic act is to tell the truth—even when your government calls it treason.

text:
A Decision Is Not the Same as the Capability to Act

Two households receive the same energy-price shock and make the same rational response: they cut consumption. One absorbs it — savings buffer it, an efficient home limits it, remote work removes its worst edge. The other cannot: savings deplete, retraining is deferred, work ends early. Identical behaviour. Different economy.

Economics sees the decision very well. It is largely blind to the structural conditions that determined which decisions were available in the first place.

On the 31st October, The Global Structure Network publishes the expanded institutional edition of The Household Affordability Frontier. It defines the structural threshold at which the combined financial, temporal, physical and participation costs of household life begin to restrict the capacity to accumulate and deploy productive capability — and connects three domains usually examined separately: household structural conditions, monetary transmission and heterogeneous-agent dynamics, and the allocation of long-duration capital.

The opportunity is structural: by shifting households from survival optimisation to capability investment, the Frontier converts economic participation from a trap into a mobility escalator — unlocking sustainable macroeconomic throughput and offering a route out of the inflation-stagnation loop.

For central banks, institutional investors, infrastructure capital and economic strategy teams, the practical question is straightforward: which structural costs are currently preventing existing capability from becoming productive capacity, and which forms of investment can measurably expand the residual space in which households can adapt?

The framework does not claim empirical superiority over existing approaches. It is offered as a proposed analytical architecture, not a finished model — with explicit measurement requirements, testable hypotheses and clear falsification conditions published in full. If threshold position and duration below it carry no predictive power beyond income and balance sheets, the framework fails.

What is stated here can be tested — by design.

text:
FABULOUS story!!!

He spent 11 and a half years behind bars. Now he owns the prison.

Kerwin Pittman went in in 2007 and came home in 2018. He knows how hard the first months outside can be. "Transitioning after a significant amount of time incarcerated is not one of the things that you easily overcome," he told North Carolina Health News.

So he started a nonprofit, Recidivism Reduction Educational Program Services, with mobile reentry centers and a hotline for people coming home. Then he set his sights on something much bigger.

The former Wayne Correctional Center in Goldsboro, North Carolina, closed in 2013 and sat empty for more than a decade: 19 acres and about 80,000 square feet behind barbed wire. Pittman offered $275,000, raised through foundations and fellowships, and the state approved the sale in November 2025, WRAL reported. He believes he is the first formerly incarcerated person in the U.S. to buy a prison.

Now he is turning it into a campus. Open dorms will become private rooms, and the bars are coming down. Men leaving prison will be able to live there free for up to six months, 200 to 250 at a time, while they train in HVAC, welding, plumbing and electrical work and get help with IDs, health care and jobs. The first residents are expected in 2028, Spectrum News reported.

"This is support. This is a tribe. This is community," Pittman said.

"I realized that this vision, this crazy vision that I had, was now a reality," he told Spectrum News. "And now it's time to go to work."

The best guide out of a hard place is someone who has already found the way out.

Good people exist.

text:
Taraji P. Henson earned an Oscar nomination playing Brad Pitt’s mother.

She says the paycheck ultimately covered one year of her son’s school tuition.

She asked for $500,000 for The Curious Case of Benjamin Button.

The first offer was $100,000.

They eventually agreed on $150,000 — with Henson responsible for months of hotel bills during filming.

Then came the deductions.

In her account, roughly $75,000 went to taxes. Another $45,000 went to her team, whose commission was calculated on the original fee.

That left $30,000.

Her son’s tuition that year was $30,000.

The film went on to gross about $335 million worldwide.

Years later, Gayle King asked whether she was considering leaving acting. Henson became emotional explaining how exhausting it was to keep proving her value.

She said each breakthrough seemed to disappear when the next negotiation began.

And she was clear about Pitt and Cate Blanchett. She believed they deserved their salaries. She wanted her own contribution valued more fairly.

Watch her explain the difference between a Hollywood paycheck and what actually reaches her account.

If an Oscar-nominated performance doesn’t improve your bargaining power, what does?
