text:
Zach Bryan sold himself as the honest one in country music - the ex-Navy kid who writes his own songs, hates the industry, and would never lie to you. So when his girlfriend of two years left, his side quietly offered her $12,000,000, a house, and a New York apartment - by her account - to sign a contract and disappear. All she had to give up was the right to ever tell you who he really is

In the video below, the woman who lived it tells the part the money was meant to bury. Her name is Brianna LaPaglia. She dated him for two years, and when it ended she says she was handed an NDA and a number, and told it was all hers the moment she agreed to go quiet

This is the man whose entire brand is that he is not like the others - no label games, no handlers, no act, just a guy and the truth. But the truth, the second it could hurt him, met the full machine: lawyers, a contract, and an offer that climbed into eight figures. He didn’t reach for that because he had nothing to hide. He reached for it because looking honest is worth far more than $12,000,000, and he knew exactly what it was worth

That’s the tell. A man with nothing to protect does not offer a house and a Manhattan apartment to make one person’s version of events go away. The honest-everyman image was never a by-product of who he is - it was the product, the asset the money existed to defend, and the moment a real person could put a scratch in it, he answered with a checkbook instead of the truth

Here’s what it really shows, and it’s bigger than one singer. The loudest honesty is almost always the most managed. When someone keeps telling you how real they are, how they’d never play you, how it’s just them and the truth - that insistence is rarely free, and it’s worth asking who got paid or pushed out to keep it believable. And this isn’t only famous people. It’s the partner who swears they’ve never lied to you, the friend everyone calls “the honest one,” the boss who “tells it straight” - the people you trust most, precisely because no one who knew better was ever able to warn you. That’s the part that should sit with you: you never get to hear from the ones who were bought. You can spend years loving and trusting someone on the strength of a reputation that money, not character, kept clean

Brianna LaPaglia said no, out loud, which is the only reason any of this reached you at all. Most people take the apartment. That’s the quiet machinery behind almost every spotless reputation: not that the honest ones are honest, but that the truth has a price, and nearly everyone who gets offered it signs

So here’s the question worth sitting with: of all the people you’ve quietly decided are “the real ones” - the straight-talking boss, the transparent brand, the famous face too genuine to be fake - how many have simply never been contradicted by someone who couldn’t be bought? And if the truth about them came attached to a $12,000,000 check to stay silent, how certain are you that you would ever get to hear it?

text:
Paul Singer bought Argentine bonds worth $600M on paper for pennies, then spent 15 years refusing every offer. In 2016 Argentina paid him $2.4B.

Ask him if that was patience. He’ll cut you off.

Argentina defaulted on $100B in 2001, the biggest sovereign default ever. The offer was 30 cents on the dollar, or nothing. About 75% of bondholders took it.

Singer didn’t. He started in 1977 with ~$1M, running a boring trade: buy convertible bonds, short the stock. When it stopped being enough, he ran the same trade with a government on the other side.

His edge wasn’t nerve. 30 cents is fair for a country with nothing left. But Argentina was the 8th largest economy in the world. The offer described a different country.

In 2012 he had an Argentine navy ship seized in Ghana and held it for 10 weeks.

In the 25-minute interview below, he explains why he rejects the word “patient”: patience means you had somewhere else to go. He didn’t. There was no version of the trade where he sold.

The impeachment articles are the last act of a career that already ended. They change nothing for Hegseth and nothing for the country. Voters already delivered their verdict in May. text:
One of the most powerful gifts you can give the people you lead is the gift of flexible attention…

Mark Pope, Kentucky Men’s Basketball head coach neatly outlines the benefits of attention flexibility in this wonderful video…

To me, leadership is about influence. It’s the ability to influence behaviours, thoughts, emotions, and feelings.

Great leaders influence behaviours, thoughts, emotions, and feelings by helping their people flex attention. They help their people direct their attention onto strengths. Onto what better looks like. Onto support for teammates. Onto what’s important now. Onto the characteristics that help them. Onto the game plan or the business model. Onto the objections clients will have or the dangers the opposition will pose.

Great leaders influence their people by asking the type of questions that guide attention. They suggest, hypothesise, surmise, offer choice, lend ideas…even instruct…all of which work in servitude of attentional direction.

Leaders are influences. They use a pallet of techniques and tools to guide and steer behaviours, thoughts, emotions, and feelings that help their people optimise their performance.

text:
I spent the last 15 months on the campaign trail across Michigan. I personally drove over 70,000 miles and visited every single county in this state.

I attended Trump rallies and NAACP meetings. I walked parade routes and ran volunteer nights. I studied the poll numbers, the results from message testing, and the polling on what voters actually care about.

I saw a lot of great people across the state working their butts off to get Republicans elected. And funny enough, most of those volunteers were boomers. The chronically online doomers want to blame the boomers in the party, when it was the boomers who did the vast majority of the volunteering while the “future of the party” sat around whining online.

I also saw a lot of people run their mouths before the convention and primaries, talk a lot of trash about Republican candidates, and then go into hiding after their preferred candidates had the snot beaten out of them by the GOP electorate.

I saw the Michigan College Republicans organize and carry out the largest volunteer deployment we’ll probably ever see, with no help from these so-called “party leaders.” (And no, I’m not talking about the MIGOP here.) They put their time, sweat, energy and money into supporting our candidates while self proclaimed leaders and wannabe leaders were no where to be found. The college and young republicans should remember which of their peers showed up to that, and which ones didn’t. 

I watched several statewide campaigns that were horribly underfunded, through no fault of their own, receive no help from our party’s established “influencer” core. Frankly, if those people ever reached out, it was to insult us or yell at us about something we were doing, never once offering real advice or help. Never once did they offer to use their followings to help build name recognition, instead they either went silent or continued to bad mouth other candidates. 

The people I see online talking the most about how everyone did something wrong, how they’re so much smarter than everyone else, and how they have grandiose ideas to fix the Republican Party’s problems are predominantly the latter, not the former.

Hate to break it to some of you, but posting on X and spending your days chatting with your friends in Signal groups doesn’t contribute to Republicans winning elections.

Rant over. Thanks for reading, and a reminder that those of us who were actually on the ground know and will remember who was out there with us.

INSCRIPTION HOUSE, Ariz. – Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren joined the Ts’ah Bii Kin Chapter, community members, and representatives from the Community Housing and Infrastructure Department (CHID) on November 6, 2026, to celebrate the presentation of keys to a new, debt-free home for a local family.

For the family, the occasion carried special meaning after spending six years living in a small cabin on land that has remained in their family for approximately 52 years. Generations of relatives have called the property home, and the new residence allows the family to remain close to loved ones while enjoying greater comfort, privacy, and security.

As the family walked through their new home, they expressed excitement over the spacious bedrooms, modern kitchen, new appliances, and flooring that will be easier to maintain. Everyday comforts that many take for granted now offer the family a greater sense of independence and a place they can truly call their own.

CHID Construction Supervisor Jeffrey Goodluck explained that the home features reinforced flooring, insulated exterior walls, durable construction, and accessible amenities, including wider doorways and a walk-in shower. These improvements reflect the Nygren Administration’s commitment to providing quality housing designed to serve Navajo families for years to come.

“Home is the foundation,” President Nygren said during the visit, emphasizing the importance of providing families with safe, dependable housing. He also stressed that homes should be built with sufficient insulation to keep families comfortable during power outages and other hardships.

President Nygren recognized the dedication of the Ts’ah Bii Kin Chapter’s former president and administration, along with current chapter officials, whose continued coordination and support helped bring the project to completion.

He also expressed his appreciation to CHID staff, construction personnel, contractors, and everyone whose hard work contributed to providing the family with their new home.

The turnover reflects the administration’s broader goal of delivering 1,000 homes through collaboration with CHID, the Navajo Housing Authority, the Veterans Administration, chapters, and other partners.

For a family whose roots on this land stretch back more than five decades, receiving a new home means more than improved living conditions. It means being able to remain where generations before them built their lives, surrounded by the people and memories that make this place home. Now, with keys in hand, they have the opportunity to carry that family history forward in a home built to serve them for generations to come.

text:
The Unmaking

The title page is almost bare. Across the top, in letters spaced wide apart, is one word: AGNOTOLOGY. Beneath it, in italics: The Making and Unmaking of Ignorance. Two editors are named, Robert N. Proctor and Londa Schiebinger, and the publisher is Stanford University Press. Most readers stop on the strange first word. The promise is in the subtitle, and it sits in the second to last word: Unmaking.

The book came out in May 2008. Its question is older, and it was set out plainly enough that it can be checked against what came after. Have we gotten better at unmaking ignorance since then, or does the book still describe the world we live in?

Start with the word, because it is younger than it looks. Proctor is a Stanford historian of science. Before this book he had written Cancer Wars, about how politics shapes what we know and don’t know about cancer. He wanted a name for the study of how not knowing gets produced. In a postscript to the book he says where the name came from. In 1992 he put the challenge to the linguist Iain Boal, and Boal came up with the term that spring. The root is the Greek for not knowing. Proctor writes that the word was meant to suggest that not knowing has a history and is made, the way an artifact is made. The first spelling was agnatology. They changed it because agnate already meant something else: a relative on the father’s side.

The book itself took longer. It grew out of two workshops, one at Pennsylvania State University in 2003 and one at Stanford in 2005. The preface opens with one flat sentence: “We live in an age of ignorance.” The first chapter opens with an epigraph from an internal memo at the Brown and Williamson Tobacco Company, dated 1969: “Doubt is our product.”

That memo is the book’s most famous example, but Proctor makes sure it isn’t the only kind. He offers three ways of thinking about ignorance and admits there are other ways to divide the pie. The first is ignorance as a native state, the plain not knowing that every child and every science starts from. That kind is a resource, because it is where curiosity begins. The second is ignorance as a lost realm, or a selective choice. This is knowledge that existed somewhere, or could have existed, and was dropped, never pursued, or left out of the books. The third is ignorance as a strategic ploy, built on purpose, like the tobacco memo’s doubt.

He also warns against the easy reading that all ignorance is bad. He writes that no one needs or wants to know everything all the time. There is even what he calls virtuous ignorance: resistance to dangerous knowledge, or limits placed on it. The book is not against not knowing. It is against not knowing whose causes go unexamined.

The chapters follow his three kinds. Naomi Oreskes and Erik Conway wrote on how climate science became a victim of the Cold War. That is the strategic ploy, and two years later it grew into their book Merchants of Doubt, whose first chapter takes its title from the same tobacco memo. Schiebinger wrote on West Indian abortifacients, plants used to end pregnancies, and on how knowledge of them was lost. That is the lost realm. Peter Galison wrote on modern censorship. The philosopher Charles Mills wrote on what he called white ignorance. And in the fifth chapter, reprinted from the philosophy journal Hypatia, where it first appeared in 2004, Nancy Tuana wrote about orgasm.

Tuana’s chapter is the one that tests the book hardest, because its subject can be checked against a body. Her abstract makes the central claim: “Ignorance is not a simple lack.” Ignorance, she goes on, is often constructed, maintained, and spread, and it is tied to questions of who has authority, who is doubted, and who is silenced. Her first illustration is not about sex at all. American obstetricians, she notes, no longer know how to turn a breech baby. The skill hadn’t been disproved. It had simply stopped being taught. A profession can lose a skill without anyone deciding that it should.

Then she turns to the female body, and the record bears her out. In 1844 the German anatomist Georg Ludwig Kobelt described the erectile tissue that lies beneath the skin around the vaginal opening and below the pubic bone. Most of the clitoris is out of sight, and Kobelt drew much of it. But Helen O’Connell, the Australian urologist whose later work rebuilt this anatomy, notes in her 2005 review that Kobelt used the word clitoris in a limited way. He described the tissue without calling all of it by that name. The knowledge existed in 1844. The name for it was narrower than the thing.

O’Connell learned her anatomy more than a century later, and she has said the clitoris barely appeared in it. She recalls a cross-section of the female pelvis in the 1985 edition of Last’s Anatomy, the textbook she studied, that left it out entirely. In 1998 she published a dissection study with colleagues. In 2005 she published an imaging study and a review in the Journal of Urology. The review’s opening pages say it bluntly. Some recent anatomy textbooks omit a description of the clitoris, while by comparison, pages are devoted to penile anatomy.

This is Proctor’s second kind in its plainest form: a lost realm. Kobelt’s knowledge wasn’t refuted. It wasn’t suppressed by any memo either. It simply didn’t make it into the books that taught the next generations. It fell out of the curriculum, as the breech turn did.

That is where the most tempting story comes in, and it deserves a fair hearing because nearly everyone tells it. Gray’s Anatomy, the most famous anatomy textbook in English, labeled the clitoris in its 1901 edition. The 1948 edition, edited by Charles Mayo Goss, did not. The story has been told as a deliberate erasure: one editor with a pen, and a whole generation of doctors trained without the organ. O’Connell’s own review speaks of active deletion across the twentieth century. The idea goes back largely to a 1995 study by Lisa Jean Moore and Adele Clarke in the journal Feminist Studies, which compared how textbook illustrations labeled female anatomy from about 1900 to 1991.

Here the link fails, or at least fails as it is usually told. In 2022 the anatomist Joel Vilensky took the claim apart in the journal Clinical Anatomy. He argued that Moore and Clarke’s methods cannot be repeated, and that their conclusions weren’t justified because their reading of the sources was biased. That doesn’t settle it. One rebuttal doesn’t end a debate, and nobody has shown what Goss intended. But it moves the Gray’s story from fact to contested claim. And the strongest version of the story never needed a villain. Tuana’s frame works with no one holding scissors. Something can drop out of the record through neglect, embarrassment, narrow naming, or a teaching tradition that focuses on reproduction. In that light, the ignorance is no less real. It is just more ordinary, and harder to fix, because there is no one to blame.

The more striking finding is that the people working to unmake this ignorance have made some of their own along the way. For years, campaigners repeated that the clitoris had 8,000 nerve endings. The number became a rallying cry. When the surgeon Blair Peters went looking for its origin, he traced it to a single line in a book from the 1970s. The International Society for Sexual Medicine says the figure came from a study of cows. In 2022, Peters, Maria Uloko, and Paige Isabey counted nerve fibers in tissue from seven patients undergoing gender-affirming surgery. They found an average of about 5,140 fibers in each of the two dorsal nerves, more than 10,000 in all. The old number was wrong, it was used for the right cause, and it lasted for decades because it was repeated rather than checked.

The same thing happens with the word first. The sexual medicine society’s own history page says the clitoris was not fully described until 2005. A newspaper report in 2026 said O’Connell published the first comprehensive anatomical study in 1998. Each first wipes out Kobelt, the anatomist who started it all. The ignorance Tuana described keeps coming back, even in the sentences meant to correct it.

So, has the gap closed? Measured on the body Tuana wrote about, it is closing, slowly. In March 2026 a team led by Ju Young Lee at Amsterdam University Medical Center posted a preprint with the first detailed three-dimensional map of the nerves inside the clitoris. It was made with high-energy X-rays from a synchrotron, a kind of particle accelerator, sharp enough to trace nerve branches too fine for an MRI to show. The scans suggest that something medical students have been taught is wrong. The main sensory nerve was thought to taper off as it neared the glans. Instead it runs strongly all the way in. Nerves of this kind inside the penis were mapped nearly thirty years earlier. The new map comes from just two donated bodies, both of them postmenopausal women, and it has not yet been peer reviewed. O’Connell, asked about it, said the clitoris “has been deleted intellectually by the medical and scientific community.”

So here is one organ, in 2026, mapped from two bodies, in a study not yet reviewed. That’s progress, and it also measures how far behind the field is.

Look beyond the body and the record is more hopeful about the tools, and less clear about the results. The year after the book came out, Schiebinger launched a project at Stanford called Gendered Innovations. It turned her side of agnotology into methods researchers could use: ways of building sex and gender analysis into the design of a study, so the gap isn’t created in the first place. The European Commission joined in 2011 and the National Science Foundation in 2012. The project helped lay the groundwork for the European Union’s requirement that research proposals in its Horizon 2020 program address the gender dimension. That is the second kind of ignorance, the lost realm, being handled before the realm can be lost.

The field grew too. In 2015 Matthias Gross and Linsey McGoey edited the Routledge International Handbook of Ignorance Studies, and a revised second edition followed in 2022. Its publisher says ignorance, once treated as the absence of knowledge, has become a rapidly growing topic in its own right. The new chapters run from forbidden knowledge in a post-truth era to sexual injustice and willful ignorance. The book’s afterword, “Ignorance Studies: State of the Art,” is by Michael Smithson, who had written on social theories of ignorance in the 2008 volume. One of the book’s own contributors closes its successor.

Even the word escaped. Merriam-Webster now defines agnotology as the study or deliberate cultivation of ignorance. Its examples include a letter to an Idaho newspaper from May 2026 and a sociology journal from the same month. A word that began as a challenge between a historian and a linguist in 1992 now turns up in letters to the editor.

But a word spreading is not ignorance shrinking. None of the works here measures whether naming the tobacco memo’s technique made it less effective the next time it was used. Merchants of Doubt traces the same small group of scientific advisers from tobacco to acid rain to the ozone hole to climate. Its record shows that the strategic ploy survived being exposed at least once. The third kind of ignorance has a name now, and a history, and a library. Whether it has gotten weaker is a different question, and not one this record answers.

The first kind, the native state, can never close, and Proctor never claimed it would. Not knowing is where every question starts. If the unknown ever ran out, there would be nothing left to discover. The book’s first chapter ends with a set of questions for further reflection, and one of them is still open: what other kinds of work does ignorance do?

So the answer to the opening question is split three ways, following the book’s own three kinds. The native state isn’t a gap to close at all. It is the frontier. The lost realm is being recovered piece by piece, in nerve maps and in research rules. But the recovery is slow, and it carries its own errors, like the cow’s nerve count and the firsts that erase Kobelt. And the strategic ploy is better understood than ever, with no sign in this record that it has been beaten.

The title page had the order right. Across the top, the spaced letters still spell AGNOTOLOGY, and beneath them the subtitle puts one task before the other: The Making and Unmaking of Ignorance.

text:
The “LGBTQ Catholic Ministry” Outreach, founded in 2022 by James Martin, S.J., recently offered the following queer-friendly “adaptation” of the Confiteor:

I confess to our Loving God
and to you, my siblings,
That I have fallen short
in my prejudiced thoughts and my biased judgements
in my careless words and my degrading self-talk
in what I have done to cooperate with injustice
and in what I have failed to do to resist it;
Through my fear, through my complacency, through my worst errors.
Therefore I ask all my spiritual ancestors, queer saints,
and you, the human family,
to pray with me,
that together we might build a better tomorrow.
Amen.

This prayer comes from an article called “An LGBTQ Catholic guide to the Mass: Praying the Confiteor,” authored by Ariell Watson Simon, who describes herself as “queer” and lives in Missouri with her “wife.” Her essay “begins a series that explores praying with the Mass from an LGBTQ perspective.”

We hardly need to be theologians to recognize the ideological and deeply secular nature of Simon’s attempt to pervert the words and focus of the Confiteor:

"I confess to almighty God, and to you, my brothers and sisters, that I have greatly sinned, in my thoughts and in my words, in what I have done and in what I have failed to do, through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault. Therefore, I ask Blessed Mary ever virgin, all the angels and saints, and you, my brothers and sisters, to pray for me to the Lord our God."

In the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chysostom, we Eastern Catholics pray the following before receiving Holy Communion:

"O Lord, I believe and profess that you are truly Christ, the Son of the living God, who came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. . . . O God, be merciful to me, a sinner. O God, cleanse me of my sins and have mercy on me. O Lord, forgive me, for I have sinned without number."

The intent, in both the East and the West, is acknowledging that I am a sinner, in constant need of mercy and conversion. Period.

Furthermore, implicit in these prayers is a fact that cannot be erased, even if Martin, Simon, and company seek to do so: it is Jesus Christ and his Church who tell us what is sinful and what is good—not our emotions, passions, or desires, no matter how strongly they press upon us. As Fr. Aidan Nichols writes, “it is not experience we should trust but the transmutation of experience by Scripture and Tradition."

text:
Stand beside a giant steam locomotive, and the scale of America’s railroad age becomes impossible to miss.

At the Oregon Rail Heritage Center in Portland, historic engines, railroad artifacts, and an operating machine shop reveal the engineering and dedication behind these powerful machines. This working museum preserves rail history through the efforts of volunteers who maintain and restore its locomotives. Seasonal train excursions offer another way to experience that heritage; rides require separate tickets.

Little-known fact: Southern Pacific 4449, one of the center’s celebrated locomotives, helped pull the American Freedom Train during the nation’s Bicentennial celebrations, carrying exhibits of American history across the country.

Make this a stop on your Portland itinerary and get close to the remarkable machines that helped connect the Pacific Northwest.

text:
This Day in True Crime — November 9, 1973

Edmund Kemper Sentenced for Eight Murders

A History of Violence

On November 9, 1973, Edmund Kemper, known as the “Co-ed Killer,” was sentenced in Santa Cruz County, California, for eight murders. His victims included six young women, his mother, and her friend. His crimes had terrified the community and exposed a history of violence dating back to his adolescence.

Two Murders at Fifteen

In 1964, at age 15, Kemper shot and killed his paternal grandparents. He was committed to Atascadero State Hospital, where he underwent psychiatric treatment, and was released in 1969. Back in Santa Cruz, he became friendly with local police officers, who had no idea he would become the focus of a major murder investigation.

The Santa Cruz Victims

Between May 1972 and February 1973, Kemper murdered Mary Ann Pesce, Anita Luchessa, Aiko Koo, Cindy Schall, Rosalind Thorpe, and Alice Liu. Several were young women hitchhiking near college campuses when he offered them rides. He killed his victims and dismembered their remains, leaving investigators struggling to connect the disappearances and identify the person responsible.

His Mother and Her Friend

In April 1973, Kemper murdered his mother, Clarnell Strandberg, at their home. He then killed her friend, Sally Hallett. Afterward, he drove to Pueblo, Colorado, and called police on April 24 to confess. His detailed account led investigators to evidence of the killings, ending the search for the killer who had terrorized Santa Cruz.

The Verdict and Sentence

Kemper pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, but psychiatrists testified that he understood his actions. On November 8, 1973, jurors convicted him of eight counts of first-degree murder. The following day, Judge Harry F. Brauer imposed eight concurrent terms of seven years to life. Kemper requested execution, but California’s death penalty was unavailable following a 1972 state Supreme Court ruling.

WALL STREET IS REBOUNDING AFTER THE AI SELLOFF. BUT HAS ANYTHING FUNDAMENTALLY CHANGED?
US equities rebounded sharply on Monday after last week's technology-led selloff, with semiconductor stocks leading the recovery.
But what caught my attention wasn't simply the rally. It was the divergence within the AI trade.
THE MARKET REBOUND
🔹 S&P 500: +2.3%
🔹 Nasdaq Composite: +2.6%
🔹 Dow Jones: +2.2%
🔹 Semiconductor Index: More than +6%
🔹 AMD $AMD: Approximately +13%
🔹 Broadcom $AVGO: Nearly +9%
🔹 Nvidia $NVDA: Down approximately 6%
These figures are Monday intraday snapshots, not verified closing prices.
WHAT'S CHANGING
Falling oil prices may be easing some inflation concerns, while investors appear willing to buy technology stocks following last week's decline.
But Nvidia's weakness stands out.
Seeing semiconductor equipment companies, competing chipmakers and AI cloud infrastructure stocks rally while Nvidia sells off suggests investors are becoming more selective within the AI trade.
That doesn't prove AI demand is weakening, nor does it establish that Nvidia's decline is entirely company-specific.
The underlying questions surrounding AI infrastructure spending, financing costs and returns on capital haven't disappeared.
MY TAKE
I'm still bullish on the long-term AI infrastructure buildout.
That conviction hasn't changed because of a market correction, and it doesn't become stronger simply because stocks rebound.
For me, the important distinction remains between companies benefiting from rising AI demand and companies converting that demand into sustainable shareholder returns.
Hyperscalers need to demonstrate that capital spending is producing incremental revenue and cash flow.
Neoclouds need to prove that contracted capacity can support financing costs without excessive dilution.
Semiconductor companies need to sustain pricing, margins and competitive positioning as capacity expands.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
Upcoming economic data and earnings from CoreWeave $CRWV, Applied Materials $AMAT and Cisco $CSCO will offer further evidence about demand, spending and business execution.
I'll be watching utilisation, margins, capital expenditure, financing and free cash flow.
The AI opportunity remains significant. But the next phase of the trade will increasingly reward financial execution, not simply exposure to AI demand.

text:
Some Copper Foil (CF) chatter today:

Furukawa Electric announced today that it will approximately double its copper foil production capacity for AI servers. The expansion will take place at its facilities in Nikko City, Tochigi Prefecture, and Taiwan, with completion targeted for the end of fiscal year 2029.  The target is a copper foil called "F0X-WS foil," which has an extremely smooth surface. It is used to achieve high-speed, high-capacity signal transmission. The investment amount and the production capacity after the expansion have not been disclosed.  

Mitsui Mining & Smelting is also increasing production of "VSP," a copper foil with similar characteristics. The company plans to increase its monthly production capacity to 1,400 tons in fiscal year 2030, a 67% increase compared to fiscal year 2026. Amidst strong AI demand, companies are successively increasing production.

https://t.co/ZZ4UB0JpUZ

🔽 🔽 🔽

We see continued material-cost pressure for AI server boards, with Goldman Sachs expecting copper foil supplier Co-Tech to raise prices about 10% across its foil products in Q4 versus Q3.  

Co-Tech (8358 TT) makes copper foil for circuit boards. Its high-end, low-roughness foil helps reduce signal loss in the high-speed connections used by AI servers and network switches.  

Goldman reports that Co-Tech targets effective monthly capacity for HVLP3-and-above foil of approximately 833 metric tons by the end of 2027, 1,666 by the end of 2028 and 2,500 by the end of 2029. That compares with roughly 200–250 metric tons a month currently.  

Multiple customers have already secured capacity in the planned expansion, according to Goldman. The bank still expects the additions to fall short of demand from key customers.  

For board makers, a larger capacity plan therefore offers limited evidence of near-term cost relief. That will depend on how quickly usable supply grows relative to orders.

Welcome to Monday's KelticMan Daily Irish Briefing, bringing you the latest developments from Ireland, the political headlines, and the stories making an impact at home and abroad.

🇮🇪 IRELAND TODAY — THE BIG STORIES

1. PUBLIC SECTOR STRIKE: LAST-MINUTE TALKS

The Government has offered public sector workers a 10.5% pay increase over the coming years, with some lower-paid workers potentially receiving increases of up to 17.8%.

Tánaiste Simon Harris says there is a crucial window to reach an agreement before Thursday’s planned nationwide strike. Schools could close and public services face significant disruption.

The unions must now decide whether the improved offer goes far enough.

2. DUBLIN PREPARES FOR MAJOR EU SUMMIT

Ireland is preparing to welcome European leaders this week as part of its EU Presidency.

The gathering will bring significant international attention to Dublin, but security concerns and traffic disruption are expected. Gardaí and the Defence Forces are preparing for a major security operation.

🚨 U.S. SPACE FORCE & MILITARY AI: WHAT THE PUBLIC SHOULD KNOW 🇺🇸🛰️

On November 9, 2026, U.S. Space Force highlighted a Department of the Air Force initiative to expand what officials now call Super Intelligence (SI) across 15 operational mission domains.

This is not simply another AI announcement. It reflects a broader effort to move advanced AI systems from experimentation into military operations.

WHAT HAS BEEN CONFIRMED?

The Department of the Air Force released its Artificial Intelligence Strategy in April 2026. On October 27, officials outlined an implementation structure, publicly reported November 5.

The initiative involves:

• 15 operational domains spanning Air Force and Space Force missions, including intelligence, cyber, nuclear operations, and human resources.

• A designated general officer or senior civilian overseeing each domain.

• AI-assisted intelligence analysis, military decision-making, logistics, predictive maintenance, training, and operational planning.

• A three-level AI literacy program being developed for Airmen and Guardians.

The April strategy explicitly discusses shortening the time between detecting a target and engaging it, along with expanding autonomous capabilities and human-machine teaming.

THAT IS SIGNIFICANT.

The department is not merely discussing AI as an administrative assistant. Its strategy includes potential applications directly connected to combat operations.

WHAT ELSE DID OUR RESEARCH FIND?

A public federal contracting solicitation from the 16th Air Force, FA7037-23-S-C0001, includes a category for Super Intelligence technologies.

That solicitation seeks innovative capabilities, but it does not establish which companies have received contracts specifically under the new 15-domain initiative.

The Air Force’s published strategy also states that it will prioritize AI vendors whose systems permit any lawful military use.

WHAT IS STILL UNKNOWN?

We could not locate a complete publicly released version of the detailed 15-domain implementation plan.

We also could not establish:

• The full list of all 15 domains and their assigned leaders.

• Which private AI companies will provide every system.

• When each capability will become operational.

• The specific safeguards and human authorization procedures for every combat application.

These questions matter.

Military AI can offer advantages in intelligence, defense, logistics, and response times. But the public also has a legitimate interest in understanding how advanced systems are tested, governed, and held accountable, particularly when their applications may involve lethal force.

One important distinction: The term Super Intelligence in these announcements should not be mistaken for proof that the military has developed a genuinely superhuman AI.

THE DOCUMENTS ARE PUBLIC. THE COMPLETE OPERATIONAL PICTURE IS NOT.

This is not a claim of wrongdoing or a prediction about what comes next.

It is a documented modernization initiative with important unanswered questions.

Research should begin with the primary sources, not speculation.

Stay curious. Read the documents. Ask questions. And when the evidence stops, it’s perfectly acceptable to say, “I don’t know yet.”

text:
#PrinceOnThisDay - Jam of the Year at The Crown: The Full Cincinnati Gig

On 9 November 1997, Prince—then performing as the Love Symbol and billed as The Artist—delivered a roughly two-hour Jam of the Year Tour show at The Crown in Cincinnati, Ohio. The New Power Generation lineup featured Prince (vocals, guitar, bass, piano, GoldAxxe, percussion), Kirk Johnson (drums), Rhonda Smith (bass, vocals), Morris Hayes (keyboards), Kat Dyson (guitar), Mike Scott (guitar), and Marva King (vocals, percussion). No guests appeared.

The night opened with the multilingual “Please take your seats” DAT intro, then “Jam of the Year,” the James Brown cover “Talkin’ Loud and Sayin’ Nothing,” and “Let’s Work” (with an instrumental coda of “Rock ’N’ Roll Is Alive! (And It Lives in Minneapolis)”). Classics followed with “Purple Rain” and “Little Red Corvette.” “Get Yo Groove On” interpolated “Six,” while “The Most Beautiful Girl in the World” nodded to “The Glamorous Life.” The energy continued through “Face Down,” “The Ride,” and “The Cross.”

A soulful mid-section brought the Joan Osborne/Eric Bazilian cover “One of Us,” then a medley-rich “Do Me, Baby” weaving in “Adore,” “Insatiable,” “Scandalous,” and “How Come U Don’t Call Me Anymore.” “Sexy M.F.” included an instrumental of “♥ or $,” leading into “If I Was Your Girlfriend.” The piano set offered “Delirious,” “Girls & Boys,” “Darling Nikki,” “Diamonds and Pearls,” and “The Beautiful Ones,” followed by “How Come U Don’t Call Me Anymore,” “Take Me With U,” and “Raspberry Beret” (ending with a “Mr. Happy” instrumental coda). The encore closed with “(Eye Like) Funky Music” and the “Baby I’m a Star” / “1999” medley.

Attendance reached 8,715 of 14,700 capacity; tickets were $65, $45, and $35 (on sale from 25 October). An afterparty followed but no aftershow performance. The gig captured the late-1997 tour’s signature blend of Emancipation-era freedom, deep cuts, and high-energy hits on a Cincinnati stage with early-career roots for Prince.
@prince

text:
#PrinceOnThisDay - This Is the Jam of the Year: Soundcheck Secrets at The Crown 🟣🎸

On 9 November 1997, ahead of the Jam of the Year Tour stop at The Crown in Cincinnati, Ohio, Prince (as the Love Symbol / The Artist) and the New Power Generation locked in a focused soundcheck. ⚡

The same tight lineup that powered the full show was present: 🎤🎸🎹 Prince on vocals, guitar, bass, piano, GoldAxxe guitar & percussion 🥁 Kirk Johnson on drums 🎸 Rhonda Smith on bass & vocals 🎹 Morris Hayes on keyboards 🎸 Kat Dyson & Mike Scott on guitar 🎤 Marva King on vocals & percussion
No guests joined them. ✨

Documented work centered on four tracks that balanced fresh Emancipation material with deeper catalog pieces: 🎵 “Jam of the Year” (the set-opening statement of freedom) 🎵 “Face Down” 🎵 “The Cross” 🎵 “The Ballad of Dorothy Parker”
These choices let the band dial in the muscular funk grooves, spiritual weight, and nuanced storytelling that defined the era. “Dorothy Parker” pointed to the piano-driven intimacy that would later appear in the main set, while “Jam of the Year” and “Face Down” sharpened the high-energy opening and mid-show drive. 🔥

The Crown (formerly Riverfront Coliseum) offered a large arena canvas, and the soundcheck ensured the multi-instrumental flexibility Prince relied on would translate cleanly. Tickets had gone on sale 25 October at 10 a.m., with the advertised start set for 8:00 p.m. By dialing in these songs early, the band set the stage for a roughly 120-minute performance that drew 8,715 fans. 👑

The soundcheck remains a quiet but telling window into how the post-Warner NPG prepared the night’s mix of fresh funk and classic depth. 🟣
#NPG #Emancipation @prince

text:
🚨 MAKE SURE YOU READ THIS!!!

🇬🇧 “YOU ARE MY ENEMY.” — VETERAN ALLEGES THESE WORDS WERE SPOKEN BY A LABOUR MP. IF TRUE, IS THIS ACCEPTABLE?

If true, I am absolutely shocked and disgusted to read the account of how Kevin Gray, a military veteran and the newly appointed Chairman of Reform UK Blackpool North and Fleetwood, says he was treated by Labour MP Lorraine Beavers.

According to Kevin, he was approached by the MP while proudly wearing his Northern Ireland service medal.

He says she angrily confronted him over his involvement with Reform UK, using words including “Racist”, “Bigot”, “Fascist” and “Trumpism”.

Despite this, Kevin says he remained calm and extended an olive branch, asking:

“Can we get a coffee sometime without alcohol? I am not your enemy.”

Her alleged response?

“YOU ARE MY ENEMY.”

Let that sink in.

If Kevin’s account is accurate, a veteran wearing his service medal offered a civil conversation to his elected Member of Parliament, only to allegedly be told that he was her enemy.

Is this really the standard of behaviour we should expect from someone elected to represent ALL constituents, regardless of their political beliefs?

On Sunday, I had the privilege of laying a wreath at Blackpool Cenotaph as Reform UK’s Group Leader.

Earlier that morning, I stood alongside my fellow ward councillor, Shaun Brookes, who represents Labour. We put politics aside, as any decent elected representative should.

At the Cenotaph, I also spoke respectfully with the Labour MP for Blackpool South, the Labour Leader of Blackpool Council and the Leader of the Conservative Group.

Different political parties. Different opinions. But mutual respect and dignity throughout.

That is what Remembrance should be about.

We do not have to agree politically to treat one another with basic human decency.

Kevin served his country. He has every right to hold political opinions, join a democratic political party and participate in public life without being subjected to personal hostility.

And frankly, whether someone is a veteran or not, no constituent should be treated as an enemy simply because they vote differently.

I sincerely hope Lorraine Beavers MP reflects on Kevin’s account and takes the opportunity to respond.

Because public office comes with responsibility. You represent your constituents — not just those who agree with you.

We should be setting an example of tolerance, dignity and respect, particularly during Remembrance.

Political disagreement is democracy. Personal hostility is not leadership.

Kevin, thank you for your service. You have my respect and support. 🇬🇧

Assuming this account is correct, she should apologise immediately!

Lest We Forget. 🌺

It has come to our attention that letters sent by BlueCross and BlueShield of Tennessee to their TennCare (BlueCare) customers suggest their customers’ physicians may not be accessible in the unfortunate event that Ballad Health is no longer a part of the BlueCare Network.  

This is not accurate.   

Individuals who access their coverage through TennCare may choose another plan, and may, of course, keep their doctors. Ballad Health and our Ballad Health Medical Associates physicians have been, and remain, in-network with all other TennCare plans being offered in the region. These plans include UnitedHealthcare Community Plan of Tennessee and Wellpoint Tennessee.

Ballad Health continues to negotiate in good faith with BlueCross BlueShield of Tennessee with the goal of finding agreement in all plans, including commercial, exchange, Medicare Advantage and BlueCare.

Anyone eligible for TennCare who receives their coverage through TennCare will not lose TennCare regardless of the outcome of these negotiations. If Ballad Health and BlueCross BlueShield of Tennessee fail to reach an agreement on the BlueCross BlueShield TennCare plan (BlueCare) by Jan. 1, 2027, the customer may switch plans and will not lose access to their provider or physician of choice.

If any TennCare customer has questions about access to their physician, they should discuss this with their physician or contact Ballad Health at 833-8-BALLAD (225523).

text:
$LCII Q3 2026 earnings: LCI earns more per sale, but October sales fell 10%

LCI Industries makes the parts inside recreational vehicles, and it now earns more on fewer of them. Sales fell 4% from a year ago because RV manufacturers built fewer trailers, yet profit per share excluding one-offs still climbed. Interim chief executive Johnny Sirpilla credited sourcing work and cost reductions, and said they leave the group able to meet its revised full-year plan. But October sales came in 10% under last October, and by our math the plan leaves fourth-quarter sales about 13% weaker than last year's.

• Sales: $𝟗𝟗𝟐.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (-4% from a year ago, or -5% without acquired businesses)
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟐.𝟐𝟏 ($1.97 a year ago)
• Operating profit margin, excluding one-offs: 𝟖.𝟑% (7.3% a year ago)
• Full-year sales outlook: 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐨 $𝟑.𝟗-𝟒.𝟎 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (the top of the range came down $100 million)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse, because LCI's own plan now points to a much softer finish to the year. Etzkorn took $100 million off the top of the sales range and 25 cents off the profit range, and October trading was the weakest month she has described all year. The good news: cost savings widened margins again, and the repair-parts business grew 6%. Running above its own margin range for a third quarter says that range was cautious, not that RV demand has turned.

The question now is whether 2027 brings more RV production or a second year of decline. Sirpilla says dealers hold lean inventory and will restock once buyers return, while retail sales of travel trailers dropped 17% in the quarter and show no sign of a turn. Etzkorn promised the 2027 shipment forecast with the fourth-quarter results, and that number settles it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐂𝐮𝐭𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝐅𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐏𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
LCI Industries supplies the chassis, windows, furniture and appliances that go inside recreational vehicles, and most of what it sells is priced off steel and aluminium. Interim chief executive Johnny Sirpilla put the quarter down to "the ongoing pursuit of operational efficiencies and strategic cost reductions", a programme that now runs to eight to ten plant closures.

• Cost of making the products: 73.4% of sales, against 75.6% a year ago
• Sourcing and cost actions: $15.5 million of extra profit at the OEM business, $2.6 million in the aftermarket
• Prices tied to commodity indexes: $18.4 million of extra profit at the OEM business
• Operating profit margin excluding one-offs: 8.3%, against 7.3% a year ago
• Profit per share excluding one-offs: $2.21, against $1.97

The savings matter because they arrived without any help from volume. Lippert built and shipped less, so each fixed cost spread over fewer units, and that squeeze alone cost the OEM business $12.0 million of factory overhead. Sirpilla told investors the plant work remains "on pace and on target", with the last closures finishing this quarter.

What to watch: gross margin in the fourth quarter, reported in February. The supplier has held it near 27% for two quarters while sales declined; a slide back toward the 22% of last year's fourth quarter would say the cost work has run its course.

🟢 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐁𝐨𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐛𝐲 $𝟏𝟒𝟏 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧
Lippert has spent this downturn paying down debt rather than buying shares. Net borrowings, meaning what it owes minus the cash it holds, stood at $607 million at the end of September against $748 million a year earlier. The company also repaid the last $92 million of a convertible bond in cash when the bond matured in May.

That leaves borrowings at 1.4 times yearly profit before interest, tax and write-downs, down from 1.8 times in January. Finance chief Lillian Etzkorn calls that the conservative end of her 1.5-to-2.0 target range, and she put total available funding at $841 million, split between cash and an undrawn credit line.

What to watch: whether any shares are bought back before the merger closes. Lippert still holds $200 million of authorisation and used none of it in the first nine months, so leaving it unused keeps the cash inside the business that Patrick Industries will inherit.

🟢 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐚𝐢𝐫 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐁𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 $𝟏 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫
The Aftermarket segment sells replacement parts, towing gear and accessories to dealers, repair shops and vehicle owners directly, rather than to the factories that build new vehicles. Sirpilla said "nearly 2 million RVs on the road are entering the repair and replacement cycle over the next few years" and that this business has "grown to nearly $1 billion in annual revenue".

Sales reached $260 million in the quarter, 6% above last year, on higher volumes of towing and truck accessories sold into the car market. Lippert is also moving its Ranch Hand operation in Texas into a plant that will "increase our capacity by about 2.5x", and it enters that building with "20 weeks of backlog".

This earns money when nobody buys a new trailer, and at 13.0% excluding one-offs its operating margin beat the rest of the group. The caution is that growth is cooling, from 7.6% over nine months to 5.6% in the quarter, while tariffs, steel and freight took 1.1 points off the reported margin.

What to watch: aftermarket sales growth in February, set against the 7.6% of the first nine months. Management expects car-market gains "to continue to help mitigate overall decline in all aftermarket channels", so a reading below 5% would mean those gains no longer cover the RV side.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝟏𝟎% 𝐚𝐬 𝐑𝐕 𝐎𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤
Travel trailers and fifth-wheels remain Lippert's biggest market, and that market is contracting faster than the diversified parts of the group are expanding. Sales of components for those vehicles dropped 18% to $338 million, while industry production of them declined 13%. LCI blamed "a change in RV sales mix toward more lower content single axle travel trailers" as well.

Retail buyers are the deeper problem. Dealers sold 75,600 towable units in the quarter, 17% fewer than a year earlier, and they ran their stock down by another 18,200 units instead of reordering. The filing attributes weak retail demand to "inflation and higher interest rates impacting retail consumer discretionary spending".

That cuts against the company's own framing. Sirpilla said the quarter's progress and margin work "position us to achieve our updated full-year outlook", yet October sales came in near $341 million, about 10% under last October. By our math the full-year range leaves fourth-quarter sales roughly 13% below last year.

What to watch: the 2027 shipment forecast, which Etzkorn said arrives with the fourth-quarter results. A figure near this year's 285,000 to 295,000 units would mean a second year at the bottom, and cost savings would again have to carry earnings on their own.

🔴 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐏𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐥𝐢𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐋𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫
Content per unit is the dollar value of Lippert parts in an average new travel trailer, measured across twelve months, and it has been the offset to falling volumes. It reached $5,733 in the September quarter, 6% above a year earlier but below the $5,831 reported three months before that.

The growth rate shows the change more clearly. Content growth ran above 11% in each of the previous three quarters, and it halved to 6% in this one as last year's price increases lapped. Asked about the shift to cheaper trailers, Sirpilla said "we've seen consistency on that trend on the single axle" and expects more of them next year.

This matters because content growth is what keeps revenue from falling as fast as unit volumes. Single-axle trailers carry fewer and cheaper parts, so every one sold instead of a twin-axle model pulls the average down. With industry volumes off 13% and content adding 6%, the arithmetic has turned against the components maker.

What to watch: content per towable unit in February, against $5,733 today. Another slip from one quarter to the next would mean price increases have stopped covering the shift to cheaper trailers, and RV revenue would then track industry units one for one.

🔴 𝐖𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐀𝐭𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐆𝐚𝐢𝐧
Lippert earned 2.2 percentage points more gross margin than a year ago and kept almost none of it. Warehouse and transportation costs, the expense of moving parts between more than 100 plants and out to customers, reached 6.0% of sales against 4.8% a year earlier.

Spending on that line climbed 20% while sales declined 4%. Selling and administrative costs took another 0.7 points of sales, partly because $5.1 million of merger fees sit there. Together the two lines absorbed 1.9 points, which is why reported operating margin improved by only 0.3 points.

These costs are not all temporary. LCI said the aftermarket margin suffered from "investments in capacity and distribution to support the Aftermarket Segment", and the new Ranch Hand plant adds further distribution space. Rising fuel prices land here too, and Lippert cannot index them to customers the way it indexes steel.

What to watch: warehouse and transportation costs as a share of sales in February. Last year's fourth quarter ran at 5.5%, so a reading above that level would mean distribution spending keeps climbing into the seasonally weakest quarter of the year.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Five standing risks got no resolution in these materials. Each one has a specific place where the next reading will appear, and three of them land before the merger with Patrick Industries can close.

• Merger approval: LCI shareholders vote on November 18, antitrust clearance is still outstanding, and the agreement carries a $94.2 million break fee each way.
• Tariff refunds: $114.6 million of the $119.3 million claim is in hand, $31.2 million is still owed to customers, and the outcome turns on "the outcome of the U. S. government's appeal of the CIT order".
• Index pricing: Etzkorn said "it passes through both if costs go up and the prices reduce as commodities come down", so this year's price gains reverse when steel and aluminium fall.
• Leadership: Sirpilla has carried the interim title since June 3, and the board has named no permanent successor.
• RV shipment outlook: narrowed to 285,000-295,000 units, the first quarter in four without a cut to the middle; one more steady quarter would start to settle it.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐕𝐨𝐭𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐚𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐤 𝐌𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐫
LCI shareholders vote on the all-stock merger with Patrick Industries on November 18, and they would end up owning about 48% of the combined group. Sirpilla said the board reviewed an approach from Monomoy Capital and "ultimately concluded that it was not superior to the proposed merger with Patrick, so we declined it". He promised "approximately $150 million of net run rate cost synergies within 3 years of closing".

𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐋𝐢𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐭 𝐒𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐈𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠
The RV slump is not an isolated case. For both transportation and marine, Lippert says it "expect market to be down low single digits" this year, and it puts housing "down low to mid single digits". The group notes that "2026 manufactured housing unit shipments were down about 3% through August". In the aftermarket it counts on car-market gains to offset declines elsewhere.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟖𝟓.𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Unpaid customer bills grew 5.9% from a year ago while sales declined 4.2%. Measured in days of sales, they have climbed for four quarters, from 29.4 to 31.3. LCI points to seasonally higher sales earlier in the year; either way, customers are taking two days longer to pay.

𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟑.𝟕 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐚 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫  ⇘ decelerating
Stock is moving more slowly than at any point in two years: 3.7 turns a year against 4.2 a year ago and 4.2 at the end of December. The absolute figure still came down, to $746.7 million from $809.1 million in December, because raw materials fell $52.1 million.

𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟑.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Spending on plant and equipment equalled 1.4% of sales, below the 1-to-2% the group says replacement alone normally takes. Nine-month outlays of $41.9 million sit well inside the $55-65 million full-year range, so the fourth quarter carries $13-23 million of it, close to last year's $14.6 million.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬: 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 $𝟑𝟒𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
New. LCI expects October sales about 10% under last October, a steeper fall than the 4% recorded in the third quarter. Lippert names one month ahead at each set of results, and the July figure it gave three months ago was also 4% below the prior year. The fourth quarter is its weakest season.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐑𝐕 𝐰𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬: 𝟐𝟖𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟗𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐬  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from 280,000 to 300,000 units
Unchanged in the middle, narrower at the edges. Management cut this range at three straight sets of results, from 335,000-350,000 units in February, and held the middle this time. By our math, 224,500 units shipped through September leave 60,500 to 70,500 for the fourth quarter. A year earlier the industry shipped 73,100 in that quarter.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟑.𝟗 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 $𝟒.𝟎 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $3.9 billion to $4.1 billion
Cut. Etzkorn took $100 million off the top, so the middle of the range falls to $3.95 billion, about 4% below 2025. By our math that leaves fourth-quarter sales of $760 million to $860 million, roughly 13% under last year at the middle. It is the third reduction in four quarters: $4.25 billion, then $4.0 billion, now $3.95 billion.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐚𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧: 𝟕.𝟓% 𝐭𝐨 𝟖.𝟎%  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from 7.5% to 8.0%
Unchanged. Nine months in, Lippert has run at 8.8%, above the top of the range, so the plan now implies a soft finish. By our math the fourth quarter lands near 3.7%, against 4.2% a year ago. Seasonality explains part of that, because this is always the weakest quarter. Holding the range after three quarters above it leaves obvious room.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐚𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐏𝐒: $𝟖.𝟐𝟓 𝐭𝐨 $𝟖.𝟓𝟎  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $8.25 to $8.75
Cut at the top. Etzkorn said "we have tightened the range to $8.25 to $8.50", taking 25 cents off the upper end. With $7.50 already earned in nine months, the fourth quarter carries 75 cents to $1.00, against 89 cents a year ago. The middle has slipped twice since February, from $9.00 to $8.38.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬: $𝟓𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 $𝟔𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from $55 million to $65 million
Unchanged for a second quarter. Outlays reached $41.9 million through September, so the range leaves $13-23 million for the fourth quarter. LCI says the money goes into automation and lean projects. The upper bound had already been trimmed twice this year, from $80 million in February to $75 million and then $65 million.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: $𝟏𝟏𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 $𝟏𝟐𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from $115 million to $125 million
Unchanged. Nine-month depreciation and amortisation of $89.6 million points at the middle of the range. Both charges are drifting down as intangible assets from older acquisitions finish being written off, which flatters operating profit slightly next year.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤-𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞: $𝟐𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 $𝟐𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $24 million to $27 million
Cut $2 million at both ends. Nine-month expense of $17.0 million already sits near the lower bound. Forfeitures explain much of it: 168,585 performance share units lapsed after the June change of chief executive, more than three times the number granted this year.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐮𝐚𝐥 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞: 𝟐𝟓% 𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟕%  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from 25% to 27%
Unchanged. The nine-month rate matched last year at 26.1%, comfortably mid-range. The third quarter ran hotter, at 26.7% against 25.6%, because a benefit tied to company-owned life insurance policies shrank and LCI wrote off executive pay it cannot deduct.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

text:
🛰️ Larry Page reportedly thinks 99.999% of future compute will end up in space. The number is striking, but its sourcing matters.

On the November 4 episode of Invest Like the Best, Patrick O'Shaughnessy recounted a story he had heard: someone asked Page how much computing would eventually be orbital, and Page supposedly answered "five nines."

That is a secondhand anecdote. The account gives no deadline or precise definition of which computing workloads it covers. Elon Musk subsequently endorsed the prediction on X.

🏗️ Podcast guest Martin Casado argued that regulation could make orbit attractive. He cited 500 proposed U.S. legislative measures aimed at stopping data-center construction, including in Texas. That figure remains his claim; I haven't independently verified the count or scope of those proposals.

☀️ The appeal is understandable: suitable orbits offer near-continuous solar exposure and avoid some terrestrial land and grid constraints. Google is already testing the underlying hardware through Project Suncatcher, reporting its first AI response from a data-center-class TPU in orbit on October 30.

🧊 Scaling that up still requires solving difficult engineering and economic problems:

▪️ Heat rejection through radiators in a vacuum.
▪️ Radiation tolerance and reliable hardware operation.
▪️ High-bandwidth links between satellites.
▪️ Launch costs that make the complete system competitive.

Orbital compute is becoming an engineering experiment with measurable milestones. The 99.999% figure remains a speculative long-term forecast. The next useful evidence will be sustained workloads, reliable interconnects, and demonstrated costs.

Podcast: https://t.co/5ppUQwe2TD
Research: https://t.co/g7AZWC3gvW

text:
On May 2, 1995, 15 year old Kiplyn Davis left home for school in Spanish Fork, Utah.

She was a sophomore at Spanish Fork High. She made it to school that day.

She never came home.

At first, police treated her as a runaway. Kiplyn's parents knew better. But the delay cost them precious time.

Months passed. Then years. No trace of Kiplyn anywhere.

In 2003, eight years after she vanished, Kiplyn's father sat down and wrote a letter to the U.S. Attorney for Utah, begging for help.

It worked. A federal grand jury opened an investigation.

And investigators ran straight into what they called a wall of silence. A group of Kiplyn's former classmates, now grown men, had told stories that didn't line up. Five of them were eventually charged with federal perjury for lying to the grand jury.

One of them became the center of the case. His name was Timmy Brent Olsen.

His story kept changing. First, he said he saw Kiplyn walk over a hillside in Spanish Fork Canyon with another teenager, and only the other teen came back. Later, he said he'd driven up the canyon with Kiplyn and a friend, and the friend killed her with a rock.

Olsen was convicted of perjury and served time in federal prison. He led investigators into the canyon to where he said she was buried.

They found nothing.

Utah charged Olsen with murder. Another former classmate was charged with murder too. That charge was later dropped, and he pleaded no contest to a lesser charge.

In 2011, a month before his murder trial, Olsen took a plea deal. He pleaded guilty to manslaughter. Prosecutors had seven witnesses who said they'd heard him brag that he killed her.

But even in his plea, he stuck to his story. He claimed someone else hit Kiplyn in the head with a rock. He said he only helped hide her body, under some trees in the canyon, and later move it somewhere else.

He would never say who that someone was. Or where Kiplyn is now.

At his sentencing, Kiplyn's father begged him to tell them where his daughter is.

He got 1 to 15 years.

In 2021, Utah offered him a way out. A new law allowed early parole for killers who help find their victims' remains. At his parole hearing, he said he'd done everything he could.

He served every day of his 15 years.

This February, Timmy Olsen walked out of prison. No parole. No supervision. Because he pleaded guilty, he can never be tried again for her death.

31 years later, Kiplyn's parents still don't know where their daughter is buried.

The man who says he helped hide her body is free.

Why won't he tell them where she is?

text:
My friend Kuroki has taught welding for 26 years, at a technical high school in Japan.

Last spring, he watched six hundred people in Mississippi stand up and scream for a welder.

He still can't tell the story without stopping halfway.

Here's why.

In Japan, your life gets sorted at fifteen. One entrance exam. The top kids go to academic high schools. The kids who don't make it go to schools like Kuroki's.

Nobody says it out loud. Everybody knows.

Every spring, high schools hang banners: how many seniors got into which university. Kuroki's seniors go to shipyards and factories. Nobody hangs a banner for that.

For 26 years, he has watched his students cross the graduation stage in silence. Head down. A small bow. Like they were apologizing for where they were going.

Last spring, his school sent him to a high school on the Mississippi Gulf Coast. A town that builds ships. His job was to study their welding program.

Three days in, the welding teacher, a big man named Boone, said, "You picked a good week. Thursday's Signing Day."

Kuroki had seen Signing Day on TV. A star quarterback. A table. Three college hats.

That is not what he saw.

The gym was packed. The band was there. The cheerleaders were there.

At the front was a long table with a red tablecloth. No college hats.

Welding helmets. Hard hats. A pipe wrench. An electrician's tool belt.

Behind every chair stood a man in work boots and a necktie he clearly did not enjoy. The shipyard. The electric company. A plumbing outfit. An air conditioning company.

The principal took the microphone and read the first name like an NFL draft pick.

"TYLER KREBS. Pipe welder. Signing with the shipyard."

Air horns. Cowbells. Tyler's grandmother held up a poster board: MY GRANDBABY BUILDS SHIPS.

The football coach was in the front row, screaming louder than anyone. For a welder.

Next was a girl, maybe five-foot-one. Kinsley Ladner. Electrician. The old electricians in the bleachers were on their feet before the principal finished her name.

Kuroki leaned over to Boone.

"These are your top students?"

Boone didn't answer right away.

"Buddy, these are the kids who keep the lights on. Who else are we gonna stand up for?"

Then came a boy named Jace.

Everybody in that gym knew two things about Jace. He was the best welder in the county. And he couldn't read very well. He'd been held back in third grade. Kids had called him things ever since.

He sat down. He picked up the letter. He stared at it.

Six hundred people went quiet.

Boone walked over, crouched down beside him, and read it into his ear. Quietly. Line by line. The whole gym waited. Nobody looked at a phone. Nobody coughed.

Jace nodded. Picked up the pen. Signed his name.

Kuroki says he has never heard a sound like the one that gym made. He felt it in the bench.

Jace's father, a shipfitter for thirty years, came down out of the bleachers in his work shirt, pulled off his own welding cap, and put it on his son's head.

Afterward, Kuroki shook Jace's hand and asked him how it felt.

"Sir," Jace said, "that's the first time anybody ever clapped for me in a school."

Kuroki excused himself and went outside to stand by his rental car for a while.

In Japan, high school seniors who are going to work get their job offers in the fall.

Last month, Kuroki's seniors got theirs.

So he held his school's first Signing Day. In a classroom. With a red tablecloth from the 100-yen shop and three welding helmets.

The principal agreed to read the names. Kuroki asked him to read them like a draft pick. The principal practiced in his office. Everyone could hear him through the wall.

The parents came in work clothes. They didn't know the rules. They bowed. They clapped politely. Like at a funeral.

Then the principal read the name of a boy going to the same shipyard where his father has welded for 31 years.

The father stood up. He is not a loud man. He had skipped every school event for three years. Work.

He shouted his son's name. Once. Full volume.

For one second, nobody moved. Then the whole room was on its feet.

His son looked at the floor. Then at his father. Then he did something Kuroki had not seen a student do on graduation day in 26 years.

He lifted his head.

Afterward, the boy came up to Kuroki and said, in Japanese, almost exactly what Jace had said.

"Sensei, nobody has ever clapped for me at school."

Kuroki excused himself and went outside to stand by his car for a while. Again.

He had also ordered twelve air horns from America. The vice principal confiscated eleven.

Nobody knows how the twelfth one got into a grandmother's purse.

text:
The Flagler County Sheriff’s Office has arrested Melissa Jester, 41, of Bunnell after an investigation determined she used forged property deeds to steal ownership of three vacant lots in Palm Coast and then sold one of them for nearly $30,000.

On Aug. 27, the victim reported to the Sheriff’s Office that property deeds to three vacant lots she had owned in Palm Coast for about 20 years had been transferred to someone else without her authorization.

FCSO General Assignment Unit detectives determined that on June 29, 2026 deed transfer paperwork was mailed to the Flagler County Clerk of Courts, transferring all three lots to Florida Ohana Homes LLC, a company owned by Jester. The victim’s signature on the deed had been forged.

Jester paid the filing fees with a money order she purchased on June 18 under a different name at an Amscot automated teller on Palm Coast Parkway, which does not require identification.

On Sept. 10, Jester, as the company’s managing member, sold one of the lots to an unsuspecting buyer. Surveillance video from the UPS Store on Belle Terre Parkway captured Jester signing the warranty deed and having it notarized. The title company then wired $29,970 from the sale to the company’s Bank of America account.

Jester later transferred $8,000 from the company account to her personal VyStar Credit Union account, where the money was spent on hotel stays and purchases around Flagler County.

Detectives seized more than $14,000 from the company’s Bank of America account and more than $6,000 from Jester’s VyStar account, the remaining balance in each account. In total, more than $20,000 was recovered.

“Most of the deed fraud we see is run by scammers hiding in another state or another country. This one lived in Bunnell and signed the closing papers in front of a security camera in Palm Coast,” said Sheriff Rick Staly. “Our detectives followed the trail of forgeries and money and recovered most of it for the victim.”

On Friday, Nov. 6, the FCSO Problem Area Crime Enforcement Unit (PACE), with assistance from the FCSO Real Time Crime Center, located Jester driving in Bunnell. The FCSO Fugitive Apprehension Unit arrested her on a warrant for grand theft and obtaining property worth $20,000 to $50,000 by swindle. She was transported to the Sheriff Perry Hall Inmate Detention Facility, where she is being held on a $45,000 bond.

The Flagler County Clerk of Court offers a free recording activity notification service that alerts subscribers when a document is recorded in their name in Flagler County’s official records. The alert does not stop a fraudulent filing, but it gives owners an early warning so they can act quickly. Local property owners, including those that may live outside Flagler County but own property in Flagler County, can sign up for this free service at https://t.co/773jOeZPOX.

text:
On November 7, 1980, Steve McQueen died in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, at the age of 50. He had gone there for surgery after American doctors told him conventional medicine had nothing left to offer.

Terrence Stephen McQueen was born on March 24, 1930, in Beech Grove, Indiana, to a single mother. His father left when he was an infant. 

A childhood ear infection left him partially deaf, and dyslexia made school difficult. 

After a stepfather’s beatings, he left home around age nine, lived on the streets, ran with a gang, and ended up at the California Junior Boys Republic, a reform school in Chino. 

He later said the place probably kept him out of prison.
In 1947 he enlisted in the Marine Corps. He served until 1950, was demoted multiple times, spent time in the brig, and left with an honorable discharge. Back in New York he studied acting on the G.I. Bill. 

On weekends he raced motorcycles on Long Island, often winning enough money to cover his living expenses.

His film career started with the 1958 science-fiction film The Blob. The real breakthrough came with the television series Wanted: Dead or Alive, in which he played bounty hunter Josh Randall. He left the show after the 1960 Western The Magnificent Seven. 

Through the 1960s and early 1970s he starred in The Great Escape, The Thomas Crown Affair, Bullitt, The Getaway, Papillon, and the 1974 disaster film The Towering Inferno (with Paul Newman). By the mid-1970s he was the highest-paid actor in the world.

He was notoriously difficult on sets—demanding changes to lines and costumes, sometimes arriving impaired by alcohol or drugs. 

He turned down roles in Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (over billing with Newman), Dirty Harry, Apocalypse Now, and others. 

In 1969 he had planned to have dinner with Jay Sebring and Sharon Tate on the night they were murdered by members of the Manson family; afterward he began carrying a loaded gun.

In 1979 he was diagnosed with mesothelioma, a cancer linked to asbestos. He believed the exposure came from sound-stage insulation, racing gear, and work removing asbestos insulation on a troop ship while he was in the Marines. 

After conventional options were exhausted, he sought experimental treatment in Mexico, including at a clinic in Rosarito Beach. 

On November 6, 1980, surgeons in Juárez removed a large abdominal tumor. He died the next day of a heart attack.
McQueen made roughly thirty films. 

The on-screen rebel image tracked closely with the life that produced it. ❤️

Indiana prohibits the sale of cold beer

text:
2/2 — Transparency, Supply Reduction and the Real Test for WLFI Holders

Aster’s technical infrastructure makes this development particularly interesting. Its aster_spotUserFills RPC method allows observers to retrieve spot execution records, including trading pair, direction, price, quantity and timestamp, through https://t.co/r1G1IvXJJ1. However, Aster also offers Account Privacy, which can conceal subsequent trading activity through encrypted orders and stealth addresses. Selective disclosure requires a viewer pass. In this particular case, the disclosed buyback account reportedly had privacy disabled. Ordinary observers could therefore query its visible WLFIUSD1 fills without privileged access. The claim that Aster trading activity is inherently inaccessible to the public would be inaccurate. Public verification is technically possible, but it depends on the account’s privacy configuration.

The reported 78,627 USD1 in purchases represents approximately 0.79% of the 10 million USD1 deposited into Aster. This should not be interpreted as the final utilization rate. The RPC query returned a maximum of 1,000 fills, and the available data does not establish whether the reported amount captures every subsequent execution or the complete trading history. Nor does it establish the remaining account balance or prove that all deposited funds are reserved exclusively for WLFI purchases.

There is another unresolved issue: what happens to the purchased tokens? The November announcement does not establish a binding permanent-burn requirement. Without evidence of burning or another clearly defined supply-reduction mechanism, these purchases should be treated as market demand rather than guaranteed long-term value accrual. This is where the historical $65.58 million disclosure becomes relevant. World Liberty has demonstrated its ability to buy substantial amounts of WLFI, but the public evidence has not established that those purchases consistently translate into permanent supply reduction.

The November program represents progress, but it does not resolve the central question facing WLFI holders. USD1 growth, reserve revenue, WLFI market purchases and permanent supply reduction are four different things. Success in one does not automatically guarantee success in the others. The latest evidence supports a more measured conclusion: World Liberty has moved beyond announcing a buyback and has demonstrated actual WLFI spot-buying activity through its disclosed Aster account. That is meaningful. At the same time, the program remains discretionary, its full execution amount has not been established, and the final destination of purchased tokens remains unclear.

The next evidence that matters is straightforward: cumulative executed purchases, average prices, complete fill records, remaining USD1 balances and the eventual treatment of purchased WLFI. A credible buyback mechanism should not require holders to infer its effectiveness from announcements. It should allow them to verify the money spent, the tokens acquired and what ultimately happens to those tokens. For WLFI, the real milestone will not be another buyback announcement. It will be a transparent and repeatable mechanism through which USD1 ecosystem revenue produces demonstrable economic benefits for WLFI holders.
